explanationHtml:
Explanation:

After modern cataract surgery, the most common late complication is posterior capsule opacification (PCO), caused by residual lens epithelial cells proliferating on the posterior capsule, leading to gradual vision blurring.

Posterior Capsule Opacification (PCO), also known as after-cataract

Definition

Opacification of the posterior lens capsule that occurs months to years after surgery

Pathogenesis

Residual lens epithelial cells in the capsular bag proliferate, migrate, and undergo fibrous metaplasia.

Leads to progressive visual deterioration due to light scatter.

[[figure-1]]

Morphologic types
  • Elschnig pearls (pearl-type PCO)
  • Fibrous PCO

Clinical features
  • Gradual, painless decrease in vision after initial recovery
  • Glare, halos, reduced contrast sensitivity
  • Hazy fundus view
  • Slit-lamp: wrinkling, fibrosis, or pearl-like opacities on posterior capsule

Management

Nd: YAG laser posterior capsulotomy: creates a central opening in the opacified capsule to restore vision.

Complications

Early Complications (days-weeks):

  • Endophthalmitis (Option D ruled out)
  • Corneal edema
  • Wound leak
  • Retained lens matter
  • TASS (Toxic Anterior Segment Syndrome)

Late Complications (months-years):

  • PCO ( Posterior Capsule Opacification) - most common (Option B)
  • CME (Cystoid Macular Edema) (Option C ruled out)
  • Secondary glaucoma (Option A ruled out)
  • Retinal detachment
  • IOL malposition/dislocation


Reference:
  1. Parson’s Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page 662
  2. Comprehensive Ophthalmology by AK Khurana, 7th Edition, Page 221.
question: Which of the following is the most frequent late postoperative complication after modern cataract surgery?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
This is acute postoperative endophthalmitis, a vision-threatening infection occurring days after cataract surgery; it requires immediate intravitreal broad-spectrum antibiotics to rapidly control the infection.

Acute Postoperative Endophthalmitis

Etiology

Exogenous (most common): Postoperative, post-traumatic, extension from corneal ulcer

Endogenous: Hematogenous spread from systemic infection (rare)

Organisms

Acute postoperative: Staphylococcus epidermidis, S. aureus, Streptococci, Gram-negative bacilli (Pseudomonas, Klebsiella, E. coli), Bacillus

Delayed postoperative: Propionibacterium acnes, fungi

Clinical features

Cardinal Triad

  • Pain
  • Marked visual loss
  • Lid swelling

Signs: conjunctival congestion, corneal edema, hypopyon, purulent vitreous, absent fundus glow.

Management

Immediate Management:

  • Intravitreal broad-spectrum antibiotics (mainstay): (Option C)
    • Vancomycin 1 mg (Gram-positive coverage)
    • Ceftazidime 2.25 mg (Gram-negative coverage)
    • ± Dexamethasone 0.4 mg (controversial)
  • Topical fortified antibiotics as an adjunct
  • Cycloplegics (e.g., atropine 1%)
  • Systemic antibiotics: limited role, only adjunct. (Option B ruled out)

Vitrectomy: Indicated if vision is light perception or worse, dense vitritis, or no response in 48 hours.

Topical corticosteroids alone (Option A): Used only as adjuncts after antimicrobial coverage; using them without antibiotics can worsen the infection.


Bandage contact lens application (Option D) treats corneal surface problems, not intraocular infections.



Reference:

Parsons’ Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Pages 560-566.
question: A 70-year-old patient develops severe ocular pain, redness, lid edema, and sudden visual deterioration 2 days after cataract surgery. Slit-lamp shows corneal edema, hypopyon, and dense vitritis obscuring the fundus glow. What is the immediate management?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
The patient has posterior capsule opacification (PCO), and the treatment of choice is Nd:YAG laser posterior capsulotomy, which creates a central opening in the opacified capsule to restore the visual axis.

  • It is the most common late complication of cataract surgery, caused by proliferation and migration of residual lens epithelial cells over the posterior capsule.
  • Clinical features:
    • Gradual, painless decrease in vision
    • Glare, halos, and reduced contrast sensitivity.
  • Slit-lamp Examination: Elschnig pearls or fibrous opacification behind the IOL
  • Treatment of choice: Nd:YAG laser posterior capsulotomy
    • Creates a central opening in the opacified capsule
    • Restores visual axis clarity
    • Outpatient, non-invasive, standard of care.

Anterior vitrectomy (Option A): Used for vitreous loss during surgery, not for PCO.

Intravitreal steroids (Option B): Used for cystoid macular edema or uveitis, not for capsular opacification.

Intracapsular cataract extraction (Option D): Obsolete, large-incision procedure; irrelevant after IOL implantation.



Reference:

Parsons’ Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page 675.
question: A 62-year-old patient who underwent uneventful cataract surgery 2 years ago now complains of gradual, painless blurring of vision. Slit-lamp examination shows a hazy posterior capsule behind a well-centred IOL. What is the treatment of choice?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
Hypopyon refers to layered pus in the anterior chamber due to severe intraocular infection (endophthalmitis) or intense suppurative keratitis. It is not a typical spontaneous complication of senile cataract and thus is least likely.

Complications of Hypermature (Senile) Cataract:

Phacoanaphylactic uveitis

Lens protein leakage triggers immune-mediated granulomatous uveitis (Option D rued out)

Lens-induced glaucoma
  • Phacomorphic: Swollen intumescent lens pushes iris → angle-closure glaucoma.
  • Phacolytic (Option C): Lens proteins obstruct trabecular meshwork → secondary open-angle glaucoma. (Option C rued out)
  • Phacotopic: Subluxated/dislocated lens mechanically blocks the angle

Lens subluxation or dislocation

Zonular degeneration causes partial or complete lens displacement (Option A rued out)


Reference:
  1. Parsons’ Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page 626.
  2. Comprehensive Ophthalmology by AK Khurana, 7th Edition, Page 199.
question: An elderly man with long-standing, untreated cataract presents for evaluation and is scheduled for surgery after 3 weeks. During this waiting period, which of the following is least likely to occur as a complication of advanced cataract?

correctAnswer: D. Balanced salt solution plus glutathione
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

An ideal intraocular irrigating solution should closely mimic aqueous humour in pH, osmolarity, and ionic composition, and provide metabolic support to the corneal endothelium.

Balanced salt solution plus glutathione contains bicarbonate, glucose, and glutathione, which help maintain endothelial pump function, reduce oxidative stress, and preserve corneal clarity during phaco. Hence, it is the best irrigating fluid.

Normal saline (Option A) lacks essential ions like bicarbonate, magnesium, and glucose; prolonged use causes endothelial stress and corneal edema.

Ringer lactate (Option B) is better than saline but still not physiologic; lactate is not the primary buffer of aqueous humour and endothelial protection is limited.

Balanced salt solution (Option C) contains essential electrolytes and is closer to aqueous humour but lacks antioxidant and metabolic substrates required during prolonged surgery.



Reference:

Yanoff and Duker Ophthalmology, 6th Edition, Page 339.

Definitive spectacle correction after conventional ECCE is usually prescribed around 6 weeks postoperatively, once the large limbal incision has healed and sutures are removed, ensuring corneal stability. This timing allows astigmatism induced by sutures to stabilize, providing an accurate refraction.
In phacoemulsification, smaller self-sealing incisions allow spectacles to be prescribed earlier (1-2 weeks), as corneal curvature and vision stabilize faster.

question: After an uncomplicated cataract surgery with posterior chamber IOL implantation, when is definitive spectacle correction usually prescribed?

correctAnswer: D. Immature senile cataract and phacoemulsification with IOL
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient is a 65-year-old diabetic woman with painless loss of vision, which points towards cataracts, a common cause of visual impairment, especially in older individuals and those with diabetes.
  • Immature senile cataract refers to the early stages of cataract formation, where the lens becomes cloudy but is not yet completely opaque. This typically leads to gradual loss of vision without pain.
  • The standard treatment for cataracts, especially in cases with significant visual impairment, is phacoemulsification, a surgical procedure that uses ultrasound to break up the lens, followed by removal and placement of an intraocular lens (IOL) to restore clear vision.

Type of Cataract

Characteristics

Visual Impact

Cuneiform Senile Cortical Cataract
  • Wedge-shaped opacities with clear areas in between.
  • Extends from periphery to center.
  • First appears in the lower nasal quadrant. Present in both anterior and posterior cortex.
  • The radial spoke-like pattern of opacities is seen.
  • Visual disturbances are noted at a comparatively late stage (since it starts at the periphery).
  • Vision improves in bright light with contracted pupils.

Cupuliform Senile Cortical Cataract

  • Saucer-shaped opacities are typically in the central part of the posterior cortex (posterior subcapsular cataract).
  • Extends from center to periphery.
  • Causes an early loss of visual acuity.- Due to the involvement of the nodal point
  • Glares seen in PSC
  • Better vision in dim light with dilated pupils.

Stages of Cortical cataract:

Stage

Description

Characteristics

1. Stage of Lamellar Separation

Earliest stage of senile cataract
  • Formation of vacuoles and water clefts within the cortex
  • Reversible change
  • Can only be demonstrated by slit lamp examination

2. Stage of Incipient Cataract

Detectable opacities with clear areas present between. Causes visual disturbances.

Cuneiform type:

  • Wedge-shaped opacities, extending from the equator appear as radial spoke-like opacities.

Cupuliform type:

  • Saucer-shaped opacity in the central posterior cortex.

3. Immature Senile Cataract

Progression of opacification
  • Iris shadow visible (clear cortex visible) -Iris Shadow present here due to opacities + clear areas
  • Can progress to Intumescent Cataract leading to the shallow anterior chamber.

4. Mature Senile Cataract (aka intumescent cataract)

Complete opacification of cortex
  • The lens appears pearly white
  • Referred to as a "ripe cataract"
  • No iris shadow as the whole lens is opacified with a chalky white color

5. Hypermature Senile Cataract (HMSC)

Advanced stage of cataract beyond maturity

Morgagnian Hypermature Cataract:

  • Cortex liquefies
  • Nucleus sinks to the bottom
  • Bag of milky fluid appearance

[[figure-1]]

Sclerotic Hypermature Cataract:

  • The cortex disintegrates, lens and capsule shrink.
  • Deep anterior chamber
  • Iridodonesis may be present.

Incorrect Options:

Zonular cataract and lensectomy (Option A): Zonular cataract is a specific type of cataract involving changes to the lens fibers and zonules (the ligaments that hold the lens in place). While lensectomy (removal of the lens) can be performed, it is typically not the preferred term for routine cataract surgery, and this condition is not as commonly associated with the age and symptoms described here.

Rosette cataract and sugar control (Option B): A rosette cataract is a rare type of cataract that forms as a star-shaped pattern, usually associated with trauma or certain diseases, but it is not typically seen in diabetic patients or with the presentation described here. Sugar control is important for diabetes management, but it doesn't directly address the cataract-related vision loss.

Sunflower cataract and lesion extraction (Option C): A sunflower cataract is typically associated with Wilson's disease, a condition characterized by copper accumulation in tissues, leading to a distinctive appearance of the cataract. The patient does not have signs of Wilson's disease, and lesion extraction would not be appropriate for a cataract.



Reference:
  1. Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 10th edition, Pg 310
  2. Comprehensive Ophthalmology by AK Khurana, 7th edition, Pg 194-196.

question: A 65-year-old diabetic woman presents with painless loss of vision. The ocular findings are shown in the image below. What is the likely diagnosis and management for this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The child has features suggestive of Marfan syndrome:

  • Height >95th percentile
  • Arm span: height ratio >1.05
  • Long slender fingers (arachnodactyly)
  • Flat feet (pes planus)
  • Scoliosis
  • Characteristic marfanoid habitus

Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder caused by mutations in the FBN1 (fibrillin-1) gene on chromosome 15.

Ectopia lentis (subluxation of the lens)

  • Occurs in approximately 60-80% of patients.
  • Typically bilateral.
  • Lens is usually displaced superotemporally (upward and outward).
  • Caused by weakness of the zonular fibres due to defective fibrillin.

Clinical features:

Skeletal abnormalities:
  • Tall stature
  • Arachnodactyly
  • Chest wall abnormalities like pectus excavatum/Pectus carinatum
  • Thumb sign( On folding thumb, it will protrude beyond the ulnar border of palm) or wrist sign is positive
  • Increased joint laxity

CVS abnormalities:
  • Aortic root dilation
  • Mitral insufficiencies
  • Arrhythmias

Eye abnormalities:
  • Ectopia lentis or subluxation of the lens of the eye (Option D)
  • High myopia
  • Retinal detachment
  • Early cataract
  • Glaucoma
  • Blindness

Pulmonary involvement:

  • Increased risk of pneumothorax

Hypertensive Retinopathy (Option A)

  • Associated with systemic hypertension.
  • Not a characteristic feature of Marfan syndrome.

Rosette Cataract (Option B)

  • Classically associated with blunt ocular trauma.
  • Not the most common ocular finding in Marfan syndrome.

Retinitis Pigmentosa (Option C)

  • Inherited retinal dystrophy causing night blindness and peripheral field loss.
  • Not associated with Marfan syndrome.


Reference:

Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Pages 339, 340.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The corneal endothelium originates from neural crest cells, which migrate during embryogenesis to form the inner layer of the cornea.
  • Neural crest cells also contribute to other anterior segment structures, including the stroma and trabecular meshwork.

Corneal Development and Cellular Origins

  • Corneal development involves ectodermal-derived tissues.
  • Neural ectoderm-derived optic vesicles interact with cranial ectoderm → form presumptive corneal epithelium and ocular surface epithelia. (Option A ruled out)
  • Neural tube-ectoderm interactions generate neural crest cells, which are migratory and multipotent.
  • Neural crest cells migrate between the lens and corneal epithelium → form corneal endothelium and stromal keratocytes.
  • Trigeminal ganglion (from neural crest and ectodermal placodes) supplies sensory innervation to the corneal stroma and epithelium.

Mesoderm (Option C): The mesoderm is responsible for forming structures like muscles, blood vessels, and connective tissue in the body. It does not contribute to the corneal endothelium.

Surface ectoderm (Option D): The surface ectoderm forms the corneal epithelium, the outermost layer of the cornea, but not the corneal endothelium.

question: Identify the given instrument

correctAnswer: B. Visual acuity less than 3/60 in the better eye after best possible correction
explanationHtml:
Correct Option B -Visual acuity less than 3/60 in the better eye after best possible correction

Visual acuity less than 6/60 in the better eye (Option A ruled out): This level of visual acuity (or 20/200 in feet) is often referred to as legal blindness in many countries, including the United States, and is a criterion for eligibility for certain services. However, the international definition of blindness is typically more severe.

Visual acuity less than 3/60 in the better eye after best possible correction (Option B): This is the definition of blindness according to the World Health Organization (WHO) and is widely adopted for international comparison. 3/60 means a person can see at 3 meters what a person with normal vision can see at 60 meters. This is the best definition of blindness among the choices.

Visual field less than 10 degrees from fixation in the better eye (Option C ruled out): A restricted visual field can also define blindness, particularly "tunnel vision." The WHO definition of blindness includes "or corresponding visual field loss," which for blindness is typically a visual field of 10 degrees or less from fixation in the better eye. This is also a valid criterion for blindness.

Inability to perceive light in both eyes(Option C ruled out): This is known as "No Light Perception" (NLP) and represents total blindness. While this is indeed a form of blindness, it is the most severe form. The general definition of "blindness" encompasses a broader range of severe visual impairment where some light perception or very limited vision might still be present.

question: Which of the following best defines blindness ?

explanationHtml:
• Pseudoexfoliation syndrome is a condition where an abnormal protein material (pseudoexfoliative material) accumulates in the anterior segment of the eye, especially on the lens capsule, pupillary margin, and the corneal endothelium.
  • This condition can cause the formation of a characteristic white, flaky material around the lens and pupil, which is the hallmark of pseudoexfoliation syndrome. It can lead to increased risk of glaucoma (due to blocked drainage of fluid), cataracts, and other complications.
  • This can lead to phacodonesis (lens wobbling).

Ocular manifestation of Pseudoexfoliation Syndrome (XFS) is characterized by the accumulation of fibrillar, proteinaceous material on various ocular structures, including

the lens, iris, and trabecular meshwork.

  • This material can be seen as flaky white deposits on the anterior lens capsule and pupillary margin, often with a distinct clear zone at the center of the lens.
  • It causes secondary open-angle glaucoma, known as pseudoexfoliative glaucoma.
  • The excessive material and pigment clog the trabecular meshwork, increasing intraocular pressure (IOP) and causing damage to the optic nerve, which leads to glaucoma.
  • It also predisposes patients to complications during cataract surgery due to weakened zonules, resulting in lens instability or phacodonesis.

Features of Pseudoexfoliation Syndrome:

  • White flaky deposits on the anterior lens capsule and iris
  • Increased trabecular meshwork pigmentation
  • Elevated IOP, leading to secondary glaucoma
  • Zonular instability and risk of lens dislocation during cataract surgery
  • Mutations in the LOXL1 gene have been strongly associated with PXF, although not all individuals with these mutations develop the disease.
  • More prevalent in elderly patients.

Intraocular foreign body (Option A): This typically causes localized symptoms such as pain, vision changes, or infection. An image of an intraocular foreign body would typically show the object within the eye, which is not characteristic of the findings in pseudoexfoliation syndrome.

Ocular trauma (Option C): Ocular trauma may lead to various findings such as bruising, swelling, or damage to the structures of the eye. It is not characterized by the deposition of material on the lens and anterior segment like in pseudoexfoliation syndrome.

Vossius ring (Option D): This is a pigmented ring on the cornea that results from trauma (usually from a blow to the eye). It is a permanent imprint of the iris pigment on the corneal endothelium and is not related to the findings of white, flaky material seen in pseudoexfoliation syndrome.



Reference:
  1. Yanoff and Duker's Ophthalmology, 5th edition, Pages 1074-1077
  2. Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology, 10th edition, Pages 382, 383, 384
question: What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Newborns are physiologically hypermetropic, with an average refractive error of approximately +2.5 to 3 diopters.
  • This occurs because the axial length of the eye is shorter at birth, and the eye grows over time, reducing hypermetropia.
  • Hypermetropia, or long-sightedness, is a refractive error in which parallel rays of light from distant objects focus behind the retina when the eye's accommodation is relaxed.

Type of Hypermetropia

Cause

Axial Hypermetropia

Shortening of the eyeball's axial length. Commonest form.

Curvatural Hypermetropia

Flatter curvature of the cornea, lens, or both.

Index Hypermetropia

Decreased refractive index of the lens, usually due to cortical sclerosis in old age or in treated diabetics.

Positional Hypermetropia

Posterior displacement of the crystalline lens.

Aphakia

Absence of the crystalline lens, either congenital or acquired (e.g., after surgery), leads to high hypermetropia.

Consecutive Hypermetropia

Overcorrected myopia after refractive surgery (e.g., LASIK, ICL) or underpowered intraocular lens (IOL) after cataract surgery.

Features:

  • Small eyeball in high hypermetropia
  • Smaller cornea
  • Shallow anterior chamber
  • Fundus Examination:
    • Optic disc - Small , ill-defined margins, possibly simulating papillitis (pseudopapillitis).
    • Retina - Shot silk appearance (shining retina).

+1 D (Option D): +1 D is below the average hypermetropia seen in newborns. This degree of refractive error is more commonly observed in older children or adults after emmetropization has occurred.

Toxic cataract:

  • Steroids - Prolonged use in high doses may cause posterior subcapsular cataracts. Children are more susceptible

  • Other causes of posterior subcapsular cataract: Galactosemia, Myotonic dystrophy, BLUNT trauma, complicated cataract, chloroquine, busulfan, NF2,

  • AACG ( Mnemonic): Atopic dermatitis- shield cataract, Amiodarone, Chlorpromazine, Gold deposit, AACG(acute angle closure glaucoma)

Incorrect Options

Glaucoma (Option B) is the most common complication of topical steroids.

Cystoid macular edema (Option C) may be associated with steroid use, but it typically presents with symptoms such as blurry vision, central vision loss, and distortion.

Retinal detachment (Option D) causes progressive loss of vision which is not consistent with the above described case.

Explanation:

True statements are 1 & 5:

  • Kayser–Fleischer (KF) ring is a golden-brown, greenish-brown, or yellow-brown ring at the corneal periphery caused by copper deposition in Descemet's membrane.
  • It is the most important ocular sign of Wilson disease (hepatolenticular degeneration), an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutation of the ATP7B gene, leading to impaired copper metabolism and copper accumulation in various tissues.

Pathogenesis

In Wilson disease, excess copper accumulates in:

  • Liver
  • Brain (especially basal ganglia)
  • Cornea
  • Kidneys

The corneal copper deposition occurs in Descemet's membrane, producing the characteristic KF ring.

Features

1. Kayser–Fleischer (KF) ring

  • Golden-brown to greenish-brown corneal ring
  • Usually starts at the superior and inferior corneal periphery and later becomes circumferential (Statement 5)
  • Best visualized by slit-lamp examination
  • Does not usually affect vision directly

KF rings are present in more than 90–95% of patients with neurological manifestations of Wilson disease, making them a very important diagnostic clue in patients presenting with tremors, dystonia, dysarthria, or other movement disorders. (Statement 1)

Although highly characteristic of Wilson disease, KF rings are not pathognomonic (Statement 2 ruled out). Similar rings may rarely be seen in other chronic cholestatic liver disorders such as:

  • Primary biliary cholangitis
  • Chronic active hepatitis

In patients presenting predominantly with hepatic involvement, KF rings are less frequent and are seen in only about 50-60% of cases. Their absence does not exclude Wilson disease. (Statement 4 ruled out)

2. Sunflower cataract

Diagnosis

  • Slit-Lamp Examination
    • Investigation of choice
    • Detects early peripheral copper deposition
  • Laboratory Findings in Wilson Disease
    • Decreased serum ceruloplasmin
    • Increased urinary copper excretion
    • Increased hepatic copper concentration

Treatment

Treatment is directed at the underlying Wilson disease:

  • Penicillamine (most commonly tested)
  • Trientine
  • Zinc therapy

With successful copper-chelation therapy, KF rings may gradually fade or disappear.

Desferrioxamine (Desferroxamine) is an iron chelator used in iron overload states and has no role in Wilson disease. (Statement 3 ruled out)



Reference:
  1. Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics, 21st Edition, Pages 2103-04
  2. Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 267.

Accurate intraocular lens (IOL) power calculation is challenging in patients who have previously undergone myopic LASIK/PRK, because corneal refractive surgery alters the anterior corneal curvature and causes standard keratometry-based formulas to underestimate the required IOL power.

Haigis-L Formula

The Haigis-L formula is specifically designed for patients who have undergone:

  • Myopic LASIK
  • Myopic PRK
  • Other corneal refractive procedures

It does not require pre-LASIK data and is one of the most commonly used formulas for IOL power calculation in such eyes.

Therefore, Haigis-L is the preferred formula in a patient with previous myopic LASIK.

Cataract Surgery in Post-LASIK Eyes

Challenges

  • Inaccurate keratometry readings

Short Eyes

  • Holladay II

Normal Axial Length Eyes

  • Useful in normal eyes but not specifically designed for post-LASIK IOL calculations.

The fundus photograph shows multiple yellow, well-defined lipid deposits arranged in clusters around the macular area, characteristic of hard exudates seen in diabetic retinopathy, particularly diabetic maculopathy.

  • Hard exudates are bright yellow, well-defined deposits caused by leakage of fluid rich in lipids and proteins from damaged retinal capillaries.
  • They often form around microaneurysms and, in the macular region, can create a star-shaped pattern (macular fan/ star), which is seen most commonly in diabetic retinopathy (although it can also be seen in Hypertensive retinopathy).

Hard and Soft Exudates:

Feature

Soft Exudates (Cotton-Wool Spots)

Hard Exudates

Appearance
  • Cloud-like, small, ill-defined, whitish patches
  • Bright yellow, well-defined lipid deposits

Formation Mechanism
  • Caused by ischemia and axonal swelling; blockage of axoplasmic flow
  • Formed by leakage of fluid rich in proteins and lipids

Location
  • Superficial retinal layers, often seen around the optic nerve
  • Seen around leaking microaneurysms, especially in the macula

Common Shape
  • Indistinct and variable; may change shape quickly
  • Radial, star-shaped figure in the macula (macular fan/star)

Main Causes
  • Hypertensive retinopathy (Most common cause) (Option A)
  • Diabetic retinopathy
  • Toxemia of pregnancy
  • Lupus erythematosus (LE)
  • Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN)
  • Retinopathy associated with AIDS
  • Diabetic retinopathy (Most common cause)
  • Hypertensive retinopathy
  • Coats' disease
  • Circinate retinopathy

Image

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Flame-Shaped Hemorrhages, Hypertension (Option C)

  • Flame hemorrhages follow the nerve fiber layer
  • Appear as linear or flame-shaped red lesions
  • Common in hypertensive retinopathy
  • No flame-shaped hemorrhages are visible in the image.

Soft Exudate, Central Retinal Vein Occlusion (Option D): CRVO typically shows:

  • Diffuse retinal hemorrhages ("blood and thunder" appearance)
  • Dilated tortuous veins
  • Cotton-wool spots
  • Disc edema
  • These findings are absent in the image.

Diabetic Retinopathy

Diabetic retinopathy is a microvascular complication of diabetes mellitus caused by chronic hyperglycemia leading to retinal capillary damage, leakage, and ischemia.

Fundus Findings

Hard Exudates

  • Yellow-white, well-defined deposits of lipid and protein
  • Result from leakage of lipoproteins from incompetent retinal capillaries and microaneurysms
  • Commonly seen in diabetic retinopathy
  • Often arranged in a circinate (ring-like) pattern around leaking microaneurysms

Other Features of Diabetic Retinopathy

  • Non-Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (NPDR)
    • Microaneurysms (earliest clinically visible sign)
    • Dot and blot hemorrhages
    • Hard exudates
    • Cotton-wool spots
    • Venous beading
    • IRMA (Intraretinal Microvascular Abnormalities)
  • Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR)
    • Neovascularization of disc (NVD)
    • Neovascularization elsewhere (NVE)
    • Vitreous hemorrhage
    • Tractional retinal detachment

Surgical Steps of Conventional ECCE:

  • Eye Stabilization: Superior rectus suture for downward gaze(known as bridle suture)
  • Conjunctival Flap Creation: A fornix-based flap will be used to expose the limbus.
  • Limbal Incision: Partial-thickness groove across the limbus.
  • Anterior Chamber Access: Entry with a razor blade knife or keratome.
  • Viscoelastic Injection: Maintains chamber depth and protects the cornea.
  • Anterior Capsulotomy/ Capsulorrhexis: Methods include can-opener, linear capsulotomy, envelope, or CCC. Tryphan blue dye is usually injected. (Option B)

[[figure-1]]

  • Corneoscleral Section Completion: Extending the incision.
  • Hydrodissection: Separates the lens from the capsule. (Option A)
  • Nucleus Removal: Methods include pressure/counter pressure or irrigating wire vectis.
  • Lens Cortex Aspiration: Using a two-way cannula. (I/A) (Option D)
  • IOL Implantation: Posterior chamber IOL into the capsular bag. (Option C)
  • Incision Closure: With sutures.
  • Viscoelastic Removal: Followed by refilling the anterior chamber with irrigating fluid.
  • Conjunctival Flap Repositioning: Secured in place.
  • Subconjunctival Injections: Dexamethasone and gentamicin.
  • Eye Patching: Final step.

Types of Cortical Cataract:

Type of Cataract

Characteristics

Visual Impact

Cuneiform Senile Cortical Cataract
  • Wedge-shaped opacities with clear areas in between.
  • Extends from periphery to center.
  • First appears in the lower nasal quadrant. Present in both anterior and posterior cortex.
  • The radial spoke-like pattern of opacities is seen.
  • Visual disturbances are noted at a comparatively late stage (since it starts at the periphery).
  • Vision improves in bright light with contracted pupils.

Cupuliform Senile Cortical Cataract

  • Saucer-shaped opacities are typically in the central part of the posterior cortex (posterior subcapsular cataract).
  • Extends from center to periphery.
  • Causes an early loss of visual acuity.- Due to the involvement of the nodal point
  • Glares seen in PSC
  • Better vision in dim light with dilated pupils.

Stages of Cortical cataract:

Stage

Description

Characteristics

1. Stage of Lamellar Separation

Earliest stage of senile cataract
  • Formation of vacuoles and water clefts within the cortex
  • Reversible change
  • Can only be demonstrated by slit lamp examination

2. Stage of Incipient Cataract

Detectable opacities with clear areas present between. Causes visual disturbances.

Cuneiform type:

  • Wedge-shaped opacities, extending from the equator appear as radial spoke-like opacities.

Cupuliform type:

  • Saucer-shaped opacity in the central posterior cortex.

Progression of opacification
  • Iris shadow visible (clear cortex visible) -Iris Shadow present here due to opacities + clear areas
  • Can progress to Intumescent Cataract leading to the shallow anterior chamber.

4. Mature Senile Cataract (aka intumescent cataract)

Complete opacification of cortex
  • The lens appears pearly white
  • Referred to as a "ripe cataract"
  • No iris shadow as the whole lens is opacified with a chalky white color

5. Hypermature Senile Cataract (HMSC)

Advanced stage of cataract beyond maturity

Morgagnian Hypermature Cataract:

  • Cortex liquefies
  • Nucleus sinks to the bottom
  • Bag of milky fluid appearance

[[figure-5]]

Sclerotic Hypermature Cataract:

  • The cortex disintegrates, lens and capsule shrink.

explanationHtml:
• In diabetic patients, sorbitol accumulation in the lens plays a critical role in the development of diabetic cataracts. This process is primarily mediated by the polyol pathway, where glucose is converted to sorbitol via the enzyme aldose reductase. Sorbitol accumulates in the lens because it is poorly permeable across the lens membrane, leading to osmotic stress and cellular damage, which promotes cataract formation.

Glucose Metabolism in the Lens:

The lens uses glucose through several metabolic pathways:

  1. Glycolytic pathway: This is the primary pathway where about 80% of glucose is metabolized anaerobically.

  2. Pentose Phosphate pathway (HMP shunt): Responsible for metabolizing 15% of glucose.

  3. Kreb's citric acid cycle: A small proportion of glucose is metabolized through this oxidative pathway.

  4. Sorbitol pathway: In healthy individuals, this pathway is minimally active. However, in diabetic and galactosemic patients, excess glucose is converted into sorbitol by aldose reductase. The accumulation of sorbitol leads to osmotic imbalance, which causes lens fiber swelling and opacity, resulting in cataracts.

Glucose (Option A): Although glucose is involved in cataract formation, it is not directly responsible for the development of diabetic cataracts. In the lens, glucose is metabolized via several pathways, but it is the conversion of glucose to sorbitol (via the polyol pathway) that leads to osmotic stress and cataract formation in diabetes.

Fructose (Option B): Fructose does not significantly contribute to diabetic cataracts. While fructose is metabolized in the body, it is not the primary substance implicated in lens opacity in diabetic patients. The key factor in diabetic cataracts is sorbitol accumulation.

Lactose + Glucose (Option C): Lactose is not involved in the formation of diabetic cataracts. Although glucose plays a role in cataract formation, lactose is more relevant in galactosemic cataracts and not in diabetes-induced cataracts.



Reference:

K Khurana Comprehensive Ophthalmology 7th edition, page 186

explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - Extracapsular cataract extraction (ECCE)

  • In extracapsular cataract extraction (ECCE), the surgeon makes a larger incision on the eye's surface, typically around 10-12 mm in size. This incision allows the surgeon to remove the cataractous lens while leaving the posterior lens capsule intact. After removing the lens, the incision is usually closed with sutures, often using 10-0 nylon. ECCE requires suturing because the incision size is relatively large, and proper wound closure is necessary to ensure the eye heals correctly and maintains its structural integrity.

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Phacoemulsification: Phacoemulsification is a modern and minimally invasive cataract surgery technique. In this procedure, a small incision is made through which an ultrasonic probe (phacoemulsifier) is inserted to break up the cataract into tiny fragments that are then suctioned out. Suturing with 10-0 nylon is not commonly performed in phacoemulsification surgery because the incision size is typically very small and may not require sutures to close.

Option C - Intracapsular cataract extraction (ICCE): Intracapsular cataract extraction involves removing the entire lens, including the lens capsule, in one piece. This method is now less commonly used due to advances in surgical techniques. Suturing with 10-0 nylon is not commonly performed in ICCE surgery because the procedure involves removing the entire lens and capsule, making the need for suturing less relevant.

Option D - Manual small incision cataract surgery (MSICS): Manual small incision cataract surgery is a technique similar to ECCE but uses a smaller incision (around 6-7 mm) compared to traditional ECCE. While suturing may still be performed in MSICS, the use of 10-0 nylon is more commonly associated with traditional ECCE due to the larger incision size.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

An oil-drop cataract is a characteristic lens opacity seen in galactosemia, an inherited disorder of galactose metabolism.

Galactosemia

Inborn error of galactose metabolism

Enzyme deficiency

  • Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT)
  • Galactokinase (GK)
Pathogenesis
  • Excess galactose accumulates in the lens.
  • Galactose is converted by aldose reductase into galactitol (dulcitol).
  • Galactitol accumulates within the lens, causing osmotic swelling and lens opacification.
  • This produces the characteristic oil-drop appearance.

Type of cataract

  • Bilateral
  • “Oil droplet”
  • Central lens

[[figure-1]]

Features

  • May be reversed
  • May be prevented if milk and milk products are eliminated at an early stage
Systemic Features
  • Failure to thrive
  • Vomiting
  • Jaundice
  • Hepatomegaly
  • Intellectual disability (if untreated)
  • Increased risk of E. coli sepsis

Wilson's disease (Option B): Copper metabolism disorder. Primarily affects the liver and brain, and produces sunflower cataracts and Kayser-Fleischer ring in the cornea.

Gaucher's disease (Option C): Lysosomal storage disorder due to glucocerebrosidase deficiency. Not associated with oil drop cataracts. Gaucher cells are seen.

Tay-Sachs (Option D): Hexosaminidase A deficiency. Characteristic ocular finding is a cherry-red spot at the macula

explanationHtml:
The patient has postoperative endophthalmitis, a vision-threatening intraocular infection occurring after cataract surgery.

The key factor in management is the presenting visual acuity, as established by the Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study (EVS):

  • If visual acuity is hand movements (HM) or light perception (LP) → Pars plana vitrectomy + Intravitreal antibiotics are indicated.
  • If visual acuity is better than HM (e.g., counting fingers) → Intravitreal antibiotics alone are sufficient.

Vitrectomy helps by:

  • Removing infected vitreous and inflammatory debris,
  • Improving antibiotic penetration,
  • Reducing bacterial load and toxins,
  • Preserving retinal function.

Intravitreal antibiotic regimen (EVS protocol):

  • Vancomycin 1 mg/0.1 mL (for Gram-positive organisms)
  • Ceftazidime 2.25 mg/0.1 mL (for Gram-negative organisms)

Postoperative Endophthalmitis

Severe inflammation of the intraocular cavities caused by microbial infection following surgery, trauma, or endogenous spread.

Common Organisms

Acute Postoperative Endophthalmitis

  • Staphylococcus epidermidis (most common)
  • Staphylococcus aureus
  • Streptococci
  • Gram-negative bacilli

Chronic Postoperative Endophthalmitis: Cutibacterium (Propionibacterium) acnes

Clinical Features

  • Marked decrease in vision
  • Pain
  • Red eye
  • Lid edema
  • Hypopyon
  • Vitritis
  • Absent or poor red reflex

Intravitreal Antibiotic Injections Only (Option A)

  • Appropriate for less severe cases with relatively better vision.
  • In a patient with severe vision loss, vitrectomy is preferred.

Redo Surgery (Option C)

  • Cataract surgery is not repeated.
  • The infection itself must be treated.

Topical Antibiotics (Option D)

  • Topical drugs do not adequately penetrate the vitreous cavity.
  • Insufficient as sole therapy for endophthalmitis.

Explanation: Rosette-shaped cataract: it is a cortical cataract that starts from the posterior cortex is seen in blunt trauma.

Traumatic cataract:

  • A traumatic cataract is an acquired cataract resulting from ocular trauma, such as penetrating or blunt injuries.
  • It forms due to degeneration in previously normal lens fibers.
  • Morphological Forms
    • Subepithelial Opacities: Most common presentation.
    • Rosette Cataracts

    • [[figure-1]]

      • Early Rosette: Feathery opacities along posterior cortex suture lines; typical of concussion cataracts. (Option C)
      • Late Rosette: Develops 1-2 years post-injury, with shorter, compact sutural extensions.
      • Diffuse Concussion Cataract: Common presentation of total cataract following blunt trauma, which may accelerate senile cataract development.
  • Subepithelial Opacities (Option A) are common but do not typically present with feathery opacities along suture lines.
  • Diffuse Concussion Cataract (Option B) involves widespread lens opacity, not localized feathery patterns..

Toxic cataract (Option B) causes posterior subcapsular cataract. It can be caused by steroids, phenothiazines, mong acting miotics, amiodarone, busulfan, gold, chloroquine

Metabolic cataract (Option C):

  • Due to Diabetes mellitus
  • It can occur due to 2 enzyme deficiencies
    • Galactokinase - causes lamellar cataract
    • GPUT - causes oil drop cataract

Nuclear cataract (Option D):

  • It is due to nuclear sclerosis
  • Sclerosis can be caused due to denaturation of the protein resulting in an increase in insoluble protein and a decrease in soluble protein, and deposition of pigments such as melanin and urochrome.

question: Which of the following cataracts is seen in blunt trauma?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The image shows a congenital cataract in a 2-month-old infant.

Congenital cataract is a lens opacity present at birth or developing during the first year of life. It is one of the most important treatable causes of childhood blindness.

Visual development occurs rapidly during the first few months of life. A dense congenital cataract obstructs the visual axis and can lead to:

  • Severe deprivation amblyopia
  • Nystagmus
  • Strabismus
  • Permanent visual impairment

Therefore, visually significant congenital cataracts require urgent surgical treatment.

Management of Congenital Cataract

Preoperative Evaluation

  • Rule out associated ocular anomalies
  • TORCH screening if indicated
  • Systemic evaluation for metabolic disorders

The timing of surgery is critical because early surgery prevents deprivation amblyopia, but surgery performed very early (especially before 4 weeks of age) is associated with a higher risk of juvenile glaucoma.

Type of Cataract Recommended Management Description
Bilateral Dense Cataract Surgery at 4-10 weeks of age Prevents deprivation amblyopia; operate denser eye first if asymmetrical
Unilateral Dense Cataract Surgery at 4-6 weeks of age (latest by 6 weeks) More urgent than bilateral; requires aggressive amblyopia therapy postoperatively
Bilateral Partial Cataract Observation and regular follow-up Surgery may not be required if visual development is not affected
Partial Unilateral Cataract Conservative management Pupillary dilatation and part-time occlusion of the normal eye may be sufficient

Surgical Procedure

  1. Anterior capsulorhexis
  2. Lens aspiration
  3. Posterior capsulorhexis
  4. Limited anterior vitrectomy
  5. Intraocular lens (IOL) implantation when appropriate

Postoperative Management

  • Correction of refractive errors (spectacles/contact lenses/IOL)
  • Amblyopia therapy
  • Regular follow-up for visual rehabilitation and glaucoma surveillance



Reference:

Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 338.
question: A 2-month-old child is brought to the ophthalmology OPD with the following presentation. What is the ideal management?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option D) Posterior capsular opacification (PCO)

Explanation:

A patient presenting with gradual decrease in vision several years after cataract surgery most commonly has Posterior Capsular Opacification (PCO), also known as a secondary cataract or after-cataract.

Posterior Capsular Opacification (PCO)

  • PCO occurs due to proliferation and migration of residual lens epithelial cells onto the posterior capsule after cataract extraction.
  • It is also known as After Cataract/Secondary Cataract

Pathogenesis

  • Residual lens epithelial cells remain after surgery.
  • These cells proliferate and undergo fibrous metaplasia.
  • The posterior capsule becomes opaque, scattering light and reducing vision.

Clinical Features

  • Gradual, painless decrease in vision months to years after cataract surgery
  • Glare and halos
  • Reduced contrast sensitivity
  • Posterior capsule appears hazy/opacified on slit-lamp examination

Types of PCO

Elschnig Pearls

  • Proliferating bladder cells
  • Pearly appearance on posterior capsule

Fibrous PCO

  • Fibrous metaplasia of lens epithelial cells
  • Wrinkling and fibrosis of the capsule

Soemmering ring:

  • Whitish annular or doughnut-shaped proliferation of residual cells
  • Classically formed almost in the periphery of the capsular bag

Treatment

  • Nd: YAG laser posterior capsulotomy (treatment of choice)
    • Creates an opening in the opaque posterior capsule
    • Immediate improvement in vision in most cases

Pseudophakic Bullous Keratopathy (Option A)

  • Corneal endothelial decompensation following cataract surgery
  • Presents with:
    • Corneal edema
    • Bullae formation
    • Pain and photophobia
  • Usually occurs earlier and shows corneal findings rather than posterior capsule opacity

Corneal Dystrophy (Option B)

  • Usually hereditary
  • Causes corneal opacities independent of cataract surgery
  • Not the typical cause of vision loss years after successful cataract surgery

Posterior Subcapsular Cataract (Option C )

  • Cataract occurring in the natural crystalline lens
  • Cannot develop in an eye where the cataractous lens has already been removed
  • Therefore not a cause of visual loss 3 years after cataract surgery


Reference:

Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Pages 331, 332.
question: A patient presents with decreased vision three years after surgery and exhibits this condition. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
A diabetic cataract develops due to the accumulation of sorbitol within the lens fibers as a result of chronic hyperglycemia.

Pathogenesis

Under normal conditions, glucose in the lens is metabolized through glycolysis. In diabetes mellitus, excess glucose enters the polyol pathway, where:

  • Glucose is converted to sorbitol by the enzyme aldose reductase.
  • Sorbitol is then slowly converted to fructose by sorbitol dehydrogenase.

However, the lens has relatively low sorbitol dehydrogenase activity, leading to:

  • Accumulation of sorbitol within lens fibers
  • Osmotic influx of water
  • Lens fiber swelling and degeneration
  • Opacification of the lens (cataract formation)

Therefore, sorbitol is the substance directly responsible for diabetic cataract formation.

Types of Diabetic Cataract

True Diabetic Cataract

  • More common in young patients with uncontrolled diabetes
  • Rapid onset
  • Characterized by snowflake-like cortical opacities

Senile Cataract with Diabetes

  • Most common form
  • Diabetes accelerates age-related cataract formation
  • Usually presents as cortical or posterior subcapsular cataract

Risk Factors

  • Long-standing diabetes mellitus
  • Poor glycemic control
  • Increasing age
  • Duration of disease

Prevention

  • Good glycemic control
  • Regular ophthalmic examinations
  • Early detection and management

Glucose Metabolism in the Lens:

The lens uses glucose through several metabolic pathways:

  1. Glycolytic pathway: This is the primary pathway where about 80% of glucose is metabolized anaerobically.

  2. Pentose Phosphate pathway (HMP shunt): Responsible for metabolizing 15% of glucose.

  3. Kreb's citric acid cycle: A small proportion of glucose is metabolized through this oxidative pathway.

  4. Sorbitol pathway: In healthy individuals, this pathway is minimally active. However, in diabetic and galactosemic patients, excess glucose is converted into sorbitol by aldose reductase. The accumulation of sorbitol leads to osmotic imbalance, which causes lens fiber swelling and opacity, resulting in cataracts.

[[figure-1]]

Glucose (Option A): Glucose is the substrate entering the polyol pathway. Lens damage occurs primarily due to sorbitol accumulation, not glucose itself.

Galactitol (Option B): Galactitol (dulcitol) accumulates in the lens in galactosemia, leading to early-onset cataracts, but not in diabetic cataracts.

Fructose (Option D): While sorbitol is eventually converted to fructose by sorbitol dehydrogenase, the rate is slow in the lens, making sorbitol the primary culprit in diabetic cataracts.



Reference:
  1. AK Khurana Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th Edition, Page 186
  2. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2903955/#:~:text

explanationHtml:
• Anisometropia is defined as a difference in the refractive power (refractive error) of the two eyes.
  • The difference in power of two eyes is more than 2.5 diopters.
  • Anisometropia up to 2.5D is well tolerated and that between 2.5 and 4D can be tolerated depending upon the individual sensitivity.
  • However, if it is more than 4D, it is not tolerated and is a matter of concern.

Etiology:

  1. Congenital and developmental anisometropia: Occurs due to differential growth of the two eyeballs.
  2. Acquired anisometropia: Occur due to asymmetric age change, uniocular aphakia after removal of cataractous lens or due to implantation of IOL of wrong power

Types of Anisometropia

1. Simple Anisometropia: One eye emmetropic, the other ametropic.

2. Compound Anisometropia: Both eyes have the same type of refractive error, but of different magnitudes.

  • Compound myopic anisometropia
  • Compound hypermetropic anisometropia

3. Mixed Anisometropia (Antimetropia): One eye is myopic and the other hypermetropic.

4. Simple astigmatic anisometropia: One eye is normal, and the other has either simple myopic or hypermetropic astigmatism.

5. Compound astigmatic anisometropia: When both eyes are astigmatic but of unequal degree.

Management

  • Spectacles
  • Contact lenses (preferred in high anisometropia)
  • Refractive surgery in selected cases

Difference in visual acuity (Option A) could be caused by conditions like myopia, hypermetropia, astigmatism, and presbyopia.

Difference in axial length (Option C) of the eyeball is seen in axial myopia.

Difference in size of eyeball (Option D) is seen in conditions like Microphthalmia and Buphthalmos.



Reference:
  1. Comprehensive Ophthalmology by AK Khurana, 7th Edition, Pages 44, 45

explanationHtml:
• Bilateral ectopia lentis in a tall individual with long limbs is classic for Marfan syndrome, which is caused by mutations in the FBN1 gene on chromosome 15.
  • Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder.
  • Pathophysiology: Defective fibrillin leads to abnormal connective tissue elasticity and excess TGF-β activation.

Clinical features

  • Ocular features: Ectopia lentis (usually superotemporal lens subluxation), myopia, risk of retinal detachment.
  • Skeletal features: Tall stature, arachnodactyly, long limbs (dolichostenomelia), pectus deformities, scoliosis.
  • Cardiovascular: Aortic root dilation, aneurysm, aortic regurgitation, mitral valve prolapse—major cause of mortality.

[[figure-1]]

Management: Regular cardiovascular monitoring, beta-blockers or ARBs to slow aortic dilation, surgical repair when needed.

COL5A (Option A) mutations cause Ehlers–Danlos syndrome (classic type), presenting with hyperextensible skin, hypermobile joints, and poor wound healing, not isolated ectopia lentis.

PAX6 (Option B) is associated with aniridia and other anterior segment dysgenesis disorders, not Marfan syndrome.

TGFβR2 (Option C) mutations cause Loeys–Dietz syndrome, which shares aortic aneurysms with Marfan’s but usually has hypertelorism, bifid uvula, and no typical lens dislocation.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The image shown is of Sunset Glow Fundus in the convalescent Phase of Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada Disease.
  • The fundus has a slightly reddish appearance, mainly due to the disappearance of melanocytes in the choroid.

Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada (VKH) Syndrome

Clinical features

Clinically, the disease is categorized into four phases:


1. Prodromal phase (lasts for a few days): Neurological (meningitis, cranial nerve paresis) and auditory manifestations (tinnitus, vertigo and deafness).


2. Acute uveitic phase: Bilateral granulomatous anterior and multifocal posterior uveitis with diffuse choroidal infiltration, vitritis, papillitis and exudative retinal detachments. Dalen–Fuchs nodules can be seen in this phase.


3. Convalescent phase (follows several weeks later): Localized alopecia, poliosis and vitiligo, depigmented fundus appearance (‘sunset glow’ fundus) and depigmented limbal lesions (Sugiura sign). (Option C)


4. Chronic recurrent phase: smouldering anterior uveitis with exacerbations

  2. Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 446, 447
question: A 28-year-old woman diagnosed with Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada (VKH) disease, Fundus examination shows the following findings. What does it indicate?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The presence of a well-defined cystic lesion in the vitreous humor with surrounding inflammation, along with restricted eye movement, is characteristic of ocular cysticercosis, caused by the larval stage of Taenia solium.
  • Inflammation occurs mainly due to the release of toxins from the dead cysts.


Ocular cysticercosis

Definition

Infestation caused by Cysticercus cellulosae, the larval form of the pork tapeworm Taenia solium.

Clinical Features

Systemic Involvement:

  • Larvae can infest the CNS (neurocysticercosis), muscles, lungs, and subcutaneous tissues.
  • Neurological manifestations include seizures and headaches.

Eye involvement:

  • Orbit and adnexal cysticercosis:
    • The extraocular muscles (superior rectus- most common) form is the most common type of orbital and adnexal cysticercosis.
    • Presents as periocular swelling, proptosis, ptosis, pain, diplopia, restriction of ocular motility, strabismus, decreased vision, lid edema and orbital cellulitis.
  • Ocular cysticercosis:
    • Intraocular cysticercosis can involve either the anterior or the posterior segment (more common).
    • Presents as blurring of vision, uveitis, vitritis, scotoma, and photopsia.

Occular Toxoplasmosis (Option A): Fundoscopy shows focal necrotizing retinitis surrounded by a distinctive “headlight in the fog” appearance.

Endophthalmitis (Option B): It is usually associated with post-surgical infection, trauma, or endogenous spread. It presents with diffuse inflammation, hypopyon, and vitritis, not a well-defined cystic lesion.


Posterior uveitis due to TB (Option D): Tubercular uveitis often presents with granulomas, choroiditis, or vasculitis rather than a single cystic lesion with inflammation.

question: A 35-year-old male with a recent travel history to Africa presents with intense itching, skin nodules, and progressive vision loss. explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The most probable diagnosis in this scenario is toxoplasmosis uveitis, which is caused by Toxoplasma gondii.
  • Fundoscopy shows focal necrotizing retinitis surrounded by a distinctive “headlight in the fog” appearance.
  • An immunocompromised person living with cats is a risk factor for toxoplasmosis.

Toxoplasmosis Uveitis:

  • It is a protozoan infestation.
  • Organism: Toxoplasma gondii
  • Definitive host - cats
  • Intermediate hosts - humans
  • Systemic lesions are more common in immunocompromised patients

Clinical manifestation:

  • Most common cause of posterior uveitis and focal necrotizing retinitis (90% of cases)
  • Congenital
    • Inactive disease - Healed punched out heavily pigmented chorioretinal scars in the macular area

[[figure-1]]

  • In active inflammation - “headlight in the fog” appearance due to intense vitritis

[[figure-2]]


Cytomegalovirus (CMV) (Option A):

  • The characteristic picture is areas of necrosis with areas of vasculitis, retinal hemorrhages, and loss of fundal details giving a pizza pie appearance.


Candida albicans (Option B):

  • The characteristic picture is multiple small, round, whitish areas, which may be associated with areas of hemorrhages with pale centers (Roth's spots).

[[figure-3]]

Histoplasma capsulatum (Option D):

  • The characteristic picture is choroidal neovascular membranes or disciform lesions at the macula with well-circumscribed peripheral chorioretinal scars in the absence of inflammatory signs in the aqueous and vitreous, and associated with peripapillary pigment epithelial atrophy.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

A relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) is best detected by the alternating light test, also known as the swinging flashlight test. During this test, a light is alternately shone into each eye for 2-3 seconds, and the examiner compares the initial direct pupillary contraction and any pupillary dilation (escape). This is the standard clinical test used to assess RAPD.

Direct ophthalmoscopy (Option A): This is used to visualise the optic disc and retina directly, and cannot itself detect a pupillary conduction defect.

Red desaturation test (Option B): This test assesses optic nerve function by comparing perceived brightness of a red object between the two eyes, used as a subjective adjunct, but not the standard reliable test for RAPD.

Confrontation visual field test (Option D): This is a screening test for gross visual field defects, not for detecting pupillary reflex abnormalities.

question: A 30-year-old patient with HIV presents with vision loss and floaters. On examination, the patient has a CD4+ count of 40 cells/mm³. Fundoscopy reveals areas of necrosis with the following appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: D. The constrictor pupillae muscle is controlled by sympathetic nerves.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The constrictor pupillae muscle is controlled by parasympathetic nerves, not sympathetic.

Middle Coat of the Eye (Uveal Tract)

Choroid:

  • Characteristics:
    1. Lines the inner surface of the sclera.
    2. Connected anteriorly to the iris via the ciliary body. (Option A)
    3. Pierced posteriorly by the optic nerve.

Ciliary Body:

  • Ciliary Muscles: Smooth muscle with radial and circular fibers. (Option B)

Iris:

  • Attachment: Attached peripherally to the ciliary body; forms the iridocorneal angle (Option C).

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]



Reference:

American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO)

The ciliary body contains both radial and circular smooth muscle fibers.
The posterior layer of the iris is continuous with the ciliary body

question: Which of the following statements about the uveal tract is false?

correctAnswer: A. Start with systemic corticosteroids and consider long-term immunosuppressive therapy
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Systemic corticosteroids can provide initial relief for uveitis symptoms in Behcet’s disease, but for long-term management, immunosuppressive therapy is necessary due to the disease’s chronic nature and poor long-term prognosis with corticosteroids alone.

Behcet’s Disease

  • Obliterative vasculitis, likely due to circulating immune complexes

Treatment

  • Corticosteroids: Effective initially but not long-term
  • Immunosuppressive Drugs: Methotrexate, azathioprine, cyclosporine for resistant or severe cases

Immediate initiation of antiviral therapy (Option B): Antiviral therapy is not appropriate as Behcet’s disease is not caused by viral infection.

Use of topical antibiotics for ocular symptoms (Option C): Topical antibiotics are not effective since the uveitis is due to an autoimmune process.

Prescription of oral antihistamines for symptom relief (Option D): Oral antihistamines are not suitable for treating the autoimmune-related uveitis in Behcet’s disease.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th edition, Page 454-56

question: A 30-year-old man presents with symptoms of recurrent bilateral eye inflammation, including redness, pain, and vision loss. He also has a history of frequent oral and genital ulcers and skin rashes. He is HLA-B51 positive. What would be the most appropriate approach for managing his uveitis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Topical corticosteroids are the initial treatment for acute iridocyclitis.

Reiter's Syndrome

  • Reiter’s syndrome includes urethritis, arthritis, and conjunctivitis, often with iridocyclitis.
  • Ocular Features:
    • Acute mucopurulent conjunctivitis, possibly with superficial punctate keratitis.
    • Acute, non-granulomatous iridocyclitis occurs in 20-30% of cases.
  • Treatment:
    • Iridocyclitis: Managed with topical, periocular, and systemic corticosteroids.
    • Post Venereal form (likely due to Chlamydia): Treated with systemic tetracycline (250 mg, four times daily for 10 days).


Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th edition, Page 435-36
question: A 30-year-old man with a recent history of urethritis and arthritis presents with eye symptoms. He is positive for HLA-B27. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Secondary glaucoma is a known complication of anterior uveitis, often resulting from inflammatory trabeculitis, corticosteroid response, or synechial angle closure.
  • In this case, the patient has posterior synechiae, which can lead to pupillary block and increased intraocular pressure (IOP).
  • Chronic inflammation can also cause damage to the trabecular meshwork, leading to impaired aqueous outflow and secondary glaucoma.

Complication

Description

Complicated Cataract

Common in iridocyclitis, characterized by posterior subcapsular opacities with "polychromatic luster" and "bread-crumb" appearance.

Secondary Glaucoma

Can occur early or late due to iridocyclitis.

Cyclitic Membrane

Late complication where exudates behind the lens become organized in acute plastic iridocyclitis.

Choroiditis

Long-standing iridocyclitis can lead to choroiditis due to the continuity of the iris, ciliary body, and choroid.

Retinal Complications

Includes cystoid macular edema, macular scar/hole, epiretinal membrane, exudative retinal detachment, secondary periphlebitis retinae, retinal scars, sub-retinal fibrosis.

Papillitis

Inflammation of the optic disc, seen in severe cases of iridocyclitis.

Band-shaped Keratopathy

Common in children with Still’s disease and chronic uveitis.

Phthisis Bulbi

Final stage of chronic uveitis where the eye becomes soft, shrunken, and atrophic.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th edition, Page 425-27

Yanoff and Duker Ophthalmology, 5th edition, Page 696-97
question: A 45-year-old male presents with unilateral eye pain, photophobia, and redness for the past five days. Slit-lamp examination reveals circumcorneal injection, anterior chamber cells and flare, and posterior synechiae. Despite initial treatment with topical corticosteroids and cycloplegics, his symptoms persist, and intraocular pressure (IOP) is found to be elevated. Which of the following is the most likely complication of the condition he is suffering from?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient has acute anterior uveitis (iridocyclitis).

  • The development of elevated intraocular pressure in the presence of active inflammation and posterior synechiae is most consistent with secondary glaucoma, a common complication of anterior uveitis.
  • Increased IOP may result from inflammatory cells, fibrin, and trabeculitis impairing aqueous outflow through the trabecular meshwork.
  • In addition, posterior synechiae may progress to seclusio pupillae, producing pupillary block, iris bombe, and secondary angle-closure glaucoma.
  • Prolonged corticosteroid therapy may also contribute to ocular hypertension in susceptible individuals.
  • Other important complications of chronic or recurrent anterior uveitis include posterior synechiae, complicated posterior subcapsular cataract, cystoid macular edema, band-shaped keratopathy, hypotony, and phthisis bulbi.

Retinal detachment (Option A): Retinal detachment is not a common complication of isolated anterior uveitis. Although severe posterior uveitis may rarely lead to exudative retinal detachment, it is not suggested by this patient's presentation.

Vitreous haemorrhage (Option C): Vitreous haemorrhage is usually caused by proliferative diabetic retinopathy, retinal tears, trauma, or retinal neovascularisation.

Optic neuritis (Option D): Optic neuritis is an inflammatory demyelinating disorder of the optic nerve characterised by painful eye movements and reduced visual acuity, often associated with multiple sclerosis. It is not a recognized complication of anterior uveitis, although optic disc edema (papillitis) may rarely occur in severe intraocular inflammation.



Reference:
  1. Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Pages 425-427
  2. Yanoff and Duker Ophthalmology, 5th Edition, Pages 696- 697
question: A 45-year-old man presents with unilateral eye pain, photophobia, and redness for 5 days. Slit-lamp examination shows circumcorneal (ciliary) injection, anterior chamber cells and flare, and posterior synechiae. Despite treatment with topical corticosteroids and cycloplegics, his symptoms persist, and intraocular pressure (IOP) is elevated. Which of the following is the most likely complication of the condition he is suffering from?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Posterior uveitis is defined as the inflammation of the choroid and the retina.
  • The components of posterior uveitis include the following,
    • Choroiditis
    • Retinitis
    • Retinal vasculitis
      • Periphlebitis - Venous sheathing
      • Periarteritis - Hemorrhages

Retinitis (Option A): Inflammation of the neural retina.

  • The retina lies in the posterior segment of the globe. In many cases of posterior uveitis, the inflammation spreads from the choroid to the retina (chorioretinitis) or starts in the retina itself.


Choroiditis (Option B): Inflammation of the choroid, the vascular layer between the retina and the sclera.

  • The choroid makes up the posterior portion of the uveal tract. It is the defining feature of "true" posterior uveitis.


Retinal Vasculitis (Option C): Inflammation of the retinal blood vessels.

  • Periphlebitis - Venous sheathing
  • Periarteritis - Hemorrhages



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th edition, Page 427, 431
question: Which of the following is not a component of Posterior uveitis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The most appropriate initial treatment for intermediate uveitis, especially when it is idiopathic and presents with significant vitreous inflammation, is the periocular injection of triamcinolone.
  • This approach targets inflammation locally with fewer systemic side effects compared to systemic steroids.

Treatment (Kaplan's Modified 4-Step Protocol)

Step

Treatment

Details

1

Periocular & Systemic Steroids

Triamcinolone injection: 40 mg, 3 injections spaced 3 weeks apart.

Oral corticosteroids: Typically considered if periocular steroids are insufficient. Gradual tapering is done. (Option B)

2

Immunosuppressive Drugs

Agents: Cyclosporine, azathioprine, methotrexate, cyclophosphamide.

Close monitoring due to potential side effects.

3

Cryotherapy/Indirect Laser Photocoagulation (Option D)

Cryotherapy: Controlled cold-induced injury. Used for snowbanking when less invasive treatments fail.

Laser photocoagulation: Focused light beam treatment.

4

Pars Plana Vitrectomy (Option A)

Surgery: For severe cases or complications (e.g., tractional retinal detachment). Removes vitreous gel, and clears debris.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th edition, Page 443-45
question: What is the 1st line of treatment in a 35 year old patient presenting with Intermediate uveitis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The presence of floaters, anterior vitritis, and white snowball-like exudates near the ora serrata with mild peripheral periphlebitis are characteristic of intermediate uveitis (pars planitis).

Intermediate Uveitis: Causes and Features

Definition:
Intermediate uveitis, also known as pars planitis, primarily affects the pars plana of the ciliary body and the peripheral choroid. It mostly occurs in children and young adults, with a higher incidence in females.

Features

Common Features

Floaters

Vision deterioration due to anterior vitreous opacities

Minimal aqueous flare with occasional keratic precipitates

Anterior Vitritis

White snowball-like exudates near the ora serrata

Mild peripheral periphlebitis

[[figure-1]]

  • CMV Retinitis: Typically presents with focal retinochoroiditis rather than the diffuse features seen in intermediate uveitis. (Option A)
  • Tuberculosis: Typically causes anterior uveitis. (Option B)
  • Lyme Uveitis: May cause uveitis but typically presents with more acute dermatological symptoms, and the ocular findings are not as specific to intermediate uveitis as in this case. More commonly seen in the relapsing-remitting type. (Option D)


Reference:

Parsons Diseases of the eye, 23rd edition, Pg 553.
question: A 25-year-old female presents with floaters and gradual deterioration of vision. On examination, there is anterior vitritis with white snowball-like exudates and mild peripheral periphlebitis. No other relevant history or clinical findings. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. Conduct an HLA typing and begin treatment with topical prednisolone.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The findings are consistent with a case of anterior uveitis.
  • HLA typing is important in identifying associated systemic conditions that may cause anterior uveitis, such as Behçet's disease or VKH syndrome.
  • Topical prednisolone is a standard treatment for reducing inflammation in anterior uveitis.

Investigations for Anterior Uveitis:

Ocular Investigations Systemic Investigations
  • USG-B-Scan: To assess the posterior segment of the eye for any abnormalities.
  • Fundus Fluorescein Angiography (FFA): To evaluate the retinal and choroidal circulation and detect any leakage or abnormalities.
  • Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT)
  • Syphilis Tests:
    • VDRL
    • TPHA
  • Sarcoidosis:
    • Serum ACE Levels:
    • Chest X-Ray:
  • Mantoux Test / QuantiFERON Test
  • X-Ray Spine
  • HLA Typing:
    • HLA-B27: Associated with various types of arthritis, including ankylosing spondylitis.
    • HLA-B5 and HLA-B51: Associated with Behçet's disease.
    • HLA-DR4: Associated with VKH syndrome and sympathetic ophthalmia.

Treatment for Anterior Uveitis:

  • Topical Steroids (Treatment of Choice):
    • Prednisolone: Commonly used for reducing inflammation.
    • Loteprednol: Less potential for increasing intraocular pressure.
  • Cycloplegics (Topical):
    • Rest the ciliary muscles to relieve pain.
    • Prevent and break posterior synechiae (adhesions of the iris to the lens).
    • Improve blood supply, leading to better healing.
  • Non-Steroidal Treatment:
    • Voclosporin: Part of the Luminate program, used as a non-steroidal option.
  • For Chronic or Vision-Threatening Uveitis:
    • Monoclonal Antibodies:
      • Adalimumab: TNF-alpha inhibitor, used for severe or chronic cases.
      • Infliximab: TNF-alpha inhibitor.
    • Interferon Alpha: An option for severe cases, helps modulate the immune response.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 424, 430-433

Order a serum ACE level and start treatment with non-steroidal voclosporin.
Conduct an HLA typing and begin treatment with topical prednisolone.
Arrange for an OCT scan and administer systemic interferon-alpha.

question: A 40-year-old patient presents with eye pain, redness, and a constricted pupil. During the examination, fine, grey deposits on the corneal endothelium are noted. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in investigating and treating this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Anterior uveitis is characterized by the presence of fine, grey keratic precipitates (KPs) on the corneal endothelium, a hazy anterior chamber (aqueous flare), and a constricted pupil.

Anterior Uveitis

Examination Findings:

  • Keratic Precipitates (KPs):
    • Non-Granulomatous: Fine, grey deposits; composed of lymphocytes
    • Granulomatous: Large, greasy-looking deposits known as "mutton fat KPs"; composed of macrophages

[[figure-1]]

  • Aqueous Cells:
    • Indicator of active inflammation
  • Aqueous Flare:
    • Haziness in the anterior chamber due to leakage of proteins from inflamed tissues
  • Muddy Iris:
    • Edema in the iris caused by protein leakage
  • Miosis:
    • Constricted pupil due to toxins released from inflamed tissue
  • Nodules on the Iris:
    • Koeppe's Nodules: At the pupillary border; seen in both granulomatous and non-granulomatous uveitis
    • Busacca Nodules: At the base of the iris; seen in granulomatous uveitis

Koeppe's Nodules

[[figure-2]]

Herpes Simplex Keratitis (Option A):

  • Presents with dendritic corneal ulcers, not fine, grey keratic precipitates or a hazy anterior chamber.
  • It also usually does not involve a constricted pupil.

Conjunctivitis (Option B):

  • Does not cause keratic precipitates , hazy anterior chamber and a constricted pupil.

Acute Angle Closure Glaucoma (Option D):

  • Presents with a mid-dilated or fixed, mid-dilated pupil, severe pain, redness, and vision changes.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 424-427
question: A 35-year-old patient presents with a 1-week history of worsening eye pain and redness. On examination, a constricted pupil, a hazy anterior chamber, and deposits on the back of the cornea as shown below. Based on these findings, which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Behcet's Disease is a known systemic association with anterior uveitis, characterized by recurrent oral and genital ulcers, and uveitis.
  • Anterior uveitis, also known as iritis, is an inflammatory condition of the eye, including the iris and ciliary body.

Masquerade Syndromes:

  • Conditions that mimic the symptoms of anterior uveitis but are not primarily inflammatory in nature.
  • Neoplastic Masquerades:
    • Lymphomas
    • Anterior Segment Melanoma
    • Retinoblastoma (Option C)
    • Metastasis
  • Non-Neoplastic Masquerades:
    • Intraocular Foreign Body (Option A)
    • Old Retinal Detachment
    • Pigment Dispersion Syndrome (Option D)
    • Coats' Disease


Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology 9th ed., Page 424
question: A 50-year-old patient presents with anterior uveitis. After a detailed evaluation, the ophthalmologist considers various systemic associations and possible masquerades for the condition. Which of the following conditions is a known systemic association with anterior uveitis, but not a masquerade?

correctAnswer: B. Chronic uveitis is classified as lasting more than 6 months without interruption.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Chronic uveitis is defined as uveitis that lasts more than 3 months, not 6 months.

Classification Based on Time of Inflammatory Activity

Acute Uveitis (Option A):

  • Duration: < 3 months
  • Onset: Sudden

Chronic Uveitis:

  • Duration: > 3 months

Recurrent Uveitis (Option C):

  • Characterized by repeated episodes
  • Includes periods of inactivity between episodes

Remission (Option D):

  • No inflammatory activity for ≥ 3 months


Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8935739/

options.text: Acute uveitis is defined as having a duration of less than 3 months and typically has a sudden onset.
Chronic uveitis is classified as lasting more than 6 months without interruption.
Recurrent uveitis involves repeated episodes with periods of inactivity between them.
Remission in uveitis is defined as no inflammatory activity for 3 months or more.

question: Which of the following statements about the classification of uveitis based on the time of inflammatory activity is false?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
The structure is the ciliary body, part of the uveal tract between the iris and choroid, extending from the iris root to the ora serrata. Its pars plicata secretes aqueous humor, and contraction of the circular ciliary muscle fibers reduces zonular tension, enabling accommodation. The main blood supply comes from the long posterior ciliary arteries and anterior ciliary arteries, not the short posterior ciliary arteries.

Parts

Arterial Supply

Venous Drainage

Nerve Supply

Iris

Long posterior ciliary arteries, Anterior ciliary arteries

Vortex veins

Sensory: Trigeminal

Motor: Parasympathetic (III) to the sphincter, Sympathetic to the dilator (Option 3)

Ciliary Body

Long posterior ciliary arteries, Anterior ciliary arteries (Option 1)

Vortex veins (inner part), Anterior ciliary veins (outer part)

Sensory: Trigeminal

Motor: Oculomotor and Sympathetic

Choroid

Short posterior ciliary arteries (Option 4 ruled out)

Vortex veins

Sensory: Trigeminal

Autonomic (vasomotor)
