Parsons Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page 44.
question:
A 62-year-old woman with newly diagnosed primary open-angle glaucoma is counselled about aqueous dynamics and accommodation. The clinician explains that aqueous humor is actively secreted by a part of the uveal tract that also contains smooth muscle fibers arranged in longitudinal, oblique, and circular layers. Which of the following statements about this structure is/are correct?

  1. It is mainly supplied by long posterior ciliary arteries and anterior ciliary arteries
  2. Its posterior portion extends up to the ora serrata
  3. It contributes to accommodation by reducing zonular tension
  4. It receives its principal blood supply from short posterior ciliary arteries

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
Corectopia is defined as the displacement of the pupil from its normal central position due to an iris developmental abnormality. It may be associated with high refractive errors, including myopia, because the optical axis is altered.

Anisocoria (Option A) describes unequal pupil size, not abnormal pupil position.

Polycoria (Option B) is characterized by multiple pupillary openings, not a single displaced pupil.


Ectopia lentis (Option C) involves displacement of the crystalline lens with a visible lens edge and marked lenticular myopia, which is absent here.



Reference:

Parsons Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page 603.
question: A 6-year-old child is brought in with complaints of poor distance vision since early childhood. Refraction reveals high myopia. Slit-lamp examination shows a single pupil displaced inferonasally, with a normally positioned crystalline lens, as seen in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient has iridodialysis, a traumatic avulsion of the iris root from its attachment to the ciliary body, most commonly caused by blunt ocular trauma.

  • The sudden anteroposterior compression and equatorial expansion of the globe generate traction at the iris root, producing a D-shaped pupil with the flattened edge directed toward the site of dialysis at the limbus.
  • Patients may also present with glare, photophobia, monocular diplopia, hyphema, and, in large defects, pseudopolycoria.
  • The diagnosis is confirmed by slit-lamp examination, and management depends on the size of the dialysis and associated ocular injuries.


Endophthalmitis (Option A) presents with pain, hypopyon, and severe inflammation, not a D-shaped pupil.

Acute glaucoma (Option C) presents with sudden pain, redness, and a mid-dilated fixed pupil, not a localised D-shaped deformity.

Anterior uveitis (Option D) causes small, irregular pupils with miosis or synechiae, but not a D-shaped pupil oriented toward the limbus.



Reference:

Parsons Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page 1290.
question: A 28-year-old male presents to the emergency department after sustaining blunt ocular trauma during a road traffic accident. On slit-lamp examination, the pupil appears D-shaped, with the flat edge oriented toward the limbus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Acute anterior uveitis is an inflammation of the iris and ciliary body. Keratic precipitates (cellular deposits on the corneal endothelium) are pathognomonic, whereas aqueous flare, Busacca nodules, and festooned pupil are supportive but not definitive.

Signs of Anterior Uveitis

Cornea
  • Keratic precipitates (pathognomonic) (Option C)
  • Corneal edema

Anterior chamber

  • Aqueous cells
  • Aqueous flare (earliest sign) (Option A ruled out)
  • Hypopyon

Iris

  • Loss of normal iris pattern
  • Change in iris color
  • Iris nodules (Koeppe, Busacca) (Option B ruled out)

Pupillary

  • Constricted pupil
  • Irregular pupil shape
  • Posterior synechiae
  • Festooned pupil (segmental posterior synechiae) (Option D ruled out)

Severe cases
  • Deep irregular anterior chamber due to synechiae
  • Neovascularization


Reference:

Parsons Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Pages 546-548.
question: A 32-year-old patient presents with pain, redness, and photophobia in one eye. Slit-lamp examination reveals inflammatory changes involving the iris and ciliary body. Which of the following findings is considered pathognomonic of acute anterior uveitis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
In acute anterior uveitis, the earliest sign detectable on slit-lamp examination is aqueous flare, which results from the breakdown of the blood-aqueous barrier. Protein leakage into the aqueous humor causes the Tyndall phenomenon, making the aqueous appear hazy. This finding precedes cellular deposits and structural changes.

[[figure-1]]

Corneal edema (Option A) occurs later due to endothelial dysfunction or raised IOP, not the earliest sign.

Keratic precipitates (Option B) are pathognomonic but appear after aqueous flare.

Corneal opacity (Option D) suggests corneal pathology or advanced inflammation, not early uveitis.



Reference:
  1. Parsons Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Pages 546-548.
  2. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2841369/
question: A 35-year-old patient presents with pain, redness, and photophobia in one eye of recent onset. Slit-lamp examination is performed to identify the earliest detectable sign of anterior uveitis. Which of the following findings is most likely to be observed first?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The image depicts keratic precipitates (KPs), which are inflammatory cellular deposits characteristic of anterior uveitis (iritis/iridocyclitis).

  • They consist of aggregates of inflammatory cells that adhere to the corneal endothelium as a result of convection currents within the aqueous humor during intraocular inflammation.
  • Keratic precipitates are typically distributed in the inferior central corneal endothelium, forming a triangular pattern known as Arlt's triangle.
    • Fine KPs are usually seen in nongranulomatous anterior uveitis.
    • Mutton-fat KPs are characteristic of granulomatous anterior uveitis.

Bowman's membrane (Option A) is an acellular layer beneath the corneal epithelium and is not a site for keratic precipitate deposition.

Corneal epithelium (Option B) is affected in epithelial defects and superficial keratitis but is not the site of keratic precipitates.

Corneal stroma (Option D) is involved in stromal keratitis and stromal infiltrates, whereas keratic precipitates are deposited on the corneal endothelium in anterior uveitis.



Reference:

Parsons Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page 270.
question: A 34-year-old male presents with eye pain, redness, and photophobia. Slit-lamp examination reveals fine whitish deposits on the posterior surface of the cornea, as shown in the image. These deposits are located in which layer of the cornea?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
In acute anterior uveitis, inflammation of the iris and spasm of the sphincter muscle lead to miosis, while posterior synechiae between the iris and lens create pupillary irregularity, resulting in a small, irregular (festooned) pupil.

The pupil is often sluggish, with a muddy iris surface and color changes from vascular congestion and edema. If synechiae progress, seclusio pupillae or iris bombé may develop in advanced stages.

[[figure-1]]

Pupil Appearance

Interpretation

Normal, regular

Seen in healthy eye (Option A Ruled out)

Large, irregular

Traumatic mydriasis or acute angle-closure glaucoma (Option B Ruled out)

Small, irregular, sluggish

Miosis with posterior synechiae (Option C)

Oval, regular

Postoperative or pharmacologic effect (Option D Ruled out)


Reference:

Parsons Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page 548.
question: A 39-year-old male presents with an acute onset of eye pain, redness, and photophobia. Slit-lamp examination confirms a diagnosis of acute anterior uveitis. Which of the following pupillary appearances is most likely to be seen in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
Koeppe nodules are small granulomatous lesions located at the pupillary margin of the iris, typically seen in granulomatous anterior uveitis associated with systemic diseases like sarcoidosis and tuberculosis.

[[figure-1]]

Pupil Findings in Various Conditions

Finding

Appearance

Location

Clinical Association

Koeppe nodules

Small, pale nodules

Pupillary margin

Granulomatous uveitis

Busacca nodules

Larger nodules

Peripheral iris

Granulomatous uveitis

Lisch nodules

Pedunculated pigmented nodules

Iris surface

Neurofibromatosis type 1

Brushfield spots

Whitish spots

Peripheral iris

Down syndrome

Iris freckles

Flat pigmented spots

Iris surface

Benign

Muddy iris

Dull, blurred pattern

Entire iris

Uveitis / iridocyclitis

Sectoral iris atrophy

Patchy thinning

Part of iris

Acute angle-closure glaucoma, herpes zoster

Retina (Option A): Involved in posterior uveitis, not associated with Koeppe nodules.

Cornea (Option B): Shows keratic precipitates in uveitis, not nodules.


Conjunctiva (Option D) may show follicles or granulomas in systemic disease, but not Koeppe nodules.



Reference:

Parsons Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page 275.
question: A 42-year-old woman with a history of sarcoidosis presents with eye redness, photophobia, and mild pain. Slit-lamp examination shows small nodules at the pupillary margin consistent with Koeppe nodules. On which ocular structure are these nodules located?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
Iris bombe occurs when aqueous humor accumulates in the posterior chamber due to 360-degree posterior synechiae, leading to complete pupillary block and anterior bowing of the peripheral iris. This circumferential adhesion of the iris to the anterior lens capsule is termed ring synechiae.

Filiform synechiae (Option A): Fine, thread-like adhesions that do not cause complete pupillary block.

Confluent synechiae (Option B): Broad adhesions involving part of the pupillary margin, insufficient to cause iris bombe.

Total synechiae (Option D): Refers to extensive iris adhesion but is a nonspecific term; iris bombe is specifically due to ring synechiae.



Reference:

Parsons Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page 548.
question: A patient with chronic anterior uveitis develops forward bowing of the peripheral iris due to complete pupillary block, producing an appearance of iris bombe. Which of the following is associated with this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
Recurrent oral and genital ulcers, bilateral ocular inflammation, and a positive pathergy test are characteristic of Behçet disease, a multisystem vasculitis often causing recurrent, bilateral, nongranulomatous uveitis, with a strong association to HLA-B51.

Non-granulomatous Uveitis

Type

Causes

Acute
  • Idiopathic
  • Viral infections (mumps, influenza, adenovirus, measles)
  • Chlamydial infection
  • Lyme disease
  • Leptospirosis
  • Kawasaki disease
  • Rickettsial infections
  • HLA-B27 associated (ankylosing spondylitis, Reiter syndrome, isolated HLA-B27) (Option A ruled out)
  • Behçet disease
  • Psoriatic arthritis
  • Inflammatory bowel disease
  • Lens-induced uveitis (phacolytic, phacoanaphylactic, phacotoxic)
  • UGH syndrome (uveitis-glaucoma-hyphaema)
  • Corneal graft rejection
  • Posner-Schlossman syndrome
  • Trauma
  • Anterior segment ischaemia
  • Secondary syphilis

Chronic
  • Juvenile chronic arthritis
  • Chronic iridocyclitis of childhood
  • Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis

HLA-DR4 (Option C): Associated with Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease and rheumatoid arthritis.

HLA-Bw54 (Option D): Associated with Posner-Schlossman syndrome.

question: A 41-year-old man presents with recurrent painful oral ulcers, genital ulcers, and bilateral eye redness with pain. Ocular examination shows features of recurrent uveitis. A pathergy test is positive. This patient is most likely to have an association with which HLA type?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Growth of acid-fast bacilli on Lowenstein-Jensen medium confirms infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

  • Ocular tuberculosis usually occurs due to hematogenous spread from a pulmonary or extrapulmonary focus.
  • The most common intraocular manifestation of ocular tuberculosis is granulomatous uveitis, which commonly presents as posterior uveitis or panuveitis.
  • It may be associated with choroiditis, retinal vasculitis, vitritis, and choroidal tubercles or granulomas.
  • Management consists of anti-tubercular therapy (ATT) along with corticosteroids, when indicated, to control intraocular inflammation.

Vitreous hemorrhage (Option A) is most commonly caused by retinal vascular disorders, trauma, or proliferative diabetic retinopathy and is not a typical primary manifestation of ocular tuberculosis.

Phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis (Option B) is a delayed hypersensitivity reaction to tubercular antigens, especially in children, but it is not the most common intraocular manifestation of ocular tuberculosis.

Complicated cataract (Option D) is a late complication of chronic uveitis or prolonged corticosteroid therapy rather than a primary manifestation of ocular tuberculosis.



Reference:
  1. Parsons Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page 545.

question: A 38-year-old man newly diagnosed with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection undergoes baseline ophthalmic evaluation. Fundus examination reveals multiple cotton-wool spots and retinal microaneurysms. What is the most common ocular manifestation seen in patients with HIV infection?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The fundus photograph shows fluffy yellow-white areas of necrotising retinitis with overlying retinal haemorrhages, producing the characteristic "pizza pie" ("cheese and ketchup") appearance, which is diagnostic of CMV retinitis.

  • In patients with advanced HIV infection, CMV retinitis is the most common opportunistic ocular infection, typically occurring when the CD4 count falls below 50 cells/µL.
  • Patients usually present with painless progressive visual loss, floaters, blurred vision, or visual field defects.
  • The lesions spread along retinal vessels in a brush-fire pattern and are associated with minimal vitritis, helping distinguish CMV retinitis from other infectious retinitides.

[[figure-1]]

Toxoplasma retinochoroiditis (Option A) presents with focal necrotising retinitis and dense vitritis (headlight in fog), not pizza-pie appearance.

Eales disease (Option B) causes peripheral retinal vasculitis and vitreous haemorrhage in young adults, unrelated to HIV.

Sympathetic ophthalmia (Option D): Bilateral granulomatous panuveitis following trauma or surgery, not an opportunistic retinal infection.



Reference:

Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 474.
question: A 40-year-old man with HIV presents with painless, progressive vision loss. Fundus examination shows a particular appearance, as shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option A - Acute uveitis

Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis is acute anterior uveitis, characterized by pain, redness, photophobia, ciliary flush, keratic precipitates, and a small irregular or sluggish pupil with normal or slightly low IOP.
Corneal haze results from cells and flare, and a shallow anterior chamber may occur from ciliary body congestion pushing the iris forward.

Anterior Uveitis: Most common type of uveitis affecting the anterior segment of the eye.

Clinical Features: Pain, Redness, Photophobia (sensitivity to light), Blepharospasm (involuntary blinking), Serous discharge, Blurring and diminished vision

Examination Findings:

  • Keratic Precipitates (KPs):
    • Non-Granulomatous: Fine, grey deposits; composed of lymphocytes
    • Granulomatous: Large, greasy-looking deposits known as "mutton fat KPs"; composed of macrophages
    • Location: Typically found in the lower cornea due to convection currents in aqueous humor; this area is known as Arlt's triangle

[[figure-1]]

  • Aqueous Cells:
    • Indicator of active inflammation
  • Aqueous Flare:
    • Haziness in the anterior chamber due to leakage of proteins from inflamed tissues
  • Muddy Iris:
    • Edema in the iris caused by protein leakage
  • Miosis:
    • Constricted pupil due to toxins released from inflamed tissue
  • Nodules on the Iris:
    • Koeppe's Nodules: At the pupillary border; seen in both granulomatous and non-granulomatous uveitis
    • Busacca Nodules: At the base of the iris; seen in granulomatous uveitis

[[figure-2]]

Complications: (Findings)

  • Posterior Synechiae: Iris adheres to the lens; may lead to festooned-shaped pupil

[[figure-3]]

  • Secclusio Pupil/Ring Synechiae: Adhesion along the entire pupillary border; can lead to Iris Bombe and peripheral anterior synechiae, causing angle closure glaucoma
  • Occlusio Pupil: Covers the whole surface of the lens
  • Cyclitic Membrane
  • Rubeosis Iridis: New vessel formation on the iris

Acute conjunctivitis (Option B) causes diffuse redness, mucopurulent discharge, and no photophobia or small pupil.

Acute congestive glaucoma (Option C) presents with a fixed mid-dilated pupil, hazy cornea, and markedly raised intraocular pressure, not seen here.

Central retinal artery occlusion (Option D) causes sudden painless loss of vision, with a pale retina and cherry-red spot, not pain or redness.

question: A 32-year-old patient presents with blurred vision, photophobia, and mild ocular pain. Examination reveals aqueous flares and keratic precipitates in the anterior chamber. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Iritis, also known as Anterior uveitis, is an inflammatory condition of the eye, including the iris and ciliary body.

Although SLE is an autoimmune disease that can affect multiple organs, iritis is less commonly seen in SLE compared to the other conditions listed. It more often causes other ocular manifestations, like dry eyes or retinal changes.

Systemic Associations and Masquerades of Iritis (Anterior Uveitis)

  • Infectious Causes:
    • Herpes Infections: Varicella Zoster, Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV)
    • Tuberculosis (TB)
    • Syphilis
    • Leprosy
  • Non-Infectious Causes:
    • With Systemic Association:
      • Sarcoidosis
      • Behçet's Disease (Option B ruled out)
      • HLA-B27 Associated Arthritis
      • Psoriatic Arthropathy (Option C ruled out)
      • Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Ulcerative Colitis (UC) > Crohn's Disease (Option D ruled out)
    • Without Systemic Association:
      • Drug-Induced: Pilocarpine, prostaglandin analogues
  • Masquerade Syndromes:
    • Definition: Conditions that mimic the symptoms of anterior uveitis but are not primarily inflammatory in nature.
    • Neoplastic Masquerades:
      • Lymphomas
      • Anterior Segment Melanoma
      • Retinoblastoma
      • Metastasis
    • Non-Neoplastic Masquerades:
      • Intraocular Foreign Body
      • Old Retinal Detachment
      • Pigment Dispersion Syndrome
      • Coats' Disease


Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology 9th ed., Page 424
question: Iritis is least associated with all of the following diseases:

explanationHtml:
Given the farmer's symptoms of pain, discharge, and history of trauma, along with the finding of white blood cells in the anterior chamber, the most likely diagnosis is hypopyon, which often results from infection or severe inflammation following eye trauma.

Fungal keratitis is a common cause of corneal ulcers following eye trauma, especially when the injury is caused by vegetative matter (such as plant material or dirt). This type of trauma provides an entry point for fungal spores.

The classic signs and symptoms of fungal keratitis include:

  • Corneal ulcer with satellite lesions (smaller ulcers surrounding the main ulcer).
  • Hypopyon (accumulation of white blood cells in the anterior chamber of the eye).
  • Mild pain, photophobia, and redness.
  • The history of vegetative matter as the cause of trauma is a significant clue, as fungi are commonly found in plant material.

Keratomycosis

[[figure-1]]

Clinical Features

  • Pain & Foreign Body Sensation
  • Watering of the eye
  • Photophobia
  • Blurred Vision
  • Redness.

Examination Findings

  • Corneal Ulcer: Greyish-white, dry-looking with elevated, rolled-out margins.
  • Pigmented Ulcer: Brownish appearance, possible with dematiaceous fungi.
  • Feathery Extensions: Delicate, finger-like projections into the surrounding stroma.
  • Sterile Immune Ring: Yellow line of demarcation where fungal antigen and host antibodies meet.
  • Satellite Lesions: Multiple small lesions around the main ulcer.
  • Hypopyon: Large, non-sterile, even with a small ulcer.

[[figure-2]]

  • Endothelial Plaque: Located under the stromal lesion, made of fibrin and leucocytes.
  • Corneal Vascularization: Typically absent in pure fungal ulcers.
  • Perforation: Rare but possible.

Investigations

  • Corneal Scraping: Performed under topical anaesthesia for microbiological examination.
  • Wet KOH Mount: Reveals filamentous fungi (branched, septate hyphae) or non-filamentous yeast-like fungi (Candida).
  • Gram's & Giemsa Stains: To detect fungal hyphae and inflammatory cells.
  • Culture: Sabouraud's agar medium is used for fungal culture.
  • PCR: Recommended for rapid identification of fungal pathogens.
  • Anterior Chamber Paracentesis: Considered if there is an intraocular extension.
  • Corneal Biopsy: Indicated for deep stromal abscess or when cultures are negative.
  • Confocal Microscopy: Used for identifying actual fungi within the cornea.

Treatment of Keratomycosis (Fungal Corneal Ulcer):

Primary Treatment: Antifungal Medications:

  • Topical Antifungal Agents:
    • Natamycin
    • Voriconazole
    • Amphotericin B (effective against Aspergillus and Fusarium)
    • Nystatin (effective against Candida)
  • Oral Antifungal Agents (for severe ulcers with specific features):
    • Ketoconazole
    • Voriconazole
    • Indications for Oral Therapy:
      • Hypopyon
      • Perforation
      • Suspicion of endophthalmitis

Surgical Management (if unresponsive to medical therapy):

  • Repeated Scraping: Removal of necrotic material
  • Cauterization Options:
    • Pure carbolic acid (100%)
    • Trichloroacetic acid (10%–20%)
    • Povidone-iodine 5%
  • Therapeutic Keratoplasty: Corneal transplantation

Hyphema (Option A): Refers to the presence of blood in the anterior chamber, often caused by trauma. While the patient did sustain trauma, the presence of pus (not blood) in the anterior chamber points to hypopyon rather than hyphema.

Aqueous flare (Option B): Refers to the presence of protein in the aqueous humor, which can be seen in inflammatory conditions, but it is generally seen as a cloudy appearance in the anterior chamber, not a white collection of cells like hypopyon.

Arlt line (Option C): This refers to a line of conjunctival scarring seen in trachoma, which is not related to the acute trauma described here and would not be associated with the findings in the anterior chamber.




Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 216, 217.
question: A farmer presents with pain and discharge in his left eye. He says that he sustained an injury caused by a leaf a few days back. What is the finding seen in the image?

explanationHtml:
Correct option: A) 1 and 2

Explanation:

Conditions where iritis is seen:

  • Behcet’s disease (Statement 3 ruled out): Characterized by recurrent uveitis, including iritis, genital involvement and oral involvement.
  • Psoriatic arthritis (Statement 4 ruled out): A seronegative spondyloarthropathy frequently associated with anterior uveitis including iritis, urethritis and arthritis.
  • Ulcerative colitis (Statement 5 ruled out): Iritis is common in inflammatory bowel disease, as it shares a systemic inflammatory pathway.
  • Rheumatoid arthritis: Iritis is rarely seen in adult-onset rheumatoid arthritis. However, it is more commonly associated with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), especially in ANA-positive cases.
  • SLE: Systemic lupus erythematosus typically affects other ocular tissues, such as the retina and optic nerve, rather than causing iritis.

Correct Option B - Atropine

Explanation:

Treatment for Anterior Uveitis:

  • Topical Steroids (Treatment of Choice):
    • Prednisolone: Commonly used for reducing inflammation.
    • Loteprednol: Less potential for increasing intraocular pressure.
  • Cycloplegics (Topical):
    • Rest the ciliary muscles to relieve pain.
    • Prevent and break posterior synechiae (adhesions of the iris to the lens).
    • Improve blood supply, leading to better healing.
    • Eg.:Atropine.
  • Non-Steroidal Treatment:
    • Voclosporin: Part of the Luminate program, used as a non-steroidal option.
  • For Chronic or Vision-Threatening Uveitis:
    • Monoclonal Antibodies:
      • Adalimumab: TNF-alpha inhibitor, used for severe or chronic cases.
      • Infliximab: TNF-alpha inhibitor.
    • Interferon Alpha: An option for severe cases, helps modulate the immune response.

Incorrect Options:

Moxifloxacin (Option A) is an antibiotic commonly used to treat bacterial infections.

Acetazolamide (Option C) is a medication primarily used to treat glaucoma by reducing the production of aqueous humor and lowering intraocular pressure.

Methotrexate (Option D) is an immunosuppressive medication commonly used in the treatment of various autoimmune and inflammatory conditions. It may be prescribed for severe or chronic cases of uveitis that do not respond to other treatments.

question: What is the specific sign that is pathognomonic for acute anterior uveitis among the options provided?

explanationHtml:
• The patient is likely experiencing sympathetic ophthalmia, a condition characterized by bilateral granulomatous panuveitis following trauma to one eye. The pathogenesis involves a delayed hypersensitivity reaction (T-cell mediated) to tyrosinase peptide antigens or melanocytes, leading to non-necrotizing granulomatous inflammation in both eyes.

Sympathetic ophthalmitis (SO)

Definition
  • Bilateral, granulomatous, panuveitis occurring after penetrating trauma where uveal prolapse may have been a feature of the trauma

Etiology and pathogenesis
  • Trauma to one eye (exciting eye) — 2 weeks to 3 months — Uveitis in the uninjured eye (sympathizing eye).
  • T-cell mediated autoimmune hypersensitivity reaction to Retinal S antigen.
  • Maximum risk upon injury to the ciliary body.

Histopathology
  • Diffuse lymphocytic infiltration of the choroid.
  • Scattered aggregates of epithelioid cells are seen, many of which contain fine granules of melanin.
  • Dalen–Fuchs nodules - granulomas located between Bruch membrane and the RPE (also seen in VKH syndrome)

[[figure-1]]

Clinical features
  • The exciting eye is frequently red and irritable.
  • The sympathizing eye develops irritation, blurred vision, photophobia and loss of accommodation causing difficulty in near vision (first symptom)
  • Anterior uveitis develops in both eyes, which may be mild or severe and is usually granulomatous

Investigations
  • Fundus exam: Dalen–Fuchs nodules, Exudative retinal detachment, vasculitis and optic disc swelling.
  • As inflammation settles, residual chorioretinal scarring may confer a ‘sunset glow’ appearance similar to VKH.
  • B-scan ultrasonography: Choroidal thickening and retinal detachment

Treatment
  • Enucleation of a severely injured eye within 10 to 14 days of the injury is effective in preventing or reducing the severity of SO
  • Steroids are the basis of initial treatment. Intravenous methylprednisolone followed by high-dose oral prednisolone is given for several months and gradually tapered according to response. Supplementary topical steroids and cycloplegics may be given

Causes of Panuveitis:

[[figure-2]]

MCP: Multifocal Choroiditis and Panuveitis, BSRC: Birdshot Retinochoroidopathy, ABD: Acute Bilateral Diffuse Uveal Retinitis, VKH: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Disease, SFU: Sarcoid-Associated Fuchs Uveitis, TB: Tuberculosis, HSV: Herpes Simplex Virus, VZV: Varicella-Zoster Virus, ARN: Acute Retinal Necrosis

Acute anterior uveitis (Option A): While acute anterior uveitis can occur in sympathetic ophthalmitis, it is not the most characteristic feature. Inflammatory involvement is not limited to just the anterior uvea in sympathetic ophthalmitis, as it typically progresses to involve all layers (hence panuveitis).

Pars planitis (Option B) is a type of intermediate uveitis that primarily affects the pars plana of the eye, but it is not typically associated with sympathetic ophthalmitis. It is a distinct form of uveitis, not related to penetrating trauma or autoimmune responses following injury.

Chronic anterior uveitis (Option D): This is not the typical presentation in sympathetic ophthalmitis. While inflammation can persist, it is more commonly panuveitis (involving both anterior and posterior segments), rather than isolated chronic anterior uveitis.



Reference:
  • Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th edition, page 449.
  • Yanoff and Duker Ophthalmology, 5th edition, page 770.
  • Uveitis- A Quick Guide to Essential Diagnosis by C. Stephen Foster, edition 1, page 3.

question: On ophthalmologic examination, the presence of Koeppe's nodules is observed in a patient diagnosed with sarcoidosis. In which area of the eye are these nodules typically observed?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option A - HLA B27

Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation of blurring vision, photophobia, redness, pain ,and keratic precipitates are suggestive of anterior uveitis. Patients with acute anterior uveitis with joint pain is suggestive of arthritis associated with uveitis. The disease affects young males who are positive for HLA B27. Among patients with ankylosing spondylitis, 90% of them belong to the HLA-B27 antigenic group.

Ankylosing Spondylitis (AS) / Marie Strumpell Disease

Definition

Chronic inflammatory disease primarily affecting the axial skeleton (spine and sacroiliac joints), leading to pain, stiffness, and spinal fusion (bamboo spine).

Etiology

Unknown; genetic (HLA-B27) and environmental factors involved. HLA-B27 is positive in 90% of cases, but not all carriers develop AS.

Pathophysiology

Inflammation at entheses → Erosive changes → New bone formation → Syndesmophytes → Spinal fusion (ankylosis).

[[figure-1]]

Clinical Features

Musculoskeletal Symptoms:

  • Chronic low back pain (worse after inactivity, better with activity)
  • Limited spinal mobility
  • Enthesitis (Achilles, plantar fascia)
  • Peripheral arthritis (hips, shoulders, knees)

Extra-articular Symptoms:

  • Ocular: Anterior uveitis (pain, redness, photophobia)
  • Cardiovascular: Aortic regurgitation, conduction issues
  • Pulmonary: Apical fibrosis
  • Gastrointestinal: Associated with IBD

Diagnosis

Based on clinical features, imaging studies, and HLA-B27 gene presence. Modified New York Criteria:

Clinical Criteria:

  • Low back pain > 3 months (improves with exercise, not with rest)
  • Limited lumbar spine motion (sagittal/frontal planes)
  • Reduced chest expansion (relative to age/sex)

Radiographic Criteria (X-ray): Bilateral sacroiliitis (grade 2-4) or unilateral sacroiliitis (grade 3-4)

Radiological Features:

  • Blurring/haziness of sacroiliac joint

[[figure-2]]

  • Juxta-articular sclerosis
  • Vertical/bridging syndesmophytes
  • Squaring of vertebrae

[[figure-3]]

  • Bamboo spine
  • Trolley track sign
  • Dagger sign

[[figure-4]]

  • Shiny corner sign/Romanus lesion (inflammatory lesions at edges of vertebrae)

[[figure-5]]

MRI: Early detection of inflammation

Clinical Tests:

For Sacroiliitis:

  • Gaenslen’s test
  • Patrick/FABER test
  • Figure of 4 test
  • Pump handle test

For Lumbar Spine:

Schober/ Modified Schober test

[[figure-6]]

Laboratory Tests
  • HLA-B27 positive (90% of cases)
  • ESR, CRP: Elevated during active disease, but can be normal

Differential Diagnosis
  • Mechanical low back pain
  • Other spondyloarthropathies (e.g., psoriatic arthritis)
  • Degenerative disc disease
  • Fibromyalgia

Treatment

Non-Pharmacological:

  • Physical therapy (mobility/posture exercises)
  • Patient education on disease and exercise importance

Pharmacological:

  • NSAIDs (first-line for pain, stiffness)
  • TNF inhibitors (for NSAID-resistant cases)
  • IL-17 inhibitors (Secukinumab)
  • Sulfasalazine (for peripheral arthritis)
  • Corticosteroids (short-term flare control)

Surgical:

  • Hip replacement (for severe hip involvement)
  • Spinal surgery (for severe deformities/fractures)

Complications
  • Spinal fractures (minimal trauma)
  • Cardiac issues (aortic regurgitation, conduction defects)
  • Osteoporosis leading to fracture risk

HLA B51 (Option B) It is associated with Behcet's syndrome with anterior uveitis. Behcet's syndrome is characterized by bilateral recurrent oral ulcers, genital ulcers, uveitis, and skin lesions.

HLA B47 (Option C) Is associated with congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency. It is characterized by symptoms like diarrhea, vomiting, arrhythmias, and low blood pressure.

HLA B57 (Option D) Is associated with the detection of abacavir hypersensitivity and slow progression of HIV.



Reference:
  • Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopedics and Trauma, 10th edition, Page 72-76.
  • https://www.niams.nih.gov/health-topics/ankylosing-spondylitis
question: A 26-year-old patient came with complaints of blurring of vision, photophobia, redness, pain in the left eye, and joint pain. Upon examination keratic precipitates and aqueous cells were observed. Which of the following major histocompatibility complex is be associated with this condition?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option A - Uvea

Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation of penetrating injury to the left eye and subsequent reduced near vision, pain, redness, and photophobia along with nodules on fundus i.e., Dalen-Fuchs nodules are suggestive of Sympathetic ophthalmitis.

Sympathetic ophthalmitis (SO)

Definition

Bilateral, granulomatous, panuveitis (Option A) occurring after penetrating trauma where uveal prolapse may have been a feature of the trauma

Etiology and pathogenesis
  • Trauma to one eye (exciting eye) — 2 weeks to 3 months — Uveitis in the uninjured eye (sympathizing eye).
  • T-cell mediated autoimmune hypersensitivity reaction to Retinal S antigen.
  • Maximum risk upon injury to the ciliary body.

Histopathology
  • Diffuse lymphocytic infiltration of the choroid.
  • Scattered aggregates of epithelioid cells are seen, many of which contain fine granules of melanin.
  • Dalen–Fuchs nodules - granulomas located between Bruch membrane and the RPE (also seen in VKH syndrome)

[[figure-1]]

Clinical features
  • The exciting eye is frequently red and irritable.
  • The sympathizing eye develops irritation, blurred vision, photophobia and loss of accommodation causing difficulty in near vision (first symptom)
  • Anterior uveitis develops in both eyes, which may be mild or severe and is usually granulomatous

Investigations
  • Fundus exam: Dalen–Fuchs nodules, Exudative retinal detachment, vasculitis and optic disc swelling.
  • As inflammation settles, residual chorioretinal scarring may confer a ‘sunset glow’ appearance similar to VKH.
  • B-scan ultrasonography: Choroidal thickening and retinal detachment

Treatment
  • Enucleation of a severely injured eye within 10 to 14 days of the injury is effective in preventing or reducing the severity of SO
  • Steroids are the basis of initial treatment. Intravenous methylprednisolone followed by high-dose oral prednisolone is given for several months and gradually tapered according to response. Supplementary topical steroids and cycloplegics may be given

Options B, C, and D are incorrect.



Reference:
  • Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th edition, page 449.
  • Yanoff and Duker Ophthalmology, 5th edition, page 770.
question: A 25-year-old male patient with a penetrating injury to the left eye was treated with corneoscleral suturing. Two months later, he returned with complaints of reduced near vision, pain, redness, and sensitivity to light in his right eye. Direct ophthalmoscopy revealed nodules in the fundus. Which part of the eye is affected?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The image shows a festooned pupil, a classic sign that occurs when a mydriatic is instilled in an eye with pre-existing posterior synechiae.
  • This confirms the underlying diagnosis of Acute Anterior Uveitis.
  • Drug of Choice: Atropine (1%) is the most potent and long-acting mydriatic/cycloplegic.
  • It is specifically preferred in cases with severe inflammation or established synechiae because milder agents may not be strong enough to break the adhesions.

Phenylephrine (Option B): It is a mydriatic (alpha-agonist) but has no cycloplegic action, and is rarely used alone for uveitis pain relief.

Scopolamine (Option C) is a potent cycloplegic and mydriatic agent used in uveitis. However, it has a shorter duration of action (3-7 days) compared to Atropine (7-10 days), making Atropine the preferred agent for sustained effect in severe cases.

Miotics (Option D): Drugs like Pilocarpine constrict the pupil. They are contraindicated in acute anterior uveitis as they increase pain (ciliary spasm) and promote synechiae formation.



Reference:
  1. Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Pages 429, 432.
  2. AK Khurana, Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th Edition, Page 561
question: A patient came with redness and pain, and the pupil was dilated to break posterior synechiae. Looking at the dilated pupil, which drug was likely used?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical scenario with the findings of keraitc precipitates is diagnostic of acute anterior uveitis (Iridocyclitis).
  • Acute Anterior Uveitis is strongly associated with HLA-B27-positive. Spondyloarthropathies (e.g., Ankylosing Spondylitis, Reactive Arthritis).
  • Approximately 50% of patients with acute anterior uveitis are HLA-B27 positive.
  • Therefore, HLA-B27 typing is the most relevant initial screening investigation for systemic etiology in this presentation.

Anti-CCP Antibodies (Option B) is a specific marker for Rheumatoid Arthritis. RA is more commonly associated with Scleritis or Keratoconjunctivitis Sicca (Dry Eye).

ANA (Option C): Antinuclear Antibody is associated with Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA). JIA-associated uveitis is typically chronic, bilateral, and painless, seen in young girls.

X-ray (Option D): While X-ray of the Sacroiliac joints is used to diagnose Ankylosing Spondylitis, the specific serological marker asked for is HLA-B27.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Pages 424, 430.
question: A young male patient presents with acute redness and pain in one eye. Examination findings are given below. What is the investigation of choice to diagnose this condition?

correctAnswer: D. Pupillary block caused by the swollen lens
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Lens-induced glaucoma is a type of secondary angle-closure glaucoma associated with a disorder of the lens.
  • In this case, the enlarged lens prevents aqueous humor from flowing through the pupil into the anterior chamber, leading to a pupillary block.
  • The iris is pushed forward, resulting in angle closure and increased intraocular pressure.

Other options describe mechanisms for other forms of secondary glaucoma, such as uveitic glaucoma (Option A), phacodonesis (Option B), or chronic iritis ( Option C), but are not characteristic of lens-induced glaucoma.



Reference:
  1. Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology, 10th edition, Pages 377, 378, 393, 394.
  2. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK574524/

options.text: Obstruction of the trabecular meshwork by inflammatory cells
Forward displacement of the lens due to an abnormal zonular attachment
Disruption of aqueous humor flow due to posterior synechiae
Pupillary block caused by the swollen lens

question: A 65-year-old female presents with acute onset pain, redness, and blurring of vision in the right eye. On examination, her intraocular pressure (IOP) is 48 mmHg, and there is a shallow anterior chamber with a hazy cornea. Slit-lamp examination reveals an intumescent, swollen lens with the iris pushed forward. Gonioscopy shows a closed angle. What is the most likely underlying mechanism for her glaucoma?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Angelman Syndrome (AS) is a rare neurogenetic disorder caused by loss of function of the UBE3A gene on chromosome 15.
  • Ophthalmic findings that can be seen in Angelman syndrome include Strabismus, Refractive errors, Oculocutaneous albinism, It is not associated with secondary glaucoma.

Secondary Developmental/ Congenital Glaucoma

Associated Ocular Anomalies

Associated Systemic Anomalies

Glaucoma Associated with Iridodysgenesis:

  • Aniridia (Option A ruled out)
  • Familial Iris Hypoplasia
  • Congenital Ectropion Uvea
  • Congenital Microcornea
  • Congenital Nanophthalmos

Chromosomal Disorders:

  • Trisomy 13 (Patau Syndrome)
  • Trisomy 18 (Edward’s Syndrome)
  • Trisomy 21 (Down Syndrome)
  • Turner Syndrome (Option C ruled out)

Ectopia Lentis Syndromes:

  • Marfan Syndrome (Option B ruled out)
  • Weill-Marchesani Syndrome
  • Homocystinuria

Glaucoma Associated with Iridocorneal Dysgenesis:

  • Posterior Embryotoxon
  • Axenfeld-Rieger Syndrome
  • Peter's Anomaly

Phakomatosis :

  • Sturge-Weber Syndrome
  • Von Recklinghausen’s Neurofibromatosis

Metabolic Syndromes:

  • Lowe’s Syndrome
  • Hurler’s Syndrome
  • Zellweger Syndrome

Types of Congenital Glaucoma:

In ophthalmology, congenital glaucoma is classified based on whether the developmental defect is isolated to the drainage angle or associated with other ocular or systemic anomalies.


Primary Congenital Glaucoma (PCG):

This is an isolated developmental defect of the drainage angle (Trabeculodysplasia) with no other systemic or ocular abnormalities.

  • Mechanism: Failure of the angle to develop properly, often resulting in Barkan’s Membrane covering the trabecular meshwork.

  • Classic Triad: Epiphora (tearing), Photophobia (light sensitivity), and Blepharospasm (eyelid squeezing).

  • Clinical Signs:

    • Buphthalmos: The globe stretches and enlarges ("Ox-eye") because the infant's sclera is elastic.

    • Haab Striae: Horizontal or curvilinear tears in Descemet’s membrane due to corneal stretching.

Secondary Congenital Glaucoma:

The glaucoma is caused by or associated with other ocular or systemic conditions.

  • Ocular Causes: Aniridia (absent iris), Peters anomaly (corneal opacity), or Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome.

  • Systemic Syndromes:

    • Sturge-Weber Syndrome: Associated with facial Port-wine stains.

    • Lowe Syndrome: Includes congenital cataracts and renal issues.

    • Neurofibromatosis-1: Features Lisch nodules and iris hamartomas.

Congenital glaucome treatment:

Congenital glaucoma is primarily a surgical emergency.

  1. Surgery: Goniotomy (if the cornea is clear) or Trabeculotomy (if the cornea is cloudy) to physically open the angle.

  2. Medication: Used only as a temporary measure.

    • Caution: Brimonidine is contraindicated in infants due to the risk of lethal CNS depression (apnea).



Reference:
  1. Parsons Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition , Pages 483- 487
  2. emedicine.medscape.com/article/1206524-overview?form=fpf
  3. www.aao.org/education/topic-detail/congenital-glaucoma-europ
question: Which of the following conditions is not typically associated with secondary congenital glaucoma?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Congenital glaucoma is diagnosed in this infant based on corneal enlargement, clouding, Haab’s striae, and elevated intraocular pressure.
  • When corneal clouding prevents proper angle visualization, Trabeculotomy with Trabeculectomy becomes the procedure of choice.
  • Trabeculotomy helps expose Schlemm's canal to improve aqueous outflow, and trabeculectomy provides additional filtration, offering better intraocular pressure control.

Goniotomy (Option A):

  • Involves making an incision in the angle of the eye and is best suited when the angle can be visualized clearly.

Trabeculectomy with antimetabolites (Option C):

  • While this is a common and effective procedure for many glaucoma cases, it might not be the first choice in this scenario due to the presence of corneal clouding and difficulty in initial angle procedures.

Glaucoma Drainage Devices (Option D):

  • Reserved for severe, resistant cases when other surgical methods have failed.



Reference:
  1. Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology, 10th Edition, Page 401, 402, 403
  2. Parsons Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page 277, 278
question: A 6-month-old infant with congenital glaucoma has corneal enlargement, clouding, and Haab’s striae and the angle is difficult to visualize due to corneal clouding. Which surgical procedure is most appropriate for this infant?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • True Congenital Glaucoma is characterized by elevated intraocular pressure present during intrauterine life, resulting in ocular enlargement at birth.
  • The presence of Haab’s striae, early onset, enlarged corneas, and the classic triad of symptoms (watering, photophobia, and blepharospasm) are all consistent with newborn glaucoma.

Primary Congenital Glaucoma

Types

1. Newborn glaucoma/ True congenital glaucoma:

  • Typically presents within the first month of life.

2. Infantile (Option B ruled out)

  • Affects infants older than 1 month and children up to 3 years.

3. Juvenile (Option A ruled out)

  • Also known as Juvenile primary open angle glaucoma (POAG) usually occurs between 10 to 35 years of age.

Secondary Congenital Glaucoma (Option D):

  • Usually associated with other ocular or systemic anomalies, which is not indicated in this case.



Reference:
  1. Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology, 10th edition, Pages 401, 402, 403
  2. Parsons’ Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, PDF Pages 277, 278
question: A 1-month-old child presents with persistent eye watering and light sensitivity. Examination shows enlarged corneas with Haab’s striae, cloudiness, a deep anterior chamber, and thin, blue sclera. The child has had ocular enlargement since birth. The ophthalmologist suspects congenital glaucoma. Which type of glaucoma best fits this presentation?

correctAnswer: C. Increases uveoscleral outflow; Iris pigmentation
explanationHtml:
Anti-Glaucoma Drugs:

1. Prostaglandin F2α Agonists (Option C)

  • Examples: Latanoprost, Bimatoprost, Travoprost, Tafluprost
  • Mechanism: Increases uveoscleral outflow
  • Uses: First-line for primary open-angle and angle-closure glaucoma
  • Side Effects: Sandy eyes, orbital fat atrophy, anterior uveitis, cystoid macular edema, heterochromia iridis, hypertrichosis
  • Contraindications: Cystoid macular edema, diabetes mellitus

2. Beta Blockers (Option D)

  • Non-Selective: Timolol, Levobunolol, Carteolol, Metipranolol
    • More effective but contraindicated in asthma
  • Selective: Betaxolol (retinoprotective), Levobetaxolol
    • Safer in asthma
  • Mechanism: Reduces aqueous secretion from ciliary epithelium
  • Side Effects: Allergic blepharoconjunctivitis, dry eyes, corneal hypoesthesia

3. Alpha-2 Agonists (Option A)

  • Examples: Brimonidine (long-term use), Apraclonidine (IOP spikes)
  • Mechanism: Reduces aqueous production, increases uveoscleral outflow
  • Side Effects: Lid retraction, respiratory depression (Brimonidine), allergic blepharoconjunctivitis
  • Contraindications: Children <2 years
  • Brimonidine: Safest during pregnancy (Category B)

4. Miotics (Option B)

  • Examples: Pilocarpine, Physostigmine, Echothiophate
  • Mechanism: Stimulates M3 receptors, increasing trabecular outflow
  • Side Effects: Brow pain, miosis, cataract (Echothiophate), retinal tears

5. Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors

  • Examples: Acetazolamide (systemic), Brinzolamide, Dorzolamide (topical)
  • Mechanism: Inhibits aqueous secretion from ciliary epithelium
  • Uses: Acute congestive glaucoma (with IV mannitol)
  • Side Effects: Ciliary edema, secondary angle-closure glaucoma (Topiramate, Zonisamide)

6. Osmotic Agents

  • Examples: Mannitol, Glycerol

  • These work by increasing blood osmolarity, "sucking" water out of the vitreous to lower IOP quickly.

  • Intravenous Mannitol: For acute attacks.

    • Side effect: Pulmonary edema, congestive heart failure.

  • Oral Glycerol: Sweeter, but contraindicated in Diabetics (metabolized to glucose).

6. Newer Drugs

  • Netarsudil (Rho kinase inhibitor): Increases trabecular outflow; Side effect - vortex keratopathy
  • Omidenepag (PGE2 agonist): Increases both trabecular and uveoscleral outflow


Reference:

Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology, 10th edition, Pages 404 - 407

Decreases aqueous humor secretion; Allergic blepharoconjunctivitis

question: All of the following are penetrating glaucoma surgeries except:

correctAnswer: B. Selective laser trabeculoplasty for open-angle glaucoma and laser iridotomy for angle closure glaucoma
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Selective Laser Trabeculoplasty (SLT)

  • It is commonly used for open-angle glaucoma.
  • SLT improves aqueous humor outflow by targeting the trabecular meshwork, which helps lower intraocular pressure over time.

[[figure-1]]

Laser Iridotomy

  • It is used for angle closure glaucoma.
  • This procedure creates a small hole in the peripheral iris to allow better fluid drainage and relieve the blockage of the anterior chamber angle.

[[figure-2]]

Argon laser iridotomy (Option A) is used for angle closure glaucoma, not open-angle glaucoma.

  • Also, SLT is not typically used for angle closure glaucoma.

Laser iridoplasty (Option C) is used for some cases of angle closure glaucoma, particularly when the angle is very narrow or if iridotomy is not feasible.

  • However, argon laser iridotomy is the more common procedure for angle closure glaucoma.

Laser iridotomy (Option D) is not used for open-angle glaucoma; it is used for angle-closure glaucoma.

  • Similarly, laser iridoplasty is a treatment for angle closure glaucoma, not open-angle glaucoma.



Reference:
  1. Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology, 10th edition, Pages 412-416
  2. Parsons’ Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, PDF Pages 725, 726

question: Which of the following laser procedures are used for Open angle glaucoma (OAG) and angle closure glaucoma (ACG) respectively?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Medical management of Glaucoma
Topical drugs
  • Beta-blockers: Decrease the formation of aqueous humour.
    • Eg: Timolol, betaxolol
  • Alpha agonists: Have dual action i.e. they decrease the formation of aqueous and increase the trabecular outflow.
    • Eg: Adrenaline/epinephrine, dipivefrin, brimonidine, and apraclonidine
  • Miotics: These increase the trabecular outflow and open the angle blockage.
    • Eg: Pilocarpine (Option B ruled out)
  • Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors: These decrease the formation of aqueous.
    • Eg: Dorzolamide and Brinzolamide
  • Newer anti-glaucoma drugs:
    • Netarsudil: Increases the trabecular outflow and also decreases the aqueous production.
    • PGF2 alpha agonist: It increases the uveoscleral outflow
      • For eg- Latanoprost, bimatoprost, travoprost (Option A ruled out), tafluprost, and unoprostone isopropyl (Option D ruled out)
Systemic drugs
  • Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor
    • Eg: Acetazolamide
  • Hyperosmotic agents: These draw aqueous out of the eye



Reference:
  1. Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology, 10th edition, Pages 369, 370, 374, 380
  2. Parsons’ Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, PDF Pages 724, 725
question: A 65-year-old male presents to the ophthalmology clinic for a routine eye examination. During the examination, his intraocular pressure (IOP) is measured at 28 mmHg in both eyes. The ophthalmologist diagnoses him with primary open-angle glaucoma. Which of the following medications is primarily designed to lower intraocular pressure by reducing the production of aqueous humor?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Cogan-Reese Syndrome is known for its distinctive iris lesions.
  • It is characterized by the presence of pigmented nodular lesions on the iris, which can be diffuse or localized.
  • These pigmented lesions are a key feature that helps distinguish it from other ICE syndromes.

Glaucomas Associated with Iridocorneal Endothelial (ICE) Syndromes:

  • ICE Syndromes Include:
    • Progressive iris atrophy
    • Chandler's syndrome
    • Cogan-Reese syndrome
  • Pathogenesis:
    • Abnormal corneal endothelial cells proliferate to form a membrane at the angle of the anterior chamber.
    • Glaucoma is caused by secondary synechial angle closure due to contraction of this endothelial membrane.
  • Clinical Features:
    • Typically affects middle-aged women.
    • Raised intraocular pressure (IOP) associated with specific features of the causative condition:
      • Progressive iris atrophy: Iris shows corectopia, atrophy, and hole formation. (Options A & D ruled out)
      • Chandler's syndrome: Mild or no iris changes, corneal edema predominates, even at normal IOP. (Option B ruled out)
      • Cogan-Reese syndrome: Iris has pigmented nodular or diffuse lesions (also called iris nevus syndrome), and may have corneal changes. (Option C)
  • Treatment:
    • Glaucoma drainage device (artificial filtration shunt) may help control IOP.
    • Medical treatment is often ineffective.
    • Trabeculectomy surgery usually fails.



Reference:

Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology, 10th edition, Pages 397, 398
question: Which ICE syndrome is characterized by the presence of pigmented nodular lesions on the iris?

correctAnswer: B. Angle recession glaucoma typically presents with elevated IOP shortly after the trauma.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Angle recession glaucoma often develops months to years after the initial blunt trauma due to long-term fibrosis of the trabecular meshwork.
  • It is not typically associated with immediate elevated IOP.

Traumatic Glaucoma:

  • A secondary glaucoma may complicate perforating as well as blunt injuries. (Option A ruled out)
  • Causes:
    • Inflammatory Glaucoma: Results from iridocyclitis.
    • Intraocular Hemorrhage: Hyphaema inside the eye leading to glaucoma.
      • Hyphema frequently causes acute intraocular pressure elevation by blocking the trabecular meshwork (TM).
      • Ghost Cell Glaucoma: RBCs lose their iron and Hb → becomes ghost cells
        • Occurs due to haemorrhage in vitreous
    • Lens-Induced Glaucoma: Due to a ruptured, swollen, or dislocated lens. (Option C ruled out)
    • Angle-Closure: Caused by peripheral anterior synechiae formation after corneal injury. (Option D ruled out)
    • Angle Recession Glaucoma: Due to angle recession (The recession is due to a tear in the ciliary body) from blunt trauma after years (10yrs), leading to fibrosis of the trabecular meshwork over time. (Option B)

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

  • Management:
    • Medical Therapy: Includes topical 0.5% timolol and oral acetazolamide.
    • Treatment of Underlying Causes: For instance, using atropine and steroids to control inflammation.
    • Surgical Intervention: Based on the specific cause and situation.



Reference:

Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology, 10th edition, Pages 395, 396, 397

question: Which of the following statements is false about traumatic glaucoma?

  • Glaucomatocyclitic Crisis (Posner-Schlossman Syndrome) is characterized by very high IOP (often between 40 and 50 mm Hg), minimal inflammation, a few small keratic precipitates, no posterior synechiae, and recurrent episodes that resolve within days to weeks.
  • It is commonly seen in young males.
  • This can be due to
    • HLA-BW54 association has been documented.
    • CMV or H. Pylori infection.

[[figure-1]]

Secondary Angle-closure glaucoma with a pupillary block (Option A): Caused by pupillary block due to annular synechiae, leading to iris bombe and subsequent angle closure.

Secondary Angle-closure glaucoma without a pupillary block (Option B) : Results from inflammatory debris organizing in the angle, which pulls the iris over the trabecular meshwork, causing progressive angle closure and elevated IOP.

question: A 30-year-old male presents with unilateral eye discomfort, blurred vision, and seeing halos around lights. On examination, his intraocular pressure (IOP) is measured at 48 mm Hg. The anterior segment shows a few small, flat, nonpigmented keratic precipitates located inferiorly, mild redness, and an aqueous flare. The pupil is dilated, but there are no signs of a posterior synechiae. The patient reports recurrent episodes that resolve within days to weeks. Given these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. Atropine drops and oral acetazolamide
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical scenario describes a 70-year-old patient who, following trabeculectomy , experiences severe eye pain and blurred vision, elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), a shallow anterior chamber, a negative Seidel's test, which are characteristic of ciliary block glaucoma (malignant glaucoma), also known as Aqueous Misdirection Syndrome.
  • This condition occurs due to a mechanical blockage of aqueous humor flow, often after intraocular surgery.

[[figure-1]]

Pathogenesis:

  • Aqueous Misdirection: The aqueous humor is diverted posteriorly into or behind the vitreous body rather than flowing into the anterior chamber, as the ciliary processes, lens, and anterior vitreous face form a 'ciliary block' that traps the fluid in the posterior segment.

  • Pressure Build-up: As aqueous accumulates in the vitreous cavity, the volume of the posterior segment increases.

  • Forward Displacement: This increased posterior pressure pushes the lens-iris diaphragm forward.

  • Angle Closure: The forward displacement causes the anterior chamber to become uniformly shallow (both centrally and peripherally), leading to a secondary angle closure and a massive spike in IOP.

Management:

  • Medical Therapy (Initial):
    • Atropine Drops/Ointment (1%): To dilate the ciliary ring and relieve ciliary block.
    • Acetazolamide (250 mg QID): To reduce aqueous humor production.
    • Timolol Maleate (0.5%): To decrease aqueous production.
    • Intravenous Mannitol: To reduce vitreous gel volume and decrease IOP.
  • Laser Therapy: YAG laser hyaloidotomy for aphakic and pseudophakic patients.
  • Surgical Therapy: Pars plana vitrectomy with or without lensectomy if medical therapy fails within 4-5 days. (Option B ruled out)



Reference:
  1. Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology, 10th edition, Pages 381, 382, 415, 419, 420, 421
  2. Parsons’ Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, PDF Page 717
question: A 70-year-old patient with a history of glaucoma undergoes a trabeculectomy to control intraocular pressure. Postoperatively, the patient presents with severe eye pain, blurred vision, a significantly elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), and a shallow anterior chamber. Seidel's test is negative. What is the most appropriate initial treatment for this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Based on these findings, the diagnosis of neovascular glaucoma is supported by the presence of iris neovascularization and elevated IOP in the context of proliferative diabetic retinopathy.
  • Panretinal photocoagulation is the most appropriate treatment as it targets the underlying cause of neovascular glaucoma.
  • This treats the retinal ischemia, reducing the stimulus for abnormal blood vessel growth and neovascularization.

Neovascular Glaucoma (NVG)

[[figure-1]]

Treatment:

  • Panretinal Photocoagulation or Cryotherapy: Aimed at preventing further neovascularization.
  • Anti-VEGF Agents: Used as an adjunctive treatment. Help reduce neovascularization. (Option D)
  • Trabeculectomy: A surgical procedure to lower intraocular pressure, often combined with antifibroblastic agents.
  • Glaucoma Drainage Device: Artificial filtration shunt (Seton operation) can help manage IOP.
  • Causes:
    • Common:
      • Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (M/C)
      • Central retinal vein occlusion
      • Sickle-cell retinopathy
      • Eales' disease
    • Rare:
      • Chronic intraocular inflammation
      • Intraocular tumors
      • Long-standing retinal detachment
      • Central retinal artery occlusion

Topical beta-blockers and oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (Option A):

  • These medications can help manage intraocular pressure (IOP) but do not address the underlying cause of neovascular glaucoma, which is the retinal ischemia and resulting neovascularization.

Systemic corticosteroids (Option C):

  • While corticosteroids can reduce inflammation, they do not address neovascularization or the elevated IOP associated with neovascular glaucoma.


Reference:
  1. Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology, 10th Edition, Pages 387, 388, 389
  2. Parsons’ Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page 710

question: A 55-year-old Asian woman presents with acute eye pain and blurred vision. Her ophthalmologist suspects primary angle closure glaucoma (PACG). Which of the following statements about the etiopathogenesis of PACG is incorrect?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Zonular instability is a hallmark of pseudoexfoliation syndrome.
  • This can lead to phacodonesis (lens wobbling).
  • Ocular manifestation of Pseudoexfoliation Syndrome (XFS) is characterized by the accumulation of fibrillar, proteinaceous material on various ocular structures, including the lens, iris, and trabecular meshwork.
  • This material can be seen as flaky white deposits on the anterior lens capsule and pupillary margin, often with a distinct clear zone at the center of the lens.
  • It causes secondary open-angle glaucoma, known as pseudoexfoliative glaucoma.

Pathogenesis of Pseudoexfoliation Syndrome:

  • Caused by abnormal extracellular matrix metabolism leading to production of pseudoexfoliative fibrillar material.

  • Strongly associated with polymorphism of the LOXL1 gene, which is involved in elastin fiber formation.

  • Oxidative stress and impaired degradation lead to accumulation of this material.

  • Deposits occur on the lens capsule, iris, zonules, and trabecular meshwork, which may cause secondary open-angle glaucoma (Pseudoexfoliation Glaucoma).

Posterior synechiae (Option A) is incorrect because while inflammation can lead to synechiae, it is not a primary feature of pseudoexfoliation syndrome.


Corneal guttata (Option C) and Iris heterochromia (Option D) are associated with Fuchs' endothelial dystrophy, not pseudoexfoliation syndrome.


Iris heterochromia (Option D) is typically seen in Fuchs' heterochromic iridocyclitis, not pseudoexfoliation syndrome.



Reference:
  1. Yanoff and Duker's Ophthalmology, 5th Edition, Page 1074-1077
  2. Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology, 10th Edition, Page 382, 383, 384
question: A 72-year-old male presents with diminution of vision in the right eye. On slit-lamp examination, dandruff-like material is noted on the anterior lens capsule and iris. Intraocular pressure is elevated, and the patient is diagnosed with pseudoexfoliative glaucoma. Which of the following is most likely to be observed in this patient’s eye?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • This patient's presentation is consistent with pigmentary glaucoma.
  • The key features are:
    • Young, myopic male
    • Elevated IOP
    • Krukenberg spindle (vertical line of pigment on corneal endothelium)
    • Heavily pigmented trabecular meshwork
    • Iris transillumination defects
    • Symptoms exacerbated by exercise (due to pupillary movement causing increased pigment release)
  • Treatment is along the lines of POAG management, which initially includes medical treatment, with prostaglandin analogues often being the first choice due to their IOP-lowering efficacy and convenient dosing schedule. (Option C)

Nd:YAG laser peripheral iridotomy (Option A) is generally reserved for cases with pronounced iris concavity or those not responding to medical therapy.


Selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT) (Option B) is typically considered after initial medical therapy or in combination with it.


Argon laser peripheral iridoplasty (Option D) is primarily used in angle-closure glaucoma to open the angle.



Reference:
  1. Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology, 10th edition, Pages 385, 386, 387
  2. pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1495789/
question: A 25-year-old myopic male presents with intermittent blurring of vision and mild ocular pain after exercise. On examination, IOP is 28 mmHg, Slit lamp examination reveals Krukenberg spindle on corneal endothelium, trabecular pigmentation on gonioscopy. Which of the following is the first-line treatment?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Fine pigmented deposits in a vertical spindle pattern on corneal endothelium (Krukenberg spindle), mid-peripheral iris transillumination defects (symmetric), moderately raised IOP point strongly to pigment dispersion syndrome (PDS).

  • Pigment dispersion syndrome occurs when pigment granules from the iris epithelium are released into the anterior chamber and deposit on various structures, including the corneal endothelium and trabecular meshwork.
  • This can lead to trabecular outflow obstruction and subsequent glaucoma.
  • Symmetric Iris transillumination defects in the mid-peripheral iris, is characteristic of Pigment Dispersion Syndrome (PDS).

Pseudoexfoliation syndrome (Option A) presents with whitish, dandruff-like material on the lens capsule and pupillary margin.

Neovascular glaucoma (Option C) is characterized by new blood vessel growth over the iris and anterior chamber angle, often secondary to ischemic retinal diseases.


Lens-particle glaucoma (Option D) occurs when lens material enters the anterior chamber, usually after cataract surgery or lens injury.

Pigmentary Dispersion vs Pseudoexfoliation Syndrome:

Feature Pigmentary Dispersion (PDS) Pseudoexfoliation (PEX)
Typical Patient Young, myopic (nearsighted) males. Elderly patients (>60 years).
Iris Finding Mid-peripheral transillumination defects (spoke-like). Pupillary margin atrophy/transillumination.
Lens Finding No abnormal material; pigment on the back of the lens. Three-zone dandruff-like material on the anterior capsule.
Cornea Krukenberg spindle (vertical pigment line on endothelium). Diffuse pigment or PEX material on endothelium.
Zonules Normal. Weak/Fragile (risk of lens subluxation).
Gonioscopy Dense, homogenous pigment (360°). Patchy pigment + Sampaolesi Line.


Reference:

Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology, 10th Edition, Page 382, 385, 387
question: A 45-year-old male presents with unilateral eye pain, redness, and moderately elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) of 28 mmHg. On slit-lamp examination, you observe fine, pigmented deposits on the corneal endothelium in a vertical spindle pattern. The patient O/E has symmetric transillumination defects in the mid-peripheral iris. Based on these findings, which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's secondary glaucoma?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Absolute glaucoma is the final phase of Primary Angle Closure Glaucoma.

Management of absolute glaucoma

  • In absolute glaucoma, the goal of treatment is to relieve pain and reduce IOP, as vision cannot be restored.
  • Retrobulbar alcohol injection - given to relieve pain.
    • It suppresses the ciliary ganglion.
  • A cyclodestructive procedure, such as cyclocryotherapy or cyclophotocoagulation, is the most appropriate management option in this scenario as it reduces aqueous production by damaging the secretory ciliary processes aiming to reduce IOP. (Option C)
  • If pain persists despite cyclodestruction, enucleation/evisceration may be considered. (Option D)

Topical timolol and brimonidine (Option A): These medications lower intraocular pressure and are useful in eyes with visual potential. They are insufficient as definitive treatment in a painful blind eye with absolute glaucoma.

Trabeculectomy (Option B): Trabeculectomy is performed to preserve remaining vision by lowering intraocular pressure. It is not indicated in an eye with no light perception and end-stage optic nerve damage.

Evisceration (Option D): Evisceration is reserved for persistent painful blind eyes when conservative measures, including cyclodestructive procedures, fail or when the eye is unsalvageable. It is not the initial management.



Reference:
  1. pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3669490/
  2. Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology, 10th edition, Pages 379, 380, 381.

question: All of the following components of Vogt's triad are typically observed in a patient who has experienced and resolved an acute primary angle-closure glaucoma (APAC) attack except?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Primary Angle Closure Suspect (PACS) is characterized by an occludable anterior chamber angle as seen during gonioscopy but without evidence of increased IOP or glaucomatous damage.
  • This indicates a risk for potential future angle closure but does not yet present as acute angle-closure glaucoma.

PACS: Primary Angle Closure Suspect

  • Iridotrabecular contact or occludable angle of more than 3 quadrants on gonioscopy
  • No peripheral anterior synechiae
  • Intraocular pressure is normal
  • Eclipse sign of PACS - convex iris lens diaphragm
  • Treatment: Prophylactic Peripheral iridotomy (Option B) is done in both eyes with lens extraction using NdYAG laser

correctAnswer: B. It is a technique for visualizing the anterior chamber angle of the eye using a special lens
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Gonioscopy is the main method used to measure the angle of the anterior chamber

correctAnswer: B. It is more commonly seen in older patients with primary angle closure glaucoma
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Plateau iris configuration is actually more common in younger patients with primary angle closure glaucoma, not older patients.

Anatomy
  • Plateau iris is characterized by an anteriorly positioned ciliary body, which pushes the peripheral iris forward. (Option A)

  • Ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM) is particularly useful in diagnosing plateau iris configuration. (Option D)

Management
  • Due to its persistence after iridotomy, patients with plateau iris may require additional treatments such as: (Option C)
    • Argon laser peripheral iridoplasty
    • Long-term use of miotic drops

[[figure-1]]

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Goldmann perimetry is a type of manual kinetic perimetry.
  • In this technique, a stimulus of constant size and intensity is moved from a non-seeing area (usually the far periphery) towards the center of vision until the patient detects it.
  • This method allows for a detailed mapping of the visual field boundary.

[[figure-1]]

Various methods of kinetic perimetry:

Automated perimetry (Option B):

  • Static perimetry where stationary stimuli of varying intensities are presented at fixed locations in the visual field.
  • It doesn't involve moving stimuli.

Frequency doubling perimetry (Option C):

  • Static perimetry that uses a specific stimulus (a sinusoidal grating) to test contrast sensitivity and is particularly useful for detecting early glaucomatous damage.

SWAP (Option D):

  • Static perimetry technique that uses a blue light stimulus on a yellow background to selectively test the function of blue-yellow ganglion cells, which may be affected early in glaucoma.

question: A 62-year-old man with a history of Glaucoma undergoes visual field testing to assess his peripheral vision. The test involves moving a stimulus of constant size and intensity from a non-seeing area into a seeing area to determine the boundaries of his visual field. Which type of perimetry is being described?

correctAnswer: D. The visual field extends maximally in the superior direction
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Visual field is the peripheral vision.
  • It extends maximally in the temporal direction and minimally in the superior direction.

The extent of the visual field: (mnemonic: TINS)

  • Temporally: 90° to 100°
  • Inferiorly: 70°
  • Nasally: 60°
  • Superiorly: 50°


Scotoma (Option A):

  • Area of decreased vision surrounded by normal vision.

Isopter (Option B):

  • Line connecting points of equal light sensitivity and size detection in the visual field.

Physiological blind spot (Option C):

  • Corresponds to the area where the optic nerve exits the eye, which lacks photoreceptors.
  • It is a type of absolute scotoma.

question: A 58-year-old patient is being evaluated for suspected primary open-angle glaucoma. The ophthalmologist wants to perform a thorough examination of the optic nerve head to detect glaucomatous changes. Which of the following techniques is considered the examination of choice for evaluating fundus changes in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Key findings:

  • IOP = 24 mmHg → mildly elevated
  • Cup–disc ratio = 0.5 → borderline/moderate
  • Splinter (Drance) hemorrhages → early sign of glaucoma
  • Wedge-shaped RNFL defects → early structural damage

These are characteristic of early glaucomatous optic nerve damage, before marked cupping or severe vision loss occurs.

  • Early glaucomatous changes are indicated by signs such as:
    • Cup-to-disc ratio of >0.3.
    • Asymmetry of the cups: A cup-to-disc ratio difference greater than 0.2 between two eyes.
    • Splinter hemorrhages near the optic disc margin.
    • Retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) defects: Wedge-shaped dark areas seen on the red-free light examination - an early indicator of glaucomatous damage.
  • Advanced glaucomatous changes
    • Cup-to-disc ratio of 0.7–0.9
    • Significant neuroretinal rim thinning
    • Vessel bayonetting
  • Glaucomatous optic atrophy
    • Complete destruction of the neural tissue
    • Deeply excavated and white optic disc.
    • Cavernous optic atrophy - large caverns or lacunae are formed due to:
      • Raised IOP leading to modulation of lamina cribrosa.
      • Ischaemic atrophy of the nerve fibers without a corresponding increase of supporting glial tissue.

Normal eye (no glaucoma)

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Early glaucoma

[[figure-3]]

[[figure-4]]

Moderate glaucoma

[[figure-5]]

[[figure-6]]

Advanced glaucoma

[[figure-7]]

[[figure-8]]

question:
A 62-year-old woman with a family history of glaucoma presents with mild visual disturbances. Her intraocular pressure is measured to be 24 mmHg in both eyes. On dilated fundus examination, the following findings are noted:

  • The cup-to-disc ratio of 0.5
  • Splinter hemorrhages at the optic disc margin
  • Wedge-shaped retinal nerve fiber layer defects on red-free light examination

What stage of glaucomatous optic disc changes is most likely present in this patient?

correctAnswer: B. Presence of alpha zone peripapillary atrophy (PPA)
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Peripapillary atrophy (PPA) in the region around the optic nerve head - is indicative of early damage in glaucoma. It has 2 zones:

  • Alpha zone (outer):
    • Characterized by irregularities in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE).
    • Larger in size and more commonly observed in glaucomatous eyes.
  • Beta zone (inner):
    • Chorioretinal atrophy.
    • A visible white band of exposed sclera adjacent and distinct to the scleral rim.
    • Larger and more frequently seen in glaucoma.
    • Considered a risk factor for glaucoma progression.
    • The location of the beta zone often correlates with patterns of visual field loss in glaucoma patients.

[[figure-1]]

Increased retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) density in the peripapillary area (Option A):

  • The peripapillary area often shows signs of degeneration, not hyperpigmentation.

Thickening of peripapillary RNFL on optical coherence tomography (OCT) (Option C):

  • In glaucoma, the RNFL undergoes thinning, especially in the superior and inferior regions, not thickening, due to the loss of retinal ganglion cells.

Uniform retinal nerve fiber layer thickness without focal loss (Option D):

  • Glaucoma is characterized by focal thinning of the RNFL, particularly around the optic nerve head.
  • Uniform thickness is more typical in healthy eyes, whereas focal thinning is a sign of glaucomatous damage.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology: A Systematic Approach, 9th Edition, Page 354, 355.

question: A 52-year-old male presents with progressive vision loss. Fundoscopic examination reveals a vertical elongation of the optic disc and diffuse thinning of the retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL). Imaging confirms significant damage to the peripapillary region. Which of the following best describes the characteristic peripapillary change seen in glaucomatous optic neuropathy?

correctAnswer: B. Nasal displacement of retinal vessels
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In advanced glaucoma, there is progressive optic disc cupping.
  • A characteristic feature of this process is the nasal displacement of retinal vessels, as the optic nerve head undergoes excavation.
  • This displacement is caused by the pulling of the retinal vessels toward the nasal side as the cupping advances, changing the shape of lamina cribrosa.

[[figure-1]]

Inferior displacement of retinal vessels (Option A):

  • This is not characteristic of glaucomatous optic neuropathy; vessels typically shift nasally.

Arterial attenuation with increased vein diameter (Option C):

  • While arterial narrowing can be seen in certain conditions, this pattern is more typical of hypertensive retinopathy.

Radial peripapillary capillary obliteration (Option D):

  • This finding is more associated with ischemic optic neuropathy, not typical in glaucoma.



Reference:
  1. Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology: A Systematic Approach, 9th Edition, Page 352, 353
  2. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-021-83720-0/figures/5
