question: A 58-year-old woman with a long history of untreated open-angle glaucoma presents with gradual peripheral vision loss. Fundoscopic examination reveals advanced optic disc cupping. Which of the following vascular changes is most characteristic of progressive glaucomatous optic neuropathy?

correctAnswer: A. The optic disc appearance follows the ISNT rule, indicating a healthy optic nerve.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • All of the findings are consistent with early glaucomatous changes except that the disc shows superior and inferior neuroretinal rim thinning violating the ISNT rule.
  • The ISNT rule (Option A) states that, in a healthy optic nerve, the neuroretinal rim thickness typically follows a pattern, being the broadest in: Inferior > Superior > Nasal > Temporal.

The patient's optic disc shows several characteristic features of glaucomatous optic neuropathy:

1. Increased cup-to-disc ratio (0.7): A ratio greater than 0.6 is suspicious for glaucoma.

2. Superior and inferior neuroretinal rim thinning: This violates the ISNT rule.

3. Peripapillary atrophy present

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

[[figure-3]]

The cup-to-disc ratio indicates early glaucomatous damage (Option B) is correct.

  • A cup-to-disc ratio of 0.7 is considered enlarged and suspicious for glaucoma.
  • Normal cup-to-disc ratio is ≤0.3.

The absence of optic disc hemorrhages does not rule out glaucoma (Option C) is correct.

  • Their presence is a risk factor for the development and progression of glaucoma.
  • They are more common in NTG, but can also occur in healthy individuals as well as patients with systemic vascular disease.

Peripapillary atrophy is commonly associated with glaucoma and warrants further monitoring (Option D) is correct.

  • Peripapillary atrophy surrounding the optic nerve head may be of significance in glaucoma and may be a sign of early damage in patients with ocular hypertension.

ASPECT

Ocular Hypertension

Characteristic Features
  • IOP consistently above 21 mm Hg (No Damage)

question: A 58-year-old man presents for a routine eye examination. His intraocular pressure (IOP) is consistently measured at 23 mm Hg on multiple occasions. He reports no visual symptoms, and his fundus examination shows no abnormalities. Visual field testing reveals no defects. Based on these findings, which of the following diagnoses is most appropriate?

correctAnswer: B. In early POAG, IOP is consistently above 21 mm Hg.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The diagnosis of Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma (POAG) in this case is supported by significant diurnal fluctuations in intraocular pressure (IOP), characteristic optic disc cupping, and specific visual field defects.
  • In the initial stages of POAG, IOP may not be consistently elevated and often shows exaggerated diurnal variation.

Intraocular Pressure (IOP) Changes in POAG

  • Initial Stage: IOP may not be consistently high; diurnal variation (fluctuation throughout the day) is exaggerated. Repeated measurements (every 3-4 hours) are needed to detect this. (Option B)
  • Diurnal Variation Patterns:
    • Morning rise in IOP: 20% of cases
    • Afternoon rise in IOP: 25% of cases
    • Biphasic rise in IOP (morning and afternoon): 55% of cases (Option A)
  • Suspicious Variation: A variation in IOP of over 5 mm Hg is suspicious, and over 8 mm Hg is diagnostic of glaucoma.
  • Later Stages: IOP becomes consistently elevated above 21 mm Hg, typically ranging from 30 to 45 mm Hg.

  • Seasonal Variations: Higher IOP is observed in winter months. (Option C)
  • Exercise: Strenuous exercise lowers IOP temporarily. (Option D)

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • A diastolic perfusion pressure of more than 55 mm Hg is generally not considered to be a risk factor for POAG.
  • Lower diastolic perfusion pressure (<55 mm Hg) is a significant risk factor for glaucoma.

Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma (POAG):

Characteristics:

  • Intraocular Pressure: Elevated (>21 mm Hg) on multiple occasions.
  • Anterior Chamber Angle: Open and normal in appearance.
  • Optic Disc: Characteristic cupping.
  • Visual Field: Specific defects present.

Risk Factors of Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma (POAG):

  • Elevated IOP: Asymmetry of IOP of ≥4 mmHg is considered significant. (Option A)
  • Family History: Higher risk in siblings (10%) and offspring (4%). Involves polygenic inheritance with genes like MYOC, OPTN, and WDR36. (Option C)
  • Age: Increased risk with age, especially between the 5th and 7th decades of life.
  • Race: Higher prevalence and severity in Black individuals compared to Whites.
  • Myopia: Increased risk in myopic individuals. (Option D)
  • Thinner Central Corneal Thickness (CCT) (<555 µm) is an independent risk factor.
  • Cigarette Smoking: Increased risk
  • Blood Pressure: Higher prevalence in hypertensives; diastolic perfusion pressure <55 mm Hg is a significant risk factor. (Option B)
  • Thyrotoxicosis: Increased in Graves' ophthalmic disease.
  • Corticosteroid Responsiveness: Greater risk of IOP rise with topical steroid therapy.

This scenario describes total internal reflection, which occurs when light travels from a denser medium (cornea, n ≈ 1.376) to a rarer medium (air, n ≈ 1.0). The critical angle is the angle of incidence at which total internal reflection occurs, and for the cornea–air interface, it is 46 degrees.

Optical principles: Angle of the AC cannot be visualized directly through the intact cornea because light from angle structures undergoes ‘total internal reflection’ at the anterior surface of the precorneal tear. When light travels from a medium of higher to one of lower refractive index (such as cornea to air), it will be reflected at the interface between the two unless the angle of incidence is less than a certain ‘critical angle’ dependent on their refractive index difference (46° for the tear film-air interface).

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The child presents with key signs of congenital glaucoma, photophobia, watering, and a large, clear cornea. The presence of Haab’s striae strongly suggests elevated intraocular pressure in infancy. These are classic findings in buphthalmos, the infantile form of glaucoma.

Haab’s Striae: Curvilinear horizontal breaks in Descemet’s membrane due to stretching of the cornea.

  • Cause: Rapid increase in IOP causing rupture of Descemet's membrane.
  • Appearance: Double parallel lines due to endothelial healing and new basement membrane deposition.
  • Common in infants, buphthalmos may lead to severe corneal edema and, rarely, acute hydrops.

[[figure-1]]

Keratoconus (Option A) manifests in adolescence, not neonates, and presents with conical corneal protrusion.

Keratoglobus (Option B) causes diffuse corneal thinning and a globular shape but is not associated with Haab's striae or neonatal onset.


Trachoma (Option C) is a chronic conjunctival infection with scarring; not seen in neonates.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 10th Edition, Page 401-402.
question: An infant is brought for evaluation due to excessive tearing and intolerance to light. Examination shows that the tear ducts are patent, and the cornea is clear but abnormally enlarged. On further assessment, Haab’s striae are noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
This patient demonstrates classic features of Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma (POAG), which is the most common form of adult glaucoma and typically asymptomatic until advanced stages. Her repeated visits for presbyopic spectacle changes, headaches, field defects, and optic nerve changes all point toward POAG.

Signs and Symptoms of POAG:

  • Asymptomatic early course: Most patients are unaware until significant field loss occurs.
  • Headaches and nonspecific discomfort may occur.
  • Frequent changes in presbyopic correction due to gradual optic nerve damage.
  • Difficulty adapting in the dark due to peripheral vision loss.
  • Scotomas, especially in the inferior visual field, appear as the disease progresses.
  • Optic nerve head findings:
    • Cup-disc ratio >0.5 or asymmetry >0.2 between eyes.
    • Thinning or notching of the neuroretinal rim.
    • Disc hemorrhages or vessel changes indicating acquired cupping.
  • Raised intraocular pressure (IOP >21 mmHg) on multiple occasions.
  • Visual field defects: Arcuate scotomas, nasal steps, or paracentral defects.
  • Retinal nerve fiber layer loss, best visualized with red-free light or OCT.
  • Normal anterior chamber angle seen on gonioscopy (key distinguishing feature).

Intumescent cataract (Option A) presents with acute angle closure symptoms, not gradual visual changes or field defects.

Retinal detachment (Option B) presents with sudden vision loss, floaters, or photopsia, not progressive field loss or presbyopic complaints.


Senile cataract (Option D) causes gradual blurring but not scotomas or cup-disc changes, and rarely causes frequent spectacle changes in such a short time.



Reference:

Parson’s Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page 695-697.
question: A 62-year-old woman has visited the clinic three times in the last two months to change her presbyopic glasses. She also complains of difficulty adapting to dim lighting and a subtle blind spot in her lower field of vision. On fundus exam, an increased cup-to-disc ratio is noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
This patient exhibits classical signs of Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG), particularly in the context of diabetes and advancing age. The laminar dot sign indicates deep cupping of the optic disc due to glaucomatous optic nerve damage. Difficulty driving at night reflects early visual field loss, often unnoticed until daily activities are affected. Headache and vague eye pain can also be early features.

[[figure-1]]

Changes in Glaucoma

Optic Nerve Head (ONH) Changes

Peripapillary Changes
  • Pathological cupping: Progressive, irreversible axonal loss → deep cupping (even in small discs)
  • Neuroretinal rim thinning: Focal or diffuse rim loss
  • Laminar dot sign: Visible lamina cribrosa pores in advanced glaucoma
  • Sharpened disc margin: Steep rim due to tissue loss
  • Bayoneting of vessels: Sharp angulation of vessels at disc edge.

[[figure-2]]

  • Other findings: Disc Hemorrhages, Collateral Vessels.
  • Alpha Zone: Irregular pigmentation due to RPE disturbance.
  • Beta Zone: Chorioretinal atrophy adjacent to disc; strongly linked to glaucoma severity.

[[figure-3]]

Retinal Nerve Fiber Layer Changes: Disc cupping and visual field defects

Uveitis (Option A) presents with photophobia, redness, and often decreased vision. No cupping or laminar dot sign is associated.

ARMD (Option B) causes central visual loss in the elderly but does not produce headache, pain, or laminar dot sign.


Retinal detachment (Option C): Sudden painless loss of vision with flashes or floaters, not chronic progression with cupping.



Reference:

Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology, 10th Edition, Pages 352-356
question: A 63-year-old diabetic male complains of a recent onset of headache and dull ocular pain. He also reports increasing difficulty with night driving and noticing shadowy areas in his vision. On fundus examination, a laminar dot sign is observed at the optic disc. Which of the following is the most probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
This patient developed bronchospasm likely due to Timolol, a non-selective beta-blocker used in glaucoma management.

Non-selective beta-blockers block both β1 and β2 receptors, and β2 blockade in bronchial smooth muscle can exacerbate asthma and precipitate bronchospasm, even when given topically as eye drops.

Betaxolol (Option A) is a cardioselective beta-1 blocker with lesser pulmonary side effects; comparatively safer in asthmatics.

Latanoprost (Option C) is a prostaglandin analogue, primarily associated with iris pigmentation changes, not respiratory symptoms.

Aspirin (Option D): Though asthma exacerbation can occur with aspirin (Aspirin-sensitive asthma), the patient is stable on aspirin long-term for her MI, making it less likely to be the new trigger.



Reference:

Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology, 10th Edition, Page 410.
question: A 60-year-old hypertensive female with a history of myocardial infarction presents with the recent onset of shortness of breath. She has a known case of asthma for which she uses inhalational bronchodilators; her last asthma episode was 7 months ago. She was recently started on topical therapy for elevated intraocular pressure. Which of the following drugs is the most likely cause of her respiratory symptoms?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
This patient’s complaints of drowsiness and fatigue are most commonly associated with Brimonidine, an α2-adrenergic agonist.

Brimonidine crosses the blood-brain barrier and can lead to central nervous system depression, especially in susceptible individuals. It is particularly contraindicated in young children for this reason.

Timolol (Option A): Although it may cause bradycardia and fatigue, CNS depression, like drowsiness, is less prominent than with Brimonidine.

Dorzolamide (Option C) is a topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that does not typically cause CNS side effects.

Latanoprost (Option D) is a prostaglandin analogue, mainly associated with local effects like iris pigmentation, not drowsiness.



Reference:

Yanoff and Duker Ophthalmology, 6th Edition, Page 1028.
question: A 47-year-old software engineer on antiglaucoma therapy presents to the clinic complaining of excessive daytime sleepiness, fatigue, and reduced productivity at work. He is otherwise healthy and has no history of sleep disorders. Which of the following medications is most likely responsible for his symptoms?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
Mannitol is preferred for IOP control in sickle cell patients because it provides effective ocular hypotension without inducing systemic acidosis, thereby avoiding the risk of vaso-occlusive events like optic nerve infarction or anterior segment ischemia.

Oral acetazolamide (Option A) is contraindicated in sickle cell disease due to the risk of acidosis and triggering a sickling crisis.

Ciprofloxacin eye drops (Option B) are used in infectious conditions, not indicated in this acute angle-closure setting.

Atropine ointment (Option C) is a mydriatic and cycloplegic, but not the first-line treatment in acute angle-closure glaucoma.



Reference:

Parson’s Diseases of The Eye, 23rd Edition, Page 705.
question:
A middle-aged woman with sickle cell disease presents with sudden eye pain, redness, and decreased vision. Visual acuity is 6/60. Slit-lamp examination shows ciliary congestion, corneal edema, and a shallow anterior chamber, indicating raised intraocular pressure.

Which drug is most appropriate for the rapid reduction of intraocular pressure?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient has acute primary angle-closure glaucoma (APACG), an ophthalmic emergency characterized by sudden painful unilateral red eye, blurred vision, halos around lights, headache, nausea, and vomiting.

  • The image demonstrates the classic findings of circumcorneal (ciliary) congestion, a steamy cornea due to corneal edema, and a fixed or sluggish mid-dilated vertically oval pupil.
  • The condition occurs in anatomically predisposed eyes, particularly hypermetropic eyes with shallow anterior chambers, where relative pupillary block causes the peripheral iris to obstruct the trabecular meshwork, producing a rapid rise in intraocular pressure, often to 40-60 mmHg or higher.

Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma

Signs
  • Mid-dilated, vertically oval, fixed pupil
  • Corneal epithelial edema
  • Shallow anterior chamber
  • Markedly raised IOP (50-80 mmHg)
  • Conjunctival hyperemia and circumcorneal injection

Symptoms
  • Sudden, severe eye pain (usually unilateral)
  • Red eye
  • Blurred vision or haloes around lights
  • Nausea, vomiting, headache
  • Intermittent blurring or visual disturbances in subacute cases

Management

Initial Management

  • Supine position
  • Acetazolamide 500 mg (IV if IOP >50 mmHg; oral if <50)
  • Topical: Timolol 0.5%, Apraclonidine 0.5%
  • Pilocarpine 2% (repeat after 30 min; cautious if IOP ≥40 mmHg)
  • Analgesics, antiemetics

Resistant cases:

  • IV Mannitol 20% (1–2 g/kg)
  • Oral Glycerol/Isosorbide
  • Corneal indentation or paracentesis
  • Laser iridotomy/iridoplasty (after corneal clarity improves)

Definitive treatment

  • Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI)
  • Medical therapy: Pilocarpine, topical steroids, IOP-lowering drugs
  • Surgery: Phacoemulsification ± IOL; Trabeculectomy if uncontrolled

Acute retrobulbar neuritis (Option A) presents with painful eye movements and vision loss, but no visible anterior segment changes.

Acute anterior uveitis (Option C): While it can cause pain and redness, it typically presents with a constricted pupil, keratic precipitates, and lacks a mid-dilated fixed pupil.

Severe keratoconjunctivitis (Option D) presents with intense conjunctival hyperemia and discharge but does not cause corneal edema or a fixed pupil.



Reference:

Yanoff and Duker Ophthalmology, 6th Edition, Page 1064.
question: A 50-year-old female presents with an acute, painful red eye. Clinical examination reveals a mid-dilated, vertically oval pupil, corneal edema, and circumcorneal congestion as shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
The dark-room/prone-provocative test is used to provoke angle closure in susceptible individuals by simulating conditions that favour pupillary block. The patient's post-test symptoms suggest angle narrowing or closure. Atropine is a long-acting anticholinergic agent that causes mydriasis and cycloplegia. Mydriasis aggravates pupillary block by further narrowing the iridocorneal angle, especially in eyes predisposed to angle closure, and should be strictly avoided in such scenarios.

Pilocarpine (Option A) is a miotic that helps relieve pupillary block by pulling the iris away from the trabecular meshwork. It may be beneficial acutely in angle-closure situations.

Timolol (Option B) is a beta-blocker that decreases aqueous production, lowering intraocular pressure without affecting pupil size. It is safe in angle-closure suspects unless contraindicated otherwise.

Acetazolamide (Option C), a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, also reduces aqueous humor production and helps lower intraocular pressure acutely. It is often used in acute angle-closure attacks unless contraindicated (e.g., sulfa allergy).



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 10th Edition, Page 381.
question: A 36-year-old woman develops acute ocular pain following a dark-room prone-provocative test performed to assess her risk of angle closure. Which of the following medications should be avoided in her management?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
The patient shows classic features of acute primary angle-closure glaucoma (APAC), precipitated in a dim environment (e.g., movie hall) due to pupillary dilation triggering angle closure. Laser peripheral iridotomy creates an opening in the peripheral iris to bypass the pupillary block, equalizing pressure between the posterior and anterior chambers. It is the definitive procedure of choice in APAC after initial IOP control.

Procedure name

Procedure

Indication

Laser Iridotomy (Option B)

Creates a hole in the peripheral iris to relieve pupillary block and equalize AC pressure

Angle-closure glaucoma (primary or secondary).

Laser Trabeculoplasty (Option D ruled out)

A laser is applied to the trabecular meshwork to increase aqueous outflow and lower IOP

POAG, ocular hypertension; first-line or adjunct; not for congenital.

Trabeculotomy (Option A ruled out)

Opens the Schlemm canal by incising the trabecular meshwork to bypass outflow resistance

Congenital/developmental glaucoma (treatment of choice).

Trabeculectomy (Option C ruled out)

Creates a guarded fistula from the AC to the subconjunctival space, forming a filtering bleb

Resistant glaucoma, advanced POAG, failure of medical/laser therapy.


Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 10th edition, Pages 378-381.
question: A young female presents with sudden-onset severe pain in the left eye after watching a movie. She reports progressive vision loss. On examination, she has ciliary congestion, corneal edema, a shallow anterior chamber, and a mid-dilated, sluggishly reactive pupil. What is the procedure of choice for this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The gold standard instrument for measuring intraocular pressure is Goldmann applanation tonometer.

Applanation Tonometry:

  • Concept: Measures IOP based on the force needed to flatten the cornea's surface (Imbert-Fick Law: P = W/A).
  • Goldmann Applanation Tonometer: (Option B)
    • Most popular and accurate; uses a double prism on a slit lamp.
    • Technique:
      • Cornea is anesthetized and stained with fluorescein.
      • Cornea and biprisms are illuminated with cobalt blue light.
      • The prism touches the cornea, and the inner edges of two semicircles are adjusted to just touch.
      • IOP is read by multiplying the dial reading by ten.

[[figure-1]]

[1]

Variable force tonometers:

  • Goldmann applanation tonometer → Gold standard
  • Perkins tonometer (hand held version of goldmann)
    • Draeger tonometer (measures wide range of IOP)
    • Draeger tonometer is similar to Perkins
    • It has a different set of prisms
    • It operates with a motor
  • Pulsair (non-contact tonometer)
  • Tonopen (based on both indentation and applanation) (Option D)
  • Rebound tonometer

[[figure-2]]

Fixed force tonometers:

  • Maklakov tonometer
  • Barraquer tonometer

Gonioscope (Option A): Gonioscope is used to visualize the angle of the anterior chamber.

[[figure-3]]

Hertel’s exophthalmometer (Option C): Hertel’s exophthalmometer is used to measure the protrusion of the apex of the cornea from the outer orbital margin.

[[figure-4]]



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology 9th Edition, pages 29,30

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Sudden severe ocular pain, headache, nausea and vomiting, blurred vision, steamy (hazy) cornea due to corneal edema, mid-dilated fixed pupil, and markedly elevated IOP (60 mmHg) are highly characteristic of acute primary angle-closure glaucoma.

Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma (AACG):

Pathophysiology:

Most common mechanism: Pupillary block

  • Aqueous humor cannot pass normally from the posterior chamber to the anterior chamber.
  • Pressure builds behind the iris.
  • Peripheral iris bows forward (iris bombe).
  • Closure of the trabecular meshwork → sudden rise in IOP.

Risk Factors

  • Increasing age (>50 years)
  • Female sex
  • Hypermetropia (short axial length)
  • Shallow anterior chamber
  • Family history
  • Asian ethnicity
  • Pupil dilatation (darkness, stress, mydriatic drugs)

Clinical Features (Symptoms)

  • Sudden severe ocular pain
  • Red eye
  • Blurred vision
  • Colored halos around lights
  • Headache
  • Nausea and vomiting

Signs

  • Circumcorneal (ciliary) congestion
  • Steamy/hazy cornea (corneal edema)
  • Shallow anterior chamber
  • Mid-dilated, fixed/sluggish pupil
  • Markedly elevated IOP (stony-hard eyeball)
  • Reduced visual acuity

Investigations

During acute attack

  • Tonometry: markedly raised IOP (often 50-80 mmHg)
  • Slit-lamp examination: corneal edema, shallow AC
  • Gonioscopy: closed angle (usually performed after cornea clears)

After attack subsides

  • Gonioscopy (confirm angle closure)
  • Optic disc evaluation
  • Visual field testing

Management

Acute Medical Management

  • Acetazolamide 500 mg IV/oral
  • Topical Timolol
  • Topical Brimonidine
  • Mannitol IV if IOP remains very high
  • Pilocarpine after IOP begins to fall (ineffective at very high IOP)

Definitive Treatment

  • Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI) ← treatment of choice
    • Performed in the affected eye
    • Usually prophylactically in the fellow eye as well

Secondary angle closure glaucoma due to uveitis (Option B): Due to posterior synechiae or iris bombe, but develops gradually. The eye is usually quiet or inflamed but not with sudden severe pain and vomiting.

Phacomorphic glaucoma (Option C): Lens-induced secondary angle closure due to intumescent cataract. Presents in an elderly patient but with visible swollen lens and shallow anterior chamber; usually subacute onset.


Chronic simple glaucoma (Option D): Painless, asymptomatic until late. IOP mildly to moderately elevated, no corneal edema, pupil reactive, no acute symptoms.



Reference:
  1. Parson’s Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page 703, 704, 705
  2. Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Pages 374, 375

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Krukenberg spindle is characteristically seen in pigmentary glaucoma.
  • It is a vertical, spindle-shaped pigment deposition on the corneal endothelium, usually in the central region.
  • It occurs due to pigment dispersion from the iris pigment epithelium, which deposits on anterior segment structures.

Pathogenesis

  • Pigment is released from the posterior surface of the iris.
  • The liberated pigment circulates in the aqueous humor.
  • Pigment deposits on:
    • Corneal endothelium → Krukenberg spindle
    • Trabecular meshwork → increased pigmentation and impaired aqueous outflow
  • This can lead to pigmentary glaucoma, a secondary open-angle glaucoma.

Phacolytic glaucoma (Option A): Caused by leakage of lens proteins from a hypermature cataract.

Juvenile open angle glaucoma (Option C): A primary developmental abnormality of the trabecular meshwork → elevated IOP.

Primary open angle glaucoma (Option D): Chronic age-related degeneration of the trabecular meshwork. May have mild pigmentation, but Krukenberg spindle is not a characteristic feature.

Secondary Glaucoma

Secondary Glaucoma Examples / Causes
Secondary Open-Angle Glaucoma
  • Pigmentary glaucoma (Krukenberg spindle)
  • Pseudoexfoliative glaucoma
  • Steroid-induced glaucoma
  • Phacolytic glaucoma
Secondary Angle-Closure Glaucoma (with pupillary block)
  • Phacomorphic glaucoma
  • Aphakic/Pseudophakic pupillary block
  • Posterior synechiae causing iris bombe
Secondary Angle-Closure Glaucoma (without pupillary block)
  • Neovascular glaucoma
  • Malignant glaucoma
Traumatic Glaucoma
  • Angle recession glaucoma
  • Hyphema-induced glaucoma
Lens-Induced Glaucoma
  • Phacomorphic
  • Phacolytic
  • Lens-particle glaucoma
  • Phacoanaphylactic (phacoantigenic) glaucoma


Reference:
  1. Parson’s Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page 716
  2. Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Pages 381, 382.

explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - Acute angle-closure glaucoma

Explanation:

  • The clinical scenario of a 50-year-old female presenting with an acute painful red-eye and an image showing redness and congestion which gives a diagnosis of Acute angle-closure glaucoma.

Acute Angle Closure Glaucoma:

  • Acute angle-closure glaucoma is a sudden and severe form of glaucoma characterized by a rapid increase in intraocular pressure. It occurs when the drainage angle of the eye becomes blocked, leading to a buildup of fluid and pressure within the eye.

Clinical features of Glaucoma are:

  1. Sudden Painful eye.

  2. A ciliary flush around the cornea due to dilated ciliary veins, and in long-standing cases, caput medusae with prominent vessels.

  3. Cornea - initially clear but insensitive, later becoming hazy, with epithelial bullae (bullous keratopathy) or filaments (filamentary keratitis).

  4. Headache and nausea: Some individuals may experience accompanying headache, nausea, and even vomiting.

  5. Anterior chamber - very shallow.

  6. Iris - atrophic.

  7. Pupil - fixed and dilated.

  8. Optic disc - glaucomatous optic atrophy.

  9. IOP is high and the eyeball becomes stony hard.

Management of absolute glaucoma

In absolute glaucoma, the goal of treatment is to relieve pain and reduce IOP, as vision cannot be restored.

  • Retrobulbar alcohol injection - given to relieve pain. First, 1 mL of 2% xylocaine is injected followed after about 5-10 minutes by 1 mL of 80% alcohol. It suppresses the ciliary ganglion.

  • A cyclodestructive procedure, such as cyclocryotherapy or cyclophotocoagulation, is the most appropriate management option in this scenario as it reduces aqueous production by damaging the secretory ciliary processes aiming to reduce IOP.

  • If pain persists despite cyclodestruction, enucleation/evisceration may be considered.

Incorrect Options

Acute retrobulbar neuritis (Option A), also known as optic neuritis, typically presents with vision loss, eye pain, and decreased color vision. It is not characterized by redness and congestion of the eye, so it is less likely to be the correct diagnosis in this case.

Acute anterior uveitis (Option C), also known as iritis, is inflammation of the iris and the anterior chamber of the eye. It commonly presents with symptoms of a red, painful eye with photophobia (sensitivity to light) and decreased vision. The image showing redness and congestion supports this diagnosis. Acute anterior uveitis can be associated with underlying systemic conditions such as ankylosing spondylitis or reactive arthritis. It is the most likely diagnosis based on the given scenario.

Severe keratoconjunctivitis (Option D) refers to inflammation of both the cornea and the conjunctiva. While it can cause redness and irritation of the eye, it is not commonly associated with acute onset and severe pain. It is less likely to be the correct diagnosis in this case.



Reference:
  • https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3669490/#:~:text=An%20eye%20that%20has%20lost,other%20cases%2C%20it%20may%20not.
  • Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology, 10th edition, Pages 379, 380, 381.

Explanation:

The correct statements are 2 and 5.

  • First-degree relatives have a higher risk of steroid-induced glaucoma due to increased steroid responsiveness and genetic predisposition. (Statement 2)
  • Visual field defects may develop before obvious optic disc cupping; therefore, glaucomatous field loss can occasionally be present despite a seemingly normal C:D ratio. (Statement 5)

Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma (POAG)

  • Chronic, progressive optic neuropathy characterized by:
    • Optic disc cupping
    • Retinal nerve fiber layer loss
    • Characteristic visual field defects
  • Occurs in the presence of an open anterior chamber angle.

Pathogenesis

  • Increased resistance to aqueous outflow at the trabecular meshwork.
  • Leads to gradual elevation of IOP and optic nerve damage.

Risk Factors:

  • Elevated IOP: Asymmetry of IOP of ≥4 mmHg is considered significant.
  • Age: Increased risk with age, especially between the 5th and 7th decades of life.
  • Race: Higher prevalence and severity in Black individuals compared to Whites.
  • Myopia: Increased risk in myopic individuals.
  • Thinner Central Corneal Thickness (CCT) is an independent risk factor.
  • Cigarette Smoking: Increased risk
  • Blood Pressure: Higher prevalence in hypertensives; diastolic perfusion pressure <55 mm Hg is a significant risk factor.
  • Thyrotoxicosis: Increased in Graves' ophthalmic disease.

Familial Risk

  • First-degree relatives have a significantly increased risk of POAG, approximately 4-9 times higher than the general population (Statement 4).
  • They are also more likely to be steroid responders, predisposing them to steroid-induced glaucoma (Statement 2).

Clinical Features

  • Usually asymptomatic in early stages.
  • Gradual peripheral visual field loss.

Visual field defects:

  1. Isopter contraction: Earliest visual field defect
  2. Baring of the blind spot
  3. Relative paracentral scotoma: Earliest clinically significant visual field defect
  4. Siedel scotoma
  5. Arcuate (Bjerrum) scotoma
  6. Ring scotoma & Nasal step of Roenne
  7. Tubular vision in advanced disease

Functional visual field loss may occasionally be detected before obvious disc cupping becomes apparent (Statement 5).

Investigations:

  • Intraocular Pressure: Elevated (>21 mm Hg) on multiple occasions.
  • Anterior Chamber Angle: Open and normal in appearance; Microscopic trabecular meshwork pathology cannot be directly appreciated on routine gonioscopy (Statement 1)
  • Optic Disc: Characteristic cupping, normal C:D ratio in early stages (Statement 5).

Pupillary dilatation may precipitate or worsen primary angle-closure glaucoma. It is not a characteristic cause of IOP exacerbation in POAG (Statement 3).

Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma (POAG) vs Primary Angle-Closure Glaucoma (PACG)

Feature POAG PACG
Angle Open Closed/Narrow
Symptoms Usually asymptomatic Acute painful attacks possible
Pupillary dilatation effect Minimal significance May precipitate attack
Gonioscopy Open angle Occludable/closed angle
Course Chronic Acute or chronic


Reference:
  1. Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology: A Systematic Approach, 9th Edition, Page 350
  2. Comprehensive Ophthalmology - AK Khurana, 7th Edition, Page 241

explanationHtml:
Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD):

  • The pupils paradoxically dilate when the flashlight is swung from the unaffected to the affected eye due to the decreased light perception.
  • This is also called the Marcus Gunn Pupil (Option A) (first sign of optic nerve disorder).
  • Causes:
  • Optic neuritis
  • Optic neuropathy
  • Chiasmal compression
  • Intraocular hemorrhage
  • Central serous retinopathy
  • Cystoid macular edema
  • Retinal detachment
  • Optic tract lesion
  • Central or branch arterial occlusion
  • Central or branch vein occlusion
  • Anisometropic amblyopia
  • Cataract
  • Corneal scar
  • Visual pathway damage
  • Tested by Swinging Flashlight Test .
    • A bright flashlight is shone onto one pupil, causing constriction, then quickly moved to the opposite pupil to observe its response. This process is repeated multiple times to assess the pupillary reactions.
    • Normally, both pupils constrict equally, but the pupil to which light is transferred remains tightly constricted.
    • In RAPD, the affected pupil dilates when the flashlight moves from the normal to the abnormal eye.
    • The dilatation that occurs is commonly called the Marcus Gunn pupil or RAPD (Relative afferent pupillary defect).

[[figure-1]]

Adie’s Pupil (Option B) shows no reaction to light, and the near reflex is very slow and tonic. It shows pupillary constriction to 0.125% Pilocarpine due to denervation supersensitivity. Seen in Postganglionic parasympathetic pupillomotor damage.

Argyll Robertson Pupil (ARP) (Option C) shows reaction to near reflex, but light reflex (both direct and consensual) is absent, i.e. there is light near dissociation. Seen in Neurosyphilis

Hutchinson’s pupil (Option D) This refers to a fixed, dilated pupil due to a midbrain lesion or uncal herniation. It is not typically seen in glaucoma.



Reference:
  • Parsons Diseases of the eye, 23rd Edition, Pg 278, 279.
  • Yanoff & Duker Ophthalmology, 5th edition, Pg 963, 964.

explanationHtml:
• The presence of classic triad of symptoms- watering, photophobia, and blepharospasm in a 2-month old infant are all consistent with Congenital glaucoma.

Primary Congenital Glaucoma:

Types
  1. Newborn glaucoma/ True congenital glaucoma: Elevated intraocular pressure is present during intrauterine life, resulting in ocular enlargement at birth. Typically presents within the first month of life.
  2. Infantile: ≤ 3 yrs of age
  3. Juvenile: > 3 yrs of age

Pathogenesis
  • Trabeculodysgenesis
  • Angle Recess Absence
  • Iris Insertion Types:
    • Flat Insertion: Reveals the ciliary body and scleral spur.
    • Concave Insertion: Obscures the scleral spur and ciliary body.

Clinical Features
  • Classic Triad: Lacrimation, photophobia, and blepharospasm; often accompanied by eye rubbing.

[[figure-1]]

  • Corneal Signs:
    • Oedema: Early sign, may progress to permanent opacity.
    • Enlargement: Corneal diameter >13 mm confirms enlargement; >16 mm indicates poor prognosis.
  • Haab’s Striae: Tears in Descemet's membrane, visible as opaque lines.

[[figure-2]]

  • Additional Features:
    • Deep Anterior Chamber: Indicates elevated IOP.
    • Optic Disc Changes: Variable cupping and atrophy.
    • Raised IOP: Elevated but not acute.
    • Axial Myopia: Due to increased axial length.

Management

Direct Goniotomy followed by Trabeculotomy - preferred management for Congenital Glaucoma

(Buphthalmos: meaning "bull-like eyes," is a condition characterized by the enlargement of the eyeball. It typically manifests before the age of 3 years and results from the accumulation and retention of aqueous humor.)



Reference:
  • Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology, 10th edition, Pages 401, 402, 403
  • Parsons’ Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, PDF Pages 277, 278

Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation of redness, pain, keratic precipitates, aqueous flare, and increased intraocular pressure is suggestive of anterior uveitis induced glaucoma. Prostaglandin analogues are contraindicated in cases of Uveitis as it may aggravate the inflammation.

Anti-Glaucoma drugs:

Prostaglandin Analogues:

Latanoprost, Bimatoprost, Travoprost, Tafluprost

Mechanism:

Increases uveoscleral outflow

Adverse effects:

Sandy eyes, orbital fat atrophy, anterior uveitis, cystoid macular edema, heterochromia iridis, hypertrichosis

Contraindications:

Cystoid macular edema, diabetes mellitus, Anterior Uveitis (Option D)

Beta Blockers: (Option A)

  • Non-Selective: Timolol, Levobunolol, Carteolol, Metipranolol
  • Selective: Betaxolol, Levobetaxolol

Mechanism:

Reduces aqueous secretion

Adverse effects:

Allergic blepharoconjunctivitis, dry eyes, corneal hypoesthesia

Alpha-2 Agonists:

Brimonidine (long-term use), Apraclonidine (IOP spikes)

Mechanism:

Reduces aqueous production, increases uveoscleral outflow

Adverse effects:

Lid retraction, respiratory depression (Brimonidine), allergic blepharoconjunctivitis

Contraindications:

Children <2 years

Additional:

Brimonidine: Safest during pregnancy (Category B)

Miotics:

Pilocarpine, Physostigmine, Echothiophate

Mechanism:

Stimulates M3 receptors, increasing trabecular outflow

Adverse effects:

Brow pain, miosis, cataract (Echothiophate), retinal tears

Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors: (Option C)

Acetazolamide (systemic), Brinzolamide, Dorzolamide (topical)

Mechanism:

Inhibits aqueous secretion

Adverse effects:

Ciliary edema, secondary angle-closure glaucoma

Osmotic agents: (Option B)

Mannitol (IV), Glycerol (oral)

Mechanism:

Lowers IOP by creating an osmotic gradient

Adverse effects:

Cardiac overload, urinary retention

Newer Drugs:

  • Netarsudil (Rho kinase inhibitor): Increases trabecular outflow; Side effect - vortex keratopathy
  • Omidenepag (PGE2 agonist): Increases both trabecular and uveoscleral outflow


Reference:

Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology, 10th edition, Pages 404 - 407
question: Which medication should be avoided in a 30-year-old female presenting with redness, pain, increased intraocular pressure, keratic precipitates, and aqueous flare?

explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: A) Amitriptyline

Explanation:

Amitriptyline, a Tricyclic Antidepressant (TCA) should not be administered to a known case of Angle closure glaucoma due to its antagonistic action on M1 (Muscarinic) receptor.

Amitriptyline:

  • MOA: Primarily blocks Serotonin (5HT3) and Norepinephrine (NE) reuptake; also has additional blocking action on ɑ1 (adrenergic), H1 (Histamine) and M1 (Muscarinic) receptors.
  • ADRs: Orthostatic hypotension, GI disturbances, seizures, increases risk of suicidal thoughts, sexual dysfunction.
  • Contraindication: Angle closure glaucoma

Common drugs contraindicated in Angle closure glaucoma patients:

Anti-Muscarinic
  • Ipratropium bromide, Thiotropium bromide (M1)
  • Toletrodine, Oxybutinin (M3)
  • Scopolamine (M1)

Anti-Histaminics
  • Diphenhydramine, Fexofenadine (H1)
  • Cimetidine, Ranitidine (H2)

Migraine drugs
  • Sumatriptan

Anti-depressants
  • SNRI: Duloxetine and Milnacipram
  • TCA: Amitryptiline

Anti-Epileptics
  • Topiramate, Zonisamide

Antibiotics
  • Trimethoprim-Sulfametoxazole (Cotrimoxazole)

Feature

Phacomorphic Glaucoma (Option D)

Phacolytic Glaucoma (Option A)

Pathogenesis
  • Intumescent cataract blocks the pupil.
  • this pushes the iris forward,
  • blocking the anterior chamber angle,
  • leading to angle-closure glaucoma.
  • Leakage of lens proteins from a hypermature cataract clogs the trabecular meshwork.

Causes
  • Intumescent cataract (mature cataract)
  • Anterior subluxation of lens
  • Spherophakia
  • Hypermature (Morgagnian) cataract
  • Obstruction of the trabecular meshwork by lens proteins.

Clinical Features
  • Symptoms are similar to acute primary angle-closure glaucoma.
  • Shallow anterior chamber.
  • Ciliary congestion, dilated pupil, and swollen cataract is visible.
  • Closed anterior chamber angle on gonioscopy.
  • Features of acute congestive glaucoma due to high IOP.
  • Deep anterior chamber.
  • Open anterior chamber angle on gonioscopy.

Management
  • Medical Treatment: IV mannitol, systemic acetazolamide, topical beta-blockers.
  • Laser Iridotomy: To relieve angle closure.
  • Surgical Treatment: Cataract extraction with PCIOL implantation.
  • Medical Therapy: To lower IOP.
  • Surgical Treatment: Extraction of the hypermature cataract and PCIOL implantation.

Malignant glaucoma (Option B) shallowing of the anterior chamber is noticed and Seidel’s test is negative.

Fuch heterochromic iridocyclitis (Option C), low-grade flare and cells, with stellate keratic precipitates and fine filaments may be seen but IOP is not very high as in the above case.

Explanation:

The presence of classic symptoms- watering, photophobia with abnormally large cornea in a neonate are all consistent with Buphthalmos- Congenital glaucoma.

[[figure-1]]

Primary Congenital Glaucoma:

Types
  • Newborn glaucoma/ True congenital glaucoma: Elevated intraocular pressure is present during intrauterine life, resulting in ocular enlargement at birth. Typically presents within the first month of life.
  • Infantile: ≤ 3 yrs of age
  • Juvenile: > 3 yrs of age

(Buphthalmos: meaning "bull-like eyes," is a condition characterized by the enlargement of the eyeball. It typically manifests before the age of 3 years and results from the accumulation and retention of aqueous humor.)

Pathogenesis
  • Trabeculodysgenesis
  • Angle Recess Absence
  • Iris Insertion Types
    • Flat Insertion: Reveals the ciliary body and scleral spur.
    • Concave Insertion: Obscures the scleral spur and ciliary body.

[[figure-2]]

Clinical Features
  • Classic Triad: Lacrimation, photophobia, and blepharospasm; often accompanied by eye rubbing.
  • Corneal Signs:
    • Oedema: Early sign, may progress to permanent opacity.
    • Enlargement: Corneal diameter >13 mm confirms enlargement; >16 mm indicates poor prognosis.
  • Haab’s Striae: Tears in Descemet's membrane, visible as opaque lines.

[[figure-3]]

  • Additional Features:
    • Deep Anterior Chamber: Indicates elevated IOP.
    • Optic Disc Changes: Variable cupping and atrophy.
    • Raised IOP: Elevated but not acute.
    • Axial Myopia: Due to increased axial length.

Management

Direct Goniotomy followed by Trabeculotomy - preferred management for Congenital Glaucoma

Keratoconus (Option B): is frequently due to congenital weakness of cornea, though it manifests only after puberty. In keratoconus, the cornea thins near the center and progressively bulges forwards, with the apex of the cone always being slightly below the center of the cornea. Important signs include: Munson sign (acute bulge given to the lower lid when the patient looks down), acute hydrops (due to ruptures in the Descemet’s membrane), Vogt striae and Fleischer ring may be seen in the later stages.

Trachoma (Option C): is the chronic inflammatory disease affecting primarily the conjunctiva, but later secondarily affecting the lids and the cornea. The organism responsible is Chlamydia trachomatis. From the clinical point of view, the diagnostic features of trachoma depend on the following characteristics: Follicles in the upper palpebral conjunctiva (Sago-grain appearance), pannus, limbal follicles or their sequelae as Herbert pits, in later stages, typical stellate trachomatous scarring in the conjunctiva.

Keratoglobus (Option D): is a congenital anomaly in which there is hemispherical protrusion of the whole cornea, occurring bilaterally. It is familial and hereditary. It differs from buphthalmos in that the intraocular pressure is normal, cornea is clear, refractive errors are with-the-rule astigmatism, angle of the anterior chamber normal and there is no cupping of the optical disc.

[[figure-4]]

question: What is the probable diagnosis for a neonate who presents with symptoms of photophobia and excessive tearing, along with a clinical examination showing a normal tear passage and a clear, but abnormally large cornea, and the presence of Haab's striae in the eye image below?

explanationHtml:
• Vogt's triad is a clinical set of findings typically associated with acute primary angle-closure glaucoma (APAC) after an attack has been resolved.
  • The triad helps in identifying damage caused during the acute episode.

Features of APAC:

  • Descemet membrane folds
  • Iris atrophy
  • Irregular pupil
  • Glaucomflecken
  • Cataract
  • Cupping +/-

Vogt’s triad:

It may be seen in both treated and non-treated cases after an attack of acute PAC. It is characterized by:

  1. Slightly dilated non-reacting pupil (due to sphincter atrophy)
  2. Glaucomflecken (anterior subcapsular lenticular opacity)
  3. Patches of iris atrophy

[[figure-1]]

Virchow's triad (Option B): This refers to the three factors that predispose to thrombosis: stasis of blood flow, vascular injury, and hypercoagulability. It is used in the context of venous thrombosis, not glaucoma.

Hutchinson's triad (Option C): This refers to a set of findings associated with congenital syphilis, including notched incisors, interstitial keratitis, and sensorineural hearing loss.


Gaucher's triad (Option D): This refers to symptoms seen in Gaucher's disease, a genetic disorder involving lipid storage. The triad includes hepatosplenomegaly, bone pain, and anemia, unrelated to glaucoma.



Reference:
  1. Parson’s Textbook of Ophthalmology, 23rd Edition, Page 704

question: After an acute episode of angle-closure glaucoma, which triad of symptoms is typically observed?

explanationHtml:
• Atropine is not recommended for use in acute congestive glaucoma.
  • This is because atropine is an anticholinergic that causes pupil dilation, which can exacerbate the already elevated intraocular pressure in acute congestive (or angle-closure) glaucoma by further obstructing the drainage of aqueous humor from the eye. This can worsen the condition.
  • Over 60 drugs have been linked to acute angle-closure (AAC) glaucoma, particularly in individuals with ocular predispositions. These include topical anticholinergic pupil dilators (e.g., atropine, cyclopentolate) and systemic medications such as topiramate, sulfonamides, duloxetine, and phenothiazines. Patients on these medications, especially those with AAC risk factors, should have regular ophthalmic examinations.

Acute anterior uveitis (Option B): Atropine can be beneficial in this condition as it helps to relieve ciliary muscle spasms, reduces pain, prevents the formation of posterior synechiae, and keeps the pupil mobile.

Malignant glaucoma (Option C): Atropine is the first line of treatment for management of malignant glaucoma. It dilates the ciliary ring and relaxes the ciliary muscles which causes stretching of zonules that will pull back the lens, thus opening the block.

Corneal ulcer (Option D): Atropine can be used in this case to help relieve pain associated with ciliary muscle spasms, reduces pain, prevents the formation of posterior synechiae, and improve vascularity.



Reference:
  1. Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
  2. (PDF) Ophthalmic Uses of Atropine: A Review
question: In which of the following conditions is atropine not recommended for use?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • True Congenital Glaucoma is characterized by elevated intraocular pressure present during intrauterine life, resulting in ocular enlargement at birth.
  • The presence of Haab’s striae, early onset, enlarged corneas, and the classic triad of symptoms (watering, photophobia, and blepharospasm) are all consistent with newborn glaucoma.

Primary Congenital Glaucoma

Types

1. Newborn glaucoma/ True congenital glaucoma: Elevated intraocular pressure is present during intrauterine life, resulting in ocular enlargement at birth. (40% cases)

Typically presents within the first month of life.

Often associated with developmental anomalies of the anterior segment, such as primary congenital glaucoma, which can result from genetic mutations or other congenital conditions.

2. Infantile: ≤ 3 yrs of age- Infantile glaucoma is labelled when the disease manifests prior to the child's third birthday

Affects infants older than 1 month and children up to 3 years.

Can also result from genetic factors or be secondary to other conditions like Sturge-Weber syndrome or other syndromic associations.

3. Juvenile: > 3 yrs of age who develop pressure rise after 3 years but before adulthood. Also known as Juvenile primary open angle glaucoma(POAG) usually occurs between 10 to 35 years of age.

Buphthalmos, meaning "bull-like eyes," is a condition characterized by the enlargement of the eyeball. It typically manifests before the age of 3 years and results from the accumulation and retention of aqueous humor.

Pathogenesis
  • Trabeculodysgenesis: Maldevelopment of the trabeculum and iridotrabecular junction from neural crest cells impairs aqueous outflow, causing elevated IOP.
  • Angle Recess Absence: The angle recess is absent, with the iris inserting either flatly or concavely into the trabeculum.
  • Iris Insertion Types:
    • Flat Insertion: Reveals the ciliary body and scleral spur.
    • Concave Insertion: Obscures the scleral spur and ciliary body.

Clinical Features

Classic Triad: Lacrimation, photophobia, and blepharospasm; often accompanied by eye rubbing.

[[figure-1]]

Corneal Signs:

  • Oedema: Early sign, may progress to permanent opacity.
  • Enlargement: Corneal diameter >13 mm confirms enlargement; >16 mm indicates poor prognosis.

Haab’s Striae: Tears in Descemet's membrane, visible as opaque lines.

[[figure-2]]

Additional Features:

  • Thin Sclera: Appears blue due to underlying uveal tissue.
  • Deep Anterior Chamber: Indicates elevated IOP.
  • Iris Changes: Iridodonesis and atrophic patches in late stages.
  • Lens Changes: Becomes flat and may subluxate.
  • Optic Disc Changes: Variable cupping and atrophy.
  • Raised IOP: Elevated but not acute.
  • Axial Myopia: Due to increased axial length.

Incorrect Options:

Congenital Cataract (Option B): Causes a cloudy lens and poor vision, but doesn’t typically cause excessive tearing, light sensitivity, or blepharospasm.

Congenital Dacryocystitis (Option C): Leads to tearing and discharge from a blocked tear duct but doesn’t cause light sensitivity or blepharospasm.

Ophthalmia Neonatorum (Option D): Involves eye redness and discharge due to infection at birth, but doesn’t cause light sensitivity or spasms.



Reference:
  1. Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology, 10th edition, Pages 401, 402, 403
  2. Parsons’ Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, PDF Pages 277, 278

question: A patient presents with sudden painful decrease in vision and a fixed, vertically oval pupil. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option A - Phacolytic glaucoma:

  • Flare cells in the anterior chamber of the eye, cataractous lens, and unequal IOP point towards the diagnosis of phacolytic glaucoma.
  • It is a type of secondary open-angle glaucoma in which trabecular meshwork is clogged by the lens proteins, macrophages which have phagocytosed the lens proteins, and inflammatory debris.
  • Leakage of the lens proteins occurs through an intact capsule in the hypermature (Morgagnian) cataractous lens.
  • The anterior chamber may become deep, and the aqueous may contain fine white protein particles, which settle down as pseudohypopyon.
  • Anterior chamber angle is open on gonioscopy, and aqueous flare or cells may be seen in the anterior chamber.

Incorrect Options:

Option B - Malignant glaucoma:

  • In Malignant glaucoma, shallowing of the anterior chamber is noticed and Seidel’s test is negative.

Option C - Fuch heterochromic iridocyclitis:

  • In Fuch heterochromic iridocyclitis, low-grade flare and cells, with stellate keratic precipitates and fine filaments may be seen but IOP is not very high as in the above case.

Option D - Phacomorphic glaucoma:

  • In Phacomorphic glaucoma, ciliary congestion, dilated pupil, and intumescent senile cataractous lens is noted.

question: A patient presents with a vision problem in the right eye. On examination, the intraocular pressure (IOP) of the Right eye is 50 mmHg, while the IOP of the Left eye is 16 mmHg. Slit lamp examination of the right eye reveals flare cells in the anterior chamber and a cataractous lens. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Types of Tonometry:

1. Indentation Tonometry:

  • Concept: Measures IOP by how much a plunger indents the eye; softer eyes indent more than harder eyes.
  • Schiotz Tonometer:
    • Most widely used tonometer in the world.
    • Advantages: Inexpensive, simple, and reliable.
    • Disadvantages: Gives false readings in eyes with abnormal scleral rigidity (e.g., high myopes, post-surgery).

[[figure-1]]

2. Applanation Tonometry:

  • Concept: Measures IOP based on the force needed to flatten the cornea's surface (Imbert-Fick Law: P = W/A).
  • Goldmann Tonometer (Option B):
    • Most popular and accurate; uses a double prism on a slit lamp.
    • Technique:
      • Cornea is anesthetized and stained with fluorescein.
      • Cornea and biprisms are illuminated with cobalt blue light.
      • The prism touches the cornea, and the inner edges of two semicircles are adjusted to just touch.
      • IOP is read by multiplying the dial reading by ten.

[[figure-2]]

Variable force tonometers:

  • Goldmann applanation tonometer → Gold standard
  • Perkins tonometer (hand held version of goldmann)
  • Draeger tonometer (measures wide range of IOP)
    • Draeger tonometer is similar to Perkins
    • It has a different set of prisms
    • It operates with a motor
  • Pulsair (non-contact tonometer)
  • Airpuff (non-contact tonometer)
  • Grolman (non-contact tonometer)
  • Tonopen (based on both indentation and applanation) (Option D)
  • MacKay Marg (based on both indentation and applanation)
  • Rebound tonometer
  • Transpalpebral Tonometer

Fixed force tonometer:

  1. Maklakov tonometer
  2. Barraquer tonometer

Hertel’s exophthalmometer (Option A) is used to measure the degree of exophthalmos (protrusion of the eyeball) in conditions such as thyroid eye disease.

Gonioscope (Option B) is a specialized lens used to visualize the iridocorneal angle, which is important in assessing angle-closure glaucoma.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology: A Systematic Approach, 9th Edition, Page 29, 30
question: What is the gold standard method for measuring intraocular pressure in patients?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Treatment of glaucoma:

  • There are 3 types of treatment modalities:
    • Medical management
    • Laser
    • Surgery

1. Medical:

The drugs either decrease the formation of aqueous or increase the drainage to decrease IOP. This is of 2 types:

  • Topical (6 types)
  • Systemic (2 types)

Topical:

PGF2 alpha agonist:

  • It increases the uveoscleral outflow
  • First line in glaucoma
  • These are also contraindicated in uveitis and asthma
  • For eg- Latanoprost, bimatoprost, travoprost , tafluprost, and unoprostone isopropyl
  • Latanoprost causes heterochromia iridis
  • Bimatoprost increases both uveoscleral and trabecular outflow
  • Side effects: Hypertrichosis

  • Beta-blockers
    • These decrease the formation of aqueous
    • Eg: Timolol, betaxolol
    • C/I in asthma
    • S/E: corneal anesthesia and blepharoconjunctivitis

  • Alpha agonists:
    • They have dual action i.e. they decrease the formation of aqueous and increase the trabecular outflow.
    • Eg: Adrenaline/epinephrine, dipivefrin, brimonidine, and apraclonidine
    • Brimonidine is safe in pregnancy
    • Adrenaline is C/I in aphakic glaucoma

  • Miotics:
    • These increase the trabecular outflow and open the angle blockage
    • Eg: Pilocarpine
    • S/E of Pilocarpine: Pseudo myopia, retinal detachment, shallow anterior chamber, iris cysts

  • Topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitors:
    • These decrease the formation of aqueous
    • Eg: dorzolamide and brinzolamide
    • These are C/I in sulpha allergies

  • Newer anti-glaucoma drugs:
    • Netarsudil: this increases the contractile property of the trabecular meshwork, thus increasing the trabecular outflow and it also decreases the aqueous production.
    • It is a Rho-kinase inhibitor
    • S/E: vortex keratopathy

Systemic:

  • Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor
    • For eg: acetazolamide, methazolamide
    • S/E: Tingling and numbness, constipation, renal stones, and a bad metallic taste
  • Hyperosmotic agents:
    • These draw aqueous out of the eye
    • For eg: I/V mannitol (C/I in heart disease), glycerol (C/I in diabetes), isosorbide, and urea

2. Laser :

Laser trabeculoplasty can be done using argon laser (ALT), or Micropulse diode (MLT) and selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT).

3. Surgery:

  • Surgical treatment of POAG primarily consists of a fistulizing (filtration) surgery which provides a new channel for aqueous outflow and successfully controls the IOP .
  • Trabeculectomy is the most frequently performed filtration surgery nowadays.


Reference:
  1. Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology, 10th edition, Pages 369, 370, 374, 380
  2. Parsons’ Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, PDF Pages 724, 725

question: A patient complains of eye pain and difficulty seeing after watching a movie. What is the first step in management?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The trabecular meshwork is a sieve-like structure at the anterior chamber angle that is responsible for approximately 90% of aqueous humor drainage through the conventional outflow pathway.

  • It consists of three anatomical components:
    • Uveal meshwork: Innermost layer with large intertrabecular spaces that offer minimal resistance to aqueous outflow. (Option 4)
    • Corneoscleral meshwork: Thickest layer with smaller intertrabecular spaces, providing greater resistance than the uveal meshwork. (Option 1)
    • Juxtacanalicular (cribriform) meshwork: Outermost layer adjoining the inner wall of Schlemm's canal and the major site of normal aqueous outflow resistance. (Option 3)
  • Although the juxtacanalicular meshwork is continuous with the inner wall of Schlemm's canal, Schlemm's canal is not a component of the trabecular meshwork itself.



Reference:

question: A 64-year-old male with long-standing hypertension comes for a routine eye checkup. On fundoscopy, the ophthalmologist observes the following changes as shown in the image below. What is the most likely stage of hypertensive retinopathy?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The given fundus photograph demonstrates Blurred optic disc margins → Papilledema, flame-shaped hemorrhages, retinal exudates, venous dilation, and narrowed arterioles.
  • These findings, combined with very high BP (220/120 mmHg) and neurological symptoms (headache, blurred vision), confirm malignant hypertensive retinopathy, where papilledema is a hallmark and diagnostic.

  • Arteriovenous nicking (Option A): Seen in chronic hypertensive changes, not specific to acute or malignant phases.
  • Copper-wiring (Option B): Characteristic of chronic arteriosclerotic changes, not acute hypertensive crisis.
  • Hard exudates (Option D): Present in both chronic and acute stages, but not diagnostic.

question: A 45-year-old male presents with complaints of severe headache and blurred vision. His blood pressure is 220/120 mmHg. Fundoscopy image is given below. Which of the following fundus changes is most characteristic of this diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In hypertensive retinopathy, arteriolar narrowing occurs as a result of vasoconstriction and thickening of the vessel walls.
  • This causes a change in the normal A-V ratio to 1:3.
    • In normal fundoscopy, the ratio of the diameters of first- and second-order retinal arterioles to the diameters of venules is approximately 2:3.

Hypertensive Retinopathy:

  • Any long-standing HTN causes changes in retina.
  • Keith-Wagener-Barker Grading:
Grade Severity Features
Grade 1 Mild
  • Diffuse arterial attenuation
Grade 2 Moderate
  • Diffuse arterial attenuation
  • Focal arteriolar constriction
  • AV Nicking
  • Salus sign
Grade 3 Severe
  • Grade II features
  • Hemorrhage
  • Exudates
  • Gunn sign
  • Bonnet sign
  • Copper wiring
Grade 4 Malignant
  • Grade III features
  • Malignant hypertension
  • Papilledema
  • Silver wiring
  • Atherosclerotic changes:
Salus sign S-shaped deflection of the vein at arteriovenous crossing due to atherosclerotic plaque
Gunn sign Narrowing of the veins at both ends of arteriovenous crossing
Bonnet sign Dilatation (Banking) of vein on one side at arteriovenous crossing
Copper-wiring Thining of blood column due to atherosclerotic plaque
Silver wiring Narrowing of blood column due to increased atherosclerotic plaque

Pregnancy-induced HTN:

  • Presents with hypertensive retinopathy
  • Grade III hypertensive retinopathy → Indication for termination of pregnancy

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The above clinical features and fundus examination shows multiple flame-shaped hemorrhages around the disc and multiple cotton wool spots.

  • This is known as splashed-tomato appearance.
  • These findings are seen in Ischemic CRVO.
    • Another characteristic appearance seen in ischemic CRVO is 100 day glaucoma (Neovascular glaucoma)

[[figure-1]]

Non-ischemic CRVO (Option A) is more common (75% of cases), but it typically presents with milder symptoms, including gradual vision blurring and the absence or mild presence of RAPD. Fundus findings are less severe, with mild venous congestion and flame-shaped hemorrhages in the periphery.

Branch Retinal Vein Occlusion (BRVO) (Option C) typically affects a portion of the retina rather than the entire retina, and the hemorrhages are more localized to the area of the occluded vein. Vision loss is generally less severe compared to ischemic CRVO.

Diabetic Retinopathy (Option D) can present with retinal hemorrhages and macular edema, but it is not associated with sudden, severe vision loss and RAPD as in this case.

Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Goldmann Perimetry and ERG are crucial for differentiating between ischemic and non-ischemic CRVO. In ischemic CRVO, there is significant retinal ischemia leading to visual field defects and a reduction in the amplitude of the b-wave on ERG. These findings help to confirm the diagnosis of ischemic CRVO.

[[figure-1]]

  • Fundus Autofluorescence (FAF) (Option A) demonstrates fern-like perivenular hypoautofluorescence due to retinal edema in both non-ischemic and ischemic CRVO.

  • Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) (Option B) is valuable in evaluating macular edema, which may be present in both non-ischemic and ischemic CRVO. Goldmann perimetry and ERG are most useful in differentiating ischemic from non-ischemic CRVO.

  • Slit-lamp examination (Option D) is essential for detecting anterior segment changes such as neovascularization of the iris (NVI). It is mainly used to monitor for complications like neovascular glaucoma.

question: Which of the following investigations is most useful in distinguishing ischemic CRVO from non-ischemic CRVO?

correctAnswer: D. Pale retina with a cherry-red spot at the macula
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient has central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO), an ophthalmic emergency that presents with sudden, painless, profound monocular vision loss.

  • Fundus examination classically shows diffuse retinal whitening (ischemic retinal edema) with a cherry-red spot at the fovea.
  • The surrounding retina appears pale because ischemia causes edema of the inner retinal layers, whereas the thin fovea, which lacks inner retinal layers and receives its blood supply primarily from the choroidal circulation, remains relatively transparent, allowing the underlying choroidal vasculature to produce the characteristic cherry-red appearance.
  • Other findings include marked attenuation of retinal arteries, box-carring (segmentation) of the blood column, and occasionally a visible retinal embolus.

[[figure-1]]

Retinal hemorrhages and cotton-wool spots (Option A): Retinal hemorrhages and cotton-wool spots are characteristic of diabetic retinopathy, hypertensive retinopathy, and central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO).

Optic disc edema and retinal hemorrhages (Option B): Optic disc edema is characteristic of conditions such as papilledema or anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, rather than CRAO. CRAO primarily affects the retinal circulation, producing retinal ischemia with a cherry-red spot.

Dilated retinal veins with tortuosity (Option C): Dilated, tortuous retinal veins are the hallmark of central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO), often accompanied by widespread retinal hemorrhages, producing the classic "blood-and-thunder" appearance.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Pages 525, 527, 528

question: A 72-year-old man with a history of hypertension presents with sudden, painless vision loss in his right eye. Which of the following findings is most consistent with the diagnosis of central retinal artery occlusion?

correctAnswer: C. Ocular massage and anterior chamber paracentesis
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical features and fundus examination are suggestive of central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO). The goal of the initial treatment is to restore retinal blood flow. Ocular massage and anterior chamber paracentesis are commonly used methods to dislodge emboli and improve perfusion.

  • Critical time to prevent irreversible damage: 90 minutes

Treatment Options

  • Intravenous Acetazolamide: Provides sustained IOP reduction
  • Sublingual Isosorbide Dinitrate: Dilates blood vessels to improve blood flow past the blockage
  • Carbogen Breathing

Oral corticosteroids (Option A): Used for Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA), which causes an ischemic optic neuropathy, not a cherry-red spot.


Intravitreal anti-VEGF injection (Option B): Used for "wet" Macular Degeneration, Diabetic Retinopathy, or Retinal Vein Occlusion (CRVO) to reduce edema, not for acute arterial blockages.


Systemic anticoagulation therapy (Option D): Retinal tissue dies within ~90 minutes; systemic anticoagulants are too slow for acute vision rescue.

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th edition, pg: 529, 530, 531.

question: A 65-year-old male presents to the emergency department with sudden, painless vision loss in his right eye. On examination, the right eye shows a pale retina with a cherry-red spot at the macula. The patient has a history of hypertension and smoking. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment to improve retinal blood flow and potentially restore vision?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The most likely cause of future vision loss in this patient is macular edema.

Complications of Diabetic Retinopathy:

  • Macular Edema: The most common cause of vision loss in diabetic retinopathy is leakage from dilated capillaries.

[[figure-1]]

  • Vitreous Hemorrhage (VH) (Option A): Seen as blood floating in the vitreous, occluding the view of the retina. Secondary to proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) is a cause of severe vision loss in diabetic patients

  • Retinal Detachment (Option B): PDR causes scars to form in the back of the eye. When the scars pull the retina away from the back of the eye, it's called tractional retinal detachment.

  • Neovascular Glaucoma (Option D): PDR causes abnormal blood vessels to grow out of the retina and block fluid from draining out of the eye, leading to neovascular glaucoma. Can cause vision loss and blindness.

  • Rubeosis Iridis: Neovascularization of the iris is when blood vessels develop on the anterior surface of the iris in response to retinal ischemia. Prone to spontaneous hyphema as the blood vessels are fragile

[[figure-2]]

question: A 58-year-old male with a 20-year history of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes and an HbA1c of 10.5% came for an ophthalmic examination. Fundoscopy reveals microaneurysms, hard exudates, and retinal thickening. Which of the following is the most likely cause of future vision loss in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient has diabetic retinopathy with diabetic macular edema (DME), as evidenced by microaneurysms, hard exudates, and retinal thickening.

  • Diabetic macular edema is the most common cause of visual impairment in patients with diabetic retinopathy.
  • It results from breakdown of the inner blood-retinal barrier, causing leakage from microaneurysms and retinal capillaries, leading to retinal thickening, intraretinal fluid accumulation, and hard exudate deposition at the macula.
  • The risk is increased by long-standing diabetes and poor glycemic control, as in this patient.

[[figure-1]]

itreous Hemorrhage (Option A): Vitreous hemorrhage is a complication of proliferative diabetic retinopathy, resulting from rupture of fragile retinal neovascular vessels. It causes sudden painless visual loss, but it is not the most common cause of vision loss in diabetic retinopathy.

Retinal Detachment (Option B): Tractional retinal detachment occurs in advanced proliferative diabetic retinopathy due to contraction of fibrovascular membranes. Although it can cause severe vision loss, it is less common than diabetic macular edema.

Neovascular Glaucoma (Option D): Neovascular glaucoma develops when retinal ischemia stimulates VEGF-mediated neovascularisation of the iris and anterior chamber angle (rubeosis iridis), obstructing aqueous outflow and raising intraocular pressure. It is a late complication of proliferative diabetic retinopathy, not the most common cause of visual loss.

[[figure-2]]

question: A 58-year-old man with a 20-year history of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 10.5%) undergoes fundus examination. explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Tobacco amblyopia presents with loss of central vision and not with its preservation.

  • It is caused by excessive use of tobacco which leads to degeneration of ganglion cells, especially in the macula.
  • Causes centrocecal scotoma: Scotoma involving both the blind spot and the macula
  • It characteristically presents with impairment of central vision, which is bilateral and progressive, with patients complaining of difficulty in doing near work and fogginess.
  • Central vision, tubular vision, or tunnel vision refers to the loss of peripheral vision while preserving central vision.

Causes of tubular vision:

  • Terminal stage of advanced glaucomatous field defect (Option A): The visual field loss is gradual, both centrally and peripherally. The temporal island is more resistant and hence is lost only in the end, leading to loss of even light perception.
  • Advanced stage of retinitis pigmentosa (Option B): Central vision occurs in advanced cases and is lost ultimately after a prolonged duration.
  • Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) with cilioretinal artery (Option C): It provides a second arterial supply to the fovea and hence in the case of CRAO, the central vision is maintained whereas the peripheral is lost.
  • Vigabatrin: It is a drug used in the treatment of epilepsy. It can cause vision loss in 30% of infants and causes bilateral tunnel vision in adults, and causes damage to the central retina and leads to visual acuity

question: A patient is being examined for loss of vision in the ophthalmology clinic. His peripheral visual field is lost, and only his central vision remains. Which of the following would not present with central (tunnel) vision?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In retinopathy of prematurity, the premature infant's retina is vulnerable to abnormal vascular growth. The disruption of VEGF production, often due to fluctuations in oxygen levels (e.g., excess oxygen therapy), impairs the normal retinal vascular development. This can lead to abnormal blood vessel formation and progression of ROP.

  • Increased oxygen supply leading to retinal vasodilation (Option A): Excessive oxygen therapy causes retinal vessel suppression, not vasodilation.
  • Excessive blood glucose levels (Option C): ROP is not directly caused by blood glucose levels, but by oxygen fluctuations.
  • Retinal hypoxia leading to abnormal collagen formation (Option D): Hypoxia triggers VEGF production, causing abnormal vessel growth, not collagen deposition.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

    • In retinopathy of prematurity, the premature infant's retina is vulnerable to abnormal vascular growth.

  • Prolonged exposure to blue light (Option C): No scientific evidence links blue light exposure to ROP.

question: A 32-week premature infant presents with dilated and tortuous retinal vessels in the posterior pole, poor pupil dilation, and vitreous haze, indicating a progression of retinopathy of prematurity (ROP). What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Stage 3 ROP (retinopathy of prematurity without plus disease in zone II is considered to be Low risk Pre threshold. It typically warrants close observation with follow-up rather than immediate treatment unless there are signs of progression.

Anatomical classification of ROP by Zones:

Zone I

Bounded by a circle, the radius of which is twice the distance between the center of the optic disc and center of the macula.

Zone II

Extends from the edge of the zone 1 peripherally to a point tangential to the nasal ora serrata.

Zone III

Consists of residual temporal crescent of retina anterior to zone II.

  • Threshold Disease: Stage 3+ ROP with plus disease.
    • Located in zone I or II.
    • Involves 5 continuous or 8 discontinuous clock hours.
    • Requires laser therapy within 72 hours.
  • Prethreshold Disease: Classified by the Early Treatment for Retinopathy of Prematurity (ET-ROP) group into two types:

Type I

Type II

High-Risk Prethreshold Disease, requiring laser photocoagulation.

  • Zone I: Plus disease, any stage.
  • Zone I: Non-plus disease, stage 3.
  • Zone II: Plus disease, stages 2 and 3.

Low-Risk Prethreshold Disease, requiring weekly follow-up.

  • Zone I: Non-plus disease, stages 1 and 2.
  • Zone II: Non-plus disease, stage 3.

Treatment of ROP:

  1. Laser treatment: (Option A)
    • Done in the avascular peripheral retina.
    • Use diode laser or frequency doubled Nd:YAG with LIO (laser indirect ophthalmoscope) delivery.
    • Used for high-risk pre-threshold, threshold, and aggressive posterior ROP.
  2. Anti-VEGF: (Option B)
    • Bevacizumab: Effective in patients with zone I, stage 3 ROP with plus disease.
    • Zone I disease responds more than zone II.
    • Recurrence can occur following cessation of anti-VEGF treatment.
  3. Pars plana vitrectomy: For tractional retinal detachment not involving macula.

  • Cryotherapy of retina (Option D) is not preferred for stage 3 ROP, especially in zone II without plus disease. It has been largely replaced by laser therapy due to its higher risk of causing inflammation and less favorable outcomes.



Reference:

Parson’s diseases of the eye, Edition 23,PDF, Page 509,510,532-534

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Purtscher Retinopathy is a condition typically associated with trauma (especially head or chest trauma) and is characterized by multiple retinal white patches around the optic nerve head and fovea, known as Purtscher flecken, cotton wool spots, and minimal intraretinal hemorrhage.
  • The occlusion of peripapillary arterioles and embolization is the key pathophysiological mechanism. In this case, the sudden severe visual loss after trauma, along with the described retinal findings, suggests Purtscher Retinopathy.

[[figure-1]]

  • Diabetic Retinopathy (Option A) is associated with microvascular changes due to diabetes, including dot-blot hemorrhages, microaneurysms, and neovascularization, but not Purtscher flecken or trauma-related visual loss.

  • Retinal Vein Occlusion (Option B) presents with diffuse retinal hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, and optic disc swelling but is not typically linked to trauma.

  • Central Serous Retinopathy (Option D) involves serous retinal detachment usually due to stress, without the hemorrhages or cotton wool spots seen in Purtscher Retinopathy.

explanationHtml:
• Young male with sudden painless loss of vision in left eye with fundus showing peripheral retinal vasculitis, venous sheathing, and recurrent vitreous hemorrhage confirms the diagnosis of Eales’ Disease (Periphlebitis Retina)

Etiology & Pathogenesis

  • Cause: Hypersensitivity to tubercular antigen

  • Type of hypersensitivity:

    • Type IV hypersensitivity (cell-mediated)

    • Type III hypersensitivity (immune complex-mediated)

  • Cause of recurrent vitreous hemorrhage in a young male = Eales’ Disease

Management:

Initial management:

  • Systemic corticosteroids (because of inflammatory vasculitis).

Further treatment:

  • Laser photocoagulation (Option C) if required.

For vitreous hemorrhage:

  • Vitrectomy (Option D).

  • Prognosis: In Eales’ disease, prognosis after vitrectomy is very good, and patient may regain vision up to 6/6.

[[figure-1]]

Intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy (Option A) is used in conditions involving neovascularization, such as diabetic retinopathy, they are not the primary treatment for Eales disease, which is mainly driven by inflammation rather than VEGF-mediated neovascularization.
