question: A 23-year-old male presents with sudden, painless vision loss in his left eye. Fundus examination reveals peripheral retinal vasculitis, vessel sheathing and recurrent vitreous hemorrhages. Fluorescein angiography reveals vessel leakage. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

explanationHtml:
Option A: HLA B27

  • It is a case in which the patient presents with pain, photophobia, redness, and decreased vision from the last 3 days. Both eyes of the patient are affected. Examination shows the involvement of the cornea and ciliary nerve. It is the scenario of acute anterior uveitis.
  • HLA, known as human leukocyte antigen, are proteins or markers in most human cells. HLA is used by immune cells to decide which cells belong to the body and which are not.
  • HLA are strongly associated with diseases of the uvea. About 50% of acute uveitis cases are associated with the human leukocyte antigen B27. Other diseases are also associated with this, such as ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, and inflammatory bowel disease.
  • The actual role of B27 in triggering the inflammation response is still unknown. People with positive or increased HLA-B27 are more likely to have autoimmune diseases.

Option B: HLA A29

  • It is a leukocyte antigen of class 1 type. It is associated with birdshot retinochoroiditis (BRC), which affects the posterior portion of the eye with choroidal inflammation.
  • It is mostly seen in Caucasians as a rare form of uveitis. HLA A29 is a major histocompatibility complex.

Option C: HLA B51

  • HLA B51 is the major genetic factor in Behcet's syndrome. It is a hallmark of this syndrome.
  • It also shows susceptibility to the virus that can cause German measles. Patients carrying this allele have 4 times greater chances of developing Bechet's disease.

Option D: HLA DR4

  • The presence of this leukocyte antigen is found in the white blood cells. It is a genetic anomaly.
  • HLA DR4 is associated with rheumatoid arthritis. It is a large serogroup and has a moderate frequency of the alleles.


Reference:

Parsons disease of eye, 22.

question: A 23-year-old male presents to the ophthalmologist with pain, redness, photophobia or sensitivity to the light, and decreased vision from the last 3 days. Both the eyes of the patient are affected, and the patient is very irritable. Upon examination, infection of both the cornea and ciliary nerve is involved. The doctor diagnosed the patient with acute anterior uveitis. Which of the following HLA (human leukocyte antigen) is associated with uveitis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient has acute anterior uveitis (acute iridocyclitis), characterised by pain, circumcorneal redness (ciliary congestion), photophobia, and decreased vision due to inflammation of the iris and ciliary body.

  • HLA-B27 is the HLA antigen most strongly associated with acute anterior uveitis, being present in approximately 50% of cases, particularly in patients with recurrent disease.
  • HLA-B27-associated uveitis is frequently linked to seronegative spondyloarthropathies, including ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, and inflammatory bowel disease-associated arthritis.
  • It typically presents as acute, recurrent, non-granulomatous anterior uveitis, often affecting one eye at a time, although bilateral involvement may occur.

HLA-A29 (Option B): HLA-A29 is strongly associated with birdshot chorioretinopathy (birdshot retinochoroiditis), a chronic bilateral posterior uveitis characterized by multiple cream-colored choroidal lesions and vitreous inflammation.

HLA-B51 (Option C): HLA-B51 is strongly associated with Behçet disease, which commonly presents with recurrent bilateral nongranulomatous uveitis, retinal vasculitis, recurrent oral and genital ulcers, and skin lesions.

HLA-DR4 (Option D): HLA-DR4 is classically associated with rheumatoid arthritis and is not the characteristic HLA association for acute anterior uveitis.



Reference:

Parson's Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page 544

Answer: B) B

Explanation:

The Inner Nuclear Layer is made up of the cell bodies of bipolar cells, horizontal cells, and amacrine cells. It is labeled as B in the Histology image given.

[[figure-1]]

Layer

Description

1. Pigment Epithelium

Outermost layer with a single pigmented cell layer; adheres to Bruch's membrane; supports neurosensory retina, and reduces reflection.

Subretinal Space: This is the layer between the Pigment epithelium and the layer of Photoreceptors.

2. Rods and Cones Layer

Contains the outer segments of photoreceptors (rods and cones, which are the first-order neurons); rods detect low-light vision, cones manage color and detailed vision.

3. External Limiting Membrane

A porous membrane allows processes from rods and cones to pass through.

4. Outer Nuclear Layer
(Henle’s layer) (Option D)

Contains the nuclei of the photoreceptor cells (rods and cones).

5. Outer Plexiform Layer (Option C)

Includes connections between rods, cones, bipolar cell dendrites, and horizontal cells.

6. Inner Nuclear Layer (Option B)

Made up of the cell bodies of bipolar cells (which are the second-order neurons), horizontal cells, amacrine cells, and Müller cells; and also contains retinal capillaries.

7. Inner Plexiform Layer (Option A)

Houses synaptic connections between bipolar cell axons, ganglion cell dendrites, and amacrine cell processes.

8. Ganglion Cell Layer

Contains ganglion cell bodies, which serve as third-order neurons; midget cells synapse with a single bipolar cell, and polysynaptic cells synapse with multiple.

9. Nerve Fiber Layer

Composed of ganglion cell axons that form the optic nerve after passing through the lamina cribrosa.

10. Internal Limiting Membrane

The innermost layer separating the retina from the vitreous; is formed by the terminal expansions of Müller cells, serving as a basement membrane.



Reference:

Parson’s diseases of the eye, Edition 23,PDF, Page 38-41

question: A 65-year-old male with a history of hypertension and atherosclerosis presents with sudden, painless loss of vision in his left eye. On fundoscopy, you note a pale retina with a cherry-red spot at the macula. What is the most likely underlying cause of this condition?

explanationHtml:
Answer: A. Central retinal artery

Explanation:

  • The central retinal artery is the main vessel responsible for supplying the inner layers of the retina, including the nerve fiber layer, ganglion cells, and inner retinal layers.
  • The short posterior ciliary arteries primarily supply the choroid and the outer retinal layers.

Blood Supply of Retina

Retinal Blood Supply

  • Outer 4 layers of retina → Supplied by short posterior ciliary arteries
    • The same arteries also supply the choroid.
  • Inner 6 layers of retina → Supplied by central retinal artery (CRA).

Course of Central Retinal Artery

  • The CRA runs along the end of the optic nerve.
  • This happens before it enters the eye wall.

Capillary Systems in Retina

  • Two capillary systems are present:
    1. Between the outer plexiform (OP) and the inner nuclear (IN) layer
      • Capillaries are oriented perpendicular to the retina.
      • Bleeding here → Dot and blot hemorrhage.
    2. Along the nerve fiber layer
      • Capillaries are oriented parallel to the retina.
      • Bleeding here → Flame-shaped hemorrhage.

Ciliary Arteries (Branches of Ophthalmic Artery)

  • Anterior ciliary arteries
  • Posterior ciliary arteries
    • Short posterior ciliary arteries → 10–12 in number.
    • Long posterior ciliary arteries → Only 2 in number.
      • Run anteriorly.
      • Anastomose with anterior ciliary arteries → Major arterial circle.

Branches from this circle → Anastomose around the pupillary border → Minor arterial circle.

[[figure-1]]

Parson’s diseases of the eye, Edition 23, Pg 3,4,11,250-252

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

When the media is hazy, the best method for assessing the retina of this patient is indirect ophthalmoscopy.

Direct vs. Indirect Ophthalmoscopy:

Feature

Direct Ophthalmoscopy

Indirect Ophthalmoscopy

Instrument used

 [[figure-1]] [[figure-2]]

Image
  • Erect, virtual
  • Inverted, real

Magnification
  • High magnification
  • (~15x in emmetropes, more in myopes, less in hypermetropes)
  • Moderate magnification (~2.5x with a +20D lens)

Field of View
  • Small (~10° or 1-2 disc diameters)
  • Large (~35° or 8 disc diameters)

Visualization
  • Central retina only
  • Central and peripheral retina (up to the ora serrata)

Refractive Media
  • Poor visualization in hazy or cloudy media (Option A)
  • Can visualize through hazy media due to stronger illumination

Examination Distance
  • Close to the eye (~15 mm from the cornea)
  • Performed at a greater distance (~50 cm or an arm’s length)

Patient Position
  • Performed in a seated/standing position in a semi-dark room
  • Performed with the patient in a supine or sitting position

Lens Requirement
  • No external lens is required; correcting lenses for refractive errors are built into the ophthalmoscope
  • Requires a convex lens (commonly +20D) to be placed in front of the patient’s eye

Peripheral Lesion Detection
  • Limited ability to detect peripheral lesions
  • Excellent for detecting peripheral retinal lesions such as retinal detachment or tears.

Slit-Lamp Biomicroscopy (Option C): Although useful for anterior segment examination and some posterior pole assessments, it is ineffective in hazy media due to scattering of light.

Amsler grid test (Option D) is a widely used tool for monitoring vision changes, particularly in individuals at risk for age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and in other macular lesions. However, it is less effective in hazy media, such as cataracts or other opacities in the eye.

question: A 60-year-old patient with a history of diabetes comes in for a routine check-up for diabetic retinopathy. The patient also has a cataract, causing a hazy view of the ocular media. Which method of study would be most appropriate for assessing the retina of this patient?

correctAnswer: A. Hyperfluorescence due to dye pooling under detached RPE and neovascularization
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient has ARMD, a condition associated with the pooling of dye under the RPE and subretinal neovascularization, both of which lead to hyperfluorescence on FFA.

Abnormalities Detected by Fundus Fluorescein Angiography (FFA)

1. Hyperfluorescence

  • Window defect (RPE atrophy): Background choroidal fluorescence.

  • Pooling of dye under RPE: Age-related macular degeneration (Option A).

  • Pooling under sensory retina: Central serous retinopathy (CSR).

  • Leakage into neurosensory retina (inner BRB breakdown): Cystoid macular edema (CME).

  • Leakage from choroidal/retinal neovascularization: Proliferative diabetic retinopathy, subretinal neovascular membrane in ARMD.

  • Staining (dye retention in tissues): Drusen, normal optic disc (Option D).

  • Leakage from optic nerve head: Papilloedema.

2. Hypofluorescence

  • Blockage of background fluorescence: Retinal hemorrhage (Option B), hard exudates, pigmented clumps.

  • Occlusion of retinal/choroidal vasculature: Central retinal artery occlusion (Option C), diabetic retinopathy with capillary occlusion.

  • Loss of vasculature: Choroideremia, myopic degeneration.

Normal Study

[[figure-1]]

question: A 60-year-old patient with age-related macular degeneration (ARMD) undergoes Fundus Fluorescein Angiography (FFA), revealing pooling of dye under the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and leakage from newly formed vessels beneath the retina. What abnormality is most likely detected on FFA in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Answer: D. Peripheral retina

Explanation:

  • The presentation of diminished night vision and loss of peripheral vision is suggestive of a defect in the peripheral retina, which is crucial for peripheral and night vision.
  • Additionally, no abnormality was found in the posterior pole, which includes the macula, fovea, and optic disc (Options A, B, C).

[[figure-1]]

Parts of the Retina:

Part

Description

Posterior Pole

The region behind the retinal equator includes the optic disc and macula lutea; best examined using slit-lamp biomicroscopy or by direct ophthalmoscopy.

Optic Disc (Option C)

Known as the optic nerve head, it is a pink, vertically oval structure, marking the start of the optic nerve.

The physiological Cup is a depression in the optic disc through which the central retinal artery and vein pass; the absence of photoreceptors results in the physiological blind spot.

Macula Lutea (Option A)

A dark, yellow spot at the posterior pole, measuring 5.5 mm in diameter; is responsible for central, high-acuity vision and color detection.

Fovea Centralis (Option B)

Central area of the macula (1.5 mm in diameter); contains only cones and is the most sensitive part of the retina for visual acuity.

Foveola

A 0.35 mm diameter shining pit within the fovea, represents the area of highest visual acuity, with the foveal avascular zone (FAZ) surrounding it.

Peripheral Retina (Option D)

Extends from the retinal equator to the ora serrata, examined via indirect ophthalmoscopy or Goldmann three-mirror lens. It contains rods, hence responsible for night vision.

Ora Serrata

The serrated peripheral margin is where the retina ends. Here the retina is firmly attached to both the vitreous and choroid. Pars plana extends anteriorly from ora serrata.


Reference:
  1. Parson’s diseases of the eye, Edition 23,PDF, Page 37,38,40,41,739-741
  2. https://www.aao.org/eye-health/anatomy/peripheral-retina
question: A 35-year-old male presents with difficulty in vision, especially at night, and he reports bumping into objects frequently. Upon examination, he is found to have tunnel vision, and the fundus reveals no abnormalities in the posterior pole. Which region of the retina is most likely responsible for his symptoms?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Negative ERG response suggests gross disturbances in retinal circulation.

  • Electroretinography (ERG) records changes in the eye's resting potential. It is induced by a flash of light.
  • Parts of ERG:
    • A-wave: Negative wave, likely from rods and cones (photoreceptors).
    • B-wave: Large positive wave, generated by Müller cells (inner retinal layers) but reflects bipolar cell activity.
    • C-wave: Positive wave, related to the metabolic activity of the pigment epithelium (RPE), observed in dark-adapted eyes.
    • Foveal ERG provides information about the macula used in diagnosing cataracts.

[[figure-1]]

Interpretation

Response

Inference

Extinguished

Complete failure in rod and cone function (e.g., pigmentary retinal dystrophy, complete retinal artery occlusion, old retinal detachment, advanced siderosis).

Subnormal

Large areas of the retina not functioning (e.g., early retinitis pigmentosa, before ophthalmoscopic signs).

Negative

Gross disturbances in the retinal circulation.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In Best disease, the Arden ratio on EOG is typically less than 1.5, indicating abnormal retinal pigment epithelium function, which is characteristic of this condition.

Electro-oculography (EOG):

  • Measures changes in resting ocular potential via electrodes placed at inner and outer canthi when eyes move side to side.
  • Changes in potential reflect the activity of retinal pigment epithelium (regulated by the bestrophin gene) and outer segments of visual receptors.

Clinical Use:

  • Useful in detecting retinal pigment epithelium dystrophies and degenerations before visual symptoms manifest.
  • Helpful in diagnosing Best disease (Arden index <1.5) and differentiating it from adult-onset vitelliform macular dystrophy and pattern dystrophy. (Option B)
  • EOG apparatus can also be used to record eye movements in nystagmus (electronystagmography (ENG)).

Arden Index: The result is calculated by dividing the light peak (maximal potential in light) by the dark trough (minimal potential in dark).

Arden Ratio

Interpretation

>1.85

Normal

1.85-1.5

Borderline

<1.5

Abnormal

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Retinal vasoconstriction is seen in the pathogenesis of hypertensive retinopathy, whereas microvascular adhesion is seen in diabetic retinopathy.

  • CSMO (Clinically Significant Macular Edema) is defined as:
    • Any edema within 500 microns from the center of the fovea
    • Any hard exudates within 500 microns from the center of the fovea

Pathogenesis of Diabetic retinopathy (DR):

  • Diabetic macular edema → Macular ischemia (Option A) → Retinal new vessels (Option B) → Vitreous hemorrhage (Option C) → Tractional retinal detachment.

Hypertensive retinopathy:

  • Systemic hypertension causes vasoconstriction of retinal arterioles (Option D)
  • Arteriosclerosis, increased vascular permeability, and retinal hemorrhages lead to retinopathy.

question: A patient with chronic diabetes mellitus complains of diminished vision. Her fundoscopy showed clinically significant macular edema. Which of the following would not be seen as a progressive change leading to diabetic retinopathy?

correctAnswer: A. Focal laser therapy for diabetic macular edema targets leaking microaneurysms within 300 µm of the fovea.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Focal laser therapy for diabetic macular edema targets leaking microaneurysms within 500 µm of the fovea.

Type of Laser used in retinal vascular diseases: Photocoagulative lasers

  • Grid laser (Option B): Grid laser is applied for diffuse retinal thickening at least 500 microns away from the fovea and optic disc, used when multiple points leak, while focal therapy is reserved for fewer leaks.

  • Sub-threshold lasers (Option C): These are diode lasers given in very short bursts with longer intervals, minimizing collateral damage and used for sub-fovea or juxtafovea pathologies.

  • Limitations (Option D): Photocoagulative lasers carry a risk of central vision loss if the fovea is hit, can cause visual field defects, and usually require multiple sessions.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 5th edition, pg: 507, 508, 510, 511, 516, 523, 536.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Reduced blood viscosity is not a contributing factor to diabetic retinopathy; instead, increased blood viscosity is observed.

  • Diabetic Retinopathy develops due to:
    • Cellular damage: From sorbitol, AGEs, Protein kinase C activation, oxidative stress (Option A)
    • Hematological-biochemical changes: Increased blood viscosity (Option B), platelet adhesiveness, and altered lipids
    • Microangiopathy: Breakdown of the inner blood-retinal barrier (Option D), capillary damage
    • Neovascularization: Driven by increased proangiogenic factors (Option C)like VEGF and PDGF, with reduced anti-angiogenic protection.

question: A 55-year-old patient with a long history of diabetes mellitus presents for a routine eye examination. The ophthalmologist noted several findings in the retinal examination. Which of the following features is least likely to be observed in early nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR)?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The defining feature of proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) is retinal neovascularisation, which may occur as neovascularisation of the disc (NVD) or neovascularisation elsewhere (NVE).

  • Among the given options, NVD is the most specific finding confirming PDR and is associated with a higher risk of vitreous hemorrhage, tractional retinal detachment, and severe visual loss.
  • These fragile new vessels grow through the internal limiting membrane in response to retinal ischemia and increased vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) production.

Cotton-wool spots (Option A): Cotton-wool spots represent localized retinal nerve fiber layer infarctions caused by retinal ischemia. They occur in moderate to severe non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR) and are not diagnostic of proliferative disease.

Retinal hemorrhages (Option B): Retinal hemorrhages occur throughout the course of diabetic retinopathy and become more numerous in severe NPDR. They are not specific for proliferative diabetic retinopathy.

Intraretinal Microvascular Abnormalities (IRMA) (Option D): IRMA are dilated intraretinal collateral vessels that develop in response to retinal ischemia and are a feature of severe NPDR. Unlike neovascularization, they remain within the retina and do not breach the internal limiting membrane, making them pre-proliferative rather than proliferative changes.



Reference:
  1. Parsons Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Pages 291, 292
  2. Yanoff and Duker Ophthalmology, 5th Edition, Page 546
  3. Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 505

Explanation:

The presence of extensive retinal hemorrhages, venous beading, and moderate IRMA in one quadrant indicates severe non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR). For severe NPDR, the follow-up interval is every 4 months.

The 4-2-1 rule; is one or more of the:

question: A 58-year-old male with Type 2 diabetes undergoes a fundus examination, revealing extensive retinal hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, venous beading, and moderate intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA) in one quadrant. What is the most appropriate follow-up interval for this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
Optic disc hypoplasia has a congenitally small disc with reduced nerve fibers but no edema or peripapillary involvement, so the blind spot remains normal or small and does not enlarge, unlike conditions causing disc edema or peripapillary pathology.

Causes of Blind Spot Enlargement

Optic Disc Edema
  • Papilledema (raised intracranial pressure) (Option C ruled out)
  • Optic neuritis with disc edema
  • Anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (AION)
  • Hypertensive papillopathy

Peripapillary Retinal / Choroidal Disease
  • Peripapillary chorioretinitis
  • Peripapillary coloboma
  • Peripapillary atrophy (Option A ruled out)

Retinal Nerve Fibre Layer Abnormalities

Medullated (myelinated) nerve fibres extending into peripapillary retina (Option D ruled out)

Space-Occupying or Inflammatory Lesions Near Disc
  • Optic disc drusen (with apparent elevation)
  • Optic nerve head or orbital tumors

question: A patient undergoes perimetry and is found to have an enlarged physiological blind spot. Which of the following conditions does not cause expansion of the blind spot?

correctAnswer: D. They are primarily located in the ganglion cell layer
explanationHtml:
Explanation:
The cell described is the Müller cell, a specialized macroglial cell present in large numbers in the human retina that provides essential structural and metabolic support, spans the entire retinal thickness, forms the inner and outer limiting membranes, and has its nuclei in the inner nuclear layer.

Müller cell (retinal radial macroglial cell)

Anatomy

  • Span almost full retinal thickness
  • Nuclei in inner nuclear layer (Option A ruled out)
  • Form outer limiting membrane (apical) and inner limiting membrane (basal) (Option B ruled out)

Functions

  • Structural support across entire retina (Option C ruled out)
  • Ionic homeostasis (K⁺ regulation, water balance)
  • Metabolic support, waste removal, neurotransmitter recycling
  • Maintenance of inner blood-retinal barrier
  • Neuroprotection and photoreceptor support

Significance

  • Dysfunction → macular edema, gliosis, diabetic retinopathy, retinal degeneration
  • Respond to injury with gliosis and altered barrier function


Reference:
  1. Parson’s Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page 41.
  2. Gray's Anatomy, 42nd Edition, Page 808.

Explanation:
The given clinical scenario of an extremely preterm infant with rapidly progressive Zone I Stage 3 ROP without peripheral ridge formation represents aggressive posterior ROP (AP-ROP). Immediate intravitreal anti-VEGF injection is the treatment of choice due to rapid VEGF-mediated neovascularization in the immature posterior retina.

Retinopathy of Prematurity (ROP)

Epidemiology

Preterm infants <32 weeks GA or <1500 g, especially with prolonged oxygen

Pathophysiology

Phase 1: Hyperoxia → vaso-obliteration

Phase 2: Retinal hypoxia → VEGF surge → neovascularization → risk of tractional RD

Zones (retinal location)

Zone I: 2-disc diameter circle around optic disc (posterior pole)

Zone II: Macula to nasal ora serrata

Zone III: Temporal peripheral retina

Stages

Stage 1: Demarcation line

Stage 2: Elevated ridge

Stage 3: Extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation

Stage 4: Partial tractional retinal detachment

Stage 5: Total funnel retinal detachment

Screening

  • Infants <32 weeks GA or <1500 g
  • First exam: 4-6 weeks chronological age or 31-33 weeks postconception
  • Follow-up: weekly/biweekly depending on severity

Treatment

  • Immediate intravitreal anti-VEGF (Zone I AP-ROP)
  • Laser photocoagulation (Zone II threshold ROP) (Option A ruled out)
  • Observation only for mild, non-plus disease (Option C ruled out)


Prophylactic oral corticosteroids (Option D): No role for systemic steroids; increases systemic complications in preterm infants.



Reference:

Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 549.

Congenital cataract (Option C): Lens opacity causes leukocoria but lacks retinal traction or fibrovascular proliferation.

question: A premature neonate who received oxygen therapy for respiratory distress is noted to have a white pupillary reflex on examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: B. Stage 3 ROP in zone II involving 5 contiguous clock hours with plus disease
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The classical definition of threshold ROP is Stage 3 ROP with plus disease in zone I or II involving ≥5 contiguous or ≥8 cumulative clock hours.

Threshold ROP

Prethreshold ROP

Stage 3 ROP + plus disease in zone I or II, involving ≥5 contiguous or ≥8 cumulative clock hours of extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation.

Eyes not meeting full threshold but at high risk:

  • Any ROP in zone I
  • Stage 2 or 3 in zone II with plus disease
  • Stage 3 in zone II without sufficient clock hours

[[figure-1]]

Stage 3 ROP in zone I involving 5 contiguous clock hours without plus disease (Option A): Lacks plus disease, so it qualifies only as prethreshold ROP.

Stage 2 ROP in zone II involving 6 clock hours with plus disease (Option C): Stage 2 has no extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation, so it cannot be threshold.

Stage 3 ROP in zone I involving 3 clock hours with plus disease (Option D): Involves too few clock hours (<5 contiguous), so it does not meet threshold criteria.

question: Which of the following situations meets the classical definition of threshold ROP?

correctAnswer: C. Stable premature babies should ideally be transported to the ophthalmology OPD for screening
explanationHtml:
Explanation:
ROP screening is done at bedside in NICU, as premature infants are physiologically unstable and transport may cause apnea, hypothermia, or cardiorespiratory compromise.

Retinopathy of Prematurity (ROP) Screening

Who to screen
  • Infants ≤32 weeks GA or ≤1500 g
  • Sicker or heavier infants if risk factors present

Timing of first screening
  • Based on Postmenstrual Age (PMA) or Postnatal Age (PNA) (Option A ruled out)
  • Usually 32 weeks PMA or 4 weeks PNA, whichever is later
  • Extremely preterm (<28 wks GA) may need earlier screening for aggressive posterior ROP (Option B ruled out)

Location

  • Screening must be at bedside in NICU (Option C)
  • Transport risks: apnea, hypothermia, cardiorespiratory instability

Method

  • Indirect ophthalmoscopy by trained ophthalmologist (gold standard) (Option D ruled out)
  • Can use 28 D lens or wide-field imaging
  • Pupil dilation + topical anesthesia + neonatal eyelid speculum

Follow up

  • Every 1-3 weeks until retinal vascularization complete
  • ~10% need treatment
  • Long-term follow-up for refractive errors, strabismus, amblyopia


Reference:
  1. Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 540.
  2. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10981436/

question: A preterm infant born at 28 weeks of gestation is now 14 days old and recovering from respiratory distress in the NICU. The pediatrician asks when to arrange the first ROP screening. When should the baby be scheduled for examination, considering the current age of the infant?

correctAnswer: D. Duration since diabetes was diagnosed
explanationHtml:
Explanation:


Duration of diabetes is the strongest predictor of diabetic retinopathy. The risk rises with cumulative exposure of retinal microvasculature to hyperglycemia.

  • Primary determinant: Duration of diabetes is the strongest predictor; risk rises with cumulative exposure of retinal vessels to hyperglycemia. (Option D)
  • Glycemic control: Tight control slows progression but does not replace duration as the main factor. (Option C ruled out)
  • Other risk factors:
    • Hypertension → accelerates progression (Option A ruled out)
    • Nephropathy, pregnancy → worsen DR
    • Age → not a direct cause; risk depends on metabolic exposure. (Option B ruled out)

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
Fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) shows an enlarged foveal avascular zone (FAZ) with surrounding capillary non-perfusion, indicative of diabetic macular ischemia (DMI). The dark hypofluorescent area represents absent capillary perfusion.

Premacular hemorrhage (Option A) produces sharply demarcated hypofluorescence due to blocked fluorescence from blood located in the subhyaloid or sub-ILM space. Retinal vessels are obscured, and it represents a pre-retinal blood collection, not a capillary perfusion defect.

[[figure-1]]

Macular edema (Option B) shows hyperfluorescence with late leakage, often in a petaloid (flower-petal) pattern in cystoid macular edema due to dye pooling in the outer plexiform layer.

[[figure-2]]

Submacular hemorrhage (Option C) causes hypofluorescence due to blocked choroidal fluorescence, but overlying retinal vessels remain visible; it represents a space-occupying subretinal blood lesion, not a microvascular perfusion defect.

[[figure-3]]

question: A 58-year-old patient with long-standing diabetes and hypertension presents with a gradual painless reduction of central vision. Fundus fluorescein angiography shows a dark, irregular zone at the fovea with surrounding capillary dropout and an enlarged foveal avascular zone (FAZ). What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Answer: (A) Beaten bronze appearance

Explanation:

Among the given options Beaten bronze appearance is seen in the fundus examination of a patient with Stargardt disease.

Stargardt’s disease

  • The most common macular dystrophy.
  • Presents early, typically in the first decade of life.
  • Mainly a dystrophy of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE).

Fundus examination findings:

  • Beaten bronze appearance

[[figure-1]]

  • Snail-like appearance

[[figure-2]]

  • On FFA (Fundus fluorescein angiography) : Dark choroid/ silent choroid sign.(Option C)
    • Not a fundoscopy finding.
    • Due to dense lipofuscin deposition in the RPE, which blocks background choroidal fluorescence.

[[figure-3]]

  • Cotton wool spots and hard exudates (Option B): Seen in vascular retinal diseases such as diabetic retinopathy, hypertensive retinopathy, CRVO, etc.
  • Honeycomb appearance (Option D): Seen in cystoid macular edema (CME).



Reference:

AK Khurana Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th Edition, Pg.159,287, 301,304

question: Which of the following is a characteristic finding in the fundus examination of a patient with Stargardt disease?

explanationHtml:
Answer: D) Group A; Laser photocoagulation

Explanation:

  • The tumor in this case fits Group A criteria of the International Classification of Retinoblastoma:
    • Tumor confined to the retina
    • Located posterior to the equator
    • <3 mm in size
    • >3 mm from the fovea and >1.5 mm from the optic disc
    • No subretinal or vitreous seeding
  • Laser photocoagulation is an appropriate focal treatment for small tumors like this in Group A.

International Classification of Retinoblastoma (ICRB)

Group

Description

Treatment

Group A

Small intraretinal tumors (<3 mm), away from foveola/optic disc, no seeding

Focal therapy (laser photocoagulation, cryotherapy)

Group B

All remaining discrete tumors confined to retina, any size or location; no seeding

Systemic chemotherapy ± focal therapy

Group C

Local subretinal/vitreous seeding, discrete

Chemotherapy ± focal

Group D

Diffuse seeding

Chemoreduction ± external beam radiation

Group E

Extensive tumor, neovascular glaucoma, opaque media, invasion

Enucleation

question: A 14-month-old child is diagnosed with retinoblastoma in the right eye. The tumor is confined to the retina, located posterior to equator, measures 2.5 mm in greatest dimension, and is located 3.5 mm from the fovea. There is no vitreous or subretinal seeding. According to the International Classification of Retinoblastoma (ICRB), how would this tumor be classified, and what will be the appropriate treatment?

explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D) Optic nerve glioma

Explanation:
The case presented describes a classic presentation of retinoblastoma, for which optic nerve glioma is not a differential diagnosis.

  • Optic nerve gliomas usually present with proptosis, visual loss, and optic nerve swelling, but not typically with leukocoria or an intraocular mass with calcification. Various conditions other than retinoblastoma, which present as leukocoria are collectively called pseudoglioma.

Causes of Leukocoria:

  • Congenital cataract
  • Inflammatory deposits in vitreous following a plastic cyclitis or choroiditis,
  • Coloboma of the choroid,
  • Retinopathy of prematurity (Option C)
  • Persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous (Option B)
  • Toxocara endophthalmitis
  • Exudative retinopathy of Coats (Option A)

On examination, the child has strabismus. Which of the following is NOT a condition to be considered in the differential diagnosis of this presentation?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The question describes a classic presentation of retinoblastoma, which is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in children. The specific histological features in retinoblastoma is Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes

  • Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes: Rosettes with a central lumen.

[[figure-1]]

Homer-Wright rosettes (Option A), Pseudorosettes (Option C), Undifferentiated tumor cells (Option D) are histological features seen in retinoblastoma, but are not highly specific.

  • Homer Wright rosettes → pseudorosettes without lumen.

question: A 2-year-old child presents with leukocoria in the right eye. Fundus examination reveals a white, elevated mass in the retina. Histopathological examination of the tumor shows rosettes with central lumen. Which of the following is the most specific histological feature for this condition?

correctAnswer: B. Retinoblastoma typically arises from a germline mutation in the RB1 gene, followed by a second somatic mutation.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical image shows leukocoria in the left eye, suggestive of retinoblastoma. Retinoblastoma is typically caused by a germline mutation in the RB1 gene (inherited or de novo) followed by a second somatic mutation or "second hit" in the retina, leading to the development of the tumor.

Knudson’s Two-Hit Hypothesis: Development of retinoblastoma requires two hits (mutations) in the RB1 tumor suppressor gene (chromosome 13q14).

  • Hereditary cases:
    • First hit = germline mutation (inherited).
    • Second hit = somatic mutation.
    • These children often develop bilateral and multifocal retinoblastomas.
  • Sporadic cases:
    • Both hits occur as somatic mutations.
    • Tumor usually unilateral and unifocal.

  • Retinoblastoma can be inherited in an autosomal dominant manner, with affected individuals having a 100% chance of passing on the mutation (Option A): While retinoblastoma is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, this option does not explain the second-hit mechanism.
  • Affected children with retinoblastoma often have mutations in both the RB1 and TP53 genes (Option C): TP53 mutations are seen in Li-Fraumeni syndrome, not in retinoblastoma, which is primarily associated with RB1 mutations.
  • A single mutation in the RB1 gene is usually sufficient for the development of retinoblastoma in both familial and sporadic cases (Option D): A single mutation in the RB1 gene is insufficient to cause retinoblastoma; a second somatic mutation is required.


Reference:
  1. AK Khurana Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th Edition, Page 314
  2. Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 861

question: A 2-year-old child presents with the following findings as shown in the image. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in the RB1 gene. Which of the following statements best describes the genetic findings associated with this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient’s symptoms and fundoscopy findings, including fibrous tissue contraction and retinal elevation without retinal breaks, are consistent with tractional retinal detachment. In this condition, the primary treatment approach is pars plana vitrectomy, which removes the vitreous and addresses the traction caused by the fibrous tissue, thereby relieving the retinal detachment.

  • Treatment for tractional retinal detachment:
    • Pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) is the standard approach for tractional retinal detachment.
    • It involves removing cutting the vitreoretinal tractional bands and internal tamponade with either a long-acting gas or silicon oil.

[[figure-1]]

Laser photocoagulation (Option A) is used in proliferative retinopathies to prevent further neovascularization but does not address existing tractional detachment.

Cryotherapy with scleral buckling (Option B) is effective in rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, not for tractional detachment.

Pneumatic retinopexy (Option D) is not suitable for tractional or exudative detachments, as it primarily addresses rhegmatogenous detachment with retinal breaks.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 681, 683-689

question: A 55-year-old woman with a history of proliferative diabetic retinopathy presents with sudden vision changes in her right eye. She reports seeing floaters and flashes of light. On fundoscopy, there is evidence of fibrous tissue contraction and retinal elevation, but no retinal breaks are seen. What is the most appropriate treatment approach for this patient?

correctAnswer: B. Pneumatic retinopexy with gas injection
explanationHtml:
Answer: B) Pneumatic retinopexy with gas injection

Explanation:

This patient has a fresh retinal detachment with a small break in the upper quadrant. Pneumatic retinopexy is an appropriate choice for treating retinal detachments with small breaks in the superior retina.

Pneumatic retinopexy:

  • A minimally invasive quick and OP based procedure to reattach the retina.
  • Uses an intravitreal gas bubble with cryotherapy or laser to seal retinal breaks.
  • Common gases: Sulfur hexafluoride (SF6) and perfluoropropane (C3F8).
  • Used for uncomplicated retinal detachments.
  • Ideal for small breaks or multiple breaks covering less than two clock hours in the upper peripheral retina.

[[figure-1]]

  • Intravitreal anti-VEGF injection (Option A): Primarily used for neovascular diseases, such as wet AMD, but not for retinal detachment.
  • Pars plana vitrectomy with silicone oil tamponade (Option C): Usually reserved for complicated cases like extensive vitreoretinal traction or multiple breaks. In this case, the detachment is relatively simple, and pneumatic retinopexy is more suitable.
  • Drainage of subretinal fluid with diathermy to seal the break (Option D): While it can be part of the management for retinal detachment, it is not the primary treatment for simple rhegmatogenous detachments with small breaks.




Reference:

AK Khurana Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th Ed, Pg. 311, 312

question: A 60-year-old man presents with a sudden onset of flashes of light and a shadow resembling a curtain in the peripheral vision of his right eye. He denies any recent trauma. On examination, fundus evaluation reveals a retinal detachment with a retinal break in the upper temporal quadrant. What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?

explanationHtml:
Answer: A) Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment

Explanation:

  • Sudden appearance of flashes of light, followed by a dark cloud or veil in the peripheral, examination reveals a greyish reflex in the affected quadrant of the retina are the features of Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment
  • Retinal detachment refers to the separation of the neurosensory retina from the retinal pigment epithelium.

Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD):

  • “Regma” = break in the retina.
  • The break can be either:
    • Hole (degeneration, e.g., lattice degeneration in pathological myopia)
    • Tear (traction-induced, usually horseshoe-shaped)
  • Symptoms:
    • Initial flashes of light (photopsia) from traction on rods and cones.
    • Followed by curtain/wheel falling over peripheral vision.

[[figure-1]]

  • Examination: gray reflex and detached retina.

[[figure-2]]

Tractional Retinal Detachment (Option B): Often seen in proliferative diabetic retinopathy or trauma, presenting with gradual vision loss, not acute symptoms.

Exudative Retinal Detachment (Option C): Associated with systemic or ocular inflammatory diseases and presents without the classic flashes or floaters.

Macular Hole (Option D): Causes central vision loss but does not present with peripheral shadows or flashes.



Reference:

AK Khurana Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th Ed, Pg. 309, 310

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Pg. 681

question: A 55-year-old man reports the sudden appearance of flashes of light, followed by a dark cloud or veil in the peripheral vision of his left eye. Examination reveals a greyish reflex in the affected quadrant of the retina. What type of retinal detachment is most likely in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Answer: B) Best Vitelliform Macular Dystrophy

Explanation:

The given clinical features and examination findings are suggestive of Best Vitelliform Macular Dystrophy.

Best’s vitelliform macular dystrophy

  • Fundoscopy shows the classic “sunny-side up” or “egg yolk” lesion in the macula.
  • Caused by lipofuscin deposition in the macula.
  • Inheritance: autosomal dominant.
  • Disease of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE).
  • Initially, it causes a mild reduction of vision, but vision drops significantly in the later vitelliruptive stage.

[[figure-1]]

Vitelliruptive: Lesion fragments (scrambled egg appearance)

[[figure-2]]

  • Stargardt’s disease (Option A): Presents with yellowish flecks in the macula and beaten bronze/snail-track appearance.
  • Retinitis pigmentosa (Option C): A dystrophy of rods and cones, starting in the mid-periphery.
    • Classic triad: waxy disc pallor, attenuated vessels, bone-spicule pigmentation.
  • Leber’s congenital amaurosis (Option D): Severe form of retinal dystrophy presenting with early-onset blindness.


Reference:

AK Khurana Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th Ed, Pg. 301

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Pg. 631-634

question: A 10-year-old child presents with a mild reduction in vision in both eyes. Fundus examination reveals a "sunny-side up egg" appearance in the macular region with yellowish subretinal material. The child’s father has a similar history of visual impairment since childhood. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: B. Fundus examination showing flame-shaped hemorrhages
explanationHtml:
Answer: (B) Fundus examination showing flame-shaped hemorrhages

Explanation:

  • The given clinical case and examination findings are suggestive of Stargardt disease.
  • Fundus examination showing flame-shaped hemorrhages is seen in hypertensive retinopathy.

Stargardt disease

  • Also known as juvenile macular dystrophy (Option A), is the most common macular dystrophy.
  • Presents in first or second decade.

Investigations:

  • FFA: Dark choroid syndrome or silent choroid syndrome.
  • Fundus autofluorescence (Option D): Lipofuscin deposits have inherent autofluorescence, and can be detected without a dye.

Treatment

  • Avoid bright sunlight. Use sunglasses
  • Avoid vitamin A (Option C), as it promotes lipofuscinosis.


Reference:

question: A 16-year-old patient presents with progressive vision loss. On examination, the ophthalmologist notes a central scotoma and yellowish-white flecks in the macular region of the retina. A diagnosis of Stargardt disease is made. All of the following are true statements about Stargardt disease, except:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • This patient’s distortion of vision (metamorphopsia), decreased visual acuity to 6/18, history of steroid intake, with OCT showing foveal detachment, and Fluorescein angiography showing smokestack appearance, is suggestive of Central Serous Chorioretinopathy (CSR)

Central Serous Chorioretinopathy (CSCR)

  • Demographics: More common in young/middle-aged men

  • Risk factors: Stress, Type A personality, steroids

  • Symptoms:

    • Blurred central vision (decreased visual acuity, typically 6/6 → 6/18)

    • Metamorphopsia (distortion of images)

[[figure-1]]

  • OCT: Serous detachment of neurosensory retina at the fovea

[[figure-2]]

  • Fluorescein angiography: Smokestack / Inkblot appearance

[[figure-3]]

Course: Often self-limiting in the acute stage

  • Age-related macular degeneration (Option B): ARMD typically occurs in older patients (>50) and is associated with drusen and neovascularization, which are absent here.

  • Cystoid macular edema (Option C): CME usually follows ocular surgeries or inflammation and presents with cystic spaces on OCT, not the subretinal detachment seen here.

  • Retinal vein occlusion (Option D): RVO presents with retinal hemorrhages and cotton wool spots on examination, not the isolated macular elevation and leakage seen in CSCR.



Reference:

AK Khurana Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th Edition, Pg. 302, 303

question: A 35-year-old male presents with sudden distrubunce of vision in his right eye for two weeks. He reports distortion of images. He has been intermittently using corticosteroids for allergies. His Visual acuity in the right eye is 6/18. FFA and OCT findings are given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Answer: (D) Conductive deafness

Explanation:

Retinitis pigmentosa associated with sensory neural deafness- Usher syndrome

Systemic associations in Retinitis Pigmentosa

  • Refsum's disease (Option A): It is a defect in the phytanic acid metabolism. RP+ Cerebellar ataxia+ Polyneuropathy. It is managed with a low phytanic acid diet.
  • Laurence-Moon-Bardet-Biedl syndrome (Option B): involves RP, mental retardation, obesity, polydactyly, and paraplegia.
  • Usher's syndrome: It is retinitis pigmentosa (RP) with Sensory neural deafness.
  • Kearns-Sayer syndrome (Option C): involves RP, heart block, and chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO).
  • Bassen-Kornzweig syndrome involves RP, acanthocytosis, abetalipoproteinemia, and ataxia. It is managed with a low-fat diet and vitamin supplements.



Reference:

AK Khurana Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th Edition, Pg.297, 298

question: Which of the following is not related to retinitis pigmentosa?

explanationHtml:
Answer: (A) Electroretinography (ERG)

Explanation:

ERG is a sensitive diagnostic test in retinitis pigmentosa that shows reduced scotopic, subnormal responses in early disease and becomes completely extinguished in advanced disease.

Electroretinogram (ERG)

  • Investigation of choice for retinitis pigmentosa (RP).
  • ERG has an A wave, a B wave, and a small C wave (corresponding to retinal pigment epithelial activity, usually not emphasized).
  • A wave = activity of rods and cones (negative wave).
  • B wave = activity of bipolar cells.
  • In RP, both A and B waves are diminished.
  • This makes ERG the most important diagnostic tool.

[[figure-1]]

  • Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) (Option B)
    • Not significant in RP.
    • OCT is more useful in macular diseases, not in diagnosing RP.
  • Visual Field Testing (Option C)
    • Done in RP, but not the investigation of choice.
    • Important finding:
      • Early RP → Ring scotoma.
      • Late RP → Tunnel vision.
  • Electrooculogram (EOG) (Option D)
    • More significant in retinal pigment epithelial dystrophies, such as Stargardt’s disease and Best’s disease.
    • Not the main investigation for RP.




Reference:
  1. AK Khurana Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th Edition, Pg.297, 298
  2. Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Pg. 620, 621

question: A 30-year-old woman presents with progressive night blindness and gradual loss of peripheral vision over the past few years. Her family history reveals that her father had similar symptoms. On examination, you observe characteristic retinal changes, including bone spicule pigmentation. To evaluate the functional status of her retina more accurately, which diagnostic test would you choose to confirm the suspicion of retinitis pigmentosa (RP)?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The fundus photograph demonstrates the classic triad of retinitis pigmentosa (RP): bone-spicule pigmentation in the mid-peripheral retina, attenuation of the retinal arterioles, and waxy pallor of the optic disc.

  • The patient's history of progressive nyctalopia (night blindness) followed by peripheral visual field loss (tunnel vision) is characteristic of this inherited retinal dystrophy, which primarily affects rod photoreceptors before involving cones.
  • RP is genetically heterogeneous and may occur as autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked, or isolated (simplex/sporadic) disease.
  • The most common syndromic association is Usher syndrome, which combines retinitis pigmentosa with sensorineural hearing loss.
  • There is no definitive cure, and management includes genetic counselling, low-vision rehabilitation, treatment of complications, and gene therapy for selected genetic subtypes (e.g., biallelic RPE65 mutations).

Chronic Central Serous Chorioretinopathy (Option B): Chronic central serous chorioretinopathy causes serous detachment of the neurosensory retina at the macula, leading to central visual distortion. It does not produce bone-spicule pigmentation, retinal arteriolar attenuation, or waxy optic disc pallor.

Age-Related Macular Degeneration (Option C): Age-related macular degeneration primarily affects the macula and presents with drusen (dry AMD) or choroidal neovascularisation (wet AMD). It causes central, rather than peripheral, visual loss and lacks the classic RP fundus triad.

Toxoplasmic Retinochoroiditis (Option D): Toxoplasmic retinochoroiditis presents with focal necrotising retinitis and dense vitritis, producing the classic "headlight in the fog" appearance. Healed lesions form localised pigmented chorioretinal scars, not the diffuse bone-spicule pigmentation characteristic of retinitis pigmentosa.



Reference:
  1. AK Khurana Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th Edition, Pages 296, 297, 298, 303
  2. Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 623

A 32-year-old female presents with difficulty seeing in low light and peripheral vision loss that has gradually worsened over several years. On fundoscopy, the following findings are noted.

  • While chronic central serous chorioretinopathy can cause retinal pigment epithelium changes, it typically does not present with the characteristic bull's eye maculopathy appearance.

Etiological causes of bull’s eye maculopathy include:

  • Chloroquine maculopathy (Option C)
  • Hydroxychloroquine (Option A)
  • Cone dystrophy (Option B)
  • Battens disease

question:
A 32-year-old woman presents with gradual central vision loss in both eyes. Fundus examination reveals concentric rings of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) atrophy and hyperpigmentation centred on the fovea, creating a characteristic appearance. The image showing the appearance is given below:

Which of the following is least likely to be associated with this condition?

explanationHtml:
Answer: A) Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT)

Explanation:

OCT is currently considered the most sensitive modality for detecting exudative (wet) AMD as it picks up RPE detachments and early CNV changes non-invasively.

  • Wet (exudative) AMD → hallmark features:
    • Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) detachment
    • Choroidal neovascularization (CNV)

Note: Dry AMD → OCT shows outer retinal tubulations.

[[figure-1]]

  • Slit-lamp biomicroscopy (Option B): basic clinical exam, not sensitive.

  • Indocyanine green angiography (ICG) (Option C) is better for choroidal pathologies because it binds 98% to plasma proteins and persists longer, so occult CNV is better seen.

  • Fluorescein angiography (Option D) can detect CNV, but limited (misses occult CNV).

question: A 68-year-old woman presents with gradual vision loss in her right eye over the past 6 months. Her ophthalmologist suspects age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and orders further tests. What is the most sensitive modality to detect exudative AMD?

correctAnswer: D. AMD is the most common cause of permanent central visual loss after 6th decade
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Age-related Macular Degeneration (AMD) is a nonhereditary degeneration involving the choriocapillaris, Bruch's membrane, retinal pigment epithelium, and photoreceptors. It is the most common cause of permanent central visual loss after 6th decade.

  • AMD is a nonhereditary degeneration (Option A) primarily affecting the macula involving the choriocapillaris, Bruch's membrane, retinal pigment epithelium, and photoreceptors.
  • Wet AMD accounts for only 10% of all AMD cases but is responsible for 90% of severe vision loss in AMD patients (Option B).
  • Choroidal neovascularization is a characteristic of wet AMD, not dry AMD. Dry AMD is characterized by drusen, RPE abnormalities, and geographic atrophy (Option C).

Angioid streaks are crack-like dehiscences in Bruch's membrane, appearing as irregular reddish-brown or gray lines radiating from the optic disc.

  • Asymptomatic angioid streaks do not require treatment.
  • However, anti-VEGF therapy can be used to prevent choroidal neovascularization.

Angioid Streaks:

  • Associations:
    • Pseudoxanthoma elasticum (PXE) - Most common
    • Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
    • Paget's disease
    • Sickle cell disease (Option B)
  • Complication: Choroidal neovascularization (CNV) frequently develops in affected patients (Option C)
  • Treatment: Anti-VEGF therapy for choroidal neovascularization

question: Which of the following statements about angioid streaks is incorrect?

explanationHtml:
Answer: D) Optic disc edema

Explanation:

The patient's history and fundus findings are consistent with pathological myopia.

  • Pathological myopia is a progressive form of myopia characterized by excessive axial elongation of the eyeball and degenerative changes in the retina and choroid.
  • Optic disc edema is not a feature of pathological myopia; the disc may appear tilted, but edema is absent unless there is another pathology (e.g., papilledema, optic neuritis).

Pathological Myopia

  • Pathological/degenerative/progressive myopia is a rapidly progressive error that starts in childhood at 5-10 years of age and results in high myopia (>-6D) during early adult life.
  • Features:

Foster-Fuchs spots (Option A)

[[figure-1]]

Lattice degeneration (Option B)

[[figure-2]]

Posterior staphyloma (Option C)

[[figure-3]]

question: A 28-year-old woman with a history of high myopia since childhood presents for a routine eye examination. She reports occasional floaters and difficulty seeing at night. On fundus examination, the ophthalmologist notes a tilted optic disc, peripapillary atrophy, and a myopic crescent. Which of the following is NOT typically associated with the condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Cystoid Macular Edema (CME) is associated with fluid accumulation in the outer plexiform and inner nuclear layers of the retina, leading to cystoid spaces.

  • The OCT findings of multiple cystic spaces centered around the foveola.
  • Fundus Fluorescein Angiography shows leakage and dye accumulation in the macular region, with a "flower petal appearance" in late frames.
  • The history of recent cataract surgery further supports this diagnosis, as CME is a known postoperative complication. (also known as Irvine-Gass syndrome)

Causes of Cystoid Macular Edema (CME)

  • Post cataract surgery- Irvine-Gass syndrome
  • Diabetic retinopathy
  • Retinal vein occlusion
  • Uveitis.
  • Retinitis pigmentosa.
  • Drugs: Niacin, epinephrine

Fluorescein Angiography: Shows leakage and dye accumulation in the macular region, with a "flower petal appearance" in late frames.

Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT): Demonstrates loss of foveal depression, cystoid spaces, and overall retinal thickening.

  • Diabetic Retinopathy (Option A): Typically shows diffuse retinal thickening and other diabetic changes, not the cystoid spaces seen in CME.

  • Central Retinal Vein Occlusion (Option B): Often associated with retinal hemorrhages and diffuse edema, but CME's cystoid spaces are more specific.

  • Central Serous Retinopathy (Option D) is characterized by "ink-blot" or "smoke-stack" leakage patterns on FFA, and neurosensory retinal and RPE detachment on OCT. CSR typically does not present with the cystoid pattern seen in CME.



Reference:

AK Khurana Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th Edition, Pages 303, 304, 305

question: A 65-year-old presents with visual blurring in the left eye, 20/40 vision, and a history of cataract surgery three months ago. Fundus examination shows retinal thickening and a dull foveal reflex. OCT and FFA findings are given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Vitreous Hemorrhage (VH):

  • Seen as blood floating in the vitreous, occluding the view of the retina.
  • Secondary to proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) is a cause of severe vision loss in diabetic patients.
  • Absence of fundus glow is a feature of Vitreous hemorrhage
  • In PDR, fibrovascular tissue lies flat on the retina or attaches to the posterior vitreous, leading to vitreous traction, retinal separation, and vessel rupture. This is the most common cause of VH in adults.

Options B, C & D: Acute anterior uveitis, Optic neuritis and Acute congestive glaucoma can also cause sudden loss of vision but there is no loss of fundus glow.

  1. Parsons Diseases of the Eye, Edition 23, page no: 289,290

question: A patient has sudden loss of vision and there is no fundus glow. There is no history of trauma, what could be the likely cause?

explanationHtml:
• The findings described in the patient—a visual acuity of 6/9, preretinal hemorrhages, and neovascularization at the optic disc—are consistent with proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR), a severe form of diabetic retinopathy.
  • In proliferative diabetic retinopathy, abnormal neovascularization (growth of new, fragile blood vessels) occurs in response to retinal ischemia. These new blood vessels are prone to leakage, causing preretinal hemorrhages and potentially leading to tractional retinal detachment.
  • Pan-retinal photocoagulation (PRP) is the first-line treatment for proliferative diabetic retinopathy. It involves the application of laser burns to the retina to ablate areas of ischemia, thereby reducing the stimulus for neovascularization. The goal is to prevent further progression, bleeding, and potential vision loss.

Abbreviated Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) classification of diabetic retinopathy

Category

Management

Non-Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (NPDR):

No Diabetic Retinopathy

Review in 12 months

Very Mild NPDR

Microaneurysms only

Review most patients in 12 months

Mild NPDR

Any or all of the: microaneurysms, retinal hemorrhages, exudates, and cotton-wool spots, up to the level of moderate NPDR. No intraretinal microvascular anomalies (IRMA) or significant beading.

Review range 6-12 months, depending on the severity of signs, stability, systemic factors, and patient's circumstances

Moderate NPDR

  • Severe retinal hemorrhages in 1-3 quadrants or mild IRMA
  • Significant venous beading can be present in no more than 1 quadrant
  • Cotton wool spots commonly present

Review in approximately 6 months

Severe NPDR

The 4-2-1 rule; is one or more of the:

  • Severe hemorrhages in all 4 quadrants
  • Significant venous beading in 2 or more quadrants
  • Moderate IRMA in 1 or more quadrants

Review in 4 months

Very severe NPDR

Two or more of the criteria for severe NPDR

Review in 2-3 months

Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR):

Mild-moderate PDR

New vessels on the disc (NVD) or new vessels elsewhere (NVE), but extent insufficient to meet the high-risk criteria

Treatment is considered according to the severity of signs, stability, systemic factors, and the patient's circumstances such as reliability of attendance for review. If not treated, review in up to 2 months

High-risk PDR

  • NVD greater than ⅓ disc area
  • Any NVD with vitreous hemorrhage
  • NVE greater than ½ disc area with vitreous hemorrhage

Treatment should be performed immediately when possible and certainly on the same day if symptomatic presentation with a good retinal view

Advanced diabetic eye disease

Is characterized by tractional retinal detachment. Significant persistent vitreous hemorrhage and neovascular glaucoma.

Vitreoretinal surgery with photocoagulation

Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR):

  • Panretinal Photocoagulation (PRP):
    • PRP of ischemic area reduces metabolic demand and prevents the release of vasoproliferative factors by conversion of hypoxic areas into anoxic areas and creates inert scars from leaking vascular anomalies.
    • Laser used: Argon, frequency-doubled YAG or diode laser
    • In PRP, the inferior quadrant of the retina is first coagulated.
    • Untreated Areas: A circular area with a radius of 2.5 DD around the fovea is left untouched during treatment.
    • Each treatment requires 2000-3000 burns, administered over two to four sessions.

Anti-VEGF Therapy:

  • Bevacizumab, ranibizumab or aflibercept are used to control neovascularization.
  • Vitreoretinal Surgery: Advanced cases with tractional retinal detachment or unresolved vitreous hemorrhage require vitrectomy.

Focal laser photocoagulation (Option A): This is typically used for treating macular edema or localized areas of retinal leakage, not for the widespread ischemic retina seen in proliferative diabetic retinopathy.

Grid laser photocoagulation (Option C): This is also used to treat macular edema but is not the treatment of choice for proliferative diabetic retinopathy.

Scleral buckling (Option D): This procedure is used for retinal detachment, often caused by traction from proliferative diabetic retinopathy, but it's not the initial treatment for PDR. Pan-retinal photocoagulation is used before considering surgery in the event of a detachment.



Reference:
  • Parsons Diseases of the Eye, Edition 23, page no: 292,293
  • Yanoff and Duker Ophthalmology,Edition 5, Page 548-551
  • Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, Edition 9, page no: 497,498
question: What should be the subsequent course of action in managing a diabetic patient who has a visual acuity of 6/9 in one eye and further investigations reveal preretinal hemorrhages with neovascularization at the optic disc?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - Diabetic retinopathy

Explanation:

  • Microaneurysms are localized outpouchings of the capillary wall that may form by focal dilatation of the capillary wall where pericytes are absent or by fusion of two arms of a capillary loop.

Diabetic retinopathy Clinical Features:

Early NPDR or Background Diabetic Retinopathy

Severe NPDR or Preproliferative Diabetic Retinopathy
  • Affects small retinal vessels.
  • Earliest sign: Microaneurysm (Option B)
    • Fluorescein angiography (FA): Tiny hyperfluorescent dots.
  • Retinal hemorrhages: Both deep, i.e., in the inner nuclear or outer plexiform layer (dot and blot hemorrhage) and superficial, i.e., in nerve fiber layer (splinter or flame-shaped) hemorrhages
  • Hard exudates:
    • White or yellow waxy patches with well-defined margins, often at the posterior pole, in the outer plexiform layer.
    • FA: Hypofluorescence with dense exudates.
  • Edema is not marked.
  • Increased inner retinal hypoxia: Leads to multiple retinal hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, venous beading, vascular loops, intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMAs), and large areas of capillary nonperfusion.
  • Cotton-Wool Spots:
    • Also called soft exudates or nerve fiber infarcts.
    • Result from ischemia, not exudation.
    • Caused by obstruction of axoplasmic flow, leading to swelling and a white, fluffy appearance.
    • FA: Focal hypofluorescence due to local ischemia.
  • Venous Beading:
    • Indicates sluggish retinal circulation.
    • Typically adjacent to large areas of capillary nonperfusion.
  • Intraretinal Microvascular Abnormalities (IRMA):
    • Dilated capillaries act as collateral channels.
    • Bypass capillary bed and is often seen adjacent to capillary nonperfusion.
    • FA: Focal hypofluorescence

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Incorrect Options:

Retinal detachment (Option A) involves the separation of the sensory retina from the underlying retinal pigment epithelium (RPE).

Uveitis (Option C) is inflammation of the uveal tract (iris, ciliary body, and choroid) and can cause symptoms such as pain, photophobia, and redness.

Glaucoma(Option D) primarily involves increased intraocular pressure, leading to optic nerve damage.

question: In which diseases are microaneurysms observed?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Neovascularization (such as on the disc) appears only in proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR), which is a more advanced stage of diabetic retinopathy, involving the growth of new blood vessels. Therefore, neovascularization of the disc is not part of very severe NPDR.

Classification of Non-Progressive Diabetic Retinopathy (NPDR)

Severity

Definition

Very mild nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy

Microaneurysms only

Mild nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy

Microaneurysms plus hard exudates, cotton-wool spots, and/or mild retinal hemorrhages

Moderate nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy

Microaneurysms plus mild intraretinal microvascular abnormalities or moderate retinal hemorrhages

Severe nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy

Any one of the following (4-2-1 Rule)

  • Severe retinal hemorrhages in four quadrants
  • Venous beading in at least two
  • Moderately severe intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA) in at least one quadrant

Very severe nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy

Any two of the following (4-2-1 Rule)

  • Severe retinal hemorrhages in four quadrants (Option C ruled out)
  • Venous beading in at least two (Option A ruled out)
  • Moderately severe intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA) in at least one quadrant (Option D ruled out)

Early NPDR or Background Diabetic Retinopathy

Severe NPDR or Preproliferative Diabetic Retinopathy
  • Affects small retinal vessels.
  • Earliest sign: Microaneurysm

  • Venous Beading:
    • Indicates sluggish retinal circulation.
    • Typically adjacent to large areas of capillary nonperfusion. (Option D)
  • Intraretinal Microvascular Abnormalities (IRMA):
    • Dilated capillaries act as collateral channels.
    • Bypass capillary bed and is often seen adjacent to capillary nonperfusion.
    • FA: Focal hypofluorescence

question: Which of the following is not seen in very severe NPDR?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option A - Amaurosis Fugax

  • Given the patient's clinical presentation of sudden, transient loss of vision in one eye, without pain, and the subsequent restoration of vision, along with the description of a curtain-like visual disturbance, is suggestive of amaurosis fugax

Incorrect Options:

Option B - Central Retinal Artery Occlusion: Central retinal artery occlusion involves the sudden blockage of the central retinal artery, leading to sudden and painless vision loss in one eye. However, in this condition, the vision loss is usually more severe and sustained, often leaving the patient with very poor vision or even complete blindness in the affected eye. The sudden and brief nature of the episode described by the patient makes central retinal artery occlusion less likely.

Option C - Central Retinal Vein Occlusion: Central retinal vein occlusion results from a blockage in the central retinal vein, causing a sudden painless loss of vision. However, the presentation of central retinal vein occlusion typically involves a more gradual and painless decrease in vision, without the sudden and transient nature of the episode described by the patient.

Option D - Hypertensive Retinopathy: Hypertensive retinopathy is associated with long-standing high blood pressure that leads to changes in the retinal blood vessels. It can cause symptoms such as blurred vision, but the sudden and transient nature of the episode, along with the complete loss and restoration of vision, is not consistent with hypertensive retinopathy.
