question: A 55-year-old male patient presents to the clinic with a complaint of sudden visual blurring that lasted for a short duration. He reports that during the episode, he completely lost vision in his left eye for a few minutes and then regained his vision. The patient denies any pain, headache, or other associated symptoms during the episode. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
• Fundoscopy shows the typical features of pale retina and cherry-red spot, and CRAO is the most likely diagnosis in this case. CRAO often presents with sudden, painless, unilateral vision loss, and it is considered an ophthalmologic emergency because of the potential for permanent vision loss.

Risk factors:

  • Atherosclerosis

  • Age

  • Hypertension

  • Cardiac Diseases

    • Atrial fibrillation: promotes blood clot formation, increasing CRAO risk

    • Mitral valve prolapse: this can lead to blood flow abnormalities and clot formation

    • Bacterial endocarditis: causes vegetation that can travel and occlude the retinal artery

  • Thrombophilic disorders

    • Hyperhomocysteinemia: elevated homocysteine levels increase clot formation risk

    • Antiphospholipid syndrome: an autoimmune disorder causing increased clot formation risk

    • Inherited anticoagulant defects: genetic conditions disrupting natural blood clotting regulation

  • Giant cell arteritis (GCA)

    • Inflammatory condition affecting blood vessels, often with severe visual loss

  • Other factors

    • Smoking

    • Diabetes mellitus

    • Oral contraceptive pills

Clinical features:

Symptoms:

  • Sudden, painless, profound vision loss

  • Painless, except in GCA: GCA-associated CRAO may present with headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, and/or pain around the temple

Clinical Signs:

  • Visual Acuity (VA): severely reduced, often to counting fingers or worse

  • Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD): Profound and sometimes total (amaurotic pupil)

Fundus Examination:

  • Retinal Whitening: Pale and opaque retina, particularly in the posterior pole

  • Cherry-Red Spot: Bright red area at the fovea due to the contrast between pale retina and underlying choroidal circulation

[[figure-1]]

  • Cattle truck appearance: Due to segmentation of blood column in retinal veins

[[figure-2]]

  • Attenuated Arteries: Narrowed and segmented retinal arterioles

  • Optic Disc Changes: Pale optic disc over time due to optic atrophy from prolonged ischemia is seen in chronic cases.

Fluorescein Angiography (FA)

  • Arterial Filling: Delayed

  • Masking of Background Fluorescence: Edematous retina blocks normal fluorescence from the choroid

  • Patent Cilioretinal Artery: Area of normal perfusion if a cilioretinal artery supplies the fovea, potentially preserving central vision

[[figure-3]]

Other Diagnostic Tests

Reveals retinal edema, structural changes, and possibly an embolic plaque within the retinal artery and other systemic causes.

  • Cranial MRI or CT

  • Carotid duplex scanning

  • Echocardiography

  • Thrombophilia screening

CRVO (Option B) (Central Retinal Vein Occlusion): Fundoscopic findings- Diffuse retinal hemorrhages (often in all quadrants), venous dilation, and cotton wool spots. The optic disc may be swollen, and there may be blood and thunder appearance. This is different from CRAO, where the retina is pale and a cherry-red spot is seen.

Diabetic Retinopathy (Option C): Fundoscopic findings- Microaneurysms, retinal hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, and hard exudates. These findings reflect chronic vascular changes in diabetes and are distinct from the acute ischemic signs seen in CRAO, which involve retinal pallor and cherry-red spots.

Cystoid Macular Edema (Option D) (CME): Fundoscopic findings- Cystic spaces in the macula, often with focal macular edema. This causes central vision blurring, but unlike CRAO, it doesn’t show retinal pallor or cherry-red spots. CME is more related to macular dysfunction rather than ischemia.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th edition, pg: 525, 527, 528
question: The image below displays the findings of a fundoscopy. What is the probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The findings of leukocoria, a cauliflower-like growth, and the presence of Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes on histopathology strongly suggest retinoblastoma, which is associated with mutations in the Rb gene.

The question describes a classic presentation of retinoblastoma, which is the MC primary intraocular malignancy in children.

The key features pointing to this diagnosis are:

  1. Age of presentation: Retinoblastoma typically occurs in young children, usually before 5 years of age.
  2. Leukocoria: This is the most common presenting sign of retinoblastoma, often described as a white pupillary reflex.
  3. Fundus examination: A white, elevated mass in the retina is characteristic of retinoblastoma.

Most specific histopathological feature of retinoblastoma is Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes, which are rosettes with a central lumen as shown in the diagram below.

[[figure-1]]

Histopathology and Diagnostic modalities for Retinoblastoma

Histopathology
  • Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes (highly specific)- These are composed of an ‘empty’ lumen surrounded by columnar cells
  • Homer-Wright rosettes - These are pseudo-rosettes and consist of cells surrounding a central lumen made up of their processes
  • Undifferentiated tumor cells
  • Areas of necrosis and calcification

Clinical Presentation
  • Leukocoria (60%)
  • Strabismus (20%)
  • Painful red eye (7%)
  • Poor vision (5%)
  • Asymptomatic (3%)

Fundus Examination
  • White, elevated mass in the retina
  • Can be endophytic, exophytic, or mixed growth

Imaging
  • CT scan: Calcification in 90% of cases
  • MRI: Better for evaluating optic nerve and extraocular extension
  • Ultrasound: Useful for initial screening

Genetic Testing
  • RB1 gene mutation on chromosome 13q14

ATP 7B gene (Option B): Mutations in the ATP7B gene are associated with Wilson's disease, a genetic disorder affecting copper metabolism, leading to copper buildup in various organs, including the liver and brain. It does not cause retinoblastoma.

Rhodopsin gene (Option C): The rhodopsin gene is associated with retinitis pigmentosa, a genetic condition causing progressive vision loss, but not with retinoblastoma.

FBN1 gene (Option D): Mutations in the FBN1 gene are responsible for Marfan syndrome, a connective tissue disorder affecting the heart, eyes, and bones, but not retinoblastoma.



Reference:

AK Khurana Textbook of Ophthalmology Edition 7th Pg. 314, 315
question: In a three-year-old boy, his parents have noticed a progressive decline in coordination over the last six months. During a physical examination, a growth resembling a cauliflower is observed in the left eye, along with leukocoria and the absence of a red reflex. Microscopic analysis of the sample reveals the presence of Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes. Which gene is associated with this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient describes a "curtain being pulled over the eye," which is a classic symptom of retinal detachment and represents progressive loss of the visual field as the retina separates.
  • The history of flashing lights (photopsia) is caused by traction on the retina as the vitreous pulls away, stimulating the photoreceptors.
  • Floaters occur due to vitreous degeneration, pigment cells, or small amounts of blood entering the vitreous cavity, often preceding retinal detachment.
  • The combination of flashes, floaters, and a curtain-like visual field defect is highly suggestive of a rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.
  • B-scan ultrasonography demonstrates a thick, highly reflective, folded membrane attached to the optic disc, which is characteristic of a detached retina. This investigation is especially useful when the fundus cannot be adequately visualized.
  • Retinal detachment is an ophthalmic emergency because prolonged separation of the neurosensory retina from the retinal pigment epithelium leads to irreversible photoreceptor damage and permanent vision loss.
  • Prompt treatment with laser photocoagulation, cryotherapy, pneumatic retinopexy, scleral buckle, or pars plana vitrectomy, depending on the type and extent of detachment, can preserve or restore vision, especially if the macula has not yet detached.

Glaucoma (Option A): It is a disease that damages the optic nerve, often caused by high pressure inside the eye. It typically causes a gradual loss or sudden loss of vision but curtain like effect is not seen.

Posterior vitreous detachment (Option B) commonly causes flashes and floaters, but it usually does not produce a curtain-like visual field defect or significant vision loss. On B-scan, the detached vitreous membrane is thinner and more mobile than the retina.

Corneal ulcer (Option D): They are painful sores on the surface of the eye that can cause redness, tearing, and sensitivity to light.



Reference:
  1. AK Khurana Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th Edition, Page 309, 310
  2. Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 681
question: A 61-year-old university professor complains of vision loss in his left eye. He compares the sensation to a curtain being pulled over his affected eye. Additionally, he experienced flashing lights and floaters a week ago. The provided image shows a B-scan of his left eye. What could be the possible diagnosis for his condition?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option A - Retinoblastoma:

  • Retinoblastoma is a malignant tumor that arises from immature retinal cells in young children, typically before the age of 5.
  • The tumor can present with leukocoria (most commonest presentation), strabismus , or an absent red reflex on examination.
  • Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes is a differentiated type of tumor characterized by columnar cells with a central lumen.

[[figure-1]]

Incorrect Options:

Option B - Neurofibroma: Neurofibromas are tumors that arise from nerve sheath cells and are often associated with the genetic disorder neurofibromatosis. In plexiform neurofibroma S-shaped deformity of the lid is observed.

Option C - Retinopathy of prematurity: It may cause retinal detachment and leukocoria but there is no history of prematurity and low birth weight.

Option D - Toxcariasis: It is a parasitic infection caused by roundworm Toxocara canis that can be acquired through ingestion of contaminated soil or food. It can present with leukocoria, strabismus, floaters, eosinophilia, and hypergammaglobulinemia.

question: A 3-year-old boy has had progressively increasing clumsiness over the past 6 months. On examination, his left eye shows leukocoria, an absent red reflex, and a cauliflower-like intraocular mass. Enucleation is performed, and histopathological examination of the specimen reveals Flexner–Wintersteiner rosettes. What is the most probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
• The most probable diagnosis in this scenario is toxoplasmosis uveitis, which is caused by Toxoplasma gondii
  • Toxoplasmosis is caused by the parasite Toxoplasma gondii and is a common cause of posterior uveitis. It can lead to punched-out lesions in the retina, which are characteristic of the disease. These lesions typically appear as well-defined, round areas of retinal scarring.
  • Fundoscopy shows focal necrotizing retinitis surrounded by a distinctive “headlight in the fog” appearance
  • An immunocompromised person living with cats is a risk factor for toxoplasmosis

Toxoplasmosis uveitis:

  • It is a protozoan infestation.
  • Organism: Toxoplasma gondii
  • Definitive host - cats
  • Intermediate hosts - humans
  • Systemic lesions are more common in immunocompromised patients

Clinical manifestation:

  • Most common cause of posterior uveitis and focal necrotizing retinitis (90% of cases)
  • Congenital
    • Inactive disease - Healed punched out heavily pigmented chorioretinal scars in the macular area

[[figure-1]]

  • In active inflammation - “headlight in the fog” appearance due to intense vitritis

[[figure-2]]

  • Acquired
    • Asymptomatic
    • Same as congenital
    • Punctate outer retinal toxoplasmosis

Treatment:

  • Quadruple therapy: Pyrimethamine + Sulfadiazine + Clindamycin + Oral steroid
  • Steroid eye drops for anterior uveitis

Posterior staphyloma (Option A): This refers to an outpouching of the sclera in the posterior part of the eye, often seen in high myopia (nearsightedness). It typically does not cause punched-out lesions on the retina.

Fundal coloboma (Option B): A coloboma is a congenital defect that can affect various parts of the eye, including the retina. It usually results in a hole or defect in the eye structure but does not typically present as punched-out lesions.

Congenital Rubella (Option C): Rubella can cause retinal changes in infants born with the infection, but it is more associated with "salt-and-pepper" retinopathy rather than punched-out lesions.



Reference:

  2. Ocular toxoplasmosis: a review of the current diagnostic and therapeutic approaches - PMC (nih.gov)

question: Which of the listed conditions is associated with the presence of punched-out lesions on the retina?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The given image shows a cherry-red spot. The orange reflex from the intact choroid stands out at the thin foveola, in contrast to the surrounding pale retina, giving rise to a ‘cherry-red spot’ appearance. Sudden loss of vision and cherry red spots are characteristic of Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO).

Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO):

Risk Factors
  • Atherosclerosis
  • Age
  • Hypertension/Cardiac Diseases
  • Thrombophilic Disorders
  • Smoking
  • Diabetes Mellitus
  • Oral Contraceptive Pills

Clinical Features

Symptoms:

  • Sudden, painless, profound vision loss.
  • Painful only in GCA: May present with headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, and/or pain around the temple.

Clinical Signs:

  • Severely reduced Visual Acuity (VA), often to counting fingers or worse.
  • Profound and sometimes total Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD), also called an amaurotic pupil.

Examination Findings

Fundus Examination:

  • Retinal Whitening: Pale and opaque retina, particularly in the posterior pole.
  • Cherry-Red Spot: Bright red area at the fovea due to the contrast between pale retina and underlying choroidal circulation.

[[figure-1]]

  • Cattle Truck Appearance: Segmentation of the blood column in retinal veins.

[[figure-2]]

  • Attenuated Arteries: Narrowed and segmented retinal arterioles.
  • Optic Disc Changes: Pale optic disc over time due to optic atrophy from prolonged ischemia (chronic cases).

Investigations

Fluorescein Angiography (FFA):

  • Delayed arterial filling.
  • Masking of background fluorescence due to edematous retina.
  • Patent Cilioretinal Artery: Area of normal perfusion of a cilioretinal artery supplies the fovea, potentially preserving central vision.

Other Diagnostic Tests:

  • Oral Antifungal Agents: Ketoconazole, Voriconazole (for severe ulcers)
  • Surgical Management:
    • Repeated Scraping: Removal of necrotic material
    • Cauterization Options: Carbolic acid (100%), Trichloroacetic acid (10%–20%), Povidone-iodine (5%)
    • Therapeutic Keratoplasty: Corneal transplantation

Reverse hypopyon (Option A): Collection of silicon oil in the anterior chamber is reverse hypopyon, usually seen as a complication of Vitreoretinal surgeries.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

A paediatric patient with leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) and Histiopathology revealing Flexner-Wintersteiner Rosettes is diagnostic of Retinoblastoma. Flexner-Wintersteiner rosette is an example of True rosette and is a highly specific feature of Retinoblastoma.

Clinical features and Diagnostic modalities for Retinoblastoma:

Clinical Presentation
  • Leukocoria (60%)
  • Strabismus (20%)
  • Painful red eye (7%)
  • Poor vision (5%)
  • Asymptomatic (3%)

Fundus Examination
  • White, elevated mass in the retina
  • Can be endophytic, exophytic, or mixed growth

Imaging
  • CT scan: Calcification in 90% of cases

Medulloblastoma (Option B): is a rapidly growing tumor of the brain, is unlikely to present with eye symptoms initially. Histopathology may reveal small round blue cells with Homer-wright pseudorosettes. IHC shows positivity for Synaptophysin+, CD56+, GFAP+.

Rhabdomyosarcoma (Option C): presents with acute painful proptosis. Usually seen in boys in the 1st decade of life. Histopathology may reveal small round blue cells with Homer-wright pseudorosettes. IHC shows positivity for Desmin+.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The above fundoscopy image given is that of ‘splashed tomato’ appearance and sudden painless loss of vision are classical features of ischaemic central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO). Splashed sauce appearance is characterized by severe tortuosity and engorgement of all branches of the central retinal vein involving the peripheral and posterior retina.

CRVO:

Risk Factors

Age > 50 years (primary risk factor), Hypertension, Diabetes Mellitus, Hyperlipidemia, Glaucoma (increased IOP), Smoking, Hypercoagulable states

Pathogenesis

Thrombosis driven by venous stasis, endothelial damage, and hypercoagulability

Types

Non-ischemic CRVO (Venous stasis retinopathy) (75% of cases)

  • Mild to moderate, unilateral blurring of vision
  • Fundus: Mild venous congestion and tortuosity, flame-shaped hemorrhages, mild macular edema

Ischemic CRVO (Hemorrhagic retinopathy)

  • Severe, sudden visual loss, massive venous engorgement, "splashed-tomato" hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, macular edema
  • Marked vein sheathing, collaterals, neovascularization, chronic cystoid edema

[[figure-1]]

Investigations
  • Ocular Exam: Visual acuity, IOP, Slit-lamp exam (NVI), Gonioscopy (NVA)
  • Goldmann Perimetry and ERG: Differentiating ischemic vs non-ischemic CRVO
  • Fundus Fluorescein Angiography (FFA): Assess retinal perfusion
  • Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT): Assess macular edema, sub-retinal fluid

Treatment
  • Systemic Management: Control of systemic conditions (hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, hyperhomocysteinemia)
  • Medical Treatment: Intravitreal anti-VEGF (e.g., Bevacizumab), intravitreal steroids (Triamcinolone, Dexamethasone implant)
  • Laser Therapy: Panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) for neovascularization
  • Surgical: Pars plana vitrectomy for complications

Complications

Neovascular glaucoma, Neovascularization of the iris (NVI), Vitreous hemorrhage, Proliferative retinopathy, Chronic macular edema

Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) (Option A): Cherry red spot seen on fundoscopy.

[[figure-2]]

Branched retinal artery occlusion (BRAO) (Option B): Focal area of ischaemia due to vascular occlusion of branch of retinal artery.

Branched retinal vein occlusion (BRAO) (Option B): Sectorial superficial retinal hemorrhages are seen on fundoscopy.

question: What is the most probable diagnosis for a 7-year-old patient who presented with a white pupillary reflex and underwent enucleation, with histopathological examination revealing the presence of Flexner Wintersteiner rosettes?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Shifting Fluid sign is seen in Exudative retinal detachment
  • Retinal detachment refers to the separation of the neurosensory retina from the retinal pigment epithelium.

Etiology:

  • Age: most common in 40-60 years.
  • Sex. More common in males (M:F - 3:2).
  • Myopia. About 40% cases of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment are myopic.
  • Aphakia and pseudophakia.
  • Trauma. It may also act as a predisposing factor.
  • Senile posterior vitreous detachment (PVD): It is associated with retinal detachment in many cases.
  • Retinal degenerations predisposed to retinal detachment: Lattice degeneration, Snail track degeneration, Acquired or degenerative retinoschisis, and Focal pigment clumps.

Type of Retinal Detachment

Clinical Features

Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment (Option C)

1. Floaters (dark spots) due to rapid vitreous degeneration.

2. Photopsia (flashes of light) caused by retinal irritation from vitreous movements.

3. Gradual visual field loss, initially localized, progressing to total vision loss as detachment spreads.

4. Dark veil/cloud in front of the eye, particularly when detachment reaches the posterior region.

[[figure-1]]

5. Sudden, painless vision loss in large, central detachment.

6. Retinal breaks may be round, horseshoe-shaped, slit-like, or large anterior dialysis.

[[figure-2]]

7. Vitreous pigments (tobacco dusting or Shaffer sign) are seen in the anterior vitreous with posterior vitreous detachment.

8. Old retinal detachment shows retinal thinning, subretinal demarcation lines (high water marks), and secondary intraretinal cysts.

Tractional Retinal Detachment (Option B)

1. Gradual, progressive visual loss

2. Typically painless

3. No associated flashes or floaters

4. Vitreoretinal bands present

5. No retinal breaks

6. Detached area - concave and localized

7. No shifting fluid

[[figure-3]]

Exudative Retinal Detachment (Option A)

1. Painless and sudden or gradual visual loss

2. No photopsia, holes/ tears, folds and undulations.

3. Smooth and convex with pigmentary disturbances

4. Rounded and fixed with neovascularization on the tumor summit.

5. Shifting fluid - changing the position of the detached area with gravity - hallmark feature.

[[figure-4]]

Retinal dialysis (Option D) involves a circumferential tear at the ora serrata, often due to trauma, but it does not exhibit the shifting fluid sign as seen in exudative detachments.



Reference:
  1. AK Khurana Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th Ed, Pg. 309, 310
  2. Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Pg. 681

Retinoblastoma

  • Retinoblastoma is the most common intraocular cancer in children.

question: A 3-year-old boy has developed progressive clumsiness over the past 6 months. His parents also noticed a white pupillary reflex (leukocoria) in his left eye. Ophthalmic examination reveals an absent red reflex in the affected eye. Enucleation of the eye is performed, and microscopic examination demonstrates Flexner–Wintersteiner rosettes. What is the most probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option A - Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO)

Explanation:

  • The presentation of sudden, painless vision loss with a cherry-red spot at the macula is suggestive of central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO).

  • Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO)

    • The central retinal artery is blocked, causing widespread retinal ischemia. Sometimes, if a cilioretinal artery is present, it can continue to supply the macula, preserving central vision even when the central retinal artery is occluded.

Clinical features:

Symptoms:

  • Sudden, painless, profound vision loss
  • Painless, except in GCA: GCA-associated CRAO may present with headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, and/or pain around the temple

Clinical Signs:

  • Visual Acuity (VA): severely reduced, often to counting fingers or worse
  • Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD): Profound and sometimes total (amaurotic pupil)

Fundus Examination:

  • Retinal Whitening: Pale and opaque retina , particularly in the posterior pole
  • Cherry-Red Spot): Bright red area at the fovea due to the contrast between pale retina and underlying choroidal circulation

[[figure-1]]

  • Cattle truck appearance: Due to segmentation of blood column in retinal veins

[[figure-2]]

  • Attenuated Arteries: Narrowed and segmented retinal arterioles
  • Optic Disc Changes: Pale optic disc over time due to optic atrophy from prolonged ischemia is seen in chronic cases.

Fluorescein Angiography (FA)

  • Arterial Filling: Delayed
  • Masking of Background Fluorescence: Edematous retina blocks normal fluorescence from the choroid
  • Patent Cilioretinal Artery: Area of normal perfusion if a cilioretinal artery supplies the fovea, potentially preserving central vision

[[figure-3]]

Other Diagnostic Tests

Reveals retinal edema, structural changes, and possibly an embolic plaque within the retinal artery and other systemic causes.

  • Cranial MRI or CT
  • Carotid duplex scanning
  • Echocardiography
  • Thrombophilia screening

Incorrect Options:

Central retinal venous occlusion (CRVO) (Option B) occurs when the central retinal vein, becomes blocked. It typically presents with sudden, painless vision loss and may be associated with retinal hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, and retinal edema.

Branched retinal artery occlusion (BRAO) (Option C) occurs when one of the branches of the central retinal artery becomes blocked, leading to a localized area of retinal ischemia. The affected area of the retina may appear pale, with associated retinal hemorrhages.

Branched retinal vein occlusion (BRVO) (Option D) occurs when one of the branches of the central retinal vein becomes blocked, resulting in impaired venous drainage from a particular area of the retina. It can lead to retinal hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, and macular edema.

  • Strabismus (20%)

question: A child presents with leukocoria and an intraocular mass. Microscopic examination reveals rosettes with scanty cytoplasm, and the mass is positive for synaptophysin and chromogranin. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) (Option B):

  • Most useful.
  • Provides high-resolution, cross-sectional images.
  • Allows detailed visualization and measurement of individual retinal layers (e.g., nerve fiber layer, photoreceptor layers).
  • Essential for diagnosing and monitoring retinal diseases.

Fundus Fluorescein Angiography (FFA) (Option A ruled out):

  • Visualizes retinal and choroidal blood vessels.
  • Highlights leakage, non-perfusion, or abnormal vasculature.
  • Does not provide layer-by-layer retinal images.

USG B-scan (Ultrasound B-scan)(Option C ruled out):

  • Uses sound waves; useful when view is obscured (e.g., hemorrhage).
  • Detects gross abnormalities (e.g., detachment, tumors).
  • Resolution not sufficient to see individual retinal layers.

Slit lamp examination(Option D ruled out):

  • Clinical tool for magnified, stereoscopic view of the retina.
  • Good for overall integrity and surface observation.
  • Does not provide cross-sectional, layer-by-layer resolution like OCT.

Yanoff & Duker Ophthalmology, 5th Edition, Page 58

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • A diabetic woman with proliferative retinopathy with gradual visual loss is most likely to be due to Tractional Retinal Detachment.
  • Retinal detachment refers to the separation of the neurosensory retina from the retinal pigment epithelium.
  • Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) leads to neovascularization on the retinal surface. These new vessels grow along with fibrous scar tissue. Over time, this fibrovascular tissue contracts and pulls the neurosensory retina away from the underlying retinal pigment epithelium, resulting in a tractional retinal detachment.

  • Key clinical clues:

    • Gradual vision loss

    • Seen in PDR and other fibrovascular conditions

    • Caused by mechanical traction - no retinal break required

  • Retinal detachment can be classified into three types:
    • Rhegmatogenous or primary retinal detachment
    • Tractional retinal detachment
    • Exudative retinal detachment

Tractional Retinal Detachment: Results from the pulling of the retina by fibrous or vascular tissue, commonly seen in fibrovascular proliferative conditions like diabetic retinopathy, without a retinal break.

[[figure-1]]

Primary or Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment (Option D and A): This is the most common type and occurs due to a retinal tear or break, allowing subretinal fluid to enter and separate the sensory retina from the pigmentary epithelium.

Exudative Retinal Detachment (Option C): Caused due to choroidal pathologies or by tumors pushing the retina or fluid accumulation under the retina due to inflammation or vascular abnormalities, without any associated retinal tear or traction.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Night Blindness is the characteristic and earliest feature of retinitis pigmentosa and may present several years before the visible changes in the retina appear.

Retinitis Pigmentosa:

  • Retinitis pigmentosa is a dystrophy of rods and cones, initially, rods are affected. (Option B ruled out)
  • Most common hereditary fundus dystrophy.
  • It can be sporadic (40-50%) or hereditary.
  • If hereditary, autosomal dominant is the most common mode of inheritance followed by autosomal recessive (AR). X-linked recessive inheritance is the least severe form.

Clinical features:

Symptoms:

  • Nyctalopia (night blindness) (Option D)
  • Peripheral visual field loss
  • Mid-peripheral superior scotoma leads to ring/ doughnut scotoma resulting in tubular/ tunnel vision. Central vision is affected in later stages (Option C ruled out)

Signs:

  • Triad of a pale waxy disc due to consecutive optic atrophy, attenuation of arteries, and pigmentation disturbance in the form of bony spicules.
  • Tapetal reflex: shinning reflex at macula - seen in female carriers of XLR inheritance.

Atypical Retinitis Pigmentosa

  • Atypical retinitis pigmentosa includes heterogeneous disorders that share clinical features with typical pigmentary retinal dystrophy.
  • Conditions included are:
  • RP sine pigmento - absence or paucity of pigment accumulation

[[figure-1]]

  • Retinitis punctata albescens - scattered whitish-yellow spots with arteriolar attenuation, usually sparing the macula.

[[figure-2]]

  • Sectoral RP - only inferior quadrants are involved.

[[figure-3]]

Investigation of Retinitis Pigmentosa

  • Electroretinography (ERG) is the investigation of choice - reduced scotopic rod in early disease and reduced photopic with progression.
  • EOG- subnormal- absence of light rise.
  • Perimetry: initially small mid-peripheral scotomas which gradually merge and may progress, leaving only a small island of residual central vision.
  • Electroretinography (ERG): There's a decreased amplitude of both "a" and "b" waves.(Option A ruled out)
  • OCT- to identify cystoid macular edema (CME).
  • Dark adaptometry: Dark adaptation time is prolonged.
  • Decreased Arden ratio may be present.

[[figure-4]]

question: Which of the following statements is incorrect about Retinitis Pigmentosa?

correctAnswer: A. 1-Retinal pigment epithelium; 2-Outer nuclear layer; 3-Inner plexiform layer; 4-Ganglion layer
explanationHtml:
Histology of Retina:

[[figure-1]]

Layers of the Retina:

[[figure-2]]

Layer

Description

1. Pigment Epithelium

Outermost layer with a single pigmented cell layer; adheres to Bruch's membrane; supports neurosensory retina, and reduces reflection.

Subretinal Space: This is the layer between the Pigment epithelium and the layer of Photoreceptors.

2. Rods and Cones Layer

Contains the outer segments of photoreceptors (rods and cones, which are the first-order neurons); rods detect low-light vision, cones manage color and detailed vision.

3. External Limiting Membrane

A porous membrane allows processes from rods and cones to pass through.

4. Outer Nuclear Layer
(Henle’s layer)

Contains the nuclei of the photoreceptor cells (rods and cones).

5. Outer Plexiform Layer

Includes connections between rods, cones, bipolar cell dendrites, and horizontal cells.

6. Inner Nuclear Layer

Made up of the cell bodies of bipolar cells (which are the second-order neurons), horizontal cells, amacrine cells, and Müller cells; and also contains retinal capillaries.

7. Inner Plexiform Layer

Houses synaptic connections between bipolar cell axons, ganglion cell dendrites, and amacrine cell processes.

8. Ganglion Cell Layer

Contains ganglion cell bodies, which serve as third-order neurons; midget cells synapse with a single bipolar cell, and polysynaptic cells synapse with multiple.

9. Nerve Fiber Layer

Composed of ganglion cell axons that form the optic nerve after passing through the lamina cribrosa.

10. Internal Limiting Membrane

The innermost layer separating the retina from the vitreous; is formed by the terminal expansions of Müller cells, serving as a basement membrane.

The Neuroglial cells, particularly the vertical Müller cells, bind the retina's neural elements. These cells provide structural support and nourish the retinal tissue.

  2. Ophthalmology by Yanoff and Duker, Edition 5, Page 421

question: Which of the following parts of the retina are correctly marked?

explanationHtml:
• Diabetic retinopathy is a progressive microvascular complication of diabetes, which can lead to proliferative changes, causing fibrovascular proliferation and subsequent tractional retinal detachment (TRD).
  • This occurs due to contraction of fibrovascular membranes over the retina, leading to vitreoretinal traction and retinal elevation.

Complications of Diabetic Retinopathy:

1. Macular Edema:

  • The most common cause of vision loss in diabetic retinopathy is leakage from dilated capillaries.
  • Clinically significant macular edema (CSME):
    • Retinal thickening at the center of the macula.
    • Retinal thickening and/or adjacent hard exudates at or within 500 µ of the center of the macula.
    • An area of retinal thickening greater than or equal to one disc area, any part of which is within 1 disc diameter of the center of the macula.
  • Types: Focal or Diffuse macular edema

  • Diagnosis:
    • Slit-lamp Biomicroscopy: Loss of foveal reflex and macular thickening
    • Fluorescein Angiography Identifies leakage and also diagnoses ischemic maculopathy.

  • Treatment:
  1. Anti-VEGF Therapy: Bevacizumab, ranibizumab or aflibercept.
    • Laser treatment should be deferred for 6 months after commencement of anti-VEGF injection.
  2. Intravitreal Triamcinolone acetonide: Reduce macular edema and improve visual acuity.
  3. Photocoagulation:
    • Focal Photocoagulation: Treatment of choice for focal diabetic macular edema (DME) not involving the center of the fovea using diode or argon burns.
    • Grid Photocoagulation: Considered in recalcitrant cases unresponsive to anti-VEGF agents or intravitreal steroids. Burns are applied to macular areas of diffuse retinal thickening, treating no closer than 500 µ from the foveola and 500 µ from the optic disc.

2. Vitreous Hemorrhage (VH):

  • Seen as blood floating in the vitreous, occluding the view of the retina.
  • Secondary to proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) is a cause of severe vision loss in diabetic patients.
  • In PDR, fibrovascular tissue lies flat on the retina or attaches to the posterior vitreous, leading to vitreous traction, retinal separation, and vessel rupture. This is the most common cause of VH in adults.

3. Retinal Detachment:

  • PDR causes scars to form in the back of the eye. When the scars pull the retina away from the back of the eye, it's called tractional retinal detachment.

4. Neovascular Glaucoma:

  • PDR causes abnormal blood vessels to grow out of the retina and block fluid from draining out of the eye, leading to neovascular glaucoma.
  • Can cause vision loss and blindness.

5. Rubeosis Iridis:

  • Neovascularization of iris, is when blood vessels develop on the anterior surface of the iris in response to retinal ischemia.
  • Prone to spontaneous hyphema as the blood vessels are fragile.
  • Treatment: Panretinal photocoagulation with or without intravitreal injection of anti-VEGF.

Posterior staphyloma (Option A): Posterior staphyloma is associated with pathologic myopia, not diabetic retinopathy. It involves progressive thinning and outward bulging of the sclera, primarily in high myopia.

Retinoschisis (Option B): Retinoschisis refers to the splitting of the retinal layers, commonly seen in degenerative retinoschisis or X-linked retinoschisis, rather than as a complication of diabetic retinopathy.

Progressive myopia (Option D): Progressive myopia is associated with axial elongation of the eyeball, typically seen in high myopia, rather than diabetic retinopathy.



Reference:

Complications of Diabetic Retinopathy:

  1. Macular Edema
  2. Vitreous Hemorrhage
  3. Retinal Detachment
  4. Neovascular Glaucoma
  5. Rubeosis Iridis
question: Which of the following is a complication of diabetic retinopathy?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Electro-oculography (EOG) is the gold standard diagnostic test for Best disease.
  • Best disease/ Best Vitelliform Macular Dystrophy (BVMD), also known as juvenile-onset vitelliform macular dystrophy, is the second most common macular dystrophy after Stargardt disease.
  • Caused by mutations in the BEST1 gene located on chromosome 11q13.
  • Bestrophin, the protein produced by this gene, functions as a transmembrane ion channel in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE).
  • Inherited in an autosomal dominant (AD) pattern.
  • Usually begins in childhood

Clinical Features:

  • Stages of the disease include:
    • Pre-vitelliform: abnormal EOG, normal fundus in asymptomatic patients.
    • Vitelliform: a characteristic "egg yolk or sunny-side up" macular lesion. The lesions can vary in size and developmental stage between the two eyes.

  • Pseudohypopyon: partially regressed lesion.
  • Vitelliruptive: Lesion fragments, visual acuity declines - “scrambled egg appearance”.

  • Atrophic: Pigment disappears, leading to RPE atrophy.
  • Visual acuity - stable early on but declines in adulthood due to complications like choroidal neovascularization (CNV), scarring, or geographic atrophy.

Diagnosis:

  • Fundus Autofluorescence (FAF): hyper autofluorescence yellowish material.
  • Fluorescein Angiography (FA): hypofluorescence due to lesion masking.
  • Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT): hyperreflective material beneath and within the RPE.
  • Electro-oculography (EOG): Severely subnormal across all stages (Arden index <1.5).
  • Hallmark- normal electroretinogram (ERG) but abnormal electrooculogram (EOG). (Option B ruled out) (Option A)
    • Best disease progresses through five stages, starting with the "egg-yolk" vitelliform lesion and potentially leading to choroidal neovascularization (CNV).
    • Asymptomatic carriers may show a reduced Arden ratio on EOG, making it useful for family screening.

Multifocal ERG (Option C): Multifocal ERG assesses macular function and can show localized dysfunction, but it is not the definitive test for Best disease.


Visual evoked potential (Option D): Visual evoked potential (VEP) evaluates optic nerve conduction and is mainly used for optic neuritis, demyelinating disorders, and optic neuropathies. It does not help in diagnosing Best disease.



Reference:
  1. AK Khurana Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th Ed, Pg. 301
  2. Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Pg. 631-634
question: Which of the following is the diagnostic investigation for Best disease?

explanationHtml:
The presentation of a white pupillary reflex (leukocoria) in a preterm infant with calcification of the globe on CT scan is most likely indicative of retinoblastoma, most common primary intraocular malignancy in children.

The key features pointing to this diagnosis are:

  1. Age of presentation: Retinoblastoma typically occurs in young children, usually before 5 years of age.
  2. Leukocoria: This is the most common presenting sign of retinoblastoma, often described as a white pupillary reflex.
  3. Fundus examination: A white, elevated mass in the retina is characteristic of retinoblastoma.

The most specific histopathological feature of retinoblastoma is Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes, which are rosettes with a central lumen as shown in the diagram below.

[[figure-1]]

Histopathology and Diagnostic modalities for Retinoblastoma

Histopathology
  • Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes (highly specific)- These are composed of an ‘empty’ lumen surrounded by columnar cells
  • Homer-Wright rosettes - These are pseudo-rosettes and consist of cells surrounding a central lumen made up of their processes
  • Undifferentiated tumor cells
  • Areas of necrosis and calcification

Clinical Presentation
  • Leukocoria (60%)
  • Strabismus (20%)
  • Painful red eye (7%)
  • Poor vision (5%)
  • Asymptomatic (3%)

Fundus Examination
  • White, elevated mass in the retina
  • Can be endophytic, exophytic, or mixed growth

Imaging
  • CT scan: Calcification in 90% of cases
  • MRI: Better for evaluating optic nerve and extraocular extension
  • Ultrasound: Useful for initial screening

Genetic Testing

RB1 gene mutation on chromosome 13q14

Retinopathy of Prematurity (Option A): While ROP is common in preterm infants, especially those born before 32 weeks gestation, it typically presents with abnormal blood vessel development in the retina.

  • Leukocoria in ROP is usually due to retinal detachment or scarring, not calcification.
  • ROP is stage-based and does not typically show calcifications on CT unless complicated by retinal detachment.

Glaucoma (Option C): Congenital glaucoma may cause enlarged corneas and optic nerve damage, but it does not usually present with white pupillary reflex or calcification.

Congenital Cataract (Option D): Congenital cataracts can also cause leukocoria, but they typically do not show calcification on CT. Cataracts are characterized by lens opacity and not calcification within the globe.

  3. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK572080/

question: A 3-month-old baby, born preterm at 33 weeks of gestation, is brought by parents with complaints of a white pupillary reflex for 2 weeks. CT revealed calcification of the globe in both eyes. What is the probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
• Irvine-Gass Syndrome, also known as cystoid macular edema (CME), is a condition commonly seen after cataract surgery.
  • The OCT finding typically shows loss of foveal depression, cystoid spaces, and overall retinal thickening, which is indicative of this syndrome.

Cystoid Macular Edema (CME)

Etiology:

  • Ocular Treatment Complications: Post-surgery (e.g., cataract extraction, retinal detachment surgery), ocular laser therapy, and topical ocular medications.
  • Retinal Vascular Disorders: Diabetic retinopathy, central and branch retinal vein occlusion, retinal telangiectasia, and hypertensive retinopathy.
  • Intraocular Inflammations: Pars planitis, uveitis.
  • Retinitis pigmentosa.
  • Vitreomacular Traction: Associated with macular epiretinal membrane (ERM) and vitreomacular traction (VMT) syndrome.
  • Systemic Diseases: Includes leukemia, chronic renal failure, and multiple myeloma.
  • Miscellaneous Causes: niacin toxicity , PG analogues (risk factor for development of CME)

Clinical Features:

  • Visual Loss: Initial minimal to moderate vision loss, potentially leading to permanent vision decrease if persistent.
  • Ophthalmoscopy: Reveals loss of foveal contour, retinal thickening, a yellow spot at the fovea, and a "honeycomb appearance" of the macula.
  • Fluorescein Angiography: Shows leakage and dye accumulation in the macular region, with a "flower petal appearance" in late frames.

Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT): Demonstrates loss of foveal depression, cystoid spaces, and overall retinal thickening.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Complications:

  • Long-standing CME may result in a lamellar macular hole.

Treatment:

  • Addressing the Cause: Intravitreal anti-VEGF or photocoagulation for diabetic CME; discontinuing causative topical medications.
  • Topical NSAIDs: Such as ketorolac, diclofenac, or profenac, are effective in preventing and treating CME.
  • Topical/Systemic Steroids: Useful in established cases.
  • Systemic Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors (CAIs): Oral acetazolamide may be beneficial, particularly in cases associated with retinitis pigmentosa.

Posner-Schlossman Syndrome (Option A): This involves high IOP and mild uveitis, but is not associated with macular edema as seen in Irvine-Gass Syndrome.

Central Serous Retinopathy (Option C): is characterized by "ink-blot" or "smoke-stack" leakage patterns on FFA, and neurosensory retinal and RPE detachment on OCT. CSR typically does not present with the cystoid pattern seen in CME.

Elschnig's Pearls (Option D): Clustered, vacuolated subcapsular epithelial cells along the posterior capsule.

[[figure-3]]



Reference:

AK Khurana Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th Edition, Pg. 303, 304, 305
question: A patient presents with vision problems and has a history of cataract surgery. OCT finding is shown below. What is the syndrome most likely associated with these findings?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient’s presentation and presence of bony spicules, pale waxy disc, and attenuated arteries are the classic triad of findings seen in retinitis pigmentosa.

[[figure-1]]

The Triad of retinitis pigmentosa includes a pale waxy disc due to consecutive optic atrophy, attenuation of arteries, and pigmentation disturbance in the form of bony spicules.

  • Retinitis pigmentosa is a dystrophy of rods and cones, initially, rods are affected.
  • Most common hereditary fundus dystrophy.
  • It can be sporadic (40-50%) or hereditary.
  • If hereditary, autosomal dominant is the most common mode of inheritance followed by autosomal recessive (AR). X-linked recessive inheritance is the least severe form.

Clinical features:

Symptoms:

  • Nyctalopia (night blindness)
  • Peripheral visual field loss
  • Mid-peripheral superior scotoma leads to ring/ doughnut scotoma resulting in tubular/ tunnel vision

Signs:

  • Triad of a pale waxy disc due to consecutive optic atrophy, attenuation of arteries, and pigmentation disturbance in the form of bony spicules.
  • Tapetal reflex: shining reflex at macula - seen in female carriers of XLR inheritance.

Investigation of Retinitis Pigmentosa

  • Electroretinography (ERG) is the investigation of choice - reduced scotopic rod in early disease and reduced photopic with progression.
  • EOG - subnormal - absence of light rise.
  • Perimetry: initially small mid-peripheral scotomas which gradually merge and may progress, leaving only a small island of residual central vision.
  • Electroretinography (ERG): There's a decreased amplitude of both "a" and "b" waves.
  • OCT - to identify cystoid macular edema (CME).
  • Dark adaptometry: Dark adaptation time is prolonged.
  • Decreased Arden ratio may be present.

Treatment of Retinitis Pigmentosa:

  • The treatable RP includes Refsum's disease and Bassen-Kornzweig syndrome.

The treatment includes-

  • Regular follow-ups: Annual check-ups help detect complications, provide support, and track new treatment options.
  • Low-vision aids: Includes devices, rehabilitation, and access to social services. Avoid smoking.
  • Light protection:
    • Outdoor sunglasses blocking wavelengths up to 550 nm with side protection.
    • Indoors, amber lenses blocking 511–527 nm may enhance contrast sensitivity.
  • Treatment for CMO: Oral acetazolamide or topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitors may reduce cystoid macular edema.
  • Vitamin A: High-dose vitamin A (15,000 units/day) provides marginal benefits but should be used with caution due to risks like liver toxicity and increased lung cancer risk in smokers. Avoid during pregnancy. Lutein, possibly with zeaxanthin, is a safer alternative.
  • A retinal implant (ARGUS-II) can also be performed.
  • Low-vision aids (LVA) can also be used.
  • It can also lead to cone dystrophy.

Retinal hemorrhage (Option B): Presents with retinal bleeding (dot, blot, flame-shaped, or preretinal hemorrhages), not bone-spicule pigmentation or nyctalopia.

Diabetic retinopathy (Option C): Characterized by microaneurysms, retinal hemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton-wool spots, and neovascularization; night blindness is not a typical presenting symptom.

Hypertensive retinopathy (Option D): Shows arteriolar narrowing, AV nicking, flame-shaped hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, hard exudates, and papilledema (in severe cases), but not bone-spicule pigmentation.



Reference:
  1. AK Khurana Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th Edition, Pages 297, 298
  2. Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Pages 620, 621
question: A patient presents with a gradual loss of night vision and peripheral vision. What is the most likely diagnosis based on fundoscopy findings?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment

Explanation:

  • A myopic patient with flashes (photopsia), floaters, and a deep anterior chamber suggests posterior vitreous detachment with retinal tear. This allows liquefied vitreous to pass into the subretinal space, leading to rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.
  • Key mechanism: Myopia → long axial length → retinal thinning + lattice degeneration → Retinal hole formation→Fluid entry under retina→Rhegmatogenous RD
  • Deep anterior chamber in this context is due to elongation of the globe and posterior shift of the lens–iris diaphragm in high myopia.

Type of Retinal Detachment

Clinical Features

Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment

1. Floaters (dark spots) due to rapid vitreous degeneration.

2. Photopsia (flashes of light) caused by retinal irritation from vitreous movements.

3. Gradual visual field loss, initially localized, progressing to total vision loss as detachment spreads.

4. Dark veil/cloud in front of the eye, particularly when detachment reaches the posterior region.

[[figure-1]]

5. Sudden, painless vision loss in large, central detachment.

6. Retinal breaks may be round, horseshoe-shaped, slit-like, or large anterior dialysis.

[[figure-2]]

7. Vitreous pigments (tobacco dusting or Shaffer sign) are seen in the anterior vitreous with posterior vitreous detachment.

8. Old retinal detachment shows retinal thinning, subretinal demarcation lines (high water marks), and secondary intraretinal cysts.

Tractional Retinal Detachment (Option C ruled out)

1. Gradual, progressive visual loss

2. Typically painless

3. No associated flashes or floaters

4. Vitreoretinal bands present

5. No retinal breaks

6. Detached area - concave and localized

7. No shifting fluid

[[figure-3]]

Exudative Retinal Detachment (Option A ruled out)

1. Painless and sudden or gradual visual loss

2. No photopsia, holes/ tears, folds and undulations.

3. Smooth and convex with pigmentary disturbances

4. Rounded and fixed with neovascularization on the tumor summit.

5. Shifting fluid - changing the position of the detached area with gravity - hallmark feature.

[[figure-4]]


Central serous retinopathy (Option D): Localized serous detachment of the neurosensory retina at the macula, seen in young stressed males; presents with central vision blurring and metamorphopsia, not flashes/floaters.



Reference:

.
question: A myopic patient presents with complaints of flashes and floaters. On examination, a deep anterior chamber is seen. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Looping in all quadrants is not a criterion in severe NPDR.

Abbreviated Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) classification of diabetic retinopathy

Category

Management

Non-Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (NPDR):

No Diabetic Retinopathy

Review in 12 months

Very Mild NPDR

Microaneurysms only

Review most patients in 12 months

Mild NPDR

Any or all of the: microaneurysms, retinal hemorrhages, exudates, and cotton-wool spots, up to the level of moderate NPDR. No intraretinal microvascular anomalies (IRMA) or significant beading.

Review range 6-12 months, depending on the severity of signs, stability, systemic factors, and patient's circumstances

Moderate NPDR

  • Severe retinal hemorrhages in 1-3 quadrants or mild IRMA
  • Significant venous beading can be present in no more than 1 quadrant
  • Cotton wool spots commonly present

Review in approximately 6 months

Severe NPDR

The 4-2-1 rule; is one or more of the:

  • Severe hemorrhages in all 4 quadrants (Option B ruled out)
  • Significant venous beading in 2 or more quadrants (Option D ruled out)
  • Moderate IRMA in 1 or more quadrants (Option A ruled out)

Review in 4 months

Very severe NPDR

Two or more of the criteria for severe NPDR

Review in 2-3 months


Reference:

  • Yanoff and Duker Ophthalmology,Edition 5, Page 548-551

question: A 72-year-old patient, with a history of cataract surgery and diabetes mellitus, presents with decreased vision one month after surgery. Examination reveals a honeycomb appearance or flower petal pattern of the retina. What is the likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: D. Night vision is lost late and rare
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Night Blindness is the characteristic and earliest feature of retinitis pigmentosa and may present several years before the visible changes in the retina appear.
  • It occurs due to degeneration of the rods.

Retinitis Pigmentosa

Retinitis pigmentosa (RP), or pigmented retinal degeneration, denotes a clinically and genetically diverse group of inherited diffuse retinal degenerative diseases initially predominantly affecting the rod photoreceptors, with subsequent less marked degeneration of cones and retinal pigment epithelium (Option B).

  • Most common hereditary fundus dystrophy.
  • It can be sporadic (40-50%) or hereditary.
  • If hereditary, autosomal dominant is the most common mode of inheritance followed by autosomal recessive (AR). X-linked recessive inheritance is the least severe form.

question: Which of the following statements is incorrect about Retinitis pigmentosa?

explanationHtml:
• Rheumatoid arthritis, especially when poorly controlled, can cause systemic vasculitis, including involvement of the retinal arterioles.

  • Branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO) typically presents as a sectoral visual field defect opposite to the involved retinal segment, here, inferior retinal ischemia causes superior field loss.

  • The process is acute, painless, and results from focal vasculitis or embolic occlusion of a branch retinal artery.

Branch Retinal Artery Occlusion (BRAO)

Branch Retinal Artery Occlusion (BRAO) is an acute retinal vascular emergency caused by occlusion of one of the branches of the central retinal artery, resulting in ischemia of the retinal territory supplied by that branch.

Unlike Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO), only a segment of the retina is affected.

Etiology:

1. Embolic disease (Most common)

  • Carotid artery atherosclerosis (most common source)
  • Cardiac emboli
    • Atrial fibrillation
    • Valvular heart disease
    • Infective endocarditis
  • Cholesterol (Hollenhorst) emboli
  • Platelet-fibrin emboli
  • Calcific emboli

2. Vasculitis

  • Giant cell arteritis (especially age >50 years)
  • Rheumatoid vasculitis (rare)
  • Systemic lupus erythematosus
  • Polyarteritis nodosa

3. Hypercoagulable states

  • Antiphospholipid syndrome
  • Protein C/S deficiency
  • Factor V Leiden mutation
  • Hyperhomocysteinemia

Risk Factors:

  • Hypertension
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Hyperlipidemia
  • Smoking
  • Carotid artery disease
  • Cardiac disease
  • Advanced age

Clinical Features

Symptoms

  • Sudden
  • Painless
  • Monocular vision loss
  • Partial loss of vision corresponding to the involved retinal sector
  • Visual field defect:
    • Inferior retinal artery occlusion - Superior visual field defect
    • Superior retinal artery occlusion - Inferior visual field defect

Fundus Findings

  • Acute stage
    • Sectoral retinal whitening along the affected arterial territory
    • Attenuated retinal artery
    • Visible embolus at arterial bifurcation (sometimes)
    • Macula usually spared unless involved

Investigations

1. Ocular

  • Fundus examination
  • Optical coherence tomography (OCT)
  • OCT angiography
  • Fluorescein angiography
  • Visual field testing

2. Systemic evaluation

  • Carotid Doppler ultrasound
  • ECG
  • Echocardiography
  • Lipid profile
  • Blood sugar
  • ESR and CRP (to exclude giant cell arteritis in older patients)

Management

BRAO is considered an ocular stroke, and urgent systemic evaluation is recommended.

Acute measures (benefit is limited and mainly if presentation is within hours)

  • Ocular massage
  • Reduction of intraocular pressure
    • Acetazolamide
    • Topical antiglaucoma medications
  • Anterior chamber paracentesis (selected cases)
  • Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (selected centers)

Treat the underlying cause:

  • Antiplatelet therapy (if embolic)
  • Carotid endarterectomy if indicated
  • Control hypertension
  • Diabetes management
  • Statin therapy
  • Anticoagulation when indicated (e.g., atrial fibrillation)

Prognosis depends on site of occlusion, macular involvement and duration of ischemia

Most patients retain good central visual acuity if the fovea is not involved, but permanent visual field defects are common.

Central retinal artery occlusion (Option B): Causes complete, sudden vision loss, not sectoral (field) loss.

Branch retinal vein occlusion (Option C): Causes sectoral hemorrhages with gradual vision loss and tortuous veins, not acute ischemia or field defect.

Central retinal vein occlusion (Option D) : Produces diffuse retinal hemorrhages (“blood and thunder” appearance), not localized field loss.



Reference:

Parson's Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Pages 773, 776
question: A patient with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis who has been noncompliant with treatment presents with sudden, painless superior field loss in one eye for the past week. Fundus examination shows retinal whitening in the inferior retina with a corresponding superior visual field defect. What is the most likely cause of this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Muscae volitantes, i.e. floating black opacities in front of the eyes is one of the symptoms in patients with pathological myopia.
  • This is likely due to Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment due to the traction in posterior vitreous detachment.
  • This causes the pigment to disperse in the vitreous cavity. This is called schafer’s sign or Tobacco dust.

Retinal Detachment (RD)

RD refers to separation of the neurosensory retina (NSR) from the RPE. This results in the accumulation of subretinal fluid (SRF) in the potential space between the NSR and RPE.

Etiology:

  • Age: most common in 40-60 years.
  • Sex. More common in males (M:F - 3:2).
  • Myopia. About 40% cases of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment are myopic.
  • Aphakia and pseudophakia.
  • Trauma. It may also act as a predisposing factor.
  • Senile posterior vitreous detachment (PVD): It is associated with retinal detachment in many cases.
  • Retinal degenerations predisposed to retinal detachment: Lattice degeneration, Snail track degeneration, Acquired or degenerative retinoschisis, and Focal pigment clumps.

Retinal detachment can be classified into three types:

  1. Rhegmatogenous or primary retinal detachment
  2. Tractional retinal detachment
  3. Exudative retinal detachment

Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment: This is the most common type and occurs due to a retinal tear or break, allowing subretinal fluid to enter and separate the sensory retina from the pigmentary epithelium.

Tractional Retinal Detachment: Results from the pulling of the retina by fibrous or vascular tissue, commonly seen in fibrovascular proliferative conditions like diabetic retinopathy, without a retinal break.

Exudative Retinal Detachment: Caused due to choroidal pathologies or by tumors pushing the retina or fluid accumulation under the retina due to inflammation or vascular abnormalities, without any associated retinal tear or traction.

Type of Retinal Detachment

Clinical Features

Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment
  1. Floaters (dark spots) due to rapid vitreous degeneration.
  2. Photopsia (flashes of light) caused by retinal irritation from vitreous movements.
  3. Gradual visual field loss, initially localized, progressing to total vision loss as detachment spreads.
  4. Dark veil/cloud in front of the eye, particularly when detachment reaches the posterior region.

[[figure-1]]

  1. Sudden, painless vision loss in large, central detachment.
  2. Retinal breaks may be round, horseshoe-shaped, slit-like, or large anterior dialysis.

[[figure-2]]

  1. Vitreous pigments (tobacco dusting or Shaffer sign) are seen in the anterior vitreous with posterior vitreous detachment.
  2. Old retinal detachment shows retinal thinning, subretinal demarcation lines (high water marks), and secondary intraretinal cysts.

Tractional Retinal Detachment
  1. Gradual, progressive visual loss
  2. Typically painless
  3. No associated flashes or floaters
  4. Vitreoretinal bands present
  5. No retinal breaks
  6. Detached area - concave and localized
  7. No shifting fluid

[[figure-3]]

Tractional RD associated with anteroposterior and bridging traction

Exudative Retinal Detachment
  1. Painless and sudden or gradual visual loss
  2. No photopsia, holes/ tears, folds and undulations.
  3. Smooth and convex with pigmentary disturbances
  4. Rounded and fixed with neovascularization on the tumor summit.
  5. Shifting fluid - changing the position of the detached area with gravity - hallmark feature.

[[figure-4]]

Subarachnoid hemorrhage (Option A): Subarachnoid hemorrhage causes subhyaloid hemorrhage.

Vitreous hemorrhage (Option C): Vitreous hemorrhage is caused by blunt force trauma.

Branched retinal artery occlusion (Option D): Branched retinal artery occlusion presents with cherry red spot in the retina.



Reference:

Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology, 10th Edition, Pages 667-700
question: A 22-year-old patient with high myopia and thick glasses presents with floaters in his eyes. What is the likely cause of this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Central serous retinopathy is characterized by sudden painless loss of vision. The other causes of sudden painless loss of vision are as follows:
    • Optic neuritis
    • Methyl alcohol amblyopia
    • Nonischaemic central retinal vein occlusion.

Central Serous Chorioretinopathy (CSCR) (Option D)

  • CSCR is characterized by the spontaneous detachment of the neurosensory retina in the macular region, with or without retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) detachment.

Pathogenesis: Increased sympathetic drive and corticosteroids affect choroidal vascular permeability, raising hydrostatic pressure, and leading to RPE defects and serous detachment of the neurosensory retina.

Risk Factors:

  • Males aged 20-50
  • Type A personality, Emotional stress, Steroid use
  • Systemic lupus erythematosus, Cushing's disease
  • Pregnancy (3rd trimester)

Clinical Manifestations:

  • Sudden painless vision loss (6/9 - 6/24)
  • Relative positive scotoma, micropsia, and metamorphopsia
  • Recurrence in 30-50% of cases

Examination Findings:

  • Mild macular elevation with circular ring reflex
  • RPE detachment (yellow-grey elevations)
  • Absence or distortion of the foveal reflex
  • Subretinal deposits

Investigations:

  • Fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA): Shows "ink-blot" or "smoke-stack" leakage patterns.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

  • Indocyanine green (ICG): Shows hyperfluorescence due to choroidal hyperpermeability.
  • OCT: Shows neurosensory retinal and RPE detachment.

[[figure-3]]

[[figure-4]]

[[figure-5]]

Treatment:

  1. Conservative: Reassurance; spontaneous resolution in 80-90% of cases within 1-6 months.
  2. Laser Photocoagulation: For cases lasting more than 3 months, recurrent cases, and those with permanent vision loss in the other eye due to CSCR.
  3. Photodynamic Therapy (PDT): For severe, sub-foveal leaks, or chronic cases.
  4. Anti-VEGF: Considered if choroidal neovascularization (CNV) develops.

Incorrect Options:

Chemical injuries to the eyeball and acute congestive glaucoma (Option A and B) typically present with pain.

Acute iridocyclitis (Option C) is associated with pain, photophobia, and redness, rather than painless vision loss.



Reference:

AK Khurana Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th Edition, Pg. 302, 303

question: Which of the following conditions is associated with the curtain falling sign?

correctAnswer: D. Homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing
explanationHtml:
Correct Option D - Homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing

  • This is the correct answer. This condition involves a loss of vision on the same side of both eyes, but with the central field of vision intact. This condition is usually associated with a stroke that affects the occipital lobe of the brain, which processes visual information. The patient's symptoms - inability to see on the left side from both eyes, but with central vision intact - align with this condition.

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Quadrantanopia: This is a type of visual field loss that happens in one of the four quarters of the visual field. But, the patient's symptoms indicate a loss of vision on the left side completely in both eyes, not just a quarter of the visual field.

Option B - Heteronymous hemianopia: This condition involves loss of half the field of view on different sides in each eye. For example, the right half in one eye and the left half in the other. But, the patient's symptoms suggest the same side (left) of both eyes is affected.

Option C - Homonymous hemianopia: This is a condition in which a patient loses half of the field of view on the same side in both eyes. This can occur because of stroke or brain injury. However, the patient's central vision remains intact, which suggests macular sparing.

He reports that he is unable to see on the left side from the left eye and the left side from his right eye. However, he notices that his central vision remains intact and unaffected. explanationHtml:
• Grade 4 hypertensive retinopathy is characterized by severe retinal changes including:

    • Flame-shaped hemorrhages

    • Cotton wool spots

    • Papilledema (disc edema)

  • Presence of disc edema distinguishes Grade 4 from Grade 3, which has hemorrhages and cotton wool spots but no disc edema.

  • Symptoms such as blurred vision and headache indicate malignant hypertension often associated with Grade 4.

Keith-Wagner Classification of Hypertensive Retinopathy

Grade Fundus Findings Clinical Features
Grade 1 Mild arteriolar narrowing Usually asymptomatic
Grade 2 Moderate arteriolar narrowing + AV nicking Often asymptomatic or mild symptoms
Grade 3 Grade 2 + Flame-shaped hemorrhages + Cotton wool spots + hard exudates Visual symptoms possible
Grade 4 Grade 3 + Papilledema (disc edema) Malignant hypertension symptoms like headache, blurred vision

Grade 1 (Option A): Incorrect, only mild arteriolar narrowing without hemorrhages or edema.

Grade 2 (Option B): Incorrect, involves AV nicking but no hemorrhages or disc edema.

Grade 3 (Option C): Incorrect, has hemorrhages and cotton wool spots but no disc edema.

question: A 55-year-old hypertensive patient presented with complaints of blurred vision and headaches. On retinal examination, the following findings were observed: multiple flame-shaped hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, and disc edema. Based on the Keith-Wagner classification, which grade of hypertensive retinopathy is this patient most likely classified as?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
The clinical presentation describes the classic triad of Retrobulbar Neuritis:

  • Pain on eye movement (due to the traction of extraocular muscles on the inflamed optic nerve sheath)
  • Presence of a Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (indicating optic nerve dysfunction)
  • Normal optic disc appearance

This is famously described as the condition where "the patient sees nothing, and the doctor sees nothing."

Optic Neuritis → an inflammatory demyelination of the optic nerve often associated with Multiple Sclerosis.

  • When the inflammation occurs at the optic disc, it is called papillitis (showing a swollen disc).
  • When the inflammation occurs behind the globe, it is called retrobulbar neuritis, and because the nerve head is not yet involved in the swelling, the fundus examination remains normal during the acute phase.

Anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (AION) (Option A) presents as sudden, painless vision loss in older patients. Furthermore, the fundus examination would reveal significant disc edema (swelling) and potentially splinter hemorrhages, rather than a normal disc.

Papilledema (Option B) refers to swelling of the optic disc due to increased intracranial pressure. A fundus examination would show a blurred, elevated, and swollen disc, not a normal one. It is also usually bilateral and not associated with pain on eye movement.

Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) (Option D) presents as sudden, profound, and painless vision loss. A fundus examination would not be normal; it would show a classic "cherry-red spot" at the macula and a pale, opaque retina.
question: A middle-aged female patient presents with pain on eye movement. Relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) is present, and a normal optic disc on fundus examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Hyphema is defined as the presence of blood in the anterior chamber of the eye.
  • It is a common complication of blunt trauma (e.g., ball injury) caused by a tear in the iris or ciliary body vessels.
  • Red blood cells settle at the bottom of the anterior chamber due to gravity (forming a fluid level).
  • Management
    • General
      • Exclude coagulopathy / haemoglobinopathy
      • Stop anticoagulants (with medical liaison)
      • Avoid NSAIDs, Semi-upright position, Protective eye shield
    • Medical
      • IOP control: Beta-blockers, Prostaglandins, CAIs
      • Avoid miotics
      • Topical steroids → ↓ inflammation, ↓ rebleed
      • Atropine → large hyphema
      • Antifibrinolytics (ACA / tranexamic acid) → recurrent/high-risk bleed
      • Hyperosmotics → selective use (high threshold in sickle cell)
    • Surgical (~5%)
      • Indications:
        • Total hyphema
        • IOP > 50 mmHg for 2 days
        • IOP > 35 mmHg for 5 days
      • Procedures:
        • AC paracentesis / surgical evacuation
        • ± Glaucoma filtration surgery

Hypopyon (Option A) refers to the presence of pus in the anterior chamber, appearing as a yellowish-white level. It is seen in corneal ulcers or endophthalmitis.

[[figure-1]]

Iridodialysis (Option C) is the disinsertion of the iris root from the ciliary body, creating a D-shaped pupil or a second false pupil at the periphery.

[[figure-2]]

Vitreous hemorrhage (Option D) obscures the red reflex and fundus view but is not seen as a fluid level in the anterior chamber.

[[figure-3]]

  1. Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Pages 390-391.
  2. AK Khurana, Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th Edition, Pages 524.
question: A baby sustains an eye injury after being hit by a ball. On examination, an image of the eye is shown to have blood settling in the anterior chamber. Identify the condition.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The fundus finding of a Cherry Red Spot against a pale background in a patient with sudden, painless vision loss is pathognomonic for Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO).

  • The occlusion of the central retinal artery causes infarction and edema of the inner retinal layers, making the retina appear cloudy white.
  • The fovea is the thinnest part of the retina and lacks these inner layers. Therefore, the underlying vascular choroid remains visible as a bright red spot, contrasting sharply with the surrounding white ischemic retina.

Conditions Associated with Cherry Red Spot:

  1. Tay-Sachs Disease (GM2 Gangliosidosis) - Most common metabolic cause.
  2. Niemann-Pick Disease (Types A and B).
  3. Sandhoff Disease.
  4. GM1 Gangliosidosis (Generalized Gangliosidosis).
  5. Sialidosis (Mucolipidosis Type I) - known as Cherry Red Spot-Myoclonus Syndrome.
  6. Farber’s Disease (Lipogranulomatosis).
  7. Commotio Retinae (Berlin’s Edema) - Following blunt trauma to the eye.
  8. Gaucher’s Disease.

Central retinal vein occlusion (Option B) presents with a Blood and Thunder appearance (or Tomato splash appearance), characterized by widespread retinal hemorrhages, dilated tortuous veins, and cotton wool spots.

Retinal detachment (Option C) presents with a history of flashes/floaters and a curtain falling over the vision. Fundoscopy shows a greyish, elevated, mobile retina with subretinal fluid.

Optic neuritis (Option D) is characterized by sudden vision loss accompanied by pain on eye movement. Fundoscopy typically shows a hyperemic, swollen disc (papillitis) or a normal fundus (retrobulbar neuritis).



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 528-529.
question: A patient presents with sudden painless loss of vision. The fundus photograph is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The examination shown is the swinging flashlight test, which is used to detect a Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD), also known as the Marcus Gunn pupil.
  • RAPD indicates reduced afferent input through the optic nerve or severe retinal disease, while the efferent pupillary pathway remains intact.
  • Normally, shining light into either eye produces equal constriction of both pupils due to the consensual light reflex.
  • In a patient with a right optic nerve lesion, illumination of the left (normal) eye causes both pupils to constrict normally.
  • However, when the light is quickly moved to the right (affected) eye, the reduced afferent signal causes both pupils to dilate relative to their previously constricted state, producing the characteristic RAPD.
  • The history of sudden painless visual loss in the right eye further supports involvement of the right optic nerve.

Left oculomotor nerve (CN III) (Option A) supplies the parasympathetic efferent fibers responsible for pupillary constriction. A lesion of the left oculomotor nerve produces a dilated, poorly reactive left pupil, often associated with ptosis and ophthalmoplegia. It does not produce a relative afferent pupillary defect, because the afferent visual pathway remains intact.

Left optic nerve (CN II) (Option B) would produce an RAPD only when the left eye is illuminated. In this case, the abnormal response occurs when light is directed into the right eye, making a left optic nerve lesion inconsistent with the examination findings.

Right oculomotor nerve (CN III) (Option C) causes an efferent pupillary defect, resulting in a fixed dilated right pupil with impaired direct and consensual constriction, often accompanied by ptosis and limitation of extraocular movements. The swinging flashlight test specifically evaluates the afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex, making an isolated oculomotor nerve lesion an unlikely explanation for the observed response.



Reference:
  • Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 781
  • https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3588138/
  • https://radiopaedia.org/articles/relativeafferent-pupillary-defect

When the light is moved from the left eye to the right eye, both pupils paradoxically dilate instead of constricting. This finding is most consistent with a lesion involving which of the following structures?

  • Although vessels that leave the disc are also obscured, which corresponds to Grade 3, the overall presentation falls under Grade 4.

Grading of Papilledema (Modified Frisen Scale)

Grade 1: C-shaped halo nasally.

Grade 2: Circumferential halo around the optic disc.

Grade 3: Obscuration of one or more major vessels leaving the disc.

Grade 4: Obscuration of major vessels on the disc.

Grade 5: Complete obscuration of all vessels on and leaving the disc

question: A 62-year-old patient with papilledema has been examined. On fundoscopic examination of the eye obscuration of major blood vessels is found on the disc & vessels leaving the disc, with a significant halo around the disc. According to the Frisen grading system, what is the grade of papilledema?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Papilledema typically presents with blurring of the optic disc margins, enlargement of the blind spot, and engorged and tortuous retinal veins.
  • As the disc swells, the physiological cup size usually decreases.
  • An increased cup-to-disc ratio is more indicative of glaucomatous changes rather than papilledema.

Papilloedema:

  • Swelling of the optic disc due to increased intracranial pressure
  • Characteristic Features:
    • Passive oedema without inflammation.
    • Swelling primarily in the optic nerve head in front of the lamina cribrosa.
    • Engorged, tortuous small blood vessels (Option D) and swollen nerve fibres.
    • Axoplasmic stasis with swollen, disrupted mitochondria.
    • Retinal changes include macular star and cotton-wool spots.
  • Signs:
    • Initial blurring of optic disc margins. (Option C)
    • Enlargement of the blind spot due to the separation of the retina. (Option B)
    • Hyperaemia, swelling, and engorgement of disc vessels.
    • Potential for haemorrhages, exudates, and macular star formation.
    • Chronic cases may lead to optic atrophy and visual loss.


Reference:

Parsons Diseases of the eye, 23rd Edition, Pg - 842,843

Yanoff & Duker Ophthalmology, 5th edition, Pg - 883

question: A 50-year-old patient presents with worsening headaches and visual disturbances. Fundoscopic examination reveals optic disc swelling. Which of the following is least likely to be associated with this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • A lesion in the left oculomotor nerve would disrupt parasympathetic signals to the left iris muscles, preventing the left pupil from constricting.
  • This results in dilating the left pupil regardless of light stimuli, while the right eye's responses remain unaffected.

[[figure-1]]


Light Reflex:

  • Direct Light Reflex: Constriction of the pupil in the same eye that is directly exposed to light.
  • Indirect (Consensual) Light Reflex: Constriction of the pupil in the opposite eye when light is shone into one eye.

[[figure-2]]

Optic Nerve

(Option A)
  • Direct and consensual reactions are lost on the affected side
  • Both are retained on the opposite side (Option D ruled out)
  • Near reflex and lid reflex remain intact.

Nuclear / Supranuclear Lesion (Option B)

Ipsilateral absolute pupillary paralysis.
