explanationHtml:
Neurosyphilis is a complication of syphilis that affects the nervous system. It occurs in the tertiary stage of syphilis, typically years after the initial infection. The condition can present with a variety of neurological symptoms, including altered sensation, coordination difficulties, and speech problems, as seen in the patient. Specific features of this case, including absent pupillary light reaction with intact accommodation, are highly suggestive of Argyll Robertson pupils, which is a classic sign of neurosyphilis.

Neurosyphilis and Argyll Robertson Pupils:

  1. Pupillary Light Reflex Absent: The pupillary light reflex is mediated by the optic nerve (CN II) and oculomotor nerve (CN III). In neurosyphilis, the optic nerve is often involved, leading to loss of the pupillary light reflex.
  2. Accommodation Reflex Present: Despite the absence of the light reflex, the accommodation reflex (the ability of the pupil to constrict when focusing on a near object) remains intact, which is typical in Argyll Robertson pupils. This occurs because the pathways responsible for accommodation (afferent via the optic nerve and efferent via the oculomotor nerve) are not usually affected in neurosyphilis.
  3. Other Symptoms: The patient may also present with neurological symptoms such as sensory disturbances, motor coordination problems (ataxia), and speech difficulties, all of which can be part of neurosyphilis.

Spirochetal uveitis:

  • Organism: Treponema pallidum
  • Anterior uveitis:
    • It can present as granulomatous or non-granulomatous iritis typically in the secondary syphilis stage
    • Iris roseola - dilated iris vessels that develop into nodules
    • ‘Plastic’ iritis occurs in congenital syphilis and Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction

[[figure-1]]

  • Posterior uveitis:
    • It occurs as disseminated, peripheral, or diffuse choroiditis.
  • Treatment: Systemic penicillin

Horner's Syndrome (Option B): This condition is caused by disruption of the sympathetic pathway to the eye and presents with ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis. It does not cause absent pupillary light reflex or preserved accommodation reflex.

Papilledema (Option C): Papilledema is swelling of the optic disc due to increased intracranial pressure, which can affect vision but would not explain the absence of the light reflex with preserved accommodation. It also doesn't account for the coordination and speech problems.

Optic Neuritis (Option D): Optic neuritis involves inflammation of the optic nerve, which can cause vision changes, but it does not typically cause the combination of absent light reflex with intact accommodation. Also, optic neuritis usually doesn't present with the full range of neurological symptoms seen here.

On examination, it is noted that the pupillary light reaction is absent, but the accommodation reaction is present. Which condition is most likely responsible for this presentation?

explanationHtml:
• The Right Superior Oblique (RSO) and the Left Inferior Rectus (LIR) are the yoke muscles involved in levodepression (the downward movement of both eyes when the gaze is directed to the left).
  • Right Superior Oblique (RSO): The superior oblique muscle in the right eye helps depress the eye when it is abducted (pushed outward).
  • Left Inferior Rectus (LIR): The inferior rectus muscle in the left eye helps depress the eye.
  • These two muscles coordinate to cause the downward movement of the eyes when looking to the left.

Yoke muscles

  • Yoke muscles are pairs of extraocular muscles, one in each eye, that work together to ensure coordinated eye movements in the same direction.
  • These muscles function according to Hering's Law of Equal Innervation, which ensures that corresponding muscles in both eyes receive equal neural impulses for synchronised movement.
  • Hering’s Law of Equal Innervation would mean that the right lateral rectus (yoke muscle) should be balanced with the left medial rectus (vs Sherrington’s law: This law about reciprocal innervation states that increased innervation and contraction of a muscle is automatically associated with reciprocal decrease in innervation and contraction of its antagonist).
  • The yoke muscle pairs facilitate various eye movements:

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

  • Horizontal Gaze (Left or Right):
    • Leftward Gaze (Levoversion):
      • Left Lateral Rectus (abducts the left eye)
      • Right Medial Rectus (adducts the right eye)
    • Rightward Gaze (Dextroversion):
      • Right Lateral Rectus (abducts the right eye)
      • Left Medial Rectus (adducts the left eye)
  • Vertical Gaze (Up or Down):
    • Upward Gaze (Elevation):
      • Right and Left Superior Rectus (elevate the eyes)
      • Right and Left Inferior Oblique (assist in elevation)
    • Downward Gaze (Depression):
      • Right and Left Inferior Rectus (depress the eyes)
      • Right and Left Superior Oblique (assist in depression)
  • Inward Gaze (Convergence):
    • Both Medial Rectus muscles contract to bring the eyes inward (toward the nose) during near-vision tasks, such as reading.

LSO and RIR (Option A): Incorrect because LSO (Left Superior Oblique) helps in depression but not for levodepression. RIR (Right Inferior Rectus) is also involved in depression but doesn't pair with LSO for this movement.

RIO and LIR (Option C): RIO (Right Inferior Oblique) assists with elevation, not depression. LIR does help in depression, but they don't work together for levodepression.

LIO and RIR (Option D): LIO (Left Inferior Oblique) assists with elevation, not depression. RIR does help in depression, but this pair is not correct for levodepression.



Reference:
  • Yanoff & Duker Ophthalmology, 5th edition, Pg- 1193,1194

question: A young patient presents with progressive visual distortion. Based on the ocular finding shown in the image, what is the investigation of choice to confirm the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The examination shown is the cover test, which is used to detect manifest strabismus (tropia) by assessing ocular alignment.
  • During the test, one eye is covered while the examiner observes the movement of the uncovered eye.
  • If the uncovered eye moves to take up fixation, it indicates that it was previously misaligned.
  • In esotropia, the affected eye is deviated medially (inward). When the normal eye is covered, the deviated eye moves outward (temporally) to assume fixation, confirming the presence of a manifest convergent squint.
  • Esotropia is the most common form of childhood strabismus and, if left untreated, may result in amblyopia, loss of binocular vision, and impaired stereopsis.

Exotropia (Option B) is a form of divergent strabismus, in which the affected eye deviates laterally (outward). During the cover test, the deviated eye would move inward (nasally) to regain fixation when the fellow eye is covered. This pattern is opposite to the movement demonstrated in the video.

Hypertropia (Option C) refers to vertical misalignment, in which one eye is positioned higher than the other. During the cover test, the corrective movement would occur in the vertical plane rather than the horizontal plane. Therefore, it does not explain the outward movement of the eye observed in this case.

Nystagmus (Option D) is characterized by rhythmic, involuntary oscillatory eye movements, which may be horizontal, vertical, or torsional. The cover test is not primarily used to diagnose nystagmus, and the eye movement demonstrated represents realignment of ocular deviation rather than involuntary oscillation.



Reference:

Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology: A Systematic Approach, 9th Edition, Pages 315, 716, 717

[[figure-1]]

  • Blowout fracture (Option A): Causes mechanical restriction (commonly inferior rectus entrapment → limitation of upgaze). History of trauma would be present.
  • Thick pterygium (Option B): Can cause restricted ocular motility but is progressive and gradual, not sudden diplopia.
  • Subluxation of lens (Option C): Produces monocular diplopia (persists even when one eye is closed). Not gaze-dependent, unlike this case.


Reference:
  1. Parsons Diseases of the eye, 23rd Edition, Page 211.
  2. Yanoff & Duker Ophthalmology, 5th edition, Page 935.
  3. Comprehensive Ophthalmology, A K Khurana, 7th edition, Page 357.
question: A 45-year-old male complains of double vision, describing seeing two overlapping images when looking in a specific direction. He reports that this problem started suddenly about two weeks ago and is most noticeable when looking towards the right side. There is no history of trauma. On examination, he has limited movement of the right eye towards the right. What is the most likely cause of this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The squint/strabismus remains constant in all directions of gaze with no associated diplopia, suggesting that it is a case of concomitant squint.

Concomitant Squint/Strabismus:

  • Angle of deviation equal in all 9 gazes.
  • No limitation of eye movements, no diplopia initially.
  • Primary deviation = secondary deviation.
  • Common in early childhood/congenital.
  • Adaptations: amblyopia (negative), abnormal retinal correspondence (positive).

Incomitant Squint/Strabismus (Option B):

  • Deviation varies in different gazes.
  • Ocular movements restricted, diplopia present.
  • Late presentation; secondary deviation > primary deviation.

Paralytic Squint/Strabismus (Option C)

  • Type of incomitant squint due to paralysis of one/more EOMs.
  • History of diplopia, restricted movement toward paralyzed muscle.
  • Head often turned toward action of paralyzed muscle.
  • Secondary deviation > primary deviation.

Pseudo-strabismus (Option D)

  • Eyes actually aligned, only appear misaligned.
  • Causes:
    • Pseudo-esotropia → epicanthal folds, high myopia (negative angle kappa)
    • Pseudo-exotropia → telecanthus, hypertelorism, high hypermetropia (positive angle kappa)

[[figure-1]]



Reference:

Yanoff & Duker Ophthalmology, 5th Edition, Pages 1211, 1217
question: A 7-year old child is brought to the clinic by her parents due to concerns about her right eyes appearing misaligned. On examination, her squint remains constant in all directions of gaze. She does not report any diplopia, and there are no limitations in eye movement. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The child has concomitant (comitant) squint, characterised by a constant angle of deviation in all directions of gaze, full extraocular movements, and equal primary and secondary deviations.

  • It commonly develops during early childhood and is not associated with extraocular muscle paralysis.
  • Most children with longstanding concomitant squint do not experience diplopia because of sensory adaptations, including suppression, amblyopia, and abnormal retinal correspondence (ARC).

[[figure-1]]

Incomitant Squint (Option B): Incomitant squint is characterised by a variable angle of deviation in different directions of gaze, often with restricted ocular movements. Diplopia is common, particularly in acquired cases.

Paralytic Squint (Option C): Paralytic squint is a type of incomitant strabismus caused by paralysis of one or more extraocular muscles. It presents with restricted eye movements, diplopia, abnormal head posture, and secondary deviation greater than primary deviation.

Pseudostrabismus (Option D): In pseudostrabismus, the eyes are normally aligned, but facial features such as prominent epicanthal folds, a broad flat nasal bridge, telecanthus, hypertelorism, or a positive angle kappa create the false appearance of ocular misalignment. Ocular alignment and motility are normal.



Reference:

Yanoff & Duker Ophthalmology, 5th Edition, Pages 1211, 1217
question: AA 7-year-old child is brought by her parents because they have noticed that her right eye appears deviated. On examination, the angle of deviation remains the same in all directions of gaze, ocular movements are full, and the child does not complain of diplopia. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Woman with head tilt to right, left hypertropia and hypertropia increases on right gaze or on left gaze in adduction. These are classic features of left superior oblique (CN IV) palsy.

  • Superior oblique: depresses, intorts, abducts the eye.
  • In paralysis, hypertropia worsens:
    • On gaze towards opposite side (right gaze) → depression by SO needed.
    • On adduction → SO acts as primary depressor; palsy → hypertropia.
  • Head tilt toward opposite shoulder is compensatory to reduce diplopia (Bielschowsky head tilt test).

Right superior oblique (Option A): Palsy would affect right eye, not left hypertropia.

Right inferior oblique (Option C): Palsy would reduce elevation in adduction of right eye, not hypertropia in left eye.

Left inferior oblique (Option D): Palsy would reduce elevation in adduction of left eye, but SO palsy presents with hypertropia, not limitation of elevation.



Reference:
  1. www.researchgate.net/publication/345627720_Keys_to_Solve_Park-3_Step_Test
  2. eyewiki.org/Three_Step_Test_for_Cyclovertical_Muscle_Palsy
question: A 65 year old woman presented to the OPD with her head tilted towards the right side. On examination, she was having left hypertropia which increases on looking right or medially. The muscle which is most likely paralyzed is:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient has left superior oblique palsy (left trochlear nerve palsy).

  • The superior oblique primarily intorts, secondarily depresses the adducted eye, and tertiarily abducts the eye.
  • Paralysis of the left superior oblique results in left hypertropia, which becomes more pronounced on right gaze (contralateral gaze) and during adduction of the left eye, when the superior oblique normally functions as the principal depressor.
  • Patients typically adopt a compensatory head tilt to the opposite shoulder (right side) to minimise vertical diplopia.
  • On the Bielschowsky head tilt test, tilting the head toward the affected (left) side worsens the hypertropia, helping localise the affected superior oblique muscle.

Right Superior Oblique (Option A): Paralysis of the right superior oblique causes right hypertropia, which worsens on left gaze and right head tilt, not the left hypertropia seen in this patient.

Right Inferior Oblique (Option C) elevates the adducted right eye. Its palsy causes limited elevation in adduction of the right eye, rather than left hypertropia with compensatory right head tilt.

Left Inferior Oblique (Option D) elevates the adducted left eye. Paralysis produces defective elevation in adduction (hypotropia in upgaze) rather than the hypertropia that increases in adduction, which is characteristic of left superior oblique palsy.



Reference:

  1. http://www.researchgate.net/publication/345627720_Keys_to_Solve_Park-3_Step_Test
  2. http://eyewiki.org/Three_Step_Test_for_Cyclovertical_Muscle_Palsy
question: A 65-year-old woman presents with her head tilted toward the right shoulder. Examination reveals left hypertropia, which increases on right gaze and on adduction of the left eye. Which extraocular muscle is most likely paralyzed?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • If the patient only sees three green dots, it suggests suppression of the right eye, as the red lens over the right eye would normally allow them to see the red dot.
  • The fact that only green dots are seen indicates that the right eye is not contributing to vision.

WORTH’S FOUR DOT TEST

  • Setup: Red lens over the right eye, green lens over the left eye; patient views 4 lights (1 red, 2 green, 1 white).
  • Interpretation:
    • Normal binocular vision (Option D): Sees all 4 lights; no squint.
    • Abnormal retinal correspondence: Sees all 4 lights despite manifest squint.
    • Right eye suppression: Sees only 3 green lights; right eye not contributing.
    • Left eye suppression (Option C): Sees only 2 red lights; left eye not contributing.
    • Alternating suppression: Sees 3 green and 2 red lights alternately.
    • Diplopia (Option A): Sees 5 lights (2 red + 3 green); double vision present.

[[figure-1]]



Reference:

Yanoff & Duker Ophthalmology, 5th edition, Pages 1206, 1207
question: A 40-year-old patient presents for binocular vision assessment. The ophthalmologist performs the Worth’s Four Dot Test. The patient wears red-green glasses and reports seeing three green dots. What does this finding most likely indicate?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In the Maddox rod test, if the vertical red line (seen by the right eye) appears to the right of the white light, it suggests that the eyes are converging, which is indicative of esophoria.

MADDOX ROD TEST

  • Patient is asked to fixate on a point light in the centre of a Maddox tangent scale at a distance of 6 metres.
  • A Maddox rod is placed in front of one eye with the axis of rod parallel to the axis of deviation.
  • The Maddox rod converts the point source into a line.
  • Thus, the patient will see a point light with one eye and a red line with the other.
  • Due to dissimilar images of the two eyes, fusion is broken and heterophoria becomes manifest.

[[figure-1]]

  • Exophoria (Option B): Eye deviates outward → line appears to the left of the light.

  • Right hyperphoria (Option C): Vertical deviation → Maddox rod placed horizontally (line vertical) detects vertical deviations. Not relevant here.

  • Left hyperphoria (Option D): Vertical deviation of left eye → line placement differs; not indicated in this case.



Reference:

smartoptometryacademy.com/maddox-rod-test-all-you-need-to-know/
question: During a Maddox rod test, the patient is asked to view a distant light source. With the Maddox rod placed in front of the right eye, the patient reports seeing a vertical red line to the right of the white light. What type of ocular misalignment does this result suggest?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Pseudo-Von Graefe Sign is due to aberrant regeneration of the third cranial nerve following a palsy.
  • The co-contraction of the levator palpebrae superioris and inferior rectus muscles leads to eyelid retraction on downgaze, distinguishing it from other conditions.
  • This Pseudo-Von Graefe Sign is not associated with pupil abnormalities, and the pupil typically remains unaffected.

[[figure-1]]

Von Graefe’s Sign (Option A) is seen in Graves’ disease, characterized by delayed descent of the upper eyelid during downgaze caused by restrictive orbitopathy affecting the eyelid.

[[figure-2]]

Hutchinson’s Pupil (Option B): Typically seen in uncal herniation, characterized by a unilateral dilated pupil that is unresponsive to light due to compression of the third cranial nerve, often associated with raised intracranial pressure.

[[figure-3]]

Marcus Gunn Jaw-Winking Phenomenon (Option D) involves ptosis that improves with jaw movement due to aberrant innervation between the trigeminal nerve (motor division for the jaw) and the levator palpebrae superioris.



Reference:

Parsons Diseases of the eye, 23rd Edition, Page 1032
question: A 45-year-old male presents with eyelid retraction on downgaze. He has a history of ocular nerve injury. Which of the following best describes this condition?

correctAnswer: A. Duane Retraction Syndrome Type I
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The child presents with:
    • Limited abduction of the left eye
    • Globe retraction and narrowing of the palpebral fissure on adduction
    • Widening of the palpebral fissure on attempted abduction
  • This clinical picture is characteristic of Duane Retraction Syndrome (DRS) Type I, the most common subtype.

Duane Retraction Syndrome Type II (Option B): Incorrect because it shows limited adduction with normal abduction, which is the reverse of this case.

Duane Retraction Syndrome Type III (Option C): Incorrect as both abduction and adduction are limited, not just abduction.

Sixth Cranial Nerve Palsy (Option D): Incorrect because, although there is limited abduction, there is no globe retraction or palpebral fissure change on adduction.



Reference:

Yanoff & Duker Ophthalmology, 5th edition, Page 1215
question: A 7-year-old girl has limited abduction of the left eye, with globe retraction and narrowing of the palpebral fissure on adduction and widening of the fissure on attempted abduction. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The Given Clinical scenario with facial weakness, lateral gaze impairment & weakness on the left side of the body along with ventral pontine lesion points toward Millard-Gubler Syndrome

Syndromes Associated with Abducens Nerve:

  • Gradenigo Syndrome (Option A):
    Mastoiditis → petrous apex inflammation → VI nerve palsy + facial pain (V nerve) + deafness.

  • Moebius Syndrome (Option C):
    Congenital → VI & VII palsy, esotropia/exotropia, orofacial dysmorphism, feeding/speech difficulty.

  • Foville Syndrome (Option D):
    Dorsal pons lesion → VI palsy + VII palsy + contralateral hemiparesis + central Horner.



Reference:
  1. Yanoff & Duker Ophthalmology, 5th edition, Page 1215
  2. Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 230
question: A 60-year-old patient presents with the following symptoms: right-sided facial weakness, right-sided lateral gaze impairment, and weakness on the left side of the body. Imaging reveals a ventral pontine lesion. Which of the following syndromes best describes this patient's condition?

correctAnswer: C. Head turn towards the same side, avoiding diplopia
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In sixth cranial nerve palsy, the affected eye cannot abduct properly, leading to diplopia that often improves with a head turn towards the affected side.
  • This compensatory mechanism helps align the eyes to avoid double vision.
  • CN VI supplies the lateral rectus → abduction deficit → esotropia (inward eye).
  • Typical clinical features:
    • Horizontal diplopia (not vertical).
    • Diplopia worse on gaze toward the affected side.
    • Compensatory head turn towards the affected side to reduce diplopia.
    • Pupils are not affected (parasympathetics travel with CN III, not VI).

Vertical diplopia (Option A): Seen in CN IV palsy (superior oblique), not CN VI.

Pupils are affected (Option B): Pupillary involvement is a feature of CN III palsy, not CN VI.

Crossed Diplopia (Option D): Crossed diplopia = seen in exotropia (outward deviation), but CN VI palsy causes esotropia → uncrossed diplopia.



Reference:

Yanoff & Duker Ophthalmology, 5th edition, Pages 933, 934

options.text: Head turn towards the same side, avoiding diplopia

question: A 45-year-old man has double vision and an inward deviation of his left eye. On examination it is found to be associated with 6th Cranial Nerve Palsy. What finding is typical for sixth cranial nerve palsy?

correctAnswer: A. Diplopia relieves while going downstairs
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In trochlear nerve palsy, there is vertical diplopia which worsens while going downstairs

Trochlear Nerve (CN IV) Palsy:

  • Clinical Features:
    • Hypertropia (Option C)
    • Increase in hypertropia on opposite gaze (Option D)
    • Excyclotorsion (outward rotational movement of the eye)
    • Vertical Diplopia - Increases on Downgaze
    • Depressed Chin with face towards the opposite side
    • Head tilt towards the opposite side (Option B)
    • Poor depression in adduction is typical.
    • Crossed Diplopia

[[figure-1]]



Reference:
  1. Yanoff & Duker Ophthalmology, 5th edition, Pages 932, 934
  2. Parsons Diseases of the eye, 23rd Edition, Page 992

options.text: No diplopia with head tilt away from the left side
Increase in hypertropia on opposite gaze

question: A 45-year-old patient reports diplopia and is found to have left trochlear nerve palsy. Which of the following findings is not typically associated with it?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Brown's Syndrome is a congenital ocular motility disorder caused by the fibrous tightening of the superior oblique tendon, causing a restriction in eye movement due to issues, and is not associated with third cranial nerve (CN III) palsy.

Syndromes associated with Third Cranial Nerve Palsy (Oculomotor Nerve):

Weber’s Syndrome (Option A)

  • Lesion: Midbrain, involving CN III fascicle + corticospinal tract.
  • Features: Ipsilateral CN III palsy + contralateral hemiplegia.

Benedikt’s Syndrome (Option B)

  • Lesion: Midbrain, involving CN III fascicle + red nucleus.
  • Features: Ipsilateral CN III palsy + contralateral tremor/involuntary movements.

Nothnagel’s Syndrome (Option C)

  • Lesion: Midbrain, involving CN III fascicle + superior cerebellar peduncle.
  • Features: Ipsilateral CN III palsy + ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia.


Reference:
  1. Yanoff & Duker Ophthalmology, 5th edition, Page 931, 932
  2. Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 231
  3. AK Khurana Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th Edition, Page 372
question:
A 65-year-old patient presents with the following findings.

Which of the following is least likely to be associated with this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The given scenario is diagnosed as paralytic strabismus, caused by 3rd nerve (oculomotor) palsy in which accommodation is completely lost due to paralysis of the ciliary muscles.

[[figure-1]]

  • Ptosis is present (Option A): Levator palpebrae superioris (CN III) is paralysed → drooping of the eyelid.

  • Mydriasis is present (Option B): If the parasympathetic fibers are involved (especially in compressive lesions), the pupil is dilated.

  • Pupil is fixed (Option C): When parasympathetic fibers are affected the pupil is dilated and poorly reactive (appears fixed).



Reference:
  1. Parsons Diseases of the eye, 23rd Edition, Pages 1000, 1024, 1027.
  2. Yanoff & Duker Ophthalmology, 5th edition, Pages 938, 968.
  3. Comprehensive Ophthalmology, A K Khurana, 7th edition, Page 369.
question: A 60-year-old man presents with sudden onset double vision and difficulty aligning his eyes, which began three weeks ago. He has a history of hypertension and recently experienced a mild stroke. Examination reveals that his eye is positioned downward and outward. Which of the following statements about this condition is incorrect?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • A–V pattern strabismus: Difference in horizontal deviation between upgaze and downgaze.
  • Diagnostic criteria:
    • A-pattern: Difference ≥ 10 prism dioptres (PD).
    • V-pattern: Difference ≥ 15 PD.

[[figure-1]]



Reference:
  1. Yanoff & Duker Ophthalmology, 5th edition, Page 1221, 1222.
  2. Comprehensive Ophthalmology, A K Khurana, 7th edition, Pages 371, 372.
question: How much is the difference in deviation between upward gaze and downward gaze in A-V pattern strabismus?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The Spiral of Tillaux refers to the spiral arrangement of the insertion points of the extraocular muscles on the sclera, which is essential for coordinating eye movements and maintaining proper ocular alignment.

Order of Insertion (Spiral of Tillaux):

Medial Rectus

Inserts closest to the limbus, about 5.5 mm from the limbus.

Inferior Rectus

Inserts 6.5 mm from the limbus.

Lateral Rectus

Inserts 6.9 mm from the limbus

Superior Rectus

Inserts the farthest, about 7.7 mm from the limbus.

[[figure-1]]

Annulus of Zinn (Option A) is a fibrous ring at the back of the orbit around the optic nerve. It serves as the origin for the four rectus muscles (lateral, medial, superior, and inferior), providing a stable attachment point that allows these muscles to control eye movement.

[[figure-2]]

Scleral spur (Option C) is the part of the sclera in the anterior chamber angle and plays a role in the drainage of aqueous humour.

Tenon’s capsule (Option D) is the fascial sheath that surrounds the eye and helps provide structural support.



Reference:

Yanoff & Duker Ophthalmology, 5th Edition, Pages 1190,1191
question: Which of the following is known for its specific pattern of muscle insertions around the sclera, essential for the alignment and movement of the extraocular muscles?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The child has mixed accommodative esotropia, in which both significant hypermetropia and a high accommodative convergence/accommodation (AC/A) ratio contribute to the esotropia.

  • The +6.50 D hypermetropia causes excessive accommodative effort to maintain clear vision, leading to increased accommodative convergence (refractive component).
  • The fact that the esotropia is greater during near fixation indicates a high AC/A ratio (non-refractive component).
  • The coexistence of these two mechanisms is diagnostic of mixed accommodative esotropia.
    Management includes full cycloplegic hyperopic correction, with bifocal lenses considered if a significant near deviation persists despite appropriate refractive correction.

Accommodative Refractive Esotropia (Option A): Refractive accommodative esotropia is caused solely by uncorrected hypermetropia, with a normal AC/A ratio. The angle of esotropia is similar for distance and near fixation, unlike the increased near deviation seen in this patient.

Accommodative Non-refractive Esotropia (Option B): Non-refractive accommodative esotropia is caused by a high AC/A ratio with little or no significant hypermetropia. Esotropia is predominantly greater at near, but marked hypermetropia (+6.50 D) is not a typical feature.

Infantile Esotropia (Option D): Infantile esotropia presents as a large-angle constant esotropia developing before 6 months of age. It is not related to accommodation or hypermetropia and does not characteristically worsen during near fixation.



Reference:
  1. Parsons Diseases of the eye, 23rd Edition, Pages 979, 980, 982.
  2. Yanoff & Duker Ophthalmology, 5th edition, Pages 1212, 1213.
  3. Comprehensive Ophthalmology, A K Khurana, 7th edition, Page 363.
question: A 3-year-old girl presents with esotropia, which increases on focusing near objects. This issue has progressively worsened over the past few months, and she has difficulty with close visual tasks. A refractive error of +6.50 D has been identified. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The scenario describes a case of stereopsis, and the appropriate test is the Titmus fly test.

  • Stereopsis is the ability to perceive the 3rd dimension (depth perception).
  • Titmus fly test:
    • The patient has to wear polarized glass, and the fly will be seen from different angles.
    • Evaluate how well the child can perceive the relative depth of the images.

HESS chart (Option A) is used to measure the degree of deviation, especially if torsional, and particularly to measure any progressive increase or decrease by Hess screen test.

Cover-uncover test (Option B): This test is used to detect manifest (tropia) and latent (phoria) strabismus by covering one eye and then uncovering it to observe any corrective movement. It evaluates ocular misalignment, not depth perception.

Maddox rod test (Option D) is used for detection of latent squint.



Reference:
  1. Parsons Diseases of the eye, 23rd Edition, Page 257.
  2. Yanoff & Duker Ophthalmology, 5th edition, Page 1208.
  3. Comprehensive Ophthalmology, A K Khurana, 7th edition, Page 355.
question: A 10-year-old child is having trouble catching a ball, climbing stairs, and performing fine motor tasks. She has a tendency to avoid activities requiring precise hand skills. No developmental delay was detected. Which of the following tests would be appropriate for diagnosing her condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The above image depicts the Bruckner test, showing a brighter reflex in a squinted eye.

Bruckner Test:

  • The examiner sits at arm’s length in front of the patient and shines the beam of a direct ophthalmoscope onto the patient’s eyes, wide enough to illuminate both eyes simultaneously.
  • Fundus reflex is depicted as,
    • Squinted eye: Brighter reflex
    • Fixing eye (normal eye): Dark or dull reflex

[[figure-1]]

Hirschberg test (Option A) involves throwing light into the eye from a distance and the patient is asked to look at the light (an infant does this reflexively). A rough indication of the angle of the squint can be obtained from the position of the corneal reflex.

[[figure-2]]

Prism cover test (Option C): In the prism bar cover test, prisms of increasing strength (apex towards the deviation) are placed before one eye while the patient fixates with the other; the cover–uncover test is repeated until no corrective movement occurs, and the deviation is then measured in prism dioptres

[[figure-3]]

Krimsky test (Option D): In this test, the patient fixates on a point light while prisms of increasing power (apex towards the squint) are placed before the normal eye until the corneal light reflex is centered in the squinting eye; the prism power needed corresponds to the squint angle in prism dioptres.

[[figure-4]]



Reference:

Parsons Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page 960, 961
question: The parents of an 8-month-old girl have observed her eyes misaligning, especially when she focuses on objects up close, with one eye occasionally turning inward. They consulted an ophthalmologist, who conducted the test shown below. What is the name of this test?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The above image depicts Hirschberg’s test, which is used to indicate the angle of squint by measuring the light reflex on the cornea.

Hirschberg’s Test

  • The angle of the squint can be roughly estimated (Option A) by observing the position of the corneal reflex when light is directed into the eye.

[[figure-1]]

  • Procedure
    • Shine light into both eyes (ophthalmoscope/torch).
    • Patient fixates on distant light source.
  • Findings
    • Fixing eye: Reflex in centre of pupil (Option B).
    • Squinting eye: Reflex decentred.
    • At pupillary border → ~18–20° deviation
    • Between pupillary border & limbus → ~35°
    • At limbus → ~45° (Option C)

[[figure-2]]



Reference:
  1. Parsons Diseases of the eye, 23rd Edition, Page 965, 966
  2. Yanoff & Duker Ophthalmology, 5th Edition, Page 1199
  3. A K Khurana Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th Edition, Page 365

In an aligned eye, the reflex is centred

question: A 10-year-old boy's parents noticed his left eye turning inward, especially when tired or focusing on near objects. An ophthalmologist diagnosed strabismus and performed the test shown below. Which statements about this test are correct?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The Maddox Rod Test is primarily subjective.
  • It requires the patient to interpret the position of lines projected onto their retina, and their perception is used to measure the angle of deviation.
  • This contrasts with purely objective tests, which rely on direct measurements or observations without relying on the patient's subjective interpretation of visual stimuli.

[[figure-1]]

Objective Tests

Subjective Tests
  • Corneal Light Reflex Test (Hirschberg Test (Option D), Krimsky Test)
  • Bruckner Test
  • Cover-Uncover Test (Option C)
  • Prism Bar Test (Option B)
  • Synoptophore
  • Maddox Rod Test
  • Maddox Wing Test
  • Lancaster Red-Green Test
  • Hess Screen
  • Haploscopic Devices (Major Amblyoscope)


Reference:
  1. Parsons Diseases of the eye, 23rd Edition, Pages 973, 974
  2. Yanoff & Duker Ophthalmology, 5th edition, Pages 1198, 1199, 1200
question: A 32-year-old patient presents with eye strain and headaches. The ophthalmologist plans to perform a series of tests to evaluate the patient’s strabismus. All of the following are objective tests used to assess strabismus except?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Distinguishes between mechanical restriction and neurogenic palsy.
  • Procedure: Examiner passively moves the eyeball with forceps.
    • If resistance → mechanical restriction (e.g., muscle entrapment, dysthyroid orbitopathy).
    • If free movement → nerve palsy.

Hess Screen Test (Option A) measures the degree of misalignment but does not differentiate between mechanical restriction and nerve palsy directly.

Cover Test (Option C) is useful for detecting and measuring deviations but not for determining the cause of limited movement.

Worth’s 4-Dot Test (Option D) assesses binocular vision and suppression but does not provide specific information about mechanical restrictions or nerve palsy.



Reference:
  1. Parsons Diseases of the eye, 23rd Edition, Pages 964, 965
  2. Yanoff & Duker Ophthalmology, 5th edition, Page 1201
question: A 35-year-old patient presents with increased diplopia on upward gaze and restricted movement of the left eye. The patient also has a history of recent orbital trauma. To determine whether the limitation is due to a mechanical restriction or a nerve palsy, which of the following tests is most appropriate?

explanationHtml:
• The given image is of Cover-Uncover Test which is used to differentiate between latent squint (heterophoria) and manifest squint (heterotopia).

Cover–Uncover Test

  • Purpose: Differentiate latent squint (heterophoria) from manifest squint (heterotropia).
  • Covers horizontal & vertical deviations (not torsional).

Cover Test

  • Detects tropias (manifest squint).
  • Procedure: Cover one eye → observe uncovered eye for movement.
    • Nasal movement: Exotropia
    • Temporal movement: Esotropia
    • Upward movement: Hypotropia
    • Downward movement: Hypertropia
  • Deviation quantified with prism cover test.

Uncover Test

  • Detects phorias (latent squint).
  • Cover one eye → remove → if eye moves to refixate → phoria/intermittent tropia.
  • Alternate cover test maximizes dissociation; prisms quantify.

Other Tests

  • Maddox Rod (Option A): Detects/quantifies heterophoria; not for latent vs manifest distinction.

  • Synoptophore (Option B): Measures squint angle, binocular vision, fusion; not for phoria vs tropia.

  • Maddox Wing (Option D): Measures eso/exophoria; mainly for latent deviations.



Reference:

Yanoff & Duker Ophthalmology, 5th Edition, Page 1199,1200
question: A 10-year-old patient presents to the clinic with complaints of occasional double vision and eye strain during schoolwork. On examination, you suspect she may have a squint and perform the following test. What is this test known as?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Squint / Strabismus:

  • A condition where the visual axes of both eyes do not meet at a point (Misalignment of Visual axes)
    • Esotropia: Inward misalignment of the eyes. (Common in Hypermetropes)
    • Exotropia: Outward misalignment of the eyes. (Common in Myopes)

question: A 32-year-old patient presents with diplopia and difficulty looking upwards and to the right, with limited elevation of the right eye. You suspect a lesion affecting a muscle responsible for vertical movement. Which axis describes the rotational movement, and which muscle is likely affected?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Sherrington’s Law of Reciprocal Innervation of the same eye, states that when one muscle contracts (agonist), its opposing muscle (antagonist) in the same eye must relax to allow coordinated movement.

  • Hering’s Law (Option A) refers to the equal innervation of corresponding eye muscles to ensure simultaneous and symmetrical movements.
  • Henle’s law of accommodation (Option C) refers to anatomical observations related to the length-tension relationship in muscles, particularly in the context of accommodation in the eye.
  • Donder’s Law (Option D) pertains to the torsional movements of the eye.

explanationHtml:

Given that the left eye fails to adduct and diplopia is more noticeable during right gaze, it suggests that the left medial rectus is not functioning properly.

  • In INO, the ipsilateral medial rectus fails to adduct due to MLF lesion.
  • The contralateral lateral rectus becomes overacting, often with nystagmus, as it tries to abduct unopposed.
  • Here, left medial rectus fails → right lateral rectus shows overaction.

Left Lateral Rectus (Option B)

  • Abducts the left eye in left gaze.

question: A 25-year-old patient presents with a condition in which, upon examination, the left eye fails to adduct during right gaze. The patient reports diplopia, which is more noticeable when looking to the right. Which extraocular muscle is most likely overacting in this patient's condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient has left internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) caused by a lesion of the left medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF).

  • This interrupts the pathway connecting the right abducens nucleus to the left oculomotor nucleus, resulting in failure of adduction of the left eye during right gaze, while convergence is usually preserved.
  • The right lateral rectus demonstrates abducting nystagmus, which is clinically described as overaction due to increased innervational drive (Hering's law of equal innervation) attempting to compensate for the impaired adduction of the opposite eye.
  • In young adults, multiple sclerosis is the most common cause of INO, whereas brainstem infarction is more common in older patients.

[[figure-1]]

Right Medial Rectus (Option A): The right medial rectus adducts the right eye during left gaze. It is not involved in right gaze and does not exhibit overaction in left INO.

Left Lateral Rectus (Option B): The left lateral rectus abducts the left eye during left gaze. It is not responsible for the abnormal findings during right gaze.

Left Medial Rectus (Option D): The left medial rectus muscle is structurally normal, but it fails to receive the appropriate signal due to a lesion of the left medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF). It therefore underacts during right gaze and is not the overacting muscle.



Reference:

Yanoff & Duker Ophthalmology, 5th Edition, Pages 1193, 1194

question: During a neuro-ophthalmic assessment, a patient is instructed to rapidly shift their gaze between two targets. The examiner notes quick, ballistic eye movements connecting the points of fixation. Which term best describes this type of eye movement?

correctAnswer: B. The frontal lobe controls the slow pursuit component
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Optokinetic nystagmus (OKN) is a physiological reflex elicited by moving visual stimuli, consisting of a slow pursuit phase (controlled by the parieto-occipito-temporal cortex) and a fast saccadic phase (controlled by the frontal eye fields). It is useful for detecting malingering, assessing visual function, and may show reversal in congenital motor nystagmus.

Optokinetic Nystagmus (OKN)

Phases of OKN
  • Slow phase: Smooth pursuit following the stimulus.
  • Fast phase: Saccadic refixation in the opposite direction; nystagmus is named by the fast phase

Cortical control
  • Slow phase: Parieto-occipito-temporal cortex (Option B)
  • Fast phase: Frontal eye fields

Clinical relevance
  • Detects malingering or functional blindness. (Option A ruled out)
  • Assesses visual acuity in infants or non-verbal patients.
  • Evaluates homonymous hemianopia.
  • Reversal may occur in congenital motor nystagmus due to null point shift. (Option D ruled out)

question: What is the function of the superior oblique muscle?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical scenario of secondary deviation was higher than the primary deviation during examination and forced duction test yielding negative results is suggestive of paralytic squint

Squint/Strabismus: Misalignment of the visual axis. This condition is also called Heterotropia.

  • Classification: It is divided into latent squint (phorias) and manifest (tropia).
  • Latent squint - classification
    • Hyperphoria
    • Exophoria
    • Esophoria
  • Manifest squint - classification
    • Esotropia/Exotropia/Hypertropia
    • Concomitant/Incomitant squint
      • Concomitant: Esotropia/Exotropia
      • Incomitant:
        1. Paralytic (paralysis of the muscles)
        2. Restrictive squint (fibrosis of the muscles)
        3. A-V pattern or pattern squint
        4. Ocular motility defects

Concomitant squint (Option A):

  • It's a type of manifest squint in which the angle of deviation remains equal in all the 9 gazes; there is no associated limitation of ocular movements .
  • Primary deviation is equal to secondary deviation.
  • Primary deviation is the amount of deviation in a squinted eye.
  • Secondary deviation: It is the amount of deviation in the normal eye (behind the cover).
  • Concomitant squint commonly occurs during early childhood or can be congenital (congenital squint).
  • Eye movements are normal and no double vision (diplopia).
  • Amblyopia develops later (negative adaptation).
  • Abnormal retinal correspondence also plays a role. It is a positive adaptation.

Incomitant squint (Option B): This condition is just the opposite of concomitant squints, where the degree of squint varies in different aspects.

  • Secondary deviation is higher than primary deviation in paralytic squint.
  • In contrast to concomitant squints, there is a late presentation.
  • There is palsy of other muscles, which causes limited ocular movements (ocular movements are restricted).
  • Diplopia is also a very important feature of inconcomitant squints.

Paralytic squint (Option C): Paralytic squint is a type of incomitant squint in which ocular deviation results from complete or incomplete paralysis of one or more extraocular muscles.

  • History of diplopia and confusion
  • Secondary deviation is greater than primary deviation.
  • Ocular movements are restricted towards the action of paralyzed muscle.
  • Head is turned towards the action of paralyzed muscle.

Pseudo-strabismus (Option D): Pseudostrabismus is a condition when the eyes are well aligned but appear to be misaligned.

  • Causes of Pseudo-esotropia:
    • Epicanthal folds
    • High myopia (high negative angle kappa)
  • Causes of Pseudo-Exotropia:
    • Telecanthus or hypertelorism
    • High hypermetropia (high positive angle kappa)

Restrictive squint (Option B)occurs when there is a limited range of movement of the affected eye due to restrictions in extraocular muscle function or mechanical factors (e.g., orbital trauma or thyroid eye disease) and would yield a positive forced duction test.



Reference:

AK Khurana 7th edition page 583, 584
question: In a 40-year-old patient with diabetes, a squint was observed. The secondary deviation was higher than the primary deviation during examination. The forced duction test yielded negative results. Which type of squint is expected to be predominant in this individual?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The image depicts limited adduction of the right eye due to weakness of medial rectus muscle seen in 3rd nerve palsy.
  • The oculomotor nerve is responsible for innervating several extraocular muscles, including the medial rectus, superior rectus, inferior rectus, and inferior oblique muscles.

Nerves of the eye:

Optic nerve (CN II)
  • Purely sensory
  • Senses the incoming light and image displayed on retina

Oculomotor nerve (CN III)
  • Innervates majority of the extraocular muscles
  • Motor innervation to the superior rectus muscle, medial rectus muscle, inferior rectus muscle, inferior oblique muscle, levator palpebrae superioris muscle, ciliary muscle, and the sphincter muscle.

Trochlear nerve (CN IV)
  • Motor innervation to the superior oblique muscle

Trigeminal Nerve (CN V)

  • Ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve provides sensory innervation to the eye
  • Afferent part of corneal and lacrimation reflex

Abducens Nerve (CN VI)
  • Motor innervation to the lateral rectus muscle

Facial Nerve (CN VII)
  • Motor innervation of the orbicularis oculi muscle
  • Efferent part of corneal and lacrimation reflex

Sympathetic Nervous System
  • Long ciliary nerves: Innervates the pupillary dilator muscles causing mydriasis

Parasympathetic nervous system
  • Short ciliary nerves: Innervates the sphincter pupillae muscles causing miosis

Incorrect Options:

6th CN palsy (Option C) This affects lateral rectus muscle and inability to abduct the eye towards the side of gaze.

4th CN palsy (Option B) This affects the superior oblique muscle, leading to difficulty in looking downward, particularly in an adducted position (e.g., difficulty descending stairs). It does not impact horizontal gaze.

7th CN palsy (Option D) This nerve innervates facial muscles, not extraocular muscles.



Reference:

question: The movement lost on left gaze as depicted in the image is seen in?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The image shows convergent squint (esotropia) — the eyes are deviated inward, a common finding in children with uncorrected hyperopia (farsightedness).

Mechanism:

  • In hyperopia, light focuses behind the retina, so the child must use accommodation (focusing effort) to bring objects into clear focus.

  • Accommodation is linked with convergence (the inward turning of the eyes).

  • Excessive accommodation therefore triggers excessive convergence, leading to accommodative esotropia.

  • This condition is especially common in young children and is corrected with convex (+) lenses, which reduce the need for accommodation.

Incorrect Options

  • A) Myopia: Causes divergence (exotropia) rather than convergence.

  • B) Astigmatism: Causes blurred vision due to irregular corneal curvature, not eye deviation

  • D) Emmetropia: Normal refractive state; no squint develops.



Reference:

Parsons Diseases of the eye, 23rd Edition, Pg - 955,957,960,963,971

question: The chart depicted in the image is ______?

explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D) Oculomotor nerve palsy

Explanation:

Given image is suggestive of Paralytic Strabismus of a patient with down and out left eye with ptosis on primary gaze with inability to elevate, adduct completely is suggestive of Oculomotor (Third) nerve palsy.

[[figure-1]]

Features of third nerve palsy

  • Ptosis: Due to paralysis of the LPS (levator palpebrae superioris) muscle
  • The eyeball is deviated down and outwards (due to actions of the lateral rectus and superior oblique muscles).
  • The pupil is fixed and dilated (due to paralysis of the sphincter pupillae muscle)
  • Ocular movements are restricted
  • Accommodation is completely lost (due to paralysis of the ciliary muscle)
  • Crossed diplopia is elicited by raising the eyelid.
  • Absence of Both direct and consensual reflexes in the affected eye
  • These compensatory head postures are motor adaptations used to minimise the effects of double vision
    • Horizontal Diplopia: The patient often tilts the head downward
    • Vertical Diplopia: The head is positioned with the chin either raised or lowered
    • Torsional Diplopia: The head is tilted sideways

Incorrect Options:

Medial Rectus Palsy (Option A): This condition is characterized by weakness or paralysis of the medial rectus muscle, which controls the eye's inward movement, often leading to an inability to ADDUCT the eye.

Trochlear Nerve Palsy (Option B): This pertains to a neurological disorder where damage to the fourth cranial nerve, or trochlear nerve, results in vertical diplopia when the patient looks down and inability to DEPRESS the eye completely .

Abducens Nerve Palsy (Option C): This is a disorder marked by the impairment of the sixth cranial nerve, resulting in lateral gaze palsy.



Reference:

Parsons Diseases of the Eye 23rd Edition, Pages 1000,1024,1027.
question: Identify the condition

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Decrease in best corrected visual acuity in one or both eyes with no apparent pathology of the eye and visual pathway is suggestive of Amblyopia.

Amblyopia: Definition, Types, and Clinical Characteristics:

Definition:

  • Partial, reversible vision loss in one or both eyes.
  • Absence of organic diseases of l ocular media, retina, visual pathway
  • The eye appears normal, but vision is impaired.

Types of Amblyopia:

Type

Cause

Key Features

Strabismic Amblyopia

The brain suppresses input from one eye due to constant squint (strabismus).

Common cause; underdevelopment of vision in the deviated eye.

Stimulus Deprivation Amblyopia

Hindered vision due to obstruction from early life (e.g., congenital cataracts, ptosis, dense central corneal opacity).

Lack of visual stimulation affects normal development.

Anisometropic Amblyopia

A significant difference in refractive error between eyes.

The brain favours the clearer eye, leading to amblyopia in the other.

Ametropic Amblyopia

High uncorrected refractive errors in both eyes.

Bilateral; is less severe compared to other types.

Meridional Amblyopia

Uncorrected astigmatism affecting specific visual meridians.

Affects one or both eyes depending on the astigmatism degree.

Clinical Characteristics:

  • Reduced Visual Acuity:
    • Affects recognition acuity more than resolution acuity.
    • Graded by severity:
      • Mild: 20/25 to 20/60
      • Moderate: 20/70 to 20/100
      • Severe: 20/200 or worse
  • Neutral Density Filter Test: Slight improvement in visual acuity through a filter (unlike organic eye diseases).
  • Crowding Phenomenon: Difficulty identifying letters on crowded charts (e.g., Snellen chart).
  • Fixation Pattern: Eccentric fixation (focusing away from the fovea) indicates severity.
  • Color Vision: Usually normal but affected in severe cases (vision below 6/36).
  • Other ocular examination: usually NO abnormalities are found (Option A)

Brain lesion (Option D): A lesion in the visual pathway can result in loss of vision but no such examination findings is mentioned.

Retinoblastoma (Option B): Retinoblastoma shows leukocoria which is absent here.

Congenital cataract (Option C): Loss of red reflex is seen in congenital cataract.

Treatment of amblyopia:

Amblyopia treatment should be started as early as possible (younger the child, better the prognosis). Amblyopia therapy works best when initiated in young children under 3 years of age and comprise:

Occlusion therapy (Option C): Occlusion of the sound (normal) eye to force use of amblyopic eye is the main stay in the treatment of amblyopia. Following methods are deployed,

  • Full-time occlusion: Up to 2 years, the occlusion should be done in 2:1, i.e. 2 days in sound eye and one day in amblyopic eye; at the age of 3 years, 3:1; at the age of 4 years, 4:1; At the age of 5 years, 5:1; and after the age of 6 years 6:1.
  • Part-time occlusion: 4-6 hours/day, as shown by Amblyopia Treatment Study (ATS), and is as effective as full-time occlusion.
  • Maintenance occlusion: After vision equalization, part-time occlusion continues until at least 8 years of age.

Given image is suggestive of Paralytic Strabismus of a patient with down and out left eye with ptosis on primary gaze with diplopia, inability to elevate, adduct completely is suggestive of Oculomotor (Third) nerve palsy.

Features of third nerve palsy

  • Ptosis: Due to paralysis of the LPS (levator palpebrae superioris) muscle
  • The eyeball is deviated down and outwards (due to actions of the lateral rectus and superior oblique muscles).
  • The pupil is fixed and dilated (due to paralysis of the sphincter pupillae muscle)
  • Ocular movements are restricted
  • Accommodation is completely lost (due to paralysis of the ciliary muscle)
  • Crossed diplopia is elicited by raising the eyelid.
  • Absence of Both direct and consensual reflexes in the affected eye
  • These compensatory head postures are motor adaptations used to minimise the effects of double vision
    • Horizontal Diplopia: The patient often tilts the head downward
    • Vertical Diplopia: The head is positioned with the chin either raised or lowered
    • Torsional Diplopia: The head is tilted sideways

Optic nerve injury (Option A): Injury to the optic nerve would cause visual disturbances.

Trochlear Nerve injury (Option C): This pertains to a neurological disorder where damage to the fourth cranial nerve, or trochlear nerve, results in vertical diplopia when the patient looks down and inability to DEPRESS the eye completely .

Abducens Nerve injury (Option D): This is a disorder marked by the impairment of the sixth cranial nerve, resulting in lateral gaze palsy.

explanationHtml:
Amblyopia, often called "lazy eye," is a condition where the vision in one eye is reduced because the brain favors the other eye. It can be caused by strabismus, but the cover-uncover test itself does not diagnose amblyopia

Cover-Uncover Test is used to differentiate between latent squint (heterophoria) and manifest squint (heterotopia).

  • Cover test: Detects Heterotropia (Manifest Squint) (Option B)
  • Uncover test: Detects Heterophoria (Latent Squint) (Option A)

Cover-Uncover Test:

  • The cover and uncover tests assess horizontal and vertical strabismus, but not torsional deviations. They also evaluate the ability of each eye to fixate on a target.

Cover Test:

  • Detects Tropias: Measures constant deviations of the visual axis.
  • Procedure:
    • Cover one eye with a paddle, thumb, or occluder.
    • Observe the uncovered eye for movement:

[[figure-1]]

  • Nasal movement: Esotropia
  • Temporal movement: Exotropia
  • Upward movement: Hypertropia
  • Downward movement: Hypotropia
  • For young children, use small toys instead of bright lights.
  • Quantify the deviation with the simultaneous prism and cover test by introducing a prism before one eye until movement stops. Repeat with the prism before the other eye.

Uncover Test:

  • Identifies latent deviations or tropias.
  • Procedure:
    • Cover one eye and then observe the covered eye when the cover is removed.
    • If the eye reverts to fixation, it indicates a phoria or intermittent tropia.
    • If the eye remains deviated, it suggests a tropia with fixation preference for the fellow eye.

[[figure-2]]

Alternate Cover Test: Detects phorias by dissociating the visual axes.

  • Alternate covering each eye to maximize visual axis dissociation.
  • Care must be taken to permit time for each eye to reside behind the cover (the cover must not be “fanned” before the eyes).
  • Use prisms to quantify phorias or tropias. If measurements are unclear, estimate the midpoint between defined movements.

Lateral Nystagmus (Option C): Nystagmus is involuntary, rhythmic eye movements. The cover-uncover test might exacerbate nystagmus, though it is not the primary test for detecting it.



Reference:

Yanoff & Duker Ophthalmology, 5th edition, Pg - 1199,1200

Displacement of one eyeball (Option B):

Diplopia

• Amblyopia (lazy eye) is treated by forcing the amblyopic eye (the weaker eye) to work, and the most common method is occlusion therapy, where the normal eye is covered (occluded) to stimulate the weaker eye.

Treatment of Amblyopia (aka Lazy eye)

  • Early treatment is essential for better visual outcomes.
  • Occlusion of Normal Eye (Occlusion Therapy)
    • Mainstay treatment involves occluding the normal eye to force the amblyopic eye to work.
    • Full-time occlusion: All waking hours or all but one hour. Schedule by Age:
      • Up to 2 years: 2:1 (2 days occluded, 1 day not)
      • 3 years: 3:1
      • 4 years: 4:1
      • 5 years: 5:1
      • 6 years and older: 6:1
    • Part-time occlusion: 4-6 hours/day, as shown by Amblyopia Treatment Study (ATS), and is as effective as full-time occlusion.
    • Maintenance occlusion: After vision equalization, part-time occlusion continues until at least 8 years of age.
    • Ensure no media opacity or refractive errors before starting occlusion therapy.
  • Other Methods
    • Penalization: Blurring vision in the sound eye with atropine or over-plus lenses.
    • Computerized Home Vision Therapy: Uses specially designed software as an adjunct to occlusion therapy.
  • Pharmacologic Manipulation
    • Levodopa/Carbidopa: Studied as an adjunct to occlusion therapy.
    • Other agents: Citicoline and omega fatty acids
  • Pleoptics: Pleoptic exercises are done to improve foveal fixation, though less commonly used now.

Observation (Option A): Passive observation is not effective for amblyopia, as early intervention is key to improving visual outcomes.

Spectacles or refraction with a near addition (Option B): These are useful for refractive errors (e.g., hyperopia) but do not directly address amblyopia unless coupled with occlusion therapy.

Radial keratotomy (Option D): This is an outdated surgical procedure for correcting refractive errors, not for treating amblyopia.



Reference:
  • Kanski’s clinical ophthalmology, John F. Salmon, 10th edition, Page no: 718-719
  • Amblyopia - PMC

Correct Option D - 4th nerve:

  • The vertical diplopia in the absence of ptosis, combined with a characteristic head posture, suggests fourth nerve disease.
  • The fourth cranial nerve controls the superior oblique muscle. The main actions of the superior oblique are intorsion and depression in adduction.
  • A compensatory head posture avoids diplopia. To compensate for the weakness of intorsion, there is a contralateral head tilt. To alleviate the weakened depression of the eye, the chin is slightly depressed
  • Peripheral lesions cause ipsilateral and nuclear lesions contralateral superior oblique weakness.

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Third nerve: Third nerve cranial palsy presents with ptosis , abduction and depression in the primary position,, dilated pupil, and limited adduction, elevation and depression .

Option C - 7 CN Palsy (Facial Nerve Palsy): The seventh cranial nerve controls the muscles of facial expression and is responsible for taste sensation on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.

explanationHtml:

Abducens Nerve (cranial nerve VI)

Type

Motor

Origin

Pons (lower border, opposite the pyramid of the medulla).

Course

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Functional component
  • General somatic efferent fibres: Arise from the abducent nucleus in the pons and supply the lateral rectus muscle of the eyeball.
  • General somatic afferent fibres carry proprioceptive sensations from the lateral rectus and terminate in the mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve.

Supply

Lateral rectus muscle of the eyeball

Clinical aspect

Lesion or injury (elevated intracranial pressure) of the abducens nerve results in paralysis of the lateral rectus muscle, leading to:

The amplitude of accommodation is at its highest in early childhood and gradually decreases as the lens loses its elasticity over time. According to standard clinical tables (such as Donders' table), the amplitude of accommodation at age 10 is approximately 14 Diopters (D).

For a child aged 7, the value is even higher, making 14 D the most appropriate choice among the options to represent the high accommodative power of a young child.

  • Amplitude of Accommodation (AoA), which measures the maximum change in the refractive power of the eye achieved by the ciliary muscle and lens.
  • As a person ages, this power declines (eventually leading to presbyopia).
  • To calculate the expected minimum amplitude, Hofstetter’s formula is often used.

Minimum AoA = 15 - 0.25 x age

For a 7-year-old, the minimum expected value is approximately 13.25 D, and the average is usually higher (around 16 D).

CORNEAL DEGENERATION

IMAGE

Arcus Senilis

  • Cause: Lipoid infiltration, common in elderly

  • Appearance: Grey/white crescent → complete ring; thicker sup/inf; sharp periphery, fades centrally; ≤1 mm wide

  • Effect: No impact on vision/vitality

  • Variants: Arcus juvenilis in young → linked to dyslipidemia

Band Shaped Keratopathy

  • Common in chronic uveitis, aphakic eyes with prolonged silicone oil, and occasionally linked to hyperparathyroidism or vitamin D poisoning.
  • Characterized by a whitish band across the cornea with round ‘holes’ or cleaves.
  • Caused by hyaline infiltration and deposition of calcareous salts in the superficial stroma.
  • Treatment options include scraping off the opacity, dissolving it with sodium edetate, or using an excimer laser.

Vortex keratopathy

  • Vortex keratopathy, also known as corneal verticillata.
  • It is a distinctive pattern of corneal epithelial deposits that appear as whorl-like (vortex) lines swirling outward toward the periphery of the cornea.
  • Etiology:
    • Drugs: Chloroquine, Amiodarone (dose related), Tamoxifen, Indomethacin, Netarsudil.
    • Fabry disease

Salzmann nodular degeneration

  • A degenerative condition of the cornea.
  • Bluish-white, avascular nodules.
  • Located in the superficial stroma and Bowman’s membrane.
  • Typically occurs in individuals with a history of previous corneal disease.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Pages 261, 262, 263, 264, 265.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

CORNEAL DEGENERATION

IMAGE

Vortex Keratopathy / Cornea verticillata

  • Appearance: Whorl-like corneal epithelial opacity

  • Causes: Drugs (amiodarone, chloroquine, phenothiazines, netarsudil, indomethacin) or Fabry disease (Option B)

[[figure-1]]

Lipid Keratopathy

  • Deposits: Whitish/yellowish cholesterol & fatty acids in cornea

  • Primary: Rare, normal serum lipids

  • Secondary: With corneal vascularization (infections, interstitial keratitis, trauma, glaucoma, iridocyclitis)

  • Fat deposits: Intracellular → extracellular with stromal necrosis (Option C)

[[figure-2]]

Salzmann nodular degeneration

  • Type: Degenerative corneal condition

  • Nodules: Bluish-white, avascular

  • Location: Superficial stroma + Bowman’s membrane (Option A)

  • Associations: Prior corneal disease

  • Course: Slowly progressive

  • Treatment: Lamellar keratoplasty

question: Which of the following statements about corneal degeneration is incorrect?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The image shows a faint opacity covering the central cornea, which suggests a Nebular opacity.
  • Although faint, a nebular opacity can severely impact vision, while also causing maximum discomfort (by inducing irregular astigmatism)
  • The irregular refraction caused by the nebula distorts the image more than a denser opacity like leucoma, leading to greater visual discomfort and blurring.

[[figure-1]]

Macular corneal opacity (Option B):

  • This semi-dense opacity affects the cornea less than a nebula regarding irregular refraction, but it still causes significant visual impairment.

[[figure-2]]

Leucomatous corneal opacity (Option C):

  • While this dense white opacity blocks light more completely, it causes less irregular refraction than a nebula.
  • If it doesn't cover the entire pupillary area, it may not affect vision as much as a nebula.

[[figure-3]]

Adherent leucoma (Option D):

  • This is a dense opacity associated with iris incarceration and is typically more significant in light blockage, but its effect on vision varies depending on the extent of iris involvement.

[[figure-4]]

Management of corneal opacity:

  • Optical Iridectomy: This procedure can be used for central macular or leucomatous opacities when vision improves with pupil dilation.
  • Phototherapeutic Keratectomy (PTK): PTK uses an excimer laser, and is effective for treating superficial corneal opacities, such as nebulae.
  • Keratoplasty
  • Cosmetic-Coloured Contact Lenses: These lenses offer a cosmetic solution for unsightly scars in the eyes without visual potential.
  • Corneal Tattooing: It is mainly reserved for firm scars in eyes with no useful vision.


Reference:

https://courseware.cutm.ac.in/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/CORNEAL-OPACITIES.pdf
question:
A 45 y/o male presents with progressively worsening vision and evident discomfort in his left eye over the past year. O/E, the following findings were observed, which caused significant blurring of his vision.

Which of the following corneal opacities is most likely causing the greatest reduction in his vision?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Multiple milky, granular deposits in the anterior corneal stroma, with a clear cornea between the deposits, indicate Granular corneal dystrophy Type 1.

Corneal dystrophies are bilateral, non-inflammatory, inherited disorders grouped by primary layer affected:

  • Anterior (Epithelial/Bowman's): Epithelial basement membrane, Meesmann, Reis-Bucklers.

  • Stromal: Granular, lattice, macular, Avellino, Schnyder, congenital stromal.

  • Posterior (Endothelial): Fuchs, CHED, PPCD.

TGFB1 Corneal Dystrophies

These dystrophies are associated with mutations in the TGFB1 gene

Lattice Corneal Dystrophy (LCD)(Option B)

LCD – Corneal dystrophy with amyloid deposits forming lattice lines in stroma.

  • LCD1: Early onset, central lattice lines, recurrent erosions → visual loss.

  • LCD2 (Gelsolin type): Later onset, peripheral lattice lines spreading centrally.

[[figure-1]]

Granular Corneal Dystrophy (GCD)

GCD – Hyaline deposits in corneal stroma.

  • GCD1: Childhood onset, milky granular anterior stromal deposits.

  • GCD2: Early onset, mixed granular + lattice deposits.

[[figure-2]]

Other Stromal Dystrophies

Macular Corneal Dystrophy (MCD)

(Option C)
  • Inheritance: Autosomal recessive

  • Features: Diffuse stromal haze + macular opacities

  • Onset: Childhood / early adulthood

  • Effect: Severe visual impairment

Schnyder Corneal Dystrophy (SCD)

(Option D)

  • Inheritance: Autosomal dominant

  • Deposits: Cholesterol crystals in stroma

  • Features: Ring-shaped corneal opacities

  • Effect: Progressive vision loss



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, Edition 9, Page- 255, 256, 257, 258, 259.
question: A 25-year-old patient presents with a history of gradual vision loss. O/E, multiple milky, granular deposits are seen in the anterior corneal stroma, with clear cornea between the deposits. Which type of stromal corneal dystrophy is most likely?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

All of the above signs are features of keratoconus.

Munson’s Sign

  • Definition: V-shaped deformity of lower lid on down gaze.

  • Mechanism: Conical cornea pushes the lower lid forward in a conical manner.

  • Seen in advanced keratoconus.

[[figure-1]]

Scissor’s Reflex

  • Seen on retinoscopy.

  • Reflex appears as two blades of a scissor moving against each other.

  • Due to irregular astigmatism in keratoconus.

Vogt’s Striae

  • Vertical, parallel lines in deep stroma/Descemet’s membrane.

  • Orientation: Parallel to steep axis of the cornea.

  • They disappear on applying pressure to the globe.

[[figure-2]]

Fleischer’s Ring

  • Iron deposition at the base of the cone.

  • Layer involved: Epithelium.

  • Appears as a yellow-brown to greenish ring on slit-lamp.

[[figure-3]]

Note

  • Fleischer’s Ring vs Kayser-Fleischer Ring:

    • Fleischer’s = iron deposition in epithelium (keratoconus).

    • Kayser-Fleischer’s = copper deposition in Descemet’s membrane (Wilson’s disease).

Treatment of Keratoconus:

  • Spectacles / Toric soft contact lens: For cylindrical correction of astigmatism
  • Choice of contact lens: Rigid gas permeable / Semi soft contact lens - for irregular cornea
  • TOC: In progressive case: C3R (Corneal collagen cross linking) with riboflavin
    • Dresden protocol
      • Instill riboflavin eye drops every 5 minutes, continuing for 30 min
      • Expose to Ultraviolet A rays for another 30 min (continuing riboflavin application)
  • Keratoplasty:
    • Penetrating keratoplasty: best prognosis in non-inflammatory conditions
    • DALK (Deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty)
  • For displaced / eccentric cones and non-progressive cases: INTACS (Intra corneal segments)



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Pages 248, 249.
question:
A 19 y/o female presents with a history of progressive worsening of vision that is not fully corrected by glasses. After evaluation, she is diagnosed with keratoconus. Which of the following examination findings are seen in keratoconus?
