explanationHtml:
Correct Option: B) Corneal topography


Explanation:

The image demonstrates Munson sign, which is suggestive of advanced keratoconus, caused by conical protrusion of the cornea.


Corneal topography is the gold standard investigation for diagnosing keratoconus, as it provides a detailed map of corneal curvature, detects early ectatic changes, and identifies asymmetric inferior steepening, even before clinical signs become evident.


Keratometry (Option A): Measures central corneal curvature only and may miss early or irregular astigmatism seen in keratoconus.


Pachymetry (Option C): Measures corneal thickness and is useful for monitoring progression, but cannot diagnose keratoconus alone.


A-scan (Option D): Used for axial length measurement and intraocular lens power calculation, not for corneal ectatic disorders.
question: A young patient presents with this sign. Diagnosis is best made by:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
In adults, endothelial density averages about 2500-3000 cells/mm². Cell count declines with age because endothelial cells do not regenerate; remaining cells enlarge to cover defects.

Age Group

Endothelial Cell Density (cells/mm²)

At birth

3500-4000

Young adults

2500-3000

Old age (around 80 years)

~2000

Clinical Significance: Endothelial cell loss may occur due to surgical trauma, inflammation, or corneal dystrophies. When the cell density drops below approximately 500 cells/mm², the endothelium can no longer maintain corneal clarity, leading to corneal edema and decompensation.

800-1200 cells/mm² (Option A): Significantly reduced reserve; increased risk of postoperative corneal edema.

300-600 cells/mm² (Option B): Critically low density; corneal decompensation likely.

3500-4200 cells/mm² (Option D): Typical of neonates and infants, not adults.



Reference:

Parsons Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page 312.
question: A 58-year-old patient is evaluated before cataract surgery. Specular microscopy shows normal endothelial morphology and adequate reserve to maintain corneal deturgescence. Which of the following values most closely represents the expected endothelial cell density in such an adult?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
The given clinical scenario refers to Microcornea, a developmental anomaly characterized by a reduced horizontal corneal diameter.

Developmental Anomalies of Cornea

Microcornea
  • Horizontal corneal diameter ≤ 10 mm in children/adults (Option B)
  • < 9 mm in newborns (Option C ruled out)
  • Globe size usually normal
  • Associated with hypermetropia and shallow anterior chamber

Megalocornea

  • Diameter ≥ 12 mm (≥ 13 mm after 2 years)
  • Associated with high myopia, astigmatism
  • Often X-linked recessive

Cornea Plana
  • Abnormally flat cornea
  • Causes high hypermetropia

Keratoglobus / Keratectasia
  • Severe corneal thinning with generalized protrusion
  • May be linked to raised IOP or intrauterine keratitis

Microphthalmos

  • Entire eye is small
  • Axial length ≥ 2 SD below normal

Nanophthalmos
  • Small but structurally normal eye
  • Associated with hypermetropia, strabismus

Anophthalmos

Complete absence of the globe


Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th edition, Page 270.
question: A child presents for ophthalmic evaluation due to an abnormally small-appearing cornea. On examination, the horizontal corneal diameter is found to be reduced. Microcornea is diagnosed when the horizontal corneal diameter measures below which of the following values?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Among the given options, Neisseria gonorrhoeae can invade an intact corneal epithelium, causing rapidly progressive corneal ulceration even in the absence of trauma or a pre-existing epithelial defect.

  • Organisms that can penetrate intact corneal epithelium:
    • Neisseria gonorrhoeae
    • Neisseria meningitidis
    • Corynebacterium diphtheriae
    • Haemophilus aegyptius
    • Listeria
    • Shigella
  • Corneal defenses: Intact epithelium, tear film, and antimicrobial factors prevent infection; most bacteria need an epithelial defect to invade.
  • Clinical significance: Gonococcal keratitis causes hyperacute purulent conjunctivitis with rapid corneal involvement and a high risk of perforation, making it an ophthalmic emergency.

Incorrect Options:

Streptococcus pneumoniae (Option A) requires epithelial defect; causes serpiginous ulcer.

Staphylococcus aureus (Option B): Opportunistic; needs epithelial compromise.

Moraxella lacunata (Option D) causes angular conjunctivitis; corneal infection needs a defect.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th edition, Page 173.
question: A patient develops rapidly progressive corneal ulceration despite no history of trauma or epithelial defect. Which organism is known to invade an intact corneal epithelium?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
Fortified cefazolin eye drops are used at 5% concentration in combination with an aminoglycoside (e.g., tobramycin) for broad-spectrum coverage.

  • Rationale: Poor corneal vascularity requires high local antibiotic concentrations; fortified drops are prepared from injectable forms.
  • Cefazolin action: First-generation cephalosporin effective against gram-positive organisms (Staphylococcus, Streptococcus).
  • Initial management: Start intensive topical broad-spectrum antibiotics; escalate to fortified drugs if needed.
  • Common fortified regimen: Cefazolin 5%, Tobramycin 1.3%, Vancomycin 5%.
  • Adjuncts: Cycloplegics (e.g., atropine 1%), vitamins A & C, analgesics.
  • Non-healing Corneal Ulcers: Debridement, chemical cautery, or conjunctival flap.
  • Threatened perforation: Lower IOP, cyanoacrylate glue, bandage contact lens.


Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th edition, Page 217.
question: A young woman presents with sudden onset severe ocular pain, photophobia, tearing and a corneal epithelial defect with stromal infiltrate on slit-lamp examination. A bacterial corneal ulcer is diagnosed. What concentration of topical cefazolin is recommended in fortified therapy?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
The clinical scenario is classical for fungal keratitis, particularly infection by filamentous fungi such as Fusarium and Aspergillus, which are the most common cause of fungal keratitis.

Fungal Keratitis

Etiopathogenesis
  • Filamentous fungi (Fusarium, Aspergillus), hyphal organisms.
  • Usually, after plant matter trauma; yeast (Candida) affects immunocompromised eyes.

Predisposing factors

Trauma, chronic ocular disease, steroids, contact lenses, diabetes, and immunosuppression.

Clinical features
  • Gradual onset of pain, photophobia, blurred vision, discharge
  • Filamentous keratitis signs:
    • Grey-white corneal infiltrate with feathery margins
    • Satellite lesions

[[figure-1]]

  • Ring infiltrates or branching extensions
  • Stromal necrosis and thinning
  • Endothelial plaque and hypopyon

[[figure-2]]

  • Possible anterior uveitis, raised IOP, or endophthalmitis

Investigations

Corneal scraping, KOH mount, Gram/Giemsa, culture on Sabouraud agar

Management

  • Topical antifungals: Natamycin 5% (first choice), econazole, and amphotericin B.
  • Adjuncts: Cycloplegics, cautious antibiotics.
  • Systemic: Voriconazole/itraconazole for deep lesions.
  • Procedures: Debridement, keratoplasty, tissue adhesive if needed.

Gram-positive cocci (Option A) produce suppurative ulcer with dense infiltrate, not feathery margins.

Acanthamoeba (Option C): Severe pain out of proportion, ring infiltrate but history of water exposure or contact lenses.

Herpes simplex virus (Option D): Dendritic epithelial lesions, reduced corneal sensation.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th edition, Pages 218-220.
question: A farmer presents with gradually increasing ocular pain, photophobia and blurred vision after minor trauma with plant matter. Slit lamp shows a dry-looking corneal ulcer with feathery margins, satellite lesions and an endothelial plaque. A hypopyon is present. Which organism group is most likely responsible?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
The stromal infiltrates in fungal keratitis result from a Type III immune complex-mediated reaction, where fungal antigens form complexes with antibodies, activating complement and neutrophils, causing enzymatic stromal damage and curvilinear infiltrates.

  • Mechanism:
    • Immune complex deposition in stroma
    • Complement activation
    • Neutrophil chemotaxis
    • Enzymatic stromal destruction
    • Formation of curvilinear/ring-shaped infiltrates.

[[figure-1]]

Type I (IgE-mediated reaction) (Option A): Immediate allergy, e.g., vernal keratoconjunctivitis.

Type II (antibody-mediated cytotoxic reaction) (Option B): Targets cell surface antigens; not seen in corneal ulcers.

Type IV (delayed, cell-mediated reaction) (Option D): Seen in granulomatous infections; not typical for microbial keratitis infiltrates.



Reference:
  1. Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 218-220.
  2. Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases,10th Edition, Page 210-212.
question: A farmer develops a corneal ulcer after injury with plant material. Slit-lamp shows a dry ulcer with feathery margins and stromal infiltrates arranged in a curvilinear pattern. Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is mainly responsible for these stromal infiltrates?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
Topical steroids are strictly contraindicated in fungal corneal ulcers because they suppress the immune response and worsen fungal infections, increasing the risk of corneal melting and perforation.

Topical steroids are strictly contraindicated because they:

  • Promote fungal growth.
  • Suppress host cell-mediated immunity, reducing the body’s ability to fight infection.
  • Increase the risk of stromal melting and corneal perforation.
  • Mask clinical signs, potentially delaying diagnosis.
  • Increase the chances of endophthalmitis.

Vernal keratoconjunctivitis (Option A): Steroids are used in severe disease to control allergic inflammation.

Stromal keratitis (Option B): Often immune-mediated (e.g., herpetic stromal keratitis); steroids are indicated with antiviral cover.

Atopic dermatitis ocular involvement (Option C): Steroids may be required to control inflammation.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th edition, Page 216.
question: A patient with infectious keratitis presents to the OPD. In which of the following ocular conditions are topical steroids strictly contraindicated?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
Eye trauma with vegetative matter causing a dry corneal ulcer with feathery edges and satellite lesions indicates Fusarium fungal keratitis, for which the drug of choice is topical Natamycin due to its strong activity against filamentous fungi.

  • Risk factor: Eye trauma with vegetative matter (common in agricultural workers)
  • Symptoms: Gradually progressive eye pain and photophobia
  • Slit-lamp findings:
    • Dry corneal ulcer
    • Feathery margins
    • Satellite lesions
  • Diagnosis: Fungal keratitis
  • Causative organism: Fusarium (filamentous fungus)
  • Drug of choice: Topical Natamycin 5% → Most effective against filamentous fungi, including Fusarium and Aspergillus.

Amphotericin B (Option A): More effective against yeasts (e.g., Candida) and has limited efficacy against filamentous fungi like Fusarium.

Fluconazole (Option B): Has poor activity against filamentous fungi and is ineffective for Fusarium keratitis.

Nystatin (Option D): Primarily active against Candida species and is not used for filamentous fungal keratitis.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th edition, Pages 219-220.
question:
A 38-year-old agricultural worker presents with gradually worsening eye pain and photophobia following trauma with vegetative matter. Slit-lamp examination reveals a dry corneal ulcer with feathery edges and satellite lesions. Corneal culture grows Fusarium species.

Which of the following is the drug of choice for treatment?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Extensive corneal vascularization is not seen in keratomycosis (fungal keratitis). In fact, corneal neovascularization is typically absent, especially in the acute stages.

[[figure-1]]

Feathery extensions at the margins of the corneal ulcer (Option A): These are characteristic finger-like projections at the ulcer margins caused by filamentous fungi.

Sterile immune ring (Option C): Also known as Wessely ring, formed at the interface of fungal antigens and host antibodies.

[[figure-2]]

Endothelial plaque (Option D): Dense, whitish deposits of fibrin and leukocytes under the stromal lesion.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 216, 217

question: A 45 y/o man from a tropical region presents with a painful red eye, significant watering, and sensitivity to light after working in a garden with decaying plant material. The patient is diagnosed with keratomycosis. Which of the following is not an examination finding in keratomycosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The innermost layer of the cornea is the endothelium which consists of a single layer of hexagonal cells.
  • These cells are crucial for maintaining corneal transparency by regulating fluid balance within the cornea through an active pump mechanism.

  • Corneal transparency results from multiple structural and physiological factors acting together.

    • These include stromal collagen architecture, precise hydration control by the endothelium, an intact epithelium and tear film, avascularity, and absence of myelin in corneal nerves.

Layers of Cornea

Epithelium

(Option C ruled out)
  • The outermost layer comprises 5-6 layers of non-keratinized, stratified squamous epithelial cells.
  • Acts as a barrier, protecting the cornea and preventing tear fluid from entering the underlying stroma.
  • The basal cells at the limbus are stem cells responsible for regenerating the corneal epithelium.

Bowman’s Membrane

(Option D ruled out)
  • Located just beneath the epithelium, this acellular layer is 12 µm thick and composed of densely packed collagen fibrils.
  • It is a protective barrier to the stroma but cannot regenerate if damaged and heals by scarring.

Stroma

(Option A ruled out)
  • Making up about 90% of the cornea's thickness (approximately 0.5 mm thick), the stroma consists of collagen fibrils arranged in parallel layers.
  • Nearly uniform interfibrillar spacing and ordered fibril organization minimize light scatter, allowing destructive interference of scattered light and thus maintaining clarity.
  • These fibrils are embedded in a hydrated matrix of proteoglycans - Chondroitin and Keratan Sulphate (keratan sulphate maintains corneal transparency).

Pre-Descemet's Membrane (Dua's Layer)
  • This layer, discovered in 2013, is about 15 µm thick, acellular, and lies just above Descemet's membrane.
  • It is strong and resistant to air penetration.

Descemet's Membrane
  • A robust basement membrane of the corneal endothelium is made of collagen and glycoproteins.
  • It is tense, but when torn, curls inwards on itself.
  • It can regenerate if damaged and is resistant to trauma and pathological processes.

Endothelium

(Option B)
  • The innermost layer consists of a single layer of flat, hexagonal cells.
  • These cells are crucial for maintaining corneal transparency by regulating fluid balance within the cornea through an active pump mechanism.

  • Using ion transporters (notably Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and associated bicarbonate systems), it pumps fluid from the stroma into the aqueous, maintaining a relatively dehydrated stroma and preventing edema and loss of transparency.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

  • The pre-corneal tear film creates a smooth, optically regular anterior refracting surface over the corneal epithelium.

    • This smooth, well-distributed layer fills in minor epithelial irregularities, reduces surface scatter, and provides an optically polished interface for incoming light.

  • The cornea is normally avascular, with nutrition coming from tears, aqueous humor, and perilimbal vessels.

    • Absence of blood vessels avoids hemoglobin, cellular elements, and vessel walls in the optical path, reducing scatter and helping keep the tissue clear.

  • Corneal nerves lose their myelin sheaths as they enter the cornea, remaining non-myelinated within the transparent zone.

    • Lack of myelin (which is opaque) and fine caliber of these fibers reduce light scatter, helping preserve transparency while still allowing high corneal sensitivity.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 204.
question: Which layer of the cornea is primarily responsible for maintaining its transparency by regulating fluid content?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The cornea uses both aerobic and anaerobic metabolism.

  • But the primary pathway = aerobic metabolism.

Oxygen & Nutrition

  • Oxygen comes mainly from the atmosphere (tear film).

  • Nutrients diffuse from the aqueous humor and limbal vessels.

Lens

  • In the lens, the primary metabolism is anaerobic.

  • ~80% of glucose in the lens is metabolized via anaerobic glycolysis.

Anaerobic Glycolysis in Cornea

  • If anaerobic glycolysis is activated in cornea → corneal edema.

  • Mechanism:

    • Lactic acid accumulates → metabolic acidosis.

    • This inhibits the Na⁺/K⁺ pump of endothelial cells.

    • Pump failure → hydration of cornea → corneal edema.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 204.
question: What is the primary metabolism of cornea?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Corneal Nerve Supply is not directly involved in maintaining transparency.
  • It provides sensation to the cornea but does not influence the clarity of the corneal tissue.

Factors Responsible for Corneal Transparency:

  1. Corneal Epithelium and Tear Film (Option A)
  2. Arrangement of Corneal Lamellae
  3. Avascularity (Option B)
  4. Barrier Function
  5. Endothelial Pumps (Option D)
  6. Evaporation
  7. Normal Intraocular Pressure (IOP)
  8. Swelling Pressure (SP)
  9. Corneal Crystals/Proteins


Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 204.
question: Which of the following factors is not responsible for maintaining corneal transparency?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Instrument

Image

Keratometry

  • Definition: Objective measurement of central corneal curvature to assess astigmatism

  • Principle: Image size analysis of anterior cornea using visible doubling

  • Normal Values: Average ~45 D; >45 D in keratoconus

  • Types: Javal-Schiotz, Bausch & Lomb

[[figure-1]]

Auto refractive Keratometer

Keratoscopy / Placido’s Disc

  • Disc with alternating black & white rings

  • Assesses corneal surface smoothness & curvature

  • Normal: Uniform, sharp ring reflections

  • Abnormal: Distorted rings → corneal irregularities

[[figure-2]]

Corneal Topography

  • Evaluates anterior corneal curvature

  • Produces colour-coded maps (shape, curvature, elevation)

  • Uses: Diagnose keratoconus, plan refractive surgery

  • Limitation: No information on posterior corneal surface

[[figure-3]]

Corneal Tomography (Pentacam)

  • Measures anterior & posterior corneal surfaces

  • Gives 3D corneal structure

  • Detects subclinical keratoconus

  • Assesses refractive surgery candidates

  • Uses Scheimpflug imaging for accurate measurements

  • Helpful in pre-op evaluation & disease monitoring

[[figure-4]]


Reference:
  1. Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 209
  2. www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK562157/#:~:text=Corneal%20topography%20evaluates%20the%20anterior%20surface%20of%20the%20cornea%20and,indications%2C%20and%20interpret%20its%20findings
question:
Match the following corneal assessment techniques with their correct descriptions:

1) Keratometry

a) Measures both anterior and posterior corneal surfaces.

2) Placido's Disc

b) Assesses the smoothness and curvature of the corneal surface.

3) Corneal Topography

c) Evaluate the anterior curvature of the cornea and generate colour-coded maps.

4) Corneal Tomography (Pentacam)

d) Measures the curvature of the central cornea.

correctAnswer: D. Aesthesiometer measures corneal sensation by evaluating the second cranial nerve
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Aesthesiometer (Esthesiometer) measures corneal sensation by evaluating the ophthalmic branch of the fifth cranial nerve (trigeminal nerve), not the second cranial nerve (optic nerve).
  • The fifth cranial nerve is responsible for sensory input from the cornea, which includes detecting tactile sensations.
  • The second cranial nerve (optic nerve) is primarily involved in vision, not sensation.

INSTRUMENT

IMAGE

Pachymetry

  • Measures corneal thickness.
  • Used for diagnosing and treating glaucoma. (Option A)
  • In glaucoma workup:
    • Thick cornea → IOP overestimated by Goldmann tonometer.
    • Thin cornea → IOP underestimated.

[[figure-1]]

Specular Microscopy:

  • Noninvasive technique for photographing and assessing the corneal endothelium. (Option B)
  • Evaluates endothelial cell number + morphology.
  • Detects polymegathism (variation in size) & pleomorphism (variation in shape).

[[figure-2]]

[[figure-3]]

Esthesiometer (Aesthesiometer):

  • Measures corneal sensation (trigeminal V1)
  • Methods: Cotton tip (qualitative), Cochet-Bonnet esthesiometer (nylon filament, 0–6 cm, 11–200 mm/gm)
  • Uses: Diagnose neurotrophic keratitis (Option C) , monitor corneal health in long-term contact lens wearers

[[figure-4]]

Explanation:

  • The patient's clinical presentation, including the irregular corneal ulcer with greenish exudate and hypopyon, along with a history of contact lens use, suggests a bacterial corneal ulcer.
  • Pseudomonas aeruginosa is known for causing irregular corneal ulcers with greenish mucopurulent exudate, rapid progression, and hypopyon.
  • It is also common in contact lens-related infections.

[[figure-1]]

Etiology of Purulent Corneal Ulcer:

Corneal epithelial damage:

  • Abrasion, xerosis, exposure keratitis, keratomalacia, bullous keratopathy, neuroparalytic keratitis

Pathogens invading intact epithelium:

  • N. gonorrhoeae, N. meningitidis, C. diphtheriae, H. aegyptius, Listeria

Sources of infection:

  • Exogenous: conjunctival/lacrimal sac, foreign bodies, vegetative material, airborne/waterborne

Common bacteria:

  • General: Staph, Strep pneumoniae, Pseudomonas, Enterobacteriaceae

  • Contact lens wearers: Pseudomonas (MC), Acanthamoeba (differential)

Causative organisms:

  • Gram + cocci: Staph aureus/epidermidis, Strep pneumoniae

  • Gram – cocci: Neisseria spp.

  • Gram + bacilli: Corynebacterium, Bacillus cereus, Propionibacterium, Listeria, Clostridium

  • Gram – bacilli: Pseudomonas, Klebsiella, Proteus, E. coli, Serratia, Moraxella, H. influenzae

  • Filamentous: Actinomyces, Nocardia

  • Mycobacteria: NTM, M. tuberculosis



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, Edition 9, Page- 209, 210, 211.
question: A 32 y/o contact lens wearer presents with a red, painful eye, blurred vision, and increased sensitivity to light. Examination reveals lid swelling, conjunctival chemosis, and a large corneal ulcer with greenish exudate, rapidly expanding with hypopyon. What is the most likely cause?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The description of chronic use of corticosteroid eye drops and an ulcer that penetrates deeply into the corneal stroma, approaching Descemet's membrane, suggests a Perforating Ulcer.
  • Most common cause leading to perforation: Pseudomonas aeruginosa

[[figure-1]]

Perforating Corneal Ulcer

A perforating ulcer is a corneal ulcer that progresses through the entire thickness of the cornea, resulting in a communication between the anterior chamber and the external environment.

It represents one of the most serious complications of bacterial keratitis.

Pathogenesis

Bacterial toxins and inflammatory enzymes cause:

  • Stromal necrosis
  • Corneal melting
  • Progressive thinning

As the ulcer deepens:

Corneal ulcer → Stromal melting → Descemetocele → Perforation

Risk Factors

  • Chronic topical corticosteroid use
  • Virulent organisms (especially Pseudomonas aeruginosa)
  • Delayed treatment
  • Immunocompromised state
  • Severe bacterial keratitis

The history of prolonged steroid use is an important clue because steroids suppress local immunity and promote corneal melting.

Clinical Features

Symptoms

  • Severe pain
  • Redness
  • Photophobia
  • Watering
  • Sudden drop in vision

Signs

  • Marked corneal thinning
  • Descemetocele
  • Positive Seidel test after perforation
  • Shallow or flat anterior chamber
  • Iris prolapse may occur through the perforation

Complications

  • Endophthalmitis
  • Iris prolapse
  • Anterior synechiae
  • Adherent leucoma
  • Permanent visual loss

Management

Small Perforation

  • Cyanoacrylate glue
  • Bandage contact lens

Large Perforation

  • Tectonic graft
  • Therapeutic penetrating keratoplasty

Localized Ulcer (Option A): A localized ulcer is confined to a limited area of the cornea.


Adherent Leucoma (Option C): An adherent leucoma is a sequela or complication after a corneal perforation has occurred and healed with iris incarceration.


Sloughing Ulcer (Option D): While necrosis is present and sloughing might occur, the most immediate and critical risk associated with an ulcer extending deep into the stroma and approaching Descemet's membrane is full-thickness penetration, not merely the shedding of necrotic tissue.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Pages 211, 212, 213.
question: A 60 y/o woman presents with a painful red eye, photophobia, and a history of chronic use of corticosteroid eye drops. Examination reveals a corneal ulcer with necrosis extending deep into the corneal stroma, approaching Descemet's membrane. Which type of bacterial keratitis is this patient most at risk for?

correctAnswer: C. Topical steroids should be started immediately to reduce inflammation.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Topical steroids should not be used in bacterial keratitis as they can exacerbate the infection and delay healing.

Treatment of Bacterial Keratitis

  • Empirical Monotherapy:
    • A single fluoroquinolone (e.g., ofloxacin) is recommended but not standard practice due to high resistance rates in some regions.
    • Perforation is more likely in ulcers treated with ofloxacin.
  • Duo Therapy (Option D):
    • Use a combination of fortified cefazoline 5% and fortified tobramycin 1.3% to cover both gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria.
  • Ointments:
    • Ocular ointments can be beneficial at bedtime for milder cases and may serve as useful adjunctive therapy.
  • Cycloplegics (Option A):
    • Administer 1% atropine eye drops to reduce ciliary spasm pain, prevent posterior synechiae, increase blood supply, and decrease exudation.
    • 2% homatropine is an alternative.
  • Vitamin Supplements:
    • Vitamins A, B-complex, and C are recommended to promote early healing of the corneal ulcer.
  • Scleral involvement:
    • In Scleral or systemic involvement cases, systemic antibiotics like oral ciprofloxacin (750 mg twice daily) (Option B)or a combination of cephalosporin and aminoglycoside may be necessary.
  • Avoid Sponge/Pad and steroids.
    • Avoid using an eye sponge or pad to prevent infection from worsening by trapping bacteria.
    • Steroids should be avoided as they may exacerbate the infection and delay the healing process.



Reference:
  1. Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Pages 214, 215, 216.
  2. Ocular ointments

question: Which of the following statements about the treatment of bacterial keratitis is incorrect?

correctAnswer: C. Perform mechanical debridement and apply tissue adhesive glue.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

For impending corneal perforation, necrotic tissue is first removed (mechanical debridement), then tissue adhesive (e.g., cyanoacrylate glue) is applied to seal the thin area and prevent rupture.

  • Mechanical debridement is necessary to remove necrotic material and promote healing in a non-healing ulcer.
  • Tissue adhesive glue is indicated to prevent perforation, especially when the perforation is less than 2mm.

If the perforation is large, then penetrating keratoplasty can be done.


Increasing the frequency of antibiotic eye drops (Option A): At this stage, just increasing frequency won’t be useful.


Applying a pressure bandage and bed rest (Option B): Pressure can worsen thinning and precipitate perforation.


Topical steroids (Option D) are contraindicated as they can worsen the infection.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Pages 214, 215, 216

Keratomycosis Etiology

  • Most Common Causative Organisms:
    • Aspergillus fumigatus: Most common in India and tropical regions.
    • Fusarium (Option B): Common in warm climates like Brazil.
    • Candida albicans (Option A): More frequent in temperate climates.

question: A 60 y/o man from a tropical region presents with a painful, red eye and a corneal ulcer following recent exposure to decaying vegetable matter. Which is the most common fungal infection affecting the cornea?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient has fungal keratitis (keratomycosis), suggested by the history of corneal trauma with vegetative matter, the most common predisposing factor for filamentous fungal infection.

  • In India, Aspergillus species (especially Aspergillus fumigatus) are the most common cause of fungal keratitis, whereas Fusarium species are reported more commonly in several other tropical regions worldwide.
  • Fungal keratitis typically presents with a painful red eye, feathery-edged corneal infiltrate, satellite lesions, and hypopyon.
  • Diagnosis is confirmed by corneal scraping for microscopy and culture, and topical natamycin 5% is the first-line treatment for filamentous fungal keratitis.
  • Corneal trauma with vegetable matter is a classic risk factor for fungal keratitis.

Candida albicans (Option A): Candida albicans is the most common yeast causing fungal keratitis and typically infects previously diseased corneas or occurs in patients with chronic ocular surface disease, prolonged topical corticosteroid use, or immunocompromised states, rather than after vegetative trauma.

Fusarium species (Option B): Fusarium species are important causes of filamentous fungal keratitis and are strongly associated with vegetative trauma. They are the predominant pathogens in many parts of the world but are less common than Aspergillus in India, making this option incorrect in the Indian context.

Mucor species (Option C): Mucor species primarily cause rhino-orbito-cerebral mucormycosis, particularly in patients with uncontrolled diabetes mellitus or severe immunosuppression, and are not common causes of primary fungal keratitis.



Reference:
  1. Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 216.
  2. http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC88956/
  3. http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK493192/
  4. http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK507901/

Explanation:

  • The history of trauma with plant material, along with the presence of a corneal ulcer with feathery edges and satellite lesions, is highly suggestive of fungal keratitis.
  • Natamycin (5%) is the first-line treatment for fungal keratitis, especially caused by filamentous fungi like Fusarium and Aspergillus.
  • It is effective in treating the type of fungal infection that is suggested by the clinical presentation in this patient.

Topical Moxifloxacin (Option A):

  • Moxifloxacin is an antibiotic effective against bacterial infections, not fungal infections.
  • Given the history of trauma with plant material and the appearance of a corneal ulcer with feathery edges and satellite lesions, the most likely diagnosis is fungal keratitis.
  • Therefore, moxifloxacin would not be appropriate.

Oral Acyclovir (Option C):

  • Acyclovir is an antiviral medication used primarily for herpes simplex virus infections.
  • It would not be effective for a fungal corneal ulcer, making it an inappropriate choice in this scenario.

Intravitreal Amphotericin B (Option D):

  • Intravitreal Amphotericin B is used in cases of fungal endophthalmitis, not as an initial treatment for keratitis.
  • Although hypopyon suggests severe infection, the primary treatment should still be topical antifungal agents unless there is confirmed or high suspicion of endophthalmitis requiring intravitreal therapy.

question: A 45 y/o male presents with redness, pain, and decreased vision in his right eye. He reports a history of trauma to the eye with a plant material three days ago. O/E, there is a corneal ulcer with feathery edges and satellite lesions. Hypopyon is also noted. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanations:

  • HSV keratitis is characterized by dendritic ulcers on the cornea, which are branching, tree-like lesions.
  • HSV also commonly causes decreased corneal sensation.

[[figure-1]]

Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) Keratitis:

  • Dendritic Ulcers: Branching, tree-like ulcers.
  • Geographic Ulcers: Larger, amoeboid-shaped ulcers.
  • Stromal Keratitis: Inflammation of the corneal stroma, leading to oedema, infiltrates, and scarring.
  • Disciform Keratitis: Central, disc-shaped inflammation in the stroma.

[[figure-2]]

Adenovirus (Option A):

  • Adenoviruses are known for causing epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC) and may present with conjunctivitis and keratitis.
  • They are less likely to cause dendritic ulcers, which are specific to HSV.

Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus (HZO): (Option B)

  • Vesicles and Scars: Painful rash and blisters following the involvement of ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve.
  • Nummular Keratitis: Large, coin-shaped, subepithelial corneal infiltrates.

[[figure-3]]

Chlamydia trachomatis (Option D):

  • Chlamydia typically causes trachoma or inclusion conjunctivitis, which may involve conjunctival scarring and corneal pannus, but not dendritic ulcers.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 219, 220
question: A 45 y/o patient presents with eye redness, excessive tearing, and sensitivity to light. O/E, you observe dendritic ulcers and decreased corneal sensation. Based on these findings, which is the most likely etiological agent responsible for the patient's condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient presents with pain, redness, photophobia, and decreased vision in the right eye, along with a dendritic ulcer on the cornea.
  • This clinical picture is classic for Herpes Simplex Keratitis (HSK), an infection of the cornea caused by the herpes simplex virus (HSV).

Treatment of Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) Keratitis:

Topical Therapy:

  • Antivirals:
    • Acyclovir 3% ointment: 5 times daily.
  • Other Topical Medications:
    • Antibiotics: Prevent secondary bacterial infections, especially with epithelial defects.
    • Cycloplegics: (e.g., Homatropine 1%) Relieve pain and photophobia by paralyzing ciliary muscles and dilating the pupil.

Topical steroids and antibiotics (Option A):

  • Topical steroids are contraindicated in the treatment of active epithelial HSV keratitis, as they can suppress the immune response and worsen the viral infection, potentially leading to complications like corneal perforation.
  • Antibiotics are not needed unless there is a secondary bacterial infection, which is not indicated here.

Oral acyclovir and lubricants (Option B):

  • While oral acyclovir is used in more severe or recurrent cases of HSV keratitis, topical acyclovir is preferred as the initial treatment.
  • Lubricants can be supportive but are not the primary treatment.

Oral steroids and topical antibiotics (Option D):

  • Oral steroids are contraindicated in HSV keratitis, similar to topical steroids, as they can exacerbate the infection.
  • Topical antibiotics are unnecessary unless there's evidence of bacterial superinfection.


Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 221.
question: A 35 y/o patient presents with pain, redness, photophobia, and decreased vision in the right eye. Slit-lamp examination reveals a dendritic ulcer on the cornea. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Neurotrophic keratopathy is characterized by decreased corneal sensation and epithelial desquamation due to trigeminal nerve damage or dysfunction.
  • The patient’s history of Gasserian ganglion block, a procedure known to impair the trigeminal nerve, strongly supports this diagnosis.

Causes of Decreased Corneal Sensation:

  1. Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) Infections (Option B):
    • HSV keratitis typically presents with dendritic ulcers on the cornea and is associated with pain, photophobia, and possibly vesicular skin lesions.
    • However, the history of a Gasserian ganglion block and the description of decreased corneal sensation point more toward neurotrophic keratopathy.
  2. Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus:
    • Caused by varicella zoster virus.
    • Leads to decreased corneal sensation.
  3. Keratomalacia (Option A)
    • Result of vitamin A deficiency.
    • The cornea becomes dull and insensitive.
    • Signs include haziness and yellow infiltrates (not seen in this patient)
    • Can progress to corneal necrosis.
  4. Neurotrophic Keratopathy
  5. Neuroparalytic Keratopathy (Option D):
    • This condition occurs due to facial nerve paralysis, leading to lagophthalmos (inability to close the eye) and subsequent corneal exposure.
    • The patient's history does not suggest facial nerve paralysis, making this less likely.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 223.
question: A 50 y/o male presents with decreased vision, redness, and a dull sensation in his R/E. He has a history of trigeminal neuralgia for which he underwent a Gasserian ganglion block. O/E, there is decreased corneal sensation and epithelial desquamation. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?

explanationHtml:
Explanations:

  • The above features describe herpes zoster ophthalmicus. A chronic ocular complication she is at risk of developing is corneal scarring.

Acute Ocular Manifestations:

  • Conjunctivitis (Option C): Redness and inflammation of the conjunctiva.
  • Keratitis:
    • Punctate Epithelial Keratitis: Coarse and irregular lesions.
    • Nummular Keratitis: Larger, disc-shaped lesions.
    • Disciform keratitis.
  • Iridocyclitis: Inflammation of the iris and ciliary body, causing pain, photophobia, and blurred vision.
  • Keratouveitis and endothelitis: Leads to acute endothelial cell loss
  • Episcleritis and Scleritis (Option A): Inflammation of the episclera or sclera, resulting in pain and redness.

Chronic Ocular Manifestations:

  • Post-herpetic neuralgia
  • Corneal lesions:
    • Neuroparalytic ulceration.
    • Neurotrophic Keratopathy
    • Corneal scarring
    • Exposure keratitis
    • Mucous plaque keratitis (Sudden development of elevated mucous plaque which stains on rose bengal)
  • Lid lesions: D/t scarring. Include ptosis, trichiasis & entropion.
  • Secondary Glaucoma (Option D): Increased intraocular pressure (IOP) leading to optic nerve damage and vision loss.

Hutchinson’s rule: The eye will be involved if the nose tip is involved. As it indicates nasociliary nerve involvement.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Pages 224, 225.
question: A 65 y/o woman presents with a painful rash on her forehead and eyelid. She also reports blurred vision and photophobia. O/E, she has conjunctivitis, punctate epithelial keratitis, and iridocyclitis. Which of the following is a chronic ocular complication she is at risk of developing?

explanationHtml:
Explanations:

  • The clinical features are suggestive of Herpes zoster ophthalmicus (HZO), caused by reactivation of the Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) involving the ophthalmic (V1) division of the trigeminal nerve.

  • Corneal scarring is a common late ocular complication of HZO and results from recurrent or severe corneal inflammation (keratitis), leading to permanent corneal opacity and visual impairment.

Acute Ocular Manifestations

  • Conjunctivitis: Redness and inflammation of the conjunctiva. (Option C ruled out)
  • Keratitis:
    • Punctate epithelial keratitis
    • Nummular keratitis
    • Disciform keratitis
  • Iridocyclitis (anterior uveitis): Causes pain, photophobia, and blurred vision.
  • Keratouveitis and endotheliitis: May result in acute corneal endothelial cell loss.
  • Episcleritis and scleritis: Acute inflammation causing ocular pain and redness. (Option A ruled out)

Late (Chronic) Ocular Complications

  • Corneal scarring: Permanent corneal opacity following recurrent or severe keratitis, leading to visual impairment.
  • Neurotrophic keratopathy and neuroparalytic ulceration. (Option B):
  • Exposure keratitis.
  • Mucous plaque keratitis.
  • Lid deformities due to scarring (ptosis, trichiasis, entropion).
  • Secondary glaucoma: May occur secondary to chronic uveitis or trabecular meshwork involvement. (Option D ruled out)

Hutchinson's Sign: Vesicles on the tip of the nose (Hutchinson's sign) indicate nasociliary nerve involvement and are associated with a significantly increased risk of ocular involvement.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Pages 224, 225.
question: A 65-year-old woman presents with a painful vesicular rash over the forehead and upper eyelid, along with blurred vision and photophobia. On examination, she has conjunctivitis, punctate epithelial keratitis, and iridocyclitis due to herpes zoster ophthalmicus. Several months later, despite resolution of the acute infection, she develops permanent corneal opacity with reduced visual acuity. Which of the following best explains this late ocular sequela?

correctAnswer: B. Antiviral therapy is started within 72 hours of rash onset.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Antiviral therapy is most effective when started within 72 hours of rash onset, its effectiveness diminishes significantly after this period.
  • However, treatment may still be considered beyond 72 hours, especially in severe cases, but the benefits are reduced.

Systemic steroids alone are sufficient to manage HZO (Option A):

  • Systemic steroids should not be used as a monotherapy for HZO.
  • They must be combined with antiviral therapy to manage inflammation and pain effectively, as steroids alone do not reduce viral replication or prevent complications.

Post-Herpetic Neuralgia:

  • Up to 75% in patients over 70 (Option C)

Topical antiviral therapy is not recommended to manage eye involvement in HZO (Option D):

  • Topical antiviral therapy in combination with systemic antiviral therapy is the standard of care for managing the viral infection.


Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th edition, Page 226, 227, 229.

question: A 70 y/o woman presents with severe pain in her right eye and forehead, along with a rash that started 5 days ago. She was diagnosed with Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus (HZO). Which of the following statements is true regarding the management of her condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanations:

  • The above clinical features and examination findings are suggestive of Acanthamoeba keratitis.

Acanthamoeba keratitis is characterized by severe pain that is often out of proportion to the clinical findings, along with features such as perineural infiltrates and, in advanced cases, ring-shaped abscesses.

  • Symptoms:
    • Blurred Vision
    • Discomfort
    • Severe Pain
  • Ring lesion indicates advanced stage of the disease.

[[figure-1]]

Herpes Simplex Keratitis (Option A) typically presents with dendritic ulcers and less severe pain relative to Acanthamoeba keratitis.

Fungal Keratitis (Option B) usually presents with feathery-edged infiltrates and satellite lesions.

Bacterial Keratitis (Option D) typically presents with a more prominent purulent discharge and a dense, localized infiltrate.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Pages 211, 216, 219, 232
question: A 30 y/o contact lens wearer presents with very severe eye pain, blurred vision, and discomfort in his right eye. O/E, the following corneal finding is noted. Based on the image and the clinical presentation, which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Image

Description

Bacterial Keratitis:

[[figure-1]]
  • M/C worldwide: Staph aureus
  • M/C organism in India: Staph epidermidis
  • Neovascularization of cornea-
  • Pannus with keratitis
  • A corneal epithelial defect with circumcorneal injection, often with a hypopyon.
  • Clinical features:
    • Pain, redness, photophobia
    • Blepharospasm, discharge, diminution of vision

Fungal Keratitis:

[[figure-2]]
  • Grey or yellow-white stromal infiltrate with indistinct fluffy margins
  • Unsterile hypopyon

Superficial Punctate Keratitis:

[[figure-3]]
  • Punctate lesions
  • Seen in herpes simplex and herpes zoster

Nummular Keratitis:

[[figure-4]]
  • Characterized by fine granular subepithelial deposits surrounded by a halo of stromal haze.
  • Seen in zoster and adenoviral infections.

Dendritic Ulcer:

[[figure-5]]
  • Also known as Viral keratitis
  • Linear branching ulcer with terminal bulbs

Pseudodendritis:

[[figure-6]]
  • Corneal epithelial lesions that are smaller and finer than herpes simplex dendrites, have tapered ends without terminal bulbs.
  • Seen in Herpes zoster

Acanthamoeba keratitis

[[figure-7]]
  • Rare infection
  • Occurs in soft contact lens users, washing lenses with tap water
    • Swimming while wearing contact lenses without goggles
  • M/C infection after contact lens use: Pseudomonas

Clinical features:

  • Pain (Disproportionately more)
    • Due to perineural invasion
    • Lead to radial perineuritis - Pathognomic feature
    • Can lead to thickening of corneal nerves
  • Redness, photophobia, blepharospasm
  • Discharge, diminution of vision

On examination:

  • Ring lesion: Can be a/w abscess formation
  • Pseudo-dendrites or micro-dendrites
  • Limbitis with stromal infiltration


Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Pages 205, 211, 216, 221, 227.
question:
Match the Following:

1)

a) Bacterial Keratitis

2)

b) Superficial Punctate Keratitis

3)

c) Pseudodendritis

4)

d) Dendritic Ulcer

5)

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical features and findings point to Acanthamoeba keratitis.
  • PHMB is an amoebicidal agent effective against both the trophozoites and cysts of Acanthamoeba.
  • It is the treatment of choice for Acanthamoeba keratitis, especially when cysts are identified.

Treatment of Acanthamoeba Keratitis:

  • Debridement: Removal of infected epithelium to enhance topical medication penetration.
  • Topical Amoebicides:
    • PHMB (polyhexamethylene biguanide) 0.02% and Chlorhexidine 0.02%: Effective against both trophozoites and cysts.
    • Hexamidine: More effective than Propamidine (Brolene).
  • Topical Steroids:
    • Considered for persistent inflammation after two weeks of anti-amoebic treatment.
    • Caution against use if corneal thinning is present.
  • Pain Management: Oral NSAIDs are recommended for pain relief.
  • Therapeutic Keratoplasty: Required for cases resistant to medical therapy or when corneal perforation occurs.

Topical moxifloxacin (Option A):

  • Moxifloxacin is an antibiotic used to treat bacterial keratitis.

Oral acyclovir (Option B):

  • Acyclovir is an antiviral agent used primarily for herpes simplex keratitis.

Topical corticosteroids (Option D):

  • While corticosteroids may be used cautiously for persistent inflammation after initiating anti-amoebic treatment, they are not first-line therapy and should be avoided initially due to the risk of worsening the infection if used prematurely.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The procedure demonstrated is SMILE (Small Incision Lenticule Extraction), a minimally invasive corneal refractive surgery performed using a femtosecond laser. The laser creates a stromal lenticule within the cornea, which is removed through a small peripheral incision, thereby altering the corneal curvature and reducing its refractive power.

  • SMILE is primarily indicated for the correction of myopia, with or without myopic astigmatism, in patients with a stable refractive error and adequate corneal thickness.
  • Unlike LASIK, SMILE does not require creation of a corneal flap, resulting in better preservation of corneal biomechanics, reduced incidence of postoperative dry eye, and a lower risk of flap-related complications.
  • Appropriate patient selection includes a stable refraction, healthy ocular surface, and absence of corneal ectatic disorders.
  • Preoperative assessment includes corneal topography or tomography to exclude keratoconus and other corneal abnormalities.

Cataract (Option A) is an opacity of the crystalline lens causing progressive visual impairment. The definitive treatment is phacoemulsification with intraocular lens implantation. SMILE reshapes the cornea and has no role in treating lenticular opacities.

Glaucoma (Option C) is an optic neuropathy characterized by progressive retinal ganglion cell loss, often associated with elevated intraocular pressure. Surgical procedures such as trabeculectomy, glaucoma drainage devices, or minimally invasive glaucoma surgery (MIGS) are performed to improve aqueous humor outflow. SMILE does not lower intraocular pressure and is not a treatment for glaucoma.

Keratoconus (Option D) is a progressive ectatic disorder characterized by corneal thinning and protrusion, resulting in irregular astigmatism. Corneal refractive procedures such as SMILE are contraindicated because they may worsen corneal instability. Management includes spectacles or contact lenses in early disease, corneal collagen cross-linking to halt progression, and keratoplasty in advanced cases.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Improper contact lens hygiene, especially with exposure to contaminated water (picnic scenario, possible swimming), is a major risk factor for Acanthamoeba keratitis.
  • Acanthamoeba is a free-living protozoan found in water, soil, and air; it can adhere to contact lenses and invade the corneal epithelium, causing severe pain (often disproportionate to clinical signs), redness, tearing, and photophobia.
  • Classic sign: ring-shaped stromal infiltrate in advanced cases.

Acanthamoeba keratitis:

  1. Severe pain out of proportion to clinical findings.
  2. History of contact lens wear, especially poor hygiene or water exposure.
  3. Resistant to routine antibacterial therapy; requires specific anti-amoebic agents (e.g., polyhexamethylene biguanide, chlorhexidine).
  4. Delayed diagnosis can lead to corneal perforation and vision loss.

Examination Findings in Acanthamoeba Keratitis:

Symptoms:

  • Blurred Vision: Common in corneal conditions due to the disruption of the cornea's transparent surface.
  • Discomfort: Significant discomfort in the affected eye.
  • Severe Pain: Pain is often out of proportion to clinical signs, a key clinical clue.

Signs:

Early Disease:

  • Irregular and Greyish Epithelium: Early sign indicating amoebic invasion.
  • Pseudodendrites: Lesions resembling herpetic keratitis
  • Limbitis and Stromal Infiltrates: Inflammation at the corneal-scleral junction with diffuse or focal infiltrates in the anterior stroma.
  • Perineural Infiltrates (Radial Keratoneuritis): Hallmark sign, radial streaks extending towards the cornea's centre, pathognomonic for Acanthamoeba keratitis.

Advanced Disease:

  • Ring Abscess: Characteristic of advanced infection, where infiltrates form a ring-shaped abscess.
  • Stromal Opacification and Vascularisation: Corneal opacity and new blood vessel growth, leading to significant vision impairment.
  • Corneal Melting: Serious complication where corneal tissue breaks down, often at the infiltrate edges.
  • Scleritis: Reactive inflammation of the sclera, not a direct infection extension.

Investigations and Treatment of Acanthamoeba Keratitis:

Investigations:

  • Corneal Scraping:
    • The primary method for obtaining tissue for examination.
    • Scrape the margins and base of the lesion after applying a non-preserved topical anaesthetic.
  • Staining:
    • PAS (Periodic acid–Schiff) and Calcofluor white: Highly effective for visualizing Acanthamoeba cysts.
    • Gram and Giemsa stains: Less sensitive but can also demonstrate cysts.
  • Culture: Definitive diagnosis by culturing on non-nutrient agar with dead E. coli.
  • Additional Investigations:
    • Immunohistochemistry: Uses antibodies to detect specific Acanthamoeba antigens.
    • PCR: Useful for detecting Acanthamoeba DNA.
    • In Vivo Confocal Microscopy: Provides detailed images of Acanthamoeba cysts within the cornea.
  • Corneal Biopsy:
    • Considered if other diagnostic methods are inconclusive.

Treatment Modalities:

  • Debridement: Removal of infected epithelium to enhance topical medication penetration.
  • Topical Amoebicides:
    • PHMB (polyhexamethylene biguanide) 0.02% and Chlorhexidine 0.02%: Effective against both trophozoites and cysts.
    • Hexamidine: More effective than Propamidine (Brolene).
  • Topical Steroids:
    • Considered for persistent inflammation after two weeks of anti-amoebic treatment.
    • Caution against use if corneal thinning is present.
  • Pain Management: Oral NSAIDs are recommended for pain relief.
  • Therapeutic Keratoplasty: Required for cases resistant to medical therapy or when corneal perforation occurs.

Plasmodium (Option B): Causes malaria; does not cause keratitis or infection related to contact lenses.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Option C): Most common bacterial cause of contact lens–related keratitis; produces rapid corneal ulceration, but here the focus is on protozoal infection linked to contaminated water exposure.

Herpes simplex virus (Option D): Causes dendritic keratitis; unrelated to contact lens hygiene and not typically triggered by recent outdoor water exposure.
question: A girl returns from a picnic and develops severe eye pain. She had been using contact lenses but did not follow proper hygiene practices. What is the most likely causative organism?

explanationHtml:
Layers of Cornea

Epithelium
  • The outermost layer comprises 5-6 layers of non-keratinized, stratified squamous epithelial cells.(Option C ruled out)
  • Acts as a barrier, protecting the cornea and preventing tear fluid from entering the underlying stroma.
  • Outermost layer Apical cells have microvilli to move the tear fluid.(Option D ruled out)
  • The basal cells at the limbus are stem cells responsible for regenerating the corneal epithelium.

Bowman’s Membrane
  • Located just beneath the epithelium, this acellular layer is 12 µm thick and composed of densely packed collagen fibrils.
  • It is a protective barrier to the stroma but cannot regenerate (Option B) if damaged and heals by scarring.

Stroma
  • Making up about 90% of the cornea's thickness (approximately 0.5 mm thick), the stroma consists of collagen fibrils arranged in parallel layers.
  • These fibrils are embedded in a hydrated matrix of proteoglycans - Chondroitin and Keratan Sulphate (keratan sulphate maintains corneal transparency).

Pre-Descemet's Membrane (Dua's Layer)
  • This layer, discovered in 2013, is about 15 µm thick, acellular, and lies just above Descemet's membrane.
  • It is strong and resistant to air penetration.

Descemet's Membrane
  • A robust basement membrane of the corneal endothelium is made of collagen and glycoproteins.
  • It is tense, but when torn, curls inwards on itself.
  • It can regenerate (Option A ruled out) if damaged and is resistant to trauma and pathological processes.

Endothelium
  • The innermost layer consists of a single layer of flat, hexagonal cells.
  • These cells are crucial for maintaining corneal transparency by regulating fluid balance within the cornea through an active pump mechanism.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, Edition 9, Page- 204.

Explanation:

  • The image given above is that of Munson’s sign which is the V-shaped conformation of the lower lid produced by the ectatic cornea in downgaze seen in Keratoconus. The refractive error seen in keratoconus is myopia and irregular astigmatism leading to defective vision.

Keratoconus:

Description
  • Progressive, non-inflammatory bilateral ectatic corneal condition affecting the axial part.

Pathology
  • Involves progressive thinning and ectasia of the cornea due to defective synthesis of mucopolysaccharides and collagen.

Clinical Features
  • Defective vision due to progressive myopia and irregular astigmatism (uncorrectable by glasses) (Option B)
  • Blurred and distorted vision, glare, and halos around lights
  • Light sensitivity and ocular irritation
  • Visual loss primarily from irregular astigmatism and myopia, secondary loss from corneal scarring

Examination Findings
  • Distorted Window Reflex: Visual irregularity on corneal reflection.
  • Placido Disc Irregularity: Irregular circles.
  • Slit-Lamp Examination:
    • Thinning and ectasia of the central cornea.
    • Opacity at the apex, Fleischer Ring (brownish ring around the cone due to haemosiderin in the epithelium).
    • Folds in Descemet's and Bowman's membranes.
  • Vogt Striae: Fine, parallel striae at the apex, disappearing with external pressure.
  • Oil Droplet Reflex: Annular dark shadow separating central and peripheral cornea in distant direct ophthalmoscopy.
  • Retinoscopy: Yawning reflex (scissor reflex) with high oblique/irregular astigmatism.
  • Ophthalmoscope Findings: Irregular astigmatism and progressive myopia, poorly corrected by glasses in later stages.
  • Munson's Sign: Localized bulging of the lower lid when looking down (seen in late stages).
  • Keratometer Findings: Malformed, malaligned, and malfocused mires.
  • Corneal Topography: Sensitive method for early detection, shows corneal surface shape.

Management

Spectacle Correction:

  • Effective in the early stages, but contact lenses are more beneficial.
  • Less effective in later stages due to irregular astigmatism.

Contact Lenses:

  • Rigid gas permeable lenses improve vision in early cases.
  • Specially designed scleral lenses (e.g., Rose-K) are useful in early to moderate cases.

Corneal Collagen Cross-Linking (CXL):

  • New treatment modality to slow disease progression.
  • Involves Riboflavin (0.1%) eye drops and UVA radiation.
  • Riboflavin induces cross-linking of corneal collagen to stabilize the stroma and improve contact lens tolerance.

Keratoplasty :

  • Recommended if disease progresses or in cases of acute hydrops (Descemet's membrane tear).
  • Reserved for more advanced diseases or when other treatments fail.
  • Penetrating keratoplasty is common, but Deep Anterior Lamellar Keratoplasty (DALK) is preferred if Descemet's membrane and endothelium are intact, reducing rejection risk.

Intracorneal Ring Segments (INTACS) :

  • Effective in early to moderate cases by flattening the cornea.
  • Less effective in halting progression.


Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology 9th Edition 9, pages 248-250.

The clinical scenario of pain, redness in eyes following trauma with vegetative matter is suggestive of Fungal Keratitis.

Fungal Keratitis:

Etiology
  • Causative organism: Aspergillus fumigatus >> Fusarium
  • Predisposing factor: Vegetative matter injury (trauma) (Option C)

Clinical Features
  • SIGNS >> symptoms
  • Pain & Foreign Body Sensation

Examination Findings
  • Corneal Ulcer: Greyish-white, dry, elevated, rolled-out margins

  • Feathery Extensions: Finger-like projections in stroma
  • Sterile Immune Ring: Yellow line of demarcation
  • Satellite Lesions: Small lesions around the main ulcer
  • Hypopyon: Large, immobile, non-sterile, even in small ulcer
  • Perforation: Rare but possible

Investigations

  • Wet KOH Mount: Filamentous fungi or yeast-like fungi (Candida)
  • Culture: Sabouraud's agar for fungal culture
  • PCR: For rapid identification of pathogens
  • Corneal Biopsy: For deep stromal abscess or negative cultures

Treatment
  • Topical Antifungal Agents: Natamycin 5%, Voriconazole, Amphotericin-B, Nystatin
  • Oral Antifungal Agents: Ketoconazole, Voriconazole (for severe ulcers)
  • Surgical Management:
    • Repeated Scraping: Removal of necrotic material
    • Cauterization Options: Carbolic acid (100%), Trichloroacetic acid (10%–20%), Povidone-iodine (5%)
    • Therapeutic Keratoplasty: Corneal transplantation

Bacterial and Fungal Keratitis:

BACTERIAL KERATITIS (Option B)

FUNGAL KERATITIS

Etiology
  • S. aureus (worldwide)
  • S. epidermidis (India)
  • Aspergillus

Examination Findings
  • Fluorescein stain positive ulcer
  • Hypopyon (sterile)
  • Stromal edema
  • Descemet’s membrane folds
  • Keratic precipitates due to anterior uveitis
  • Signs >>> symptoms
  • Dry/rough ulcer
  • Has projecting ends
  • Thick immobile unsterile hypopyon
  • Satellite nodules are infective and have immune reaction- Wessley ring
  • IOP is high

Treatment
  • Empirical monotherapy: Moxifloxacin, gatifloxacin, besifloxacin
  • Duo therapy: Gram positive + gram negative. Combination of Cefazolin with Gentamicin or Cefuroxime with Gentamicin.
  • Cycloplegics and mydriatics
  • Antifungals: Natamycin 5%, amphotericin B
  • Steroids are contraindicated

Simplex Keratitis (Option A): Caused due to infection by Herpes simplex virus (HSV-1). Unlike Fungal keratitis, Simplex keratitis is acquired by kissing or in close contact with an infected person. Dendritic ulcer with budding pattern is suggestive of Simplex keratitis.

Acanthameoba keratitis (option D): Usually seen in contact lens users, pseudodendritic pattern with tapering ends is suggestive of Acanathamoeba Keratitis.

explanationHtml:
Haab's striae are horizontal breaks or scars in Descemet's membrane and are typically associated with congenital glaucoma (especially buphthalmos) rather than keratoconus. These striae occur as a result of increased intraocular pressure and are not a feature of keratoconus.

Keratoconus

[[figure-1]]

  • Definition: Progressive, non-inflammatory bilateral ectatic corneal condition affecting the axial part.
  • Pathology: Involves progressive thinning and ectasia of the cornea due to defective synthesis of mucopolysaccharides and collagen.

Clinical Features

  • Symptoms:
    • Defective vision due to progressive myopia and irregular astigmatism, uncorrectable by glasses.
    • Blurred and distorted vision, glare, halos around lights.
    • Light sensitivity and ocular irritation.
    • Visual loss mainly from irregular astigmatism and myopia; secondary loss due to corneal scarring.

Examination Findings

  • Corneal Thinning & Bulging: The Cornea thins near the centre and bulges forward, with the cone apex slightly below the corneal centre.
  • Specific Signs:
    • Distorted Window Reflex: Visual irregularity on corneal reflection.
    • Placido Disc Irregularity: Circles appear irregular.
    • Slit-Lamp Examination:
      • Thinning and ectasia of the central cornea.
      • Opacity at the apex, Fleischer Ring: Brownish ring around the cone, possibly due to haemosiderin in the epithelium.
      • Folds in Descemet's and Bowman's membranes.
      • Vogt Striae: Fine, parallel striae at the apex, best seen with a slit lamp, disappearing with external pressure (vs Haab striae: They are curvilinear breaks in Descemet's membrane, resulting acutely from stretching of the cornea in primary congenital glaucoma).

[[figure-2]]

Oil droplet reflex

  • Retinoscopy: Yawning reflex (scissor reflex) with high oblique/irregular astigmatism. (Option D ruled out)
  • Distant Direct Ophthalmoscopy: Annular dark shadow (oil droplet reflex) separating central and peripheral cornea. A ring of shadow concentric with the margin in the red reflex, resembling an oil droplet.
  • Ophthalmoscope Findings: Irregular Astigmatism: Progressive myopia and irregular astigmatism in later stages, poorly corrected by glasses. (Option C ruled out)
  • Munson's Sign: Localized bulging of the lower lid when looking down (seen in late stages). (Option B ruled out)
  • Keratometer Findings: Malformed, malaligned, and malfocused mires.
  • Corneal Topography: The most sensitive method for early detection (Forme Fruste Keratoconus) shows the shape of the corneal surface.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 248, 249.

  • Eye Finding: The child has a Kayser-Fleischer ring, a brownish-yellow copper deposit in the Descemet membrane of the cornea, which is visible on gonioscopy. This is a hallmark sign of Wilson disease.

Wilson’s disease

  • Deficiency of caeruloplasmin, leading to abnormal copper deposition in tissues.
  • Symptoms:
    • Liver disease
    • Basal ganglia dysfunction (movement disorders)

question: A child with elevated liver enzymes presented to the OPD with the following eye finding on gonioscopy. It is associated with?

correctAnswer: D. Fluorescein dye cobalt blue filter
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Fluorescein sodium

[[figure-1]]

  • Fluorescein penetrates poorly into the lipid layer of the corneal epithelium, and therefore, it does not stain normal cornea. Although fluorescein is a very effective stain for the diseased cornea, it is more difficult to detect fluorescein staining of the conjunctiva because of the poor scleral contrast. Fluorescein absorbs light in the blue spectrum (490 nm) and emits yellow-green light of a higher wavelength (530 nm), therefore staining can be more readily viewed if a cobalt blue or yellow (blue-free) filter is used. This combination is particularly useful for detecting corneal defects and ulcers.

Cobalt blue filter:

  • Cobalt blue is a filter that is commonly used in conjunction with fluorescein stain, as it enhances the fluorescence of fluorescein, making it easier to detect corneal defects. It absorbs light in the blue spectrum (around 490 nm) and helps the fluorescein stain emit a bright yellow-green fluorescence when illuminated.

Lissamine green dye

[[figure-2]]

  • It has a high affinity for staining dead and degenerated cells, including mucous strands. The dye appears to stain areas where there are disrupted intercellular junctions. Use of a green (red-free) filter shows the stained areas to appear black in color. As it is better tolerated than rose bengal, it is the preferred dye for staining the bulbar conjunctiva.

Incorrect Options:

Lissamine green dye green filter (Option A):

  • Lissamine green stains dead or degenerated cells and mucous strands on the conjunctiva, not corneal defects.
  • A green filter is used with lissamine green because it enhances contrast, making stained areas appear black. It’s not effective for fluorescein.

Lissamine green dye cobalt blue filter (Option B):

  • Lissamine green doesn’t fluoresce, so a cobalt blue filter (which works with fluorescein) won’t enhance its staining.
  • Cobalt blue is useful for fluorescein fluorescence, not for lissamine green, which requires a green filter.

Fluorescein dye green filter (Option C):

  • Fluorescein works best with a cobalt blue filter for fluorescence, not a green filter. A green filter doesn’t enhance fluorescein’s fluorescence, making it less effective for detecting corneal defects.



Reference:

Ocular surface staining: Current concepts and techniques - PMC (nih.gov)

Wilson’s disease is a genetic disorder of copper metabolism that leads to copper accumulation in various tissues, including the liver, brain, and cornea.
  • Kayser-Fleischer rings are copper deposits that form in the Descemet membrane of the cornea, appearing as a golden or greenish ring on slit-lamp examination.

Wilson’s disease

• The patient has guttate lesions in one eye and bullous keratopathy in the other. Guttate lesions indicate endothelial cell loss, while bullous keratopathy results from corneal edema due to endothelial dysfunction. These are classical features of Fuchs’ endothelial dystrophy.
  • Fuchs’ endothelial dystrophy is a bilateral, progressive corneal endothelial disorder.
  • Early sign: Guttae (drop-like excrescences on Descemet membrane) seen on slit lamp.
  • Late stage: Stromal edema → epithelial edema → bullae formation (bullous keratopathy).

Symptoms: Gradual, painless decrease in vision; glare; haloes; worse in the morning due to overnight edema.

Treatment:

  • Early: Hypertonic saline drops, hair dryer to reduce morning edema
  • Advanced: Keratoplasty (DSEK, DMEK, or PK)

Interstitial keratitis (Option B) – Chronic stromal inflammation, usually post-infectious (e.g., syphilis, HSV); presents with stromal haze and vascularization, not guttate lesions or bullous keratopathy.

Viral corneal ulcer (Option C) – Painful red eye with epithelial defect and stromal infiltrate; acute onset, not a chronic, painless, bilateral process.

Keratoconjunctivitis (Option D) – Inflammatory condition involving cornea and conjunctiva; presents with redness, pain, photophobia, discharge; not consistent with long-standing endothelial degeneration.

explanationHtml:
The corneal reflex (blink reflex) is a protective response that involves both sensory (afferent) and motor (efferent) pathways:

  • Afferent limb (sensory input): Trigeminal nerve (CN V1 - Ophthalmic division)
    • The cornea is innervated by the nasociliary branch of the ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve.
    • A light touch to the cornea (e.g., with a cotton wisp) stimulates sensory fibers, sending signals to the trigeminal sensory nucleus in the brainstem.
  • Efferent limb (motor response): Facial nerve (CN VII)
    • The facial nerve (CN VII) innervates the orbicularis oculi muscle, which causes eyelid closure in response to the stimulus.

Reflex

Afferent Nerve

Efferent Nerve

Accommodation

II (Optic nerve)

III (Oculomotor nerve)

Corneal

V₁ (Ophthalmic, nasociliary branch)

Bilateral VII (Facial nerve, temporal branch - orbicularis oculi)

Cough

X (Vagus nerve)

X (Vagus nerve, also phrenic and spinal nerves)

Gag

IX (Glossopharyngeal nerve)

X (Vagus nerve)

Jaw Jerk

V₃ (Mandibular branch, sensory from masseter)

V₃ (Mandibular branch, motor to masseter)

Lacrimation

V₁ (Ophthalmic branch) (loss of reflex does not preclude emotional tears)

VII (Facial nerve)

Pupillary

II (Optic nerve)

III (Oculomotor nerve)

Facial Nerve (CN VII) (Option A): The facial nerve is responsible for the efferent limb (motor response), not the afferent limb. It causes eyelid closure by contracting the orbicularis oculi muscle.

Oculomotor Nerve (CN III) (Option C): CN III controls extraocular muscles and the levator palpebrae superioris (eyelid elevation), but it does not mediate the corneal reflex.

Abducens Nerve (CN VI) (Option D): CN VI controls the lateral rectus muscle for eye abduction but is not involved in the corneal reflex.

explanationHtml:
Chronic Blepharitis is an inflammation of the eyelid margins that can cause symptoms such as eyelid crusting and a thready sensation between the cornea and eyelids, often due to the accumulation of secretions along the lash line. The eyelids may feel gritty or have a foreign body sensation.


Bacterial blepharitis:

Definition

Chronic infection of the anterior part of the lid margin

Synonyms

  • Chronic anterior blepharitis
  • Staphylococcal blepharitis

Causative Organisms
  • Most commonly Staphylococci (coagulase positive)
  • Rarely Streptococci, Propionibacterium acnes, and Moraxella

Clinical Features
  • Chronic irritation
  • Itching
  • Mild lacrimation
  • Gluing of cilia
  • Mild photophobia
  • Yellow crusts at the root of cilia
  • Small ulcers that bleed easily when crusts are removed
  • Red, thickened lid margins with dilated blood vessels
  • Mild papillary conjunctivitis and conjunctival hyperemia

Treatment
  • Lid Hygiene:
    • Warm compresses
    • Cotton buds dipped in dilute baby shampoo or 3% sodium bicarbonate solution
    • Avoid touching
  • Antibiotics
  • Topical Steroids
  • Ocular Lubricants

Dry Eye Syndrome (Option B): While dry eyes can cause a foreign body sensation, it typically does not cause eyelid crusting. Dry eye symptoms are more related to discomfort from insufficient tear production, but the crusting is not a hallmark feature.

Meibomian Gland Dysfunction (Option C): This condition can lead to dry eyes and eyelid discomfort due to insufficient oil production, but it doesn’t usually cause eyelid crusting in the way that blepharitis does.

Conjunctivitis (Option D): Conjunctivitis (inflammation of the conjunctiva) causes symptoms such as redness, discharge, and itching

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology 9th edition page 70-72

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Vernal keratoconjunctivitis or Spring catarrh

It is a recurrent bilateral conjunctivitis that tends to occur with the onset of warm weather. It primarily affects young children and adolescents, particularly boys.

Course

The condition typically starts in childhood and may resolve on its own over 5–10 years.

Symptoms

Burning, Itching, Photophobia (sensitivity to light), and lacrimation (excessive tearing).

Signs
  • Palpebral Form: Hypertrophied palpebral conjunctiva with a cobblestone appearance; bluish-white color; dense fibrous tissue with thickened epithelium.
  • Limbal or Bulbar Form: Opacification at the limbus, gelatinous thickening, and Horner–Trantas dots

[[figure-1]]

  • Pseudogerontoxon/cupid’s bow (which resembles arcus senilis) is a grayish-white ring at the limbus seen in severe limbal vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC).

[[figure-2]]

  • Shield ulcers are a significant complication of VKC, particularly in severe cases. These microerosions typically form on the upper third of the cornea.

[[figure-3]]

  • Mixed form: Exhibits characteristics of both the tarsal (palpebral) and limbal subtypes, typically presenting in only one eye.

Maxwell Lyon's sign is a pseudomembrane formed due to excessive mucus deposition on the papilla resulting in cobblestone papillae.

[[figure-4]]

Histology

In the palpebral form, hypertrophied papillae are observed, rich in eosinophils and other inflammatory cells.

Treatment
  • Topical therapy:
    • Antihistamines - Levocabastine & emedastine
    • Mast cell stabilizers - Sodium cromoglicate
    • Mild steroids - Fluorometholone and loteprednol etabonate,
    • Acetylcysteine can control excess mucus.
  • Local therapy: Subtarsal steroid injections and cryotherapy for severe cases.
  • Surgical treatment: Excision of giant papillae and treatment of shield ulcers with debridement and amniotic membrane or bandage contact lens.
  • Cold compresses and tinted glasses for comfort.
  • Avoid eye rubbing

Phlyctenular conjunctivitis (Option B):

  • Allergy caused by endogenous antigens → Staph. aureus and TB infection
  • It presents with watering and itching in the eyes
  • O/E: nodule of phlycten near the limbus and conjunctival congestion

Atopic keratoconjunctivitis (Option C):

  • Common in temperate regions and winters
  • Dennie-morgan folds present
  • Presence of Madarosis and Hertoghe’s sign

Autoimmune Conditions (Option D):

  • Not typically associated with Shield Ulcer: Various autoimmune diseases can affect the eyes, such as rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and Sjögren's syndrome, leading to conditions like dry eye, scleritis, and uveitis.
  • However, shield ulcers are not commonly seen as a direct manifestation of these autoimmune conditions.

question: Shield ulcer is seen in which of the following?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option A - Siderosis bulbi

  • This is the correct answer. Siderosis bulbi refers to the condition in which iron particles, usually from a previous trauma, are deposited in the eye's intraocular tissues leading to visual disturbances and discoloration. In this case, the patient's line of work in an iron factory could have exposed him to iron particles.

Incorrect Options:

Option B - Hemochromatosis: This is a genetic disorder that leads to excessive iron absorption from the diet. It affects various organs in the body, including the liver, heart, and pancreas. While it can cause a number of health problems, it is not typically associated with iron deposits in the eye or the visual disturbances described by the patient.

Option C - Retinitis pigmentosa: This is a group of rare, genetic disorders that involve a breakdown and loss of cells in the retina—which is the light sensitive tissue that lines the back of the eye. It is not typically associated with iron deposits in the eye.

Option D - Age-related macular degeneration: This is a common eye condition among people over 50. It causes blurred or reduced central vision, due to thinning of the macula, the part of the retina responsible for clear vision in your direct line of sight. It is not associated with iron deposits in the eye.
