explanationHtml:
• The image most likely represents keratoconus, characterized by the thinning and cone-shaped bulging of the cornea, leading to visual distortion and irregular astigmatism.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Keratoconus

  • Definition: Progressive, non-inflammatory bilateral ectatic corneal condition affecting the axial part.
  • Pathology: Involves progressive thinning and ectasia of the cornea due to defective synthesis of mucopolysaccharides and collagen.

Clinical Features

  • Symptoms:
    • Defective vision due to progressive myopia and irregular astigmatism, uncorrectable by glasses.
    • Blurred and distorted vision, glare, halos around lights.
    • Light sensitivity and ocular irritation.
    • Visual loss mainly from irregular astigmatism and myopia; secondary loss due to corneal scarring.

Examination Findings

  • Corneal Thinning & Bulging: The Cornea thins near the centre and bulges forward, with the cone apex slightly below the corneal centre.
  • Specific Signs:
    • Distorted Window Reflex: Visual irregularity on corneal reflection.
    • Placido Disc Irregularity: Circles appear irregular.
    • Slit-Lamp Examination:
      • Thinning and ectasia of the central cornea.
      • Opacity at the apex, Fleischer Ring: Brownish ring around the cone, possibly due to haemosiderin in the epithelium.
      • Folds in Descemet's and Bowman's membranes.
      • Vogt Striae: Fine, parallel striae at the apex, best seen with a slit lamp, disappearing with external pressure (vs Haab striae: They are curvilinear breaks in Descemet's membrane, resulting acutely from stretching of the cornea in primary congenital glaucoma).

[[figure-3]]

Oil droplet reflex

  • Retinoscopy: Yawning reflex (scissor reflex) with high oblique/irregular astigmatism.
  • Distant Direct Ophthalmoscopy: Annular dark shadow (oil droplet reflex) separating central and peripheral cornea. A ring of shadow concentric with the margin in the red reflex, resembling an oil droplet.
  • Ophthalmoscope Findings: Irregular Astigmatism: Progressive myopia and irregular astigmatism in later stages, poorly corrected by glasses.
  • Munson's Sign: Localized bulging of the lower lid when looking down (seen in late stages).
  • Keratometer Findings: Malformed, malaligned, and malfocused mires.
  • Corneal Topography: The most sensitive method for early detection (Forme Fruste Keratoconus) shows the shape of the corneal surface.

Vogt's limbal girdle (Option B): This refers to a white or grayish band at the corneal margin, but it is not associated with corneal thinning or bulging, as seen in keratoconus.

Keratoglobus (Option C): This is a rare condition where the cornea is uniformly thin and globular in shape, but it is not associated with the same irregular astigmatism and conical shape as keratoconus.

Corneal dystrophy (Option D): This is a group of inherited disorders that cause abnormal deposits in the cornea, but the presentation is different from keratoconus. It does not typically involve the corneal thinning and cone shape seen in keratoconus.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, Edition 9, Page- 248, 249.
question: What does this image indicate?

correctAnswer: A. Abnormal curvature of the cornea
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The primary cause of regular astigmatism is an abnormal curvature of the cornea, which results in different refractive powers along different meridians of the eye. This irregularity in corneal shape prevents light rays from focusing on a single point on the retina, causing blurred or distorted vision.
  • Astigmatism: A refractive error where different meridia of the eye have different refractive errors. Divided into 2 types: Regular and irregular
  • I. Regular Astigmatism: When refraction error changes uniformly from one meridian to the other. ( 2 principle meridians present)

Type

Description

With-the-Rule (WTR)

The vertical meridian has greater curvature than the horizontal meridian.

Against-the-Rule (ATR)

The horizontal meridian is more curved than the vertical meridian.

Oblique Astigmatism

Principal meridians are at oblique angles (e.g., 45° and 135°), still perpendicular to each other.

Bi-oblique Astigmatism

Principal meridians are not perpendicular to each other (e.g., 30° and 100°).

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

[[figure-3]]

Regular Astigmatism Based on Focal Lines:

[[figure-4]]

Type

Description

Simple Astigmatism

One meridian focuses on the retina; the other focuses in front (simple myopic) or behind (simple hypermetropic).

Compound Astigmatism

Both meridians focus light either in front (compound myopic) or behind (compound hypermetropic) the retina.

Mixed Astigmatism

One meridian focuses in front of the retina (myopic), and the other behind (hypermetropic).

II. Irregular Astigmatism Involves multiple, changing meridians of refractive power, making it geometrically complex.Usually due to Corneal scars.

Excessive eye rubbing (Option B) can irritate the eyes and potentially lead to infections like keratoconjunctivitis.

Prolonged exposure to bright light (Option C) can cause eye strain and discomfort.

Vitamin A deficiency (Option D) can lead to xerophthalmia characterized by night blindness and dryness of the eyes.

question: Arlt’s line is seen in?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option C - Herpes zoster ophthalmicus

Explanation:

  • The clinical scenario of a patient with history of chickenpox and cutaneous lesions seen along the course of trigeminal nerve is suggestive of Herpes zoster ophthalmicus.

Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus (HZO)

  • Affects the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve.
  • Anterior uveitis occurs in 40-50% of cases, usually within 2 weeks of skin rash onset.
  • Symptoms: mild iritis, vesicular rash on the nose, small KPs, mild aqueous flare, possible hemorrhagic hypopyon.
  • Complications: iris atrophy, secondary glaucoma, complicated cataracts.

Incorrect Options:

Chicken pox exacerbation (Option A), caused by the varicella-zoster virus, usually occurs in children and presents with a generalized vesicular rash. Reactivation of the virus in adults leads to herpes zoster rather than an exacerbation of chickenpox.

Drug allergy to acyclovir (Option B), a common antiviral medication used to treat herpes zoster, would typically present with skin rashes, itching, or swelling after drug exposure.

Herpes zoster oticus (Option D) (Ramsay Hunt syndrome) involves the facial nerve and affects the ear, causing pain, vesicular rash in the ear canal, and facial paralysis. It does not primarily affect the eye or lead to keratitis.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th edition, Page 468-71
question: What is the diagnosis for a female patient, aged 65, who has a history of chickenpox and presents at the clinic with the following findings?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option D - Soft Contact lenses:

Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation of blurred vision, severe pain after swimming in a pond with ring like lesion on examination is suggestive of Acanthamoeba keratitis.

Acanthamoeba keratitis:

It is caused by Acanthamoeba, a free-living amoeba found in water, causes severe corneal infections

Risk Factors:

  1. Contact Lens Use (Primary Risk Factor)
  2. Exposure to Contaminated Water
  3. Trauma
  4. Immunosuppression
  5. Use of Homemade Saline Solutions.
  6. Poor Lens Storage Conditions

Examination Findings in Acanthamoeba Keratitis:

Symptoms:

  • Blurred Vision: Common in corneal conditions due to the disruption of the cornea's transparent surface.
  • Discomfort: Significant discomfort in the affected eye.
  • Severe Pain: Pain is often out of proportion to clinical signs, a key clinical clue.

Signs:

Early Disease:

  • Irregular and Greyish Epithelium: Early sign indicating amoebic invasion.
  • Pseudodendrites: Lesions resembling herpetic keratitis
  • Limbitis and Stromal Infiltrates: Inflammation at the corneal-scleral junction with diffuse or focal infiltrates in the anterior stroma.
  • Perineural Infiltrates (Radial Keratoneuritis): Hallmark sign, radial streaks extending towards the cornea's centre, pathognomonic for Acanthamoeba keratitis.

Advanced Disease:

  • Ring Abscess: Characteristic of advanced infection, where infiltrates form a ring-shaped abscess.
  • Stromal Opacification and Vascularisation: Corneal opacity and new blood vessel growth, leading to significant vision impairment.
  • Corneal Melting: Serious complication where corneal tissue breaks down, often at the infiltrate edges.
  • Scleritis: Reactive inflammation of the sclera, not a direct infection extension.

Options A, B, and C are incorrect.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, Ed 9, Pg 211,216,219,232
question: What's the main risk for a 37-year-old man with blurred vision and severe pain in his right eye? He revealed that recently, he went swimming in a pond. During examination, a ring-like lesion was found, as seen in the image.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation of blurred vision, severe pain after swimming in a pond with ring like lesion on examination is suggestive of Acanthamoeba keratitis.

Acanthamoeba keratitis:

It is caused by Acanthamoeba, a free-living amoeba found in water, causes severe corneal infections

Risk Factors:

  1. Contact Lens Use (Primary Risk Factor)
  2. Exposure to Contaminated Water
  3. Trauma
  4. Immunosuppression
  5. Use of Homemade Saline Solutions.
  6. Poor Lens Storage Conditions

    Examination Findings in Acanthamoeba Keratitis:

Symptoms:

  • Blurred Vision: Common in corneal conditions due to the disruption of the cornea's transparent surface.
  • Discomfort: Significant discomfort in the affected eye.
  • Severe Pain: Pain is often out of proportion to clinical signs, a key clinical clue.

Signs:

Early Disease:

  • Irregular and Greyish Epithelium: Early sign indicating amoebic invasion.
  • Pseudodendrites: Lesions resembling herpetic keratitis
  • Limbitis and Stromal Infiltrates: Inflammation at the corneal-scleral junction with diffuse or focal infiltrates in the anterior stroma.
  • Perineural Infiltrates (Radial Keratoneuritis): Hallmark sign, radial streaks extending towards the cornea's centre, pathognomonic for Acanthamoeba keratitis.

Advanced Disease:

  • Ring Abscess: Characteristic of advanced infection, where infiltrates form a ring-shaped abscess.
  • Stromal Opacification and Vascularisation: Corneal opacity and new blood vessel growth, leading to significant vision impairment.
  • Corneal Melting: Serious complication where corneal tissue breaks down, often at the infiltrate edges.
  • Scleritis: Reactive inflammation of the sclera, not a direct extension of infection.

[[figure-1]]

Diabetes (Option A): Diabetes predisposes to some infections but is not the characteristic risk factor for Acanthamoeba keratitis.

Hypertension (Option B): Not a specific association.

Steroids (Option C): Topical steroids may worsen the infection or delay diagnosis, but they are not the primary risk factor being tested here.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Pages 211, 216, 219, 232
question: A 37-year-old man presents with blurred vision and severe pain in his right eye. He revealed that recently, he went swimming in a pond. During examination, a ring-like lesion was found, as seen in the image. What is the main risk for this condition?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option A - Keratoconus

Explanation:

Treatment of Keratoconus:

  • Spectacle Correction:
    • Effective in the early stages, but contact lenses are more beneficial.
    • Less effective in later stages due to irregular astigmatism.
  • Contact Lenses:
    • Rigid gas permeable lenses improve vision in early cases.
    • Specially designed scleral lenses (e.g., Rose-K) are useful in early to moderate cases.
  • Corneal Collagen Cross-Linking (CXL) (Option A) :
    • New treatment modality to slow disease progression.
    • Involves riboflavin (0.1%) eye drops and UVA radiation.
    • Riboflavin induces cross-linking of corneal collagen to stabilize the stroma and improve contact lens tolerance.
  • Keratoplasty :
    • Recommended if disease progresses or in cases of acute hydrops (Descemet's membrane tear).
    • Reserved for more advanced diseases or when other treatments fail.
    • Penetrating keratoplasty is common, but Deep Anterior Lamellar Keratoplasty (DALK) is preferred if Descemet's membrane and endothelium are intact, reducing rejection risk.
  • Intracorneal Ring Segments (INTACS) :
    • Effective in early to moderate cases by flattening the cornea.
    • Less effective in halting progression.

Incorrect Options:

Corneal ulcer (Option B) are treated with antibiotics, antivirals, or antifungals, depending on the cause.

Band keratopathy (Option C) involves calcium deposition in the superficial cornea and is treated with chelation therapy or surgical interventions like superficial keratectomy.

Uveitis (Option B) is inflammation of the uveal tract and is typically managed with corticosteroids, immunosuppressive agents, or biologics.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, Edition 9, Page- 249, 250.
question: For which of the subsequent diseases is collagen cross-linking therapy utilized?

correctAnswer: C. Conjunctival invasion making a flap over cornea
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Pterygium/Surfer’s eye

Definition

Pterygium is a triangular encroachment of vascularized granulation tissue covered by conjunctiva in the interpalpebral area.

[[figure-1]]

  • Parts: Cap, head, neck, body
  • Degenerative process

Aetiology

  • Common in dry, sunny climates with sandy soils
  • Ultraviolet light is a probable factor
  • Usually elderly persons

Pathology

[[figure-2]]

Histology shows collagenous degenerative changes in the vascularized subepithelial stroma.

Pathogenesis

  • Degenerative subconjunctival proliferation
  • Granulation tissue proliferates as avascularized tissue encroaches on the cornea.
  • Destroys the superficial layers of the stroma and Bowman’s membrane

Symptoms

  • Frequently follows a pinguecula
  • Often bilateral
  • Usually on the nasal side
  • Impairment of vision due to:
    • Progression into the pupillary area of the cornea
    • Induced astigmatism by corneal flattening in the axis of pterygium
  • Progressive pterygium: thick and vascular
  • Regressive pterygium: thin, pale, and atrophic
  • Ceases to grow but never disappears
  • A probe can be passed under the lesion
  • Can present as inflammed pterygium

[[figure-3]]

Signs

  • A probe cannot be passed under the lesion
  • Fusch’s spots/Islets of Vogt: small discrete whitish flecks made of pterygial epithelial cells seen in progressive pterygium and are also called the cap of the pterygium.
  • Stocker line: linear epithelial iron deposition, seen in regressive pterygium.

[[figure-4]]

Management of pterygium:

Management

  • Best left alone

Medical treatment:

  • Tear substitutes for small regressive pterygium with dry eye
  • Topical steroids for associated inflammation
  • Protection from UV rays with sunglasses

Surgical excision for:

  • Progression of lesion towards the pupillary area causing excessive astigmatism and visual impairment
  • Restricted ocular movements
  • Disfiguring
  • Diplopia

Procedures
  • Bare sclera technique:
    • The pterygium is excised from the cornea and conjunctiva, leaving a bare sclera
    • Associated with a high recurrence rate
  • Autoconjunctival graft
    • A piece of limbal conjunctival tissue from the same or the other eye or
    • An amniotic membrane graft is used to cover the bare sclera
    • Sutured at the limbus to cover the defect
  • Surgical excision with lamellar keratectomy and lamellar keratoplasty for deeply infiltrating recurrent recalcitrant pterygia
  • Old methods (not used now):
    • McRaynold’s operation
    • Postoperative use of beta irradiations

Post-operative therapy and care
  • Prevent recurrence:
    • Mitomycin C 0.02% drops
    • Complications like scleral necrosis, cataracts, and iritis


Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th edition, Page- 198, 199.

question: Which of the following is true about pterygium?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - Bacterial corneal ulcer

Explanation:

  • Bacterial corneal ulcers present with redness, pain, and discharge. Signs include a greyish-white serpiginous ulcer seen over the lower third of the cornea, indicative of the bacteria

Aetiology of Purulent Corneal Ulcer:

  • Corneal Epithelial Damage:

    • Due to Corneal abrasion, epithelial drying (xerosis, exposure keratitis), necrosis (keratomalacia), desquamation (bullous keratopathy), and trophic changes (neuroparalytic keratitis).

  • Pathogens Invading Intact Epithelium:

    • Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Corynebacterium diphtheriae, Neisseria meningitidis, Haemophilus aegyptius, Listeria species.

  • Sources of Infection:

    • Exogenous Sources: Conjunctival sac, lacrimal sac (dacryocystitis), infected foreign bodies, vegetative material, waterborne or airborne infections.

  • Common Bacteria Associated with Corneal Ulceration:

    • General: Staphylococci, Pseudomonas, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Enterobacteriaceae, Neisseria.

    • In Contact Lens Wearers: Pseudomonas is the most common cause. Acanthamoeba is another differential in contact lens misuse.

  • All causative organisms:

    • Gram-positive Cocci: Staphylococcus aureus, Staphylococcus epidermidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae.

    • Gram-negative Cocci: Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Neisseria meningitidis.

    • Gram-positive Bacilli: Corynebacterium diphtheriae, C. xerosis, Bacillus cereus, Propionibacterium acne, Listeria, Clostridium.

    • Gram-negative Bacilli: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Enterobacteriaceae (Klebsiella, Proteus, E. coli, Serratia), Moraxella lacunata, Haemophilus influenzae.

    • Gram-positive Filamentous Bacteria: Actinomyces, Nocardia.

    • Mycobacteria: Non-tuberculous mycobacteria, M. tuberculosis.

Clinical Features of Bacterial Corneal Ulcers:

Symptoms:

  • Pain and foreign body sensation.

  • Watery eye (reflex hyper lacrimation).

  • Photophobia (light intolerance).

  • Blurred vision.

  • Redness of the eye.

Signs:

  • Lid swelling.

  • Blepharospasm (lid twitching).

  • Conjunctival chemosis and hyperemia.

  • Corneal ulcer characteristics:

    • Early stage: Epithelial defect with greyish-white infiltrate.

    • Established: Yellowish-white ulcer, swollen margins, necrotic floor, stromal oedema.

  • Specific bacterial features:

    • Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pneumoniae: Oval, yellowish-white ulcer surrounded by clear cornea.

    • Pseudomonas species: Irregular ulcer with greenish exudate, rapid spread, often with hypopyon.

    • Enterobacteriaceae: Shallow ulcer with greyish-white suppuration, ring-shaped infiltrate.

  • The anterior chamber may contain pus (Hypopyon).

  • Muddy iris colour.

  • Small pupil due to iritis.

  • Possible raised intraocular pressure (inflammatory glaucoma).

Incorrect Options

Viral corneal ulcer (Option A) It is caused due to low immunity. A red, watery, and bloodshot eye is a prominent feature. There is severe eye pain and pus or other eye discharge. This can lead to vision loss and blindness.

Fungal corneal ulcer (Option C) Trauma is one of the causes of Fungal corneal ulcer. There is less pain and Hypopyon if present is thick and immobile.

Parasitic corneal ulcer (Option D) Is characterized by disproportionately severe pain and is caused by either contact lens wear or exposure to contaminated water.



Reference:
  • Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, Edition 9, Page- 209, 210, 211.

Additionally, a hypopyon measuring 4 mm was found in the anterior chamber, along with a moderate flare reaction.

Explanation:

  • Keratan sulfate and chondroitin sulfate are the major glycosaminoglycan present in the corneal stroma. They exist in the proteoglycan form and are responsible for maintaining the space between the regularly oriented layers of collagen fibrils in the stroma.

Locations of Various Mucopolysaccharides

Mucopolysaccharide

Primary Locations

Functions

Hyaluronic Acid (Option B)

Heparin (Option C)

Acts as an anticoagulant by activating antithrombin III, which inactivates thrombin and other clotting factors

Chondroitin Sulfate

Keratan Sulfate (Option A)

Dermatan Sulfate (Option D)

Skin, blood vessels, heart valves

Contributes to the structure of the skin, blood vessels, and heart valves

Correct Option A - Keratoplasty

Explanation:

  • The history of trauma to the eye and complete loss of vision and examination finding revealing congestion and corneal perforation is suggestive of uncontrolled keratitis commonly seen with bacterial keratitis. The choice of treatment for corneal perforation with uncontrolled infection penetrating is keratoplasty.

Penetrating Keratoplasty (PK):

  • It is a type of Allografting (Allo-Keratoplasty) which is the replacement of a patient’s diseased cornea with a healthy donor cornea.
  • Full-thickness grafting.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

[[figure-3]]

Indications for Penetrating Keratoplasty:

Optical
  • Corneal opacity
  • Bullous keratopathy
  • Corneal dystrophies
  • Advanced keratoconus

Therapeutic

To replace an inflamed cornea that does not respond to conventional therapy

Tectonic Graft

To restore the integrity of the eyeball, e.g., after corneal perforation (Option A) or in cases of significant corneal thinning.

Cosmetic

To improve the appearance of the eye

Complications: (ak142)

  • Early Complications:
    • Flat anterior chamber
    • Iris prolapse
    • Infection
    • Secondary glaucoma
    • Epithelial defects
    • Primary graft failure
  • Late Complications:
    • Graft rejection
    • Recurrence of disease
    • Astigmatism

Incorrect Options

Keratotomy (Option B) is used for correcting refractive error causing flattening of the cornea and reducing its focusing power.

LASIK (Option C) surgery is commonly used for keratomileusis, which is altering of the curvature of the cornea, done for refractive correction. .

Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) (Option D) is a surgical procedure done for dacryocystitis.

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, Edition 9, Page- 277
question: A 64-year-old woman with a history of trauma to the left eye 5 days back now presented with complaints of complete loss of vision. Upon examination the following findings were seen. What should be the subsequent course of action to manage this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Keratomycosis

[[figure-1]]

Clinical Features

  • Pain & Foreign Body Sensation
  • Watering of the eye
  • Photophobia
  • Blurred Vision
  • Redness.

Examination Findings

  • Corneal Ulcer: Greyish-white, dry-looking with elevated, rolled-out margins.
  • Pigmented Ulcer: Brownish appearance, possible with dematiaceous fungi.
  • Feathery Extensions: Delicate, finger-like projections into the surrounding stroma.
  • Sterile Immune Ring: Yellow line of demarcation where fungal antigen and host antibodies meet.
  • Satellite Lesions (Option D): Multiple small lesions around the main ulcer.
  • Hypopyon (Option A ruled out): Large, non-sterile, even with a small ulcer.
  • Endothelial Plaque: Located under the stromal lesion, made of fibrin and leucocytes.
  • Corneal Vascularization: Typically absent in pure fungal ulcers.
  • Perforation: Rare but possible.

Investigations

  • Corneal Scraping: Performed under topical anaesthesia for microbiological examination.
  • Wet KOH Mount: Reveals filamentous fungi (branched, septate hyphae) or non-filamentous yeast-like fungi (Candida).
  • Gram's & Giemsa Stains: To detect fungal hyphae and inflammatory cells.
  • Culture: Sabouraud's agar medium is used for fungal culture.
  • PCR: Recommended for rapid identification of fungal pathogens.
  • Anterior Chamber Paracentesis: Considered if there is an intraocular extension.
  • Corneal Biopsy: Indicated for deep stromal abscess or when cultures are negative.
  • Confocal Microscopy: Used for identifying actual fungi within the cornea.

Incorrect Options:

Dendritic ulcer on a fluorescein dye (Option B) is a characteristic finding of herpetic keratitis caused by the herpes simplex virus.

Ring abscess (Option C) is seen in Acanthamoeba keratitis commonly seen in patients using contact lens and using tap water to clean it.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, Edition 9, Page- 216, 217.

question: What is the distinguishing characteristic of a fungal ulcer?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Layers of Cornea

Epithelium

(Option D ruled out)
  • The outermost layer comprises 5-6 layers of non-keratinized, stratified squamous epithelial cells.
  • Acts as a barrier, protecting the cornea and preventing tear fluid from entering the underlying stroma.
  • The basal cells at the limbus are stem cells responsible for regenerating the corneal epithelium.

Bowman’s Membrane
  • Located just beneath the epithelium, this acellular layer is 12 µm thick and composed of densely packed collagen fibrils.
  • It is a protective barrier to the stroma but cannot regenerate if damaged and heals by scarring.

Stroma

(Option C ruled out)
  • Making up about 90% of the cornea's thickness (approximately 0.5 mm thick), the stroma consists of collagen fibrils arranged in parallel layers.
  • These fibrils are embedded in a hydrated matrix of proteoglycans - Chondroitin and Keratan Sulphate (keratan sulphate maintains corneal transparency).

Pre-Descemet's Membrane (Dua's Layer)

  • This layer, discovered in 2013, is about 15 µm thick, acellular, and lies just above Descemet's membrane.
  • It is strong and resistant to air penetration.

Descemet's Membrane (Option A ruled out)
  • A robust basement membrane of the corneal endothelium is made of collagen and glycoproteins.
  • It is tense, but when torn, curls inwards on itself.
  • It can regenerate if damaged and is resistant to trauma and pathological processes.

Endothelium

(Option B)
  • The innermost layer consists of a single layer of flat, hexagonal cells.
  • These cells are crucial for maintaining corneal transparency by regulating fluid balance within the cornea through an active pump mechanism.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, Edition 9, Page- 204.

explanationHtml:
Explantion:

  • History of trauma with vegetative matter is the single most important clue → strongly points toward fungal keratitis

  • Key clinical features of fungal keratitis:

    • Corneal ulcer with dry, feathery, irregular margins

    • Satellite lesions around the main ulcer (classic finding)

    • Hypopyon (often thick and immobile)

    • Mild to moderate pain (pain is less than expected for severity)

    • Photophobia and redness

Acanthamoeba keratitis (Option B):

  • Typically associated with contact lens use, especially with tap water

  • Causes severe pain out of proportion to signs

  • Classically shows a ring-shaped stromal infiltrate

  • Satellite lesions and hypopyon are uncommon

Viral keratitis (Option C):

  • Usually due to HSV

  • Characteristic dendritic or geographic ulcers

  • Hypopyon and satellite lesions are not typical

Bacterial keratitis (Option D):

  • Often has severe pain, purulent discharge

  • Ulcer margins are more well-defined

  • Satellite lesions strongly favor fungal rather than bacterial etiology

question: What is the probable diagnosis in a 27-year-old male with eye trauma from vegetative matter presenting with a corneal ulcer, hypopyon, satellite lesions, mild pain, photophobia, and redness?

  • It is prevalent in individuals using soft contact lens and using tap water for cleaning or swimming with the contact lens in a swimming pool.

Incorrect Options:

Option B - Naegleria fowleri: Naegleria fowleri is a free-living amoeba that can cause a rare and often fatal brain infection known as primary amoebic meningoencephalitis (PAM).

Option C - Entamoeba histolytica: Entamoeba histolytica is a parasitic amoeba that can cause amoebiasis, a gastrointestinal infection.

Option D - Balamuthia mandrillaris: Balamuthia mandrillaris is a free-living amoeba that can cause a rare and often fatal brain infection known as granulomatous amoebic encephalitis (GAE).

question: What is the likely reason for a 21-year-old student to have ocular redness, feeling of a foreign object in the eye, and excessive tearing after wearing a soft contact lens, as indicated by the corneal scraping interface contrast microscopy image?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option A - Viral keratitis:

  • The lesion in viral keratitis is typically characterized by dendritic or branching patterns on the cornea, as seen in the image.
  • Viral keratitis is a type of corneal infection caused by a virus, such as herpes simplex virus (HSV) or varicella-zoster virus (VZV).

Incorrect Options:

Option B - Fungal keratitis: The lesion in fungal keratitis often presents as an infiltrate or ulcer with feathery edges (hyphae) and satellite lesions.

Option C - Bacterial keratitis: The lesion in bacterial keratitis often presents with ulcer, stromal edema, inflammation, and keratic precipitates due to anterior uveitis.

Option D - Interstitial keratitis: This is a condition in which there is inflammation of the cornea that affects the middle layer (stroma) of the cornea. The lesion in interstitial keratitis is typically characterized by a hazy appearance of the cornea, with no obvious ulcer or infiltrate.

question: Please analyze the image provided and determine the specific abnormality or injury present.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The presence of a retrobulbar tumor, suggestive of an optic pathway glioma, along with the clinical images, demonstrates the classic features of NF1 (Neurofibromatosis Type 1).

  • Iris shows Lisch nodules, which are melanocytic hamartomas
  • S-shaped ptosis is characteristic of a plexiform neurofibroma involving the eyelid.
  • Skin lesions shown are café-au-lait spots, which are flat, hyperpigmented macules commonly seen in NF1.

NF1 (Neurofibromatosis Type 1), also known as von Recklinghausen disease

  • It is the most common phakomatosis (neurocutaneous syndrome).
  • Caused by a mutation in the NF1 gene on chromosome 17.
  • Phakomatoses are hereditary multisystem disorders affecting structures derived from the ectoderm, mainly the skin, nervous system, and eyes.
  • Diagnosis of NF1 is based on characteristic clinical criteria, including:
    • Café-au-lait macules
    • Neurofibromas/plexiform neurofibromas
    • Lisch nodules
    • Optic gliomas
    • Skeletal abnormalities
    • Family history of NF1.

Tuberous sclerosis (Option A): Its characteristic skin findings are ash-leaf spots, shagreen patches, and facial angiofibromas (adenoma sebaceum). Its primary ocular finding is a retinal astrocytic hamartoma (mulberry lesion), rather than Lisch nodules or plexiform neurofibromas.

Sturge-Weber syndrome (Option C) is characterized by a "port-wine stain" (nevus flammeus) on the face, usually following the distribution of the trigeminal nerve. The most common ocular complication is glaucoma, and it does not present with Lisch nodules or café-au-lait spots.

Von Hippel-Lindau disease (VHL) (Option D) is primarily associated with retinal capillary hemangioblastomas (vessel tumors in the retina) and systemic tumors like renal cell carcinoma and pheochromocytoma. It does not present with the iris nodules or skin pigmentation shown in the images.

question: A patient presents with skin lesions, retrobulbar tumor, and characteristic eye findings shown in the images below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
It accurately pairs each diagnostic lens with its specific magnification correction factor used during slit-lamp biomicroscopy. The standard correction factors (multipliers used to find the true size of the optic disc from the slit-beam measurement) are:

  • VOLK 90D (D): 1.3 (Factor 1)
  • Goldmann 3-mirror (C): 1.08 (Factor 4)
  • VOLK 60D (A): 1.1 (Factor 2)
  • VOLK 78D (B): 1.27 (Factor 3)

When measuring structures like the optic nerve head using a slit lamp and a diagnostic lens, the image seen is magnified or minified depending on the lens power.

  • To calculate the true physical size, the vertical height of the slit beam must be multiplied by a magnification correction factor.
  • Higher-powered lenses (like 90D) produce a smaller image, thus requiring a larger correction factor (1.3) to return to the actual size, whereas lower-powered lenses (like 60D) produce a larger image and require a smaller correction factor (closer to 1.0).

  • Thyroid Eye Disease (TED), also known as Graves' Ophthalmopathy, is the most common cause of both unilateral and bilateral proptosis in adults.

Idiopathic (Option B) is a diagnosis of exclusion, made only after specific causes like TED, tumors, or infections have been ruled out.

question: A patient presents with bilateral proptosis with restricted movements of the eye. What is the most common cause of such a condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The finding of Dendritic Ulcer are pathognomonic for Herpes Simplex Epithelial Keratitis.
  • Topical Acyclovir 3% eye ointment (5 times/day) is the gold standard antiviral therapy.
  • Atropine (cycloplegic) is added to relieve pain caused by ciliary spasm and to prevent posterior synechiae if there is secondary uveitis.

Treatment of Herpes Simplex Epithelial Keratitis:

  • First-line
    • Topical antivirals:
      • Acyclovir 3% ointment 5×/day
      • Ganciclovir 0.15% gel 5×/day
      • >99% heal in ≤2 weeks
  • Adjuncts
    • Cycloplegic: homatropine / atropine (pain relief)
    • Debridement: for resistant cases (+ antiviral cover)
    • Oral antivirals (if severe/immunocompromised/refractory):
  • Acyclovir / Valaciclovir / Famciclovir

Antibiotics (Option A) are used for bacterial ulcers presenting as a round/oval defect with stromal infiltrate.

Steroids (Option C) are absolutely contraindicated in epithelial HSV keratitis. They promote viral replication and can convert a dendritic ulcer into a massive Geographic Ulcer, leading to perforation.

Conservative management (Option D): Untreated Herpes Simplex Keratitis can progress to deeper stromal involvement (disciform keratitis), leading to permanent corneal scarring, neovascularization, and vision loss.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 221.
question: A characteristic corneal lesion is seen on fluorescein staining (image shown). What is the preferred treatment?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical scenario describes a severe refractive error between the two eyes.
  • Anisometropia is the condition where the refractive status of the two eyes differs.
  • The brain suppresses the blurred image from the eye with the higher refractive error to avoid diplopia, leading to severe vision loss (Amblyopia) and often a secondary deviation (squint).
  • Etiology
    • Congenital/developmental: differential eyeball growth
    • Acquired: Uniocular aphakia, Asymmetric aging changes, Wrong-power IOL implantation
  • Diagnosis:
    • Cycloplegic refraction / retinoscopy
    • Autorefractometry
  • Treatment
    • Spectacles → tolerated up to ~4D
    • Contact lenses → treatment of choice for high anisometropia
    • Surgical options:
      • IOL for uniocular aphakia
      • Corneal refractive surgery
      • Phakic Refractive Lenses (PRL)/ Refractive Lens Exchange (RLE) for very high anisometropia

Strabismic amblyopia (Option B) is vision loss caused primarily by misalignment.

Esotropia (Option C) is an inward deviation. On the cover test, if an eye is esotropic, it must move OUT (abduct) to take up fixation when the good eye is covered.

Pseudostrabismus (Option D) is the false appearance of a squint (usually due to a broad nasal bridge or epicanthal folds) where the visual axes are actually aligned.



Reference:
  1. Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 698.
  2. AK Khurana, Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th Edition, Page 44.
question: A patient came with a vision of 6/6 in one eye, and the other eye had less than 6/60. A refractive difference of 4D is present between the two eyes. On covering the normal eye, the deviated eye moved towards the center to take up fixation. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis is the most likely diagnosis given the patient’s age, the characteristic findings of cobblestone-like papillae on the palpebral conjunctiva
  • It commonly affects young children and adolescents, presenting with symptoms such as itching, burning, and lacrimation, and often worsens during warm weather.

Vernal keratoconjunctivitis or Spring catarrh

Symptoms

Burning, Itching, Photophobia (sensitivity to light), and lacrimation (excessive tearing).

Signs
  • Palpebral Form: Hypertrophied palpebral conjunctiva with a cobblestone appearance;dense fibrous tissue with thickened epithelium.
  • Limbal or Bulbar Form: Opacification at the limbus, gelatinous thickening, and Horner–Trantas dots
  • Pseudogerontoxon/cupid’s bow (which resembles arcus senilis) is a grayish-white ring at the limbus seen in severe limbal vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC).
  • Shield ulcers are a significant complication of VKC, particularly in severe cases. These microerosions typically form on the upper third of the cornea.
  • Mixed form: Exhibits characteristics of both the tarsal (palpebral) and limbal subtypes, typically presenting in only one eye.

Maxwell Lyon's sign is a pseudomembrane formed due to excessive mucus deposition on the papilla resulting in cobblestone papillae.

Atopic keratoconjunctivitis (Option A):

  • Seen in older patients (teens/adults) with atopy
  • More chronic, less dramatic cobblestone papillae

Bacterial conjunctivitis (Option C):

  • Purulent discharge, not intense itching
  • No cobblestone papillae

Chlamydial conjunctivitis (Option D):

  • Follicles, not papillae
  • Usually chronic with mucopurulent discharge

correctAnswer: B. Hallmark is the presence of Cobblestone papillae
explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - Hallmark is the presence of Cobblestone papillae:

Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis

  • Bilateral, Recurrent, Self-limiting conjunctivitis.

  • Young boys in 1st decade of life are affected.

  • More common in the summer.

  • More common in the tropical climate.

  • Cobblestone papillae are seen: hallmark

Horner trantas spots

Shield ulcer

Cobblestone papillae

Incorrect Options:

Option A - It is a Follicular hypertrophy:

  • The hypertrophy which occurs in the VKC is papillary, not follicular.

Option C - Mild itching is present:

Option D - Type IV hypersensitivity response:

question: A 25-year-old male presents to the ophthalmologic clinic for evaluation of his ocular lesions. After carefully assessing the eyes, the attending doctor diagnoses vernal keratoconjunctivitis. Which of the following statements is most likely associated with vernal keratoconjunctivitis?

correctAnswer: B. The hallmark is the presence of cobblestone papillae.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient has vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC), a bilateral, recurrent allergic keratoconjunctivitis that predominantly affects boys and young males living in warm, dry, tropical climates.

  • It is characterised by intense itching (Option C), photophobia, tearing, ropy mucoid discharge, and conjunctival hyperemia.
  • The hallmark finding is giant cobblestone papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva.

  • Other characteristic features include:
    • Horner-Trantas dots (collections of eosinophils and degenerated epithelial cells at the limbus) and

    • Shield ulcers, which are sterile superficial corneal ulcers caused by mechanical trauma from giant papillae and eosinophil-derived toxins.

  • VKC is mediated by both Type I (IgE-mediated) and Type IV (T-cell-mediated) (Option D) hypersensitivity mechanisms.

It is Characterized by Follicular Hypertrophy (Option A): VKC produces papillary hypertrophy, particularly giant cobblestone papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva. Follicles are more characteristic of viral or chlamydial conjunctivitis.



Reference:

A K Khurana Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 6th Edition, Pages 79-80

The hallmark is the presence of cobblestone papillae.
It is caused solely by a Type IV hypersensitivity reaction.

correctAnswer: C. Vitamin A: 2 lakhs IU in oral, 0 th , 1 st , and 14 th day
explanationHtml:

Explanation:

  • The clinical picture of night blindness, conjunctival xerosis, bitot's spot, and keratomalacia suggest the diagnosis of Xerophthalmia and the treatment is Vitamin A supplementation either orally or injectable. The rule is to inject 1 lakh IU of Vitamin A on the 0th,1st, and 14th day if given IM for a child above 1 year, or if given orally double the amount of Vitamin A given injectable. If, the child is less than 1 year half the dose.

Vitamin A: 2 lakh IU in oral, 0th, 1st, and 10th day (Option A): This option is incorrect, the last dose is given on the 14th day, not on the 10th day.


Vitamin A: 2 lakhs IU injectable, 0th, 1st, and 14th day (Option B): This option is incorrect, the dose for injectable Vitamin A above 1 year is 1Lakh, not 2 lakhs.


Vitamin A: 2 lakhs IU injectable, 0th, 1st, and 10th day (Option D): This option is incorrect, the last dose is given on the 14th day, not on the 10th day and moreover the dose given is 1 Lakh if given injectable.

question: A 3-year-old child weighing 14 kg is brought to the pediatric clinic with complaints of night blindness and dryness of the eyes. On examination, the ophthalmologist observes conjunctival xerosis, Bitot's spots, and keratomalacia. What is the appropriate treatment for this child's condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Extensive Rose Bengal staining indicates significant damage to the corneal and conjunctival epithelium, which is a feature of dry eye.


Schirmer’s Test:
  • Schirmer’s test is used to diagnose aqueous deficiency dry eye disease.

Schirmer's Test 1

  • Measures both basal and reflex tear secretions
  • Uses Whatman-41 filter paper, kept in the lower fornix at the junction of lateral one-third and medial two-thirds.
  • After 5 minutes, wetting of the filter strip from the bent end is measured.
  • Normal value: >15 mm
  • 5-10 mm: Mild to moderate keratoconjunctivitis sicca (KCS).
  • < 5 mm: Severe KCS (Option B)

Schirmer's Test 2

  • Measures only basal secretion under anesthesia

Tear Film Break-Up Time (TBUT)
  • Tear film stained with sodium fluorescein 1% is observed under a slit lamp, and time is noted after the patient blinks.
  • The interval between the complete blink and the first appearance of a ‘dark’ dry spot on the cornea is recorded as TBUT.
  • Normal: 15-35 seconds
  • < 10 seconds indicates unstable tear film. (Option A)

Rose Bengal or Lissamine Green

Stain devitalized, desiccated corneal and conjunctival epithelium red or green. (Option C)

Rose Bengal stain

Lissamine Green

Tear film Osmolality

Increased in dry eye (Option D)

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, Edition 9, Page- 160, 161, 162.

question: A 65-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis presents with dry eyes and mouth. Rose bengal staining shows conjunctival damage, and tear analysis reveals a tear-to-lysozyme ratio of 0.1. Which tear film layer is primarily deficient in this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • A yellowish, triangular patch on the conjunctiva near the limbus, typically in the elderly, associated with sun exposure and not extending onto the cornea, points towards the diagnosis of Pinguecula.

Pinguecula

Definition

A triangular patch on the conjunctiva appears yellow and resembles fat (pinguis).

Pathology

Caused by hyaline infiltration and elastotic degeneration of submucous tissue.

Etiology

Common in elderly people, particularly those exposed to strong sunlight, dust, and wind.

Clinical Feature
  • Bilateral
  • Usually stationary
  • Yellowish triangular patch near the limbus
  • Apex of the triangle is away from the cornea
  • Affects the nasal side first, followed by the temporal side

Image

[[figure-1]]

Complication

  • Inflammation of pinguecula
  • Intraepithelial abscess formation
  • Rarely calcification

Treatment

  • Generally, it requires no treatment.
  • When inflamed, treated with topical steroids.
  • May be excised when cosmetically unaccepted.

Pterygium (Option A) is a triangular, vascularized growth extending onto the cornea.

[[figure-2]]

Dermoid (Option C) appears as a lenticular yellow tumor near the corneal margin and consists of epidermoid epithelium with sebaceous glands and hair.

[[figure-3]]

Malignant melanoma (Option D) typically occurs at the limbus, is usually pigmented, and can spread or metastasize.

[[figure-4]]

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th edition, Page- 197, 198.
question: A 70-year-old man with extensive sun exposure has a yellowish, triangular patch on the nasal conjunctiva, as shown below. The lesion does not extend onto the cornea. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: D. Histology shows collagenous degenerative changes in the vascularized subepithelial stroma
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The above clinical scenario points to the diagnosis of pterygium.

Pterygium/Surfer’s eye




Pathology

Histology shows collagenous degenerative changes in the vascularized subepithelial stroma.

[[figure-1]]


Symptoms

  • Frequently follows a pinguecula
  • Often bilateral
  • Usually on the nasal side (Option B)
  • Impairment of vision due to:
    • Progression into the pupillary area of the cornea
    • Induced astigmatism by corneal flattening in the axis of pterygium
  • Progressive pterygium: thick and vascular (Option A)
  • Regressive pterygium: thin, pale, and atrophic
  • Ceases to grow but never disappears
  • A probe can be passed under the lesion
  • Can present as inflammed pterygium

[[figure-2]]

Pseudopterygium (Option C) is caused by:

  • Trauma
  • Chronic conjunctivitis
  • Thermochemical burn


Reference:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Cone dystrophy is primarily associated with day blindness (hemeralopia), which is the inability to see clearly in bright light due to poor light adaptation.

Nyctalopia/ Night Blindness is the inability to see in low-light conditions.

  • It is attributed to interference with the functions of the retinal rods.

Causes of Nyctalopia:

  • Retinitis pigmentosa

  • Peripheral cortical cataract

    • Due to a deficiency of the enzyme ornithine aminotransferase, plasma ornithine levels are elevated.

question: A 5-year-old boy from a rural area has difficulty seeing at night. Upon examination, you notice the presence of triangular, dry-white spots on the bulbar conjunctiva in both eyes. Which of the following represents the correct diagnosis and grade of xerophthalmia based on the clinical findings?

correctAnswer: B. Topical dual-acting antihistamine/mast cell stabilizer
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Topical dual-acting antihistamine/mast cell stabilizer is the first-line treatment for atopic keratoconjunctivitis.
  • It addresses both histamine release and mast cell stabilization, helping control inflammation and allergic responses.

Atopic Keratoconjunctivitis

Treatment
  • First-line therapy: Topical dual-acting antihistamine/mast cell stabilizer
  • If there is no improvement in 2-3 weeks: A brief course of topical corticosteroids. (Option A)
  • For moderate-to-severe disease requiring frequent corticosteroids - Use topical cyclosporine (2%, compounded). (Option C)
  • Eyelid Dermatitis: Topical tacrolimus is preferred over corticosteroids.

Oral antihistamines (Option D) may help with systemic symptoms, but they are not as effective for treating ocular manifestations directly.

question: A 23-year-old male presents with a history of atopic dermatitis and asthma. He complains of tearing, burning, itching sensation and blurry vision for the past week. On examination, his eyelids are thickened and swollen, with signs of meibomitis. Slit-lamp examination reveals anterior subcapsular cataracts. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment for this patient’s ocular symptoms?

correctAnswer: B. Type IV hypersensitivity reaction to endogenous bacterial antigens
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The above presentation is a case of phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis primarily mediated by a delayed-type (Type IV) hypersensitivity reaction triggered by bacterial proteins of Staphylococcus aureus or tuberculosis.
  • The child's history of TB is significant, as TB antigens can trigger this hypersensitivity response, leading to the characteristic ocular findings.
  • The immune system reacts to these antigens, causing the formation of nodules (phlyctens) and subsequent inflammation around the limbus.
  • This explains the localized inflammatory response seen in this condition.



Reference:

.

question: A 10-year-old child presents with itching, watering, and redness in both eyes. On examination, small round yellow nodules are observed near the limbus, and conjunctival congestion is noted. The child has a past h/o TB. Which of the following best explains the pathophysiology of this condition?

correctAnswer: B. The conjunctival epithelium is lined by stratified non-keratinized epithelium.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The conjunctival epithelium is composed of stratified non-keratinized epithelium.

Layers of Conjunctiva

Outer Epithelial Layer
  • Lined by stratified squamous epithelium.
  • The epithelium gradually thickens from the fornices to the limbus(Option A), becoming stratified and nonkeratinized near the corneal margin, while the palpebral conjunctiva lining the eyelids remains thinner and nonkeratinized. It contains:
    • Goblet cells
    • Melanocytes
    • Langerhans cells

Adenoid Layer (or lymphoid layer)
  • It is located below the epithelium.
  • This layer develops lymphoid tissue only after 3-4 months of age, which explains why newborns cannot produce a follicular conjunctival reaction.(Option C)

Dense Fibrous Layer
  • It is present deep in the adenoid layer, merging into the underlying tissues (lid or sclera).
  • This layer contains the vessels and nerves of the conjunctiva.(Option D)

[[figure-1]]


Reference:

KANSKI’S Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th edition, Page- 168.

question: A 2-day-old infant is evaluated for discharge from the eyes. The discharge was initially serous, but it quickly turned into mucopurulent and then purulent. On examination, the eyes are bright red and swollen. What is the most likely causative agent here?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Azithromycin stands out as the preferred systemic antibiotic or treatment of choice, given its effectiveness and convenient dosing regimen, particularly when taken orally either as a single dose or as part of a mass drug administration approach.

Management

SAFE is a WHO-recommended combination of interventions to treat trachoma and prevent it from leading to blindness

  • Surgery for cicatricial entropion and trichiasis (Tertiary prevention)
  • Antibiotics to eliminate the organism (Secondary prevention)
  • Facial cleanliness to avoid infection (Primary prevention)
  • Environmental improvement with better hygiene and sanitation (Primordial prevention)

Erythromycin (Option A) or doxycycline (Option B) may be considered, although caution is warranted with tetracyclines in pregnancy, breastfeeding, and among children, and hence, it is not preferred over azithromycin.

Signs of active trachoma

Signs of cicatricial trachoma

Conjunctival signs:

  • Conjunctival congestion
  • Follicles in the upper tarsal conjunctiva: Look like sago-grains

  • Symblepharon

Corneal signs:

  • Herbert’s follicles
  • Progressive pannus/Trachomatous pannus: The upper part of the cornea is cloudy

Trachomatous pannus

Progressive pannus

  • Corneal ulcers are common at the advancing edge of the pannus
    • Shallow, little infiltrated
    • Cause lacrimation and photophobia

    • Receding infiltration
    • Vessels extend beyond the area of infiltration and haze

  • Herbert pits: oval or circular pitted scars formed after the healing of Herbert’s follicles in the limbal area

  • Vascularized and opaque cornea.

question: An 8-year-old female is being evaluated for conjunctivitis. She gives a history of itching and mild foreign body sensation in the eyes, stickiness of the lids, and mucoid discharge from the eyes. On examination, there is conjunctival congestion. Which of the following signs would be seen in this stage of the disease?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Sudden redness, foreign body sensation and subconjunctival haemorrhage, especially after travel to a tropical region, are characteristic of acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis, caused by Coxsackievirus.

Causes of Hemorrhagic Conjunctivitis:

  • Viral:
    • Coxsackievirus

[[figure-2]]

question: A 28-year-old man develops sudden redness, Foreign body sensation and subconjunctival haemorrhage in both eyes after returning from a tropical region. His visual acuity is normal. What is the most likely causative agent?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The presence of localised inflammation, redness, and foamy discharge confined to the angles of the eyes, along with skin maceration around these areas, points towards the diagnosis of angular conjunctivitis.

  • The most common cause is Moraxella axenfeld.
  • Infection is transmitted from the nasal cavity to the eyes via contaminated fingers or handkerchiefs.
  • Treatment:
    • Oxytetracycline (1%) eye ointment applied 2-3 times a day for 9-14 days.
    • Zinc lotion is instilled during the day, and zinc oxide ointment at bedtime to inhibit the proteolytic enzyme and reduce maceration.

[[figure-1]]

Staphylococcus aureus (Option A): Staphylococcus aureus commonly causes blepharitis, hordeolum, and bacterial conjunctivitis, producing diffuse lid margin inflammation rather than the characteristic angular fissuring and foamy discharge of angular conjunctivitis.

Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Option C): Neisseria gonorrhoeae causes hyperacute purulent conjunctivitis with copious purulent discharge, marked chemosis, and rapid corneal involvement, rather than a chronic infection confined to the canthal angles.

Haemophilus influenzae (Option D): Haemophilus influenzae is a cause of acute bacterial conjunctivitis, particularly in children, presenting with diffuse conjunctival hyperemia and mucopurulent discharge, not the localized angular conjunctivitis seen in this patient.



Reference:

AK Khurana Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th Edition, Pages 66, 67
question: A 30-year-old male presents with irritation and redness at both eye corners, foamy discharge, and skin maceration as shown below. He also has chronic nasal discharge. Which organism is most likely causing his symptoms?

Aspect

Membranous Conjunctivitis

Pseudomembranous Conjunctivitis

Characteristics

  • True membranes grow into the conjunctival epithelium and are more adherent.
  • Removal of these membranes often results in significant bleeding.
  • More superficial, with no growth into conjunctival epithelium, and are less adherent than true membranes.
  • These can be removed with minimal bleeding.

Causes

  • Bacterial: Corynebacterium diphtheria.
  • Drug Reactions: Hypersensitivity reactions, Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS).
  • Chemical or thermal injury.
  • Infectious: Mild Corynebacterium diphtheria infection, Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Option B ruled out), Streptococcus pyogenes (Option D ruled out), Staphylococcus aureus, adenovirus (Option A ruled out), COVID-19.
  • Inflammatory: Hypersensitivity reactions, foreign body reactions.
  • Ligneous Conjunctivitis

Image

question: A 7-year-old child presents with the eye condition shown in the image. The child reports severe eye pain, redness, and eyelid swelling. Examination reveals an inflamed conjunctiva with thick, adherent membranes that bleed when removed. Which of the following organisms is most likely responsible for this presentation?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The presence of copious purulent discharge, tender preauricular lymphadenopathy, and Gram-negative intracellular diplococci strongly suggests gonococcal conjunctivitis, caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae also termed as acute blennorrhea/ acute purulent conjunctivitis/ hyperacute conjunctivitis, treated with single dose Ceftriaxone IM and oral Azithromycin or doxycycline (twice a day for 7 days).


Acute Mucopurulent Conjunctivitis:

  • M/c cause: Staphylococcus aureus
  • Symptoms:
    • Redness
    • Mucus discharge
    • Eyelids stick together, especially in the morning

[[figure-1]]

  • Treatment: Topical Antibiotics:
    • Broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g., chloramphenicol, lomefloxacin, ofloxacin, ciprofloxacin) applied 4-6 times daily.
    • Antibiotic ointment for lid application to prevent sticking and manage discharge.

Acute Purulent Conjunctivitis/ Hyperacute conjunctivitis/ Acute blennorrhoea:

  • M/c cause: Neisseria gonorrhoeae
  • Symptoms:
    • Fiery red conjunctiva (‘pink eye’)
    • Severe pain
    • Lid swelling
    • Copious purulent discharge
    • Pus seen in the fornices and margin of the lid
    • Matting of lashes with dirty yellow crust
    • Coloured halos
    • Tender preauricular lymphadenopathy

[[figure-2]]

  • Treatment: Systemic Antibiotics:
    • Single dose Ceftriaxone IM and oral Azithromycin or doxycycline (twice a day for 7 days)


Intravenous ampicillin (Option A) is not the first-line treatment for hyperacute conjunctivitis and is not commonly used.

Eye irrigation with saline (Option B) might provide temporary relief but does not address the underlying infection. Systemic antibiotics are needed to prevent complications.

Topical antibiotic drops (Option D) are generally insufficient for treating hyperacute conjunctivitis caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae; systemic antibiotics are required.

Explanation:

Giant Papillary Conjunctivitis

Definition

Specific allergic inflammation affecting the superior tarsal conjunctiva.

Etiology

  • Soft hydrophilic contact lenses
  • Protruding suture ends
  • Ocular prostheses

Underlying Mechanism

Hypersensitivity reactions (types I and IV)

Image

Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis (Option A) is characterized by seasonal symptoms, cobblestone-like papillae, limbal thickening with Horner-Trantas dots, and potential corneal involvement, unlike giant papillary conjunctivitis, which typically presents with large papillae associated with contact lens use.

Phlyctenular Conjunctivitis (Option C) shows small nodules near the limbus with localized congestion, not large papillae on the tarsal conjunctiva, as seen in giant papillary conjunctivitis.

Papillary Conjunctivitis (Option D) is a broad term and lacks the specificity of the large, polygonal papillae and pronounced symptoms seen in Giant Papillary Conjunctivitis, which is linked to contact lens use.

question: A 25-year-old woman with a history of soft contact lens use for the past 8 months presents with bilateral itching, redness, and watery discharge. Examination shows large, polygonal papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Given the seasonal pattern of symptoms, bilateral itching, watery discharge, mild conjunctival congestion, and the presence of small papillae point toward the diagnosis of allergic conjunctivitis.

Viral Conjunctivitis (Option A) typically presents with watery discharge and moderate conjunctival congestion.

  • It is often associated with follicles rather than papillae, and a seasonal pattern is less likely than that of allergic conjunctivitis.

Bacterial Conjunctivitis (Option C) is characterized by purulent discharge and marked conjunctival congestion.

  • While bacterial conjunctivitis can sometimes present with papillae, these are not usually as prominent or marked as those in allergic conjunctivitis.

Chlamydial Conjunctivitis (Option D) typically presents with mucopurulent discharge and moderate conjunctival congestion.

  • It is often associated with follicles, and papillae may or may not be present.
  • The lack of prominent papillae and specific seasonal patterns make it less likely than allergic conjunctivitis.



Reference:

Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th edition, Pages 170, 181.

Pharyngoconjunctival fever

Causative agent

Adenovirus (serotypes 3, 4, 7)

Symptoms

  • Common in children; often outbreak-related
  • Systemic: fever, sore throat, malaise
  • Ocular: redness, watering, foreign body sensation, mild photophobia

Signs

  • Follicular conjunctivitis
  • Conjunctival hyperemia, chemosis
  • Often starts in one eye → spreads to other

[[figure-1]]

Management

Supportive

  • Cold compresses
  • Lubricating drops
  • Topical antihistamines/mast cell stabilizers
  • Antibiotics only for secondary bacterial infection

Herpes simplex virus (Option A) causes unilateral follicular conjunctivitis with dendritic keratitis.

Chlamydia trachomatis (Option C) causes inclusion conjunctivitis, more chronic and associated with mucopurulent discharge.

The given clinical scenario of a sudden painless bright red patch over the sclera with normal vision points towards the diagnosis of subconjunctival hemorrhage (subconjunctival ecchymosis), often spontaneous in hypertension, resolves on its own, and aspirin/NSAIDs should be avoided.

Subconjunctival Hemorrhage (Subconjunctival Ecchymosis)

Cause

  • Rupture of small conjunctival vessels
  • Spontaneous in elderly or patients with systemic hypertension (Option 2)
  • Can follow minor trauma, straining, eye surgery, or systemic disorders

Clinical features

  • Benign and self-limiting (Option 3)
  • Vision and intraocular structures remain normal
  • Blood spreads under conjunctiva

Management

  • No specific treatment required (gradually absorbed in 1-3 weeks) (Option 1 ruled out)

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
The given clinical scenario of recurrent itching, ropy mucus discharge and habitual removal of mucus points toward mucus fishing behavior associated with Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis.

  • Recurrent bilateral allergic conjunctivitis in children/adolescents, more common in boys, especially in hot weather
  • Pathology: Papillae with eosinophils; thick mucus contributes to mucus fishing
  • Features:
    • Intense itching, burning, photophobia, lacrimation, thick ropy/mucoid discharge
    • Mucus fishing behaviour - habitual removal of mucus strands-worsens irritation.
  • Signs:
    • Palpebral form: Cobblestone papillae on upper tarsal conjunctiva
    • Limbal form: Gelatinous limbal thickening, Horner-Trantas dots
    • Mixed forms common; may develop superficial punctate keratitis, shield ulcers, keratoconus.
  • Management:
    • Avoid eye rubbing
    • Stepwise therapy: topical antihistamines, mast cell stabilizers, lubricants, NSAIDs, mild steroids, cyclosporine
    • Acetyl cysteine for mucus reduction
    • Severe cases: subtarsal steroid injection, cryotherapy, debridement, amniotic membrane.

Giant papillary conjunctivitis (Option A): Related to contact lens or prosthesis irritation, not seasonal allergic disease with ropy mucus.

Phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis (Option B): Hypersensitivity reaction with nodules, not associated with mucus fishing.

Atopic keratoconjunctivitis (Option D): Chronic allergic disease of adults, not typically a seasonal childhood disorder.

question: A young boy presents with intense ocular itching during summer, thick stringy discharge, and recurrent conjunctival inflammation. He frequently pulls mucus strands from the eye using his fingers, which worsens the irritation. Which condition is most closely related to this behavior?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
The given clinical scenario of upper tarsal follicles, superior keratitis, and scarring points toward Trachoma, a chronic cicatrizing keratoconjunctivitis, and a major historical cause of blindness in developing countries.

Causative Agent

Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes A, B, C (obligate intracellular bacterium)

Epidemiology

  • Common in dry, dusty, poor-hygiene regions
  • Begins in childhood; female preponderance due to caregiving roles
  • Spread via fingers, towels, flies attracted to ocular discharge

Clinical features

Symptoms: Mild early irritation, foreign body sensation, discharge; later photophobia, lacrimation, pain, and blurred vision.

Signs

  • Follicles mainly on upper tarsal conjunctiva (sago grain follicle)

[[figure-1]]

  • Papillary hypertrophy, early stellate scarring
  • Superior corneal involvement: punctate keratitis, trachomatous pannus.

[[figure-2]]

  • Limbal signs: Herbert pits

[[figure-3]]

  • Later: conjunctival scarring (Arlt’s line), entropion, trichiasis, corneal opacity

[[figure-4]]

Sequelae: Cicatricial changes → trichiasis, corneal abrasion, blindness; severity worsens with reinfection.

Vernal keratoconjunctivitis (Option A): Allergic disease with cobblestone papillae, eosinophils, and seasonal recurrence, not cicatricial scarring.


Xerophthalmia (Option B): Vitamin A deficiency causing dryness, Bitot spots and keratomalacia.


Phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis (Option D): Hypersensitivity nodules, not diffuse follicular cicatrizing disease.



Reference:

Parsons Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Pages 383-389.

The given clinical scenario describes active trachoma with established scarring and ongoing follicular disease.

McCallan Stages of Trachoma

Stage I (Option A ruled out)
  • Immature follicles, early keratopathy
  • Early disease, no scarring

Stage II (Option C ruled out)
  • Florid follicles, papillary hypertrophy, no scarring
  • Active follicular disease without cicatricial changes

Stage III (Option B)
  • Conjunctival scarring with active follicles
  • Persistent active infection; scarring present

Stage IV (Option D ruled out)
  • Marked scarring, no active follicles
  • Inactive cicatricial stage; follicles resolved.


Reference:

Parsons Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page 388-389.
question: A young girl from an endemic region has chronic eye discharge and redness. Examination shows multiple tarsal follicles, obvious conjunctival scarring, and trachomatous trichiasis. According to McCallan staging, which stage does this represent?

correctAnswer: C. Basal and reflex tear secretion
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The procedure demonstrated is the Schirmer test, which is used to assess aqueous tear production and is an important investigation in the evaluation of dry eye disease (keratoconjunctivitis sicca).
  • In the Schirmer I test (without topical anaesthesia), a standardised strip of Whatman filter paper is placed in the lower conjunctival fornix, typically at the junction of the middle and lateral third of the lower eyelid. The length of the wetted area is measured after 5 minutes.
  • Because topical anesthesia is not used, the test measures both basal tear secretion and reflex tear secretion. Reflex tearing occurs due to mild irritation produced by the filter paper.

Interpretation (Schirmer I):

  • >10 mm wetting in 5 minutes: Normal
  • 5-10 mm: Borderline or mild aqueous deficiency
  • <5 mm: Suggestive of severe aqueous tear deficiency, commonly seen in conditions such as Sjögren syndrome.

If topical anesthesia is instilled before the test (Basal Schirmer test), reflex tearing is minimized, allowing assessment of basal tear secretion alone.

Corneal epithelial integrity (Option A) is assessed using fluorescein staining, which highlights epithelial defects such as corneal abrasions, corneal ulcers, and punctate epithelial erosions. The Schirmer test does not evaluate the corneal surface; instead, it measures tear production.

Tear film stability (Option B) is assessed using the Tear Break-Up Time (TBUT) test. Following fluorescein instillation, the time between a complete blink and the appearance of the first dry spot on the cornea is measured. A TBUT of less than 10 seconds indicates an unstable tear film, whereas the Schirmer test evaluates aqueous tear secretion.

Meibomian gland function (Option D) is assessed by slit-lamp examination of the eyelid margins, expression of meibomian gland secretions, or meibography. Meibomian gland dysfunction leads to evaporative dry eye due to deficiency of the lipid layer of the tear film and is not assessed by the Schirmer test, which measures aqueous tear production.



Reference:
  • Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology: A Systematic Approach, 9th Edition, Page 160
  • https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK559159/
question: A 46-year-old woman presents with complaints of gritty sensation, intermittent blurring of vision, and dryness in both eyes for the past 8 months. The examination shown in the video is performed. What is the primary parameter being evaluated by this test?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Herbert’s pits are:

  • Small, shallow depressions at the limbus

  • Caused by healing of limbal follicles in trachoma

  • Considered pathognomonic of healed/previous trachoma

Pathophysiology

Chronic infection with Chlamydia trachomatis

  • Formation of limbal follicles → Follicles ulcerate → Heal by fibrosis → Leave behind depressed pits at the limbus = Herbert’s pits


Horner-Trantas spots (Option A): White, chalky dots at limbus composed of eosinophils in vernal keratoconjunctivitis, not trachoma.


Pannus (Option C): Superficial vascularization of cornea extending from the limbus, seen in active trachoma and other chronic keratitis.


Arlt’s line (Option D): Linear scar on the upper tarsal conjunctiva, seen in late scarring stage of trachoma, not at the limbus.

explanationHtml:
The most frequently observed eye symptom associated with COVID-19 is follicular conjunctivitis.

Follicular conjunctivitis typically presents with redness, swelling, and irritation of the conjunctiva, along with a follicular reaction on the palpebral conjunctiva. This condition has been reported in patients with COVID-19, and it is often associated with other symptoms of viral infection.

Ophthalmic conditions associated with COVID-19

Category

Conditions

Conjunctiva
  • Acute conjunctivitis
  • Unremitting conjunctivitis
  • Mild follicular conjunctivitis
  • Severe hemorrhagic conjunctivitis
  • Pseudomembrane formation
  • Keratoconjunctivitis
  • Kawasaki-like illness (MIS-C)

Sclera/Episclera
  • Episcleritis
  • Nodular episcleritis
  • Necrotizing anterior scleritis
  • Sectoral anterior scleritis

Anterior Chamber
  • Acute anterior uveitis
  • Reactivated idiopathic anterior uveitis

Retina and Choroid
  • Central retinal vein occlusion
  • Central retinal artery occlusion
  • Acute macular neuroretinopathy (AMN)
  • Paracentral acute middle maculopathy (PAMM)
  • Purtscher-like retinopathy
  • Retinal hemorrhages
  • Cotton wool spots
  • Dilated veins
  • Tortuous vessels
  • Multifocal choroiditis (associated with vaccine)
  • Serpiginous and ampiginous choroiditis
  • Acute retinal necrosis (due to herpes virus reactivation)
  • Retinal vasculitis
  • Retinal degeneration
  • Breakdown of blood-retinal barrier

Optic Nerve
  • Optic neuritis
  • Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder
  • Anti-myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (anti-MOG) antibodies
  • Papilledema
  • Elevated intracranial pressure (pseudotumor cerebri syndrome)

Extraocular Motility, Cranial Nerves
  • Cranial nerve III, IV, VI palsies
  • Binocular diplopia
  • Ocular cranial neuropathies
  • Postinfectious demyelinating conditions (e.g., Miller-Fisher syndrome, Guillain-Barré syndrome)
  • Ocular myasthenia gravis

Pupils
  • Mydriasis
  • Cholinergic super-sensitivity
  • Tonic pupils

Nystagmus
  • Visual disturbances (oscillopsia)
  • Viral-induced vestibular neuritis
  • Central vestibular nystagmus (associated with rhombencephalitis)

Visual Cortex
  • Acute stroke affecting posterior visual pathways
  • Homonymous visual field deficits
  • Posterior cerebral artery ischemic strokes

Orbit and Ocular Adnexa
  • Sinusitis
  • Orbital cellulitis
  • Bacterial orbital abscess
  • Invasive fungal rhino-orbital mucormycosis
  • Orbital myositis

Lacrimal System
  • Epiphora (tear overproduction)

Manifestations in Newborn Infants
  • Periorbital edema
  • Chemosis
  • Hemorrhagic conjunctivitis
  • Ciliary injection
  • Corneal edema
  • Rubeosis
  • Posterior synechiae
  • Retinopathy of prematurity
  • Vitreous hemorrhage
  • Cotton wool spots

Uveitis (Option A): While uveitis can occur in some cases of COVID-19, it is not the most frequent eye symptom. Uveitis refers to inflammation of the uveal tract (the iris, ciliary body, and choroid), and while it has been reported in some COVID-19 patients, it is less common than conjunctivitis.

Mucormycosis (Option B): This is a rare fungal infection that can occur in COVID-19 patients, particularly in those with diabetes or who are immunocompromised. It can cause serious orbital and sinus involvement, but it is not the most frequently observed eye symptom in COVID-19.

Papillary conjunctivitis (Option D): This refers to inflammation of the conjunctiva with prominent papillae (small, raised bumps) on the inner surface of the eyelids. While it can occur in various infections, it is not as commonly reported as follicular conjunctivitis in COVID-19.

question: A 30-year-old contact lens wearer presents with severe pain, redness and watery discharge from the eye. Which of the following stains is most useful for diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option A - Conjunctiva:

  • The symptoms of redness, sensitivity to light (photophobia), excessive tearing, and discomfort are characteristic of conjunctivitis, commonly known as pink eye. Conjunctivitis has been observed as a common ocular manifestation of COVID-19, with the conjunctiva being the most likely part of the eye to be affected. This is usually a mild viral conjunctivitis that resolves with symptomatic treatment.

Incorrect Options:

Uvea (Option B) is typically affected in uveitis. While uveitis can cause redness, sensitivity to light, and discomfort, it is less common to occur solely as a result of COVID-19. Also, uveitis typically presents with more severe signs upon examination, such as cells in the anterior chamber or posterior synechiae, which were not noted in this case.

Choroid (Option C) is a deeper structure within the eye and is not typically affected in viral conjunctivitis or mild ocular manifestations of COVID-19. Choroiditis would present with more severe symptoms and would be visible on specialized imaging such as fluorescein angiography.

Retina (Option D) would typically not be directly affected by COVID-19 or the symptoms presented in this patient. Retinal conditions, such as retinitis, often present with more severe visual changes, such as visual field defects or floaters, which were not reported here.



Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK556093/#:~:text=Ocular%20manifestations%20of%20COVID-19%20often%20present%20with%20conjunctivitis%2C%20which,Bacterial%20conjunctivitis
question: In a patient who has had contact with a COVID-19 patient, presenting with symptoms such as redness, sensitivity to light, excessive tearing, and overall discomfort, a thorough examination was conducted with no eye abnormality. Based on this information, which specific part of the eye is most likely to be affected in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - Preseptal cellulitis

Explanation:

  • Preseptal cellulitis is an infection of the eyelid and surrounding skin anterior to the orbital septum. It is characterized by eyelid swelling, erythema, fever, and tenderness, often following a minor trauma or spreading from a nearby infection, or spreading from a remote infection of middle ear and upper respiratory tract infection. In this case, the absence of significant ocular findings, such as chemosis or proptosis, along with the mild flu-like illness history, is more consistent with preseptal cellulitis

[[figure-1]]

Chandler’s Classification of Orbital Cellulitis

Stage

Description

Key Features

I - Preseptal cellulitis

Infection confined to the eyelid

Eyelid swelling, no ocular involvement

II - Orbital cellulitis (Option B)

Infection spreads to the orbit

Pain with eye movement, restricted mobility, no abscess formation, chemosis or proptosis

III - Subperiosteal abscess

Pus collection beneath periosteum

Localized pus, proptosis, pain on movement, swelling

IV - Orbital abscess

Pus collection within the orbital tissues

Severe proptosis, potential vision loss, risk of optic nerve damage

V - Cavernous sinus thrombosis

Spread of infection to the cavernous sinus

Bilateral eye involvement, headache, cranial nerve palsies

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical image shows a pterygium, which is a subconjunctival fibrovascular growth extending onto the cornea, most commonly nasally, and associated with chronic UV exposure.

  • Although pterygium and pinguecula share some pathological similarities, the statement in option D is incorrect because it describes histological changes seen in pinguecula, not pterygium.

In a pinguecula, there is:

  • Elastotic degeneration of collagen
  • Hyalinization of conjunctival connective tissue
  • No corneal invasion

In a pterygium, the pathology instead involves:

  • Fibrovascular proliferation
  • Abnormal expression of p53 due to UV-induced damage
  • Increased matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) and decreased TIMPs

Thus, option D does not correctly describe the condition shown (pterygium), making it the best answer.

Abnormal activity of p53 is seen in the pterygium tissue (Option A): This statement is correct. Pterygium is associated with abnormal p53 expression, which is a tumor suppressor gene that plays a role in regulating cell growth and preventing the formation of tumors.

Decreased activity of tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases is seen (Option B): This statement is correct. Pterygium is associated with an imbalance in the activity of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) and tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs), leading to excessive tissue remodeling.

Destruction of Bowman’s layer occurs when the pterygium invades the cornea (Option C): This statement is also correct as the lesion grows over the cornea and disrupts Bowman’s layer.
