The patient's symptoms of intense itching and sticky (ropy) discharge, along with the presence of hard, flat-topped papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva with a cobblestone appearance as shown in the image are characteristic of Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis (VKC).
Vernal keratoconjunctivitis (Spring catarrh):

  • It is a recurrent bilateral conjunctivitis that tends to occur with the onset of warm weather. It primarily affects young children and adolescents, particularly boys.
  • Type I & IV HSR reaction > Type IV HSR

Course

The condition typically starts in childhood and may resolve on its own over 5–10 years.

Symptoms

Burning, Itching, Photophobia (sensitivity to light), and lacrimation (excessive tearing).

Signs
  • Palpebral Form: Hypertrophied palpebral conjunctiva with a cobblestone appearance; bluish-white color; dense fibrous tissue with thickened epithelium.

[[figure-1]]

  • Limbal or Bulbar Form: Opacification at the limbus, gelatinous thickening, and Horner–Trantas dots

[[figure-2]]

Pseudogerontoxon/cupid’s bow (which resembles arcus senilis) is a grayish-white ring at the limbus seen in severe limbal vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC).

[[figure-3]]

  • Shield ulcers are a significant complication of VKC, particularly in severe cases. These microerosions typically form on the upper third of the cornea.

[[figure-4]]

  • Mixed form: Exhibits characteristics of both the tarsal (palpebral) and limbal subtypes, typically presenting in only one eye.
  • Maxwell Lyon's sign is a pseudomembrane formed due to excessive mucus deposition on the papilla resulting in cobblestone papillae.

[[figure-5]]

Histology

In the palpebral form, hypertrophied papillae are observed, rich in eosinophils and other inflammatory cells.

Treatment
  • Topical therapy:
    • Antihistamines - Levocabastine & emedastine
    • Mast cell stabilizers - Sodium cromoglicate
    • Mild steroids - Fluorometholone and loteprednol etabonate,
    • Acetylcysteine can control excess mucus.
  • Local therapy: Subtarsal steroid injections and cryotherapy for severe cases.
  • Surgical treatment: Excision of giant papillae and treatment of shield ulcers with debridement and amniotic membrane or bandage contact lens.
  • Cold compresses and tinted glasses for comfort.
  • Avoid eye rubbing

Trachoma (Option A): Sago-grain appearance of conjunctiva is seen in Trachoma.

[[figure-6]]

Phlyctenular conjunctivitis (Option C): Type of hypersensitivity reaction to endogenous antigens like bacterial antigens, staphylococcal & tuberculosis antigens. It presents as a small, white, or yellowish nodule (phlyctenule) near the limbus and conjunctival congestion.

Xerophthalmia (Option D): Xerophthalmia is a spectrum of ocular disease caused due to vitamin A deficiency. It is characterized by night blindness (earliest feature), conjunctival xerosis, Bitot’s spot, corneal xerosis, ulcer, keratomalacia.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology 9th edition, pages 181–186

Stage

Description

XN

explanationHtml:
• Pterygium is a fibrovascular growth that arises from the conjunctiva and extends onto the cornea, typically affecting the nasal side of the eye. (Option B ruled out)
  • The parts of a pterygium include: (Option C ruled out)
    • Head: The part that grows onto the cornea.
    • Neck: The transition zone between the conjunctiva and the cornea.
    • Body: The part on the conjunctiva.
  • Pterygium has progressive and regressive types, meaning it can either grow over time (progressive) or shrink back (regressive) in some cases. (Option D ruled out)
  • The rate of recurrence after surgical removal of pterygium is typically around 30-40%, not 95%. This high rate of recurrence is more common in certain settings (e.g., incomplete excision or lack of adjunctive treatments like conjunctival autografting or mitomycin C). A 95% recurrence rate is uncharacteristically high and is not the typical outcome. (Option A)

Pterygium/Surfer’s eye

Pseudopterygium

Definition

Pterygium is a triangular encroachment of vascularized granulation tissue covered by conjunctiva in the interpalpebral area.

  • Parts: Cap, head, neck, body
  • Degenerative process
  • Pterygium like lesion
  • Due to cicatrizing conjunctival inflammatory overgrowth

Aetiology

  • Common in dry, sunny climates with sandy soils
  • Ultraviolet light is a probable factor
  • Usually elderly persons
  • Seen at any age
  • Caused by
    • Trauma
    • Chronic conjunctivitis
    • Thermochemical burn

Pathology

Histology shows collagenous degenerative changes in the vascularized subepithelial stroma.

Pathogenesis

  • Degenerative subconjunctival proliferation
  • Granulation tissue proliferates as avascularized tissue encroaches on the cornea.
  • Destroys the superficial layers of the stroma and Bowman’s membrane


Symptoms

  • Frequently follows a pinguecula
  • Often bilateral
  • Usually on the nasal side
  • Impairment of vision due to:
    • Progression into the pupillary area of the cornea
    • Induced astigmatism by corneal flattening in the axis of pterygium
  • Progressive pterygium: thick and vascular
  • Regressive pterygium: thin, pale, and atrophic
  • Ceases to grow but never disappears
  • A probe can be passed under the lesion
  • Can present as inflamed pterygium
  • Non-progressive
  • Can be at any quadrant of the corneal limbus
  • Located away from the horizontal
  • Attached to the cornea due to scar tissue
  • Adhered to the adjacent lid
  • Always stationary

Signs

  • A probe cannot be passed under the lesion
  • Fusch’s spots/Islets of Vogt: small discrete whitish flecks made of pterygial epithelial cells seen in progressive pterygium and are also called the cap of the pterygium.
  • Stocker line: linear epithelial iron deposition, seen in regressive pterygium.
  • A probe can be passed under the neck.


Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 198, 199.

question: What is the most effective treatment for a patient who experiences considerable discomfort when reading text from paper or a screen, despite having normal visual acuity and other eye examination findings, except for a Schirmer's test result of 5mm?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - Excision with conjunctival autograft:

  • The most appropriate management for pterygium encroaching the pupillary area is surgical excision with conjunctival autograft.
  • This involves removing the pterygium tissue and replacing it with a graft of healthy conjunctival tissue taken from another area of the patient's own eye.
  • This procedure has been shown to have a low recurrence rate and a high success rate in preventing visual disturbance caused by the pterygium.

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Keratoplasty: Keratoplasty involves the surgical replacement of the cornea with a healthy donor cornea. Indicated for corneal opacities, bullous keratoplasty, corneal dystrophies, and keratoconus.

Option C - Observation: If the pterygium is not causing any visual disturbance, observation may be appropriate. However, if it is steadily progressing towards the pupillary area, it is likely to cause visual disturbances and should be managed surgically.

Option D - Beta-radiation: Beta-radiation therapy involves using low doses of radiation to prevent recurrence of the pterygium, not recommended.

  • Systemic antibiotics
  • Steroid Therapy
  • Supportive Therapy
  • Vitrectomy - if no improvement in 48-72 hours or if severe infection with vision reduced to hand movements close to the face
  • If blind - no perception of light - Evisceration.

Options A, C & D: Staph aureus, Strep. Pneumonia and H. influenzae are disease causing bacteria and do not form the normal conjunctival flora

question: Which of the following is the normal conjunctival flora?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Causes for Vitamin A Deficiency :

  • Decreased intake.
  • Obstructive jaundice: Defective absorption.
  • Liver cirrhosis: Reduce synthesis of RBP (retinol binding protein).
  • Severe malnutrition: Lack of amino acids for RBP synthesis.
  • Chronic nephrosis: RBP excretion through urine.

Vitamin A Deficiency Manifestations :

1. Ocular manifestations :

  • Vitamin A deficiency is the most significant preventable cause of blindness, especially in children below 5 in developing countries.
  • Early Signs:
    • Loss of sensitivity to green light.
    • Difficulty adapting to dim light.
    • Night blindness.
  • Prolonged Deficiency:
    • Xerophthalmia:
      • Dry, thick, keratinized conjunctiva and cornea. If untreated, it leads to corneal ulceration and ultimately results in blindness due to the formation of opaque scar tissue.
      • WHO grading of xerophthalmia:
      • Bitot's Spots: Grayish-white triangular plaques firmly adherent to the conjunctiva.
      • Keratomalacia: When xerophthalmia persists for a longer time, it progresses to keratomalacia (corneal softening).

XN
  • Night blindness.

X1
  • X1A: Conjunctival xerosis.
  • X1B: Bitot spots. (Option B)

X2
  • Corneal xerosis.

X3
  • X3A: Corneal ulceration, less than one-third.
  • X3B: Corneal ulceration, more than one-third.

XS
  • Corneal scar.

XF
  • Xerophthalmic fundus.

2. Immune Function:

  • Deficiency increases susceptibility to infections.
  • Infection reduces retinol-binding protein synthesis, lowering vitamin A levels and impairing immune responses.

3. Skin and Mucous Membrane Lesions:

  • Follicular Hyperkeratosis (Phrynoderma): Causes rough skin due to hyperkeratinization of the follicular epithelium.
  • Keratinizing Metaplasia: Affects respiratory, gastrointestinal, and genitourinary tracts.
  • Epithelium is atrophied.

4. Other General Manifestation :

  • Growth retardation due to defective synthesis of chondroitin sulfate.
  • Decreased protein synthesis.

Incorrect Options:

Pinguecula (Option A) is a degenerative conjunctival condition unrelated to Vitamin A deficiency.

Pterygium (Option C) is a fibrovascular growth extending from the conjunctiva onto the cornea, often caused by UV exposure rather than nutritional deficiency.

Stocker’s line (Option D) is an iron line seen in front of the advancing edge of a pterygium, also unrelated to Vitamin A deficiency.



Reference:

Harper Edition 32, Page no: 538.
question: Which of the following is associated with Vitamin A deficiency?

Explanation: Poor socioeconomic status suggests that the person is prone to develop infections. The above image is of Phlyctenular conjunctivitis

Phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis

Cause

Allergic reactions to endogenous antigens are often linked to bacterial infections such as Staphylococcus aureus (M/C/C in Western countries) or tuberculosis(M/C/C in India).

[[figure-1]]

Symptoms & signs
  • Watering, itching
  • Reflex blepharospasm (involuntary blinking)
  • Conjunctival congestion
  • Phlycten - Small, round, grayish, or yellowish nodules on the bulbar conjunctiva near the limbus.
  • Corneal involvement can lead to fascicular ulcers or ring ulcers.

Pathophysiology

Type IV hypersensitivity reaction.

Common Complications

Corneal involvement: Ulcers form on the cornea, leading to potential scarring.

Associated Conditions

Long-standing mild infections like tonsillitis or adenoiditis, and in populations with a high prevalence of tuberculosis.

Treatment

Local therapy:

  • Corticosteroids: Drops/ointment to reduce inflammation. Address underlying cause (e.g., tuberculosis).
  • Antibiotics
  • Cycloplegics: Paralyze ciliary muscle, relieve pain, and prevent complications.
  • Dark Glasses/Eye Shade: For photophobia relief.

General therapy:

  • Oral tetracycline or doxycycline is used in recurrent cases linked to Staphylococcal blepharitis.

Supportive: Dark glasses or eye shade.


Reference:

Parsons Diseases of the Eye 23rd Edition Pg.no.: 405-406
question: A young boy from a poor socioeconomic background presents with hyperemia and yellowish nodules at the limbus. What could be the likely diagnosis?

Explanation:

Herbert pits are small, depressed scars at the limbus that result from the resolution of limbal follicles seen in trachoma, representing healed follicular lesions that leave behind these characteristic pit-like depressions, a pathognomonic sign of past trachomatous infection.

Horner-Trantas spots (Option A): These are discrete white limbal dots composed of degenerated eosinophils, seen in vernal keratoconjunctivitis, and appear raised rather than pitted.

[[figure-1]]

Pannus (Option C): This refers to fibrovascular tissue growth over the superior cornea, seen in trachoma and other chronic conjunctival conditions, but is a vascularized membrane rather than a pit-like lesion.

[[figure-2]]

Corneal dystrophy (Option D): This refers to bilateral, inherited corneal opacities, unrelated to limbal follicular scarring.

[[figure-3]]

question: A patient presents to the outpatient department with the following findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
• A pterygium is a fibrovascular growth extending from the conjunctiva onto the cornea, often associated with UV exposure and chronic irritation.
  • The most common visual disturbance caused by a pterygium is astigmatism, due to its pulling effect on the cornea, leading to corneal distortion and irregular refraction.

Eye pain (Option A): Pterygium can cause irritation, foreign body sensation, and redness, but severe pain is not a primary feature. Pain occurs only if there is inflammation or ulceration.

Macular edema (Option B): Pterygium affects the cornea and conjunctiva, but it does not involve the retina or macula. Macular edema is seen in conditions like diabetic retinopathy or retinal vein occlusion.

Purulent discharge (Option C): Pterygium is a non-infectious degenerative condition, so it does not cause purulent discharge. Discharge may be seen in bacterial conjunctivitis or dacryocystitis.

Pterygium/Surfer’s eye

Pseudopterygium

Definition

Pterygium is a triangular encroachment of vascularized granulation tissue covered by conjunctiva in the interpalpebral area.

  • Parts: Cap, head, neck, body
  • Degenerative process
  • Pterygium like lesion
  • Due to cicatrizing conjunctival inflammatory overgrowth

Aetiology

  • Common in dry, sunny climates with sandy soils
  • Ultraviolet light is a probable factor
  • Usually elderly persons
  • Seen at any age
  • Caused by
    • Trauma
    • Chronic conjunctivitis
    • Thermochemical burn




Pathology

Histology shows collagenous degenerative changes in the vascularized subepithelial stroma.

Pathogenesis

  • Degenerative subconjunctival proliferation
  • Granulation tissue proliferates as avascularized tissue encroaches on the cornea.
  • Destroys the superficial layers of the stroma and Bowman’s membrane


Symptoms

  • Frequently follows a pinguecula
  • Often bilateral
  • Usually on the nasal side
  • Impairment of vision due to:
    • Progression into the pupillary area of the cornea
    • Induced astigmatism by corneal flattening in the axis of pterygium
  • Progressive pterygium: thick and vascular
  • Regressive pterygium: thin, pale, and atrophic
  • Ceases to grow but never disappears
  • A probe can be passed under the lesion
  • Can present as inflammed pterygium
  • Non-progressive
  • Can be at any quadrant of the corneal limbus
  • Located away from the horizontal
  • Attached to the cornea due to scar tissue
  • Adhered to the adjacent lid
  • Always stationary

Signs

  • A probe cannot be passed under the lesion
  • Fusch’s spots/Islets of Vogt: small discrete whitish flecks made of pterygial epithelial cells seen in progressive pterygium and are also called the cap of the pterygium.
  • Stocker line: linear epithelial iron deposition, seen in regressive pterygium.
  • A probe can be passed under the neck.

Management of pterygium:






Management

Best left alone

Medical treatment:

  • Tear substitutes for small regressive pterygium with dry eye
  • Topical steroids for associated inflammation
  • Protection from UV rays with sunglasses

Surgical excision for:

  • Progression of lesion towards the pupillary area causing excessive astigmatism and visual impairment
  • Restricted ocular movements
  • Disfiguring
  • Diplopia







Procedures
  • Bare sclera technique:
    • The pterygium is excised from the cornea and conjunctiva, leaving a bare sclera
    • Associated with a high recurrence rate
  • Autoconjunctival graft
    • A piece of limbal conjunctival tissue from the same or the other eye or
    • An amniotic membrane graft is used to cover the bare sclera
    • Sutured at the limbus to cover the defect
  • Surgical excision with lamellar keratectomy and lamellar keratoplasty for deeply infiltrating recurrent recalcitrant pterygia
  • Old methods (not used now):
    • McRaynold’s operation
    • Postoperative use of beta irradiations

Post-operative therapy and care
  • Prevent recurrence:
    • Mitomycin C 0.02% drops
    • Complications like scleral necrosis, cataracts, and iritis



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th edition, Page- 198, 199.
question: What is a common ocular finding in pterygium?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation is diagnostic of a pterygium.
  • A pterygium is a triangular fibrovascular subepithelial ingrowth of degenerative bulbar conjunctival tissue over the limbus onto the cornea.
  • Surgery is indicated because it is symptomatic (vision reduced to 6/18) and induces significant astigmatism.
  • Gold Standard: Pterygium Excision with Conjunctival Autograft (CAG).
  • Simple excision (bare sclera technique) has a very high recurrence rate (30-80%).
  • Using a limbal-conjunctival autograft covers the defect and creates a barrier, reducing the recurrence rate to < 5-10%.
  • Adjuncts (recurrent/high-risk cases):
    • Mitomycin-C or beta-irradiation
  • Deep corneal involvement:
    • Peripheral lamellar keratoplasty

Simple excision (Option A): Not recommended due to high recurrence.

Topical corticosteroids with sunglasses and Observation with lubricating eye drops (Options C & D) is appropriate for small, asymptomatic pterygia or to treat inflamed pterygia temporarily.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Pages 198-199.

The image shows ankyloblepharon, a congenital condition characterised by partial or complete fusion of the upper and lower eyelid margins by one or more bands of tissue, leading to difficulty opening the eye.

  • In hypothyroidism, patients may also exhibit Hertoghe's sign (Queen Anne's sign), characterised by loss of the lateral one-third of the eyebrows.

Poliosis (Option B): Poliosis refers to localised whitening or greying of the eyelashes or eyebrows due to loss of melanin. It is seen in conditions such as Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome, Waardenburg syndrome, and vitiligo.

[[figure-1]]

Tylosis (Option C): Tylosis is thickening and keratinisation of the eyelid margin, most commonly occurring as a complication of chronic blepharitis. It does not cause loss of eyelashes.

[[figure-2]]

Trichiasis (Option D): Trichiasis is misdirection of eyelashes toward the globe, causing ocular irritation, foreign body sensation, and corneal damage. The eyelashes are present but abnormally directed, not lost.

question: A 45-year-old female presents with bilateral ptosis that worsens throughout the day, particularly in the evening, and improves with rest. She also complains of double vision and generalized fatigue. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her symptoms?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The given clinical vignette suggests that the patient most likely has Horner’s syndrome, which can result from a Pancoast tumor at the apex of the lung.
  • This tumor can compress the sympathetic chain.

Features of Horner's syndrome:

  • Classic triad of symptoms:
    • Ptosis: Typically unilateral and not contralateral (Option B)
    • Miosis (Option A): constricted pupil
    • Ipsilateral facial anhidrosis (lack of sweating)
  • Loss of ciliospinal reflex
  • Enophthalmos

• Painful lid swelling with a visible opus point (localized yellowish spot of pus) at the base of an eyelash is characteristic of external hordeolum (stye).
  • An external hordeolum is an acute bacterial infection (usually Staphylococcus aureus) of the sebaceous glands of Zeis located at the eyelash follicle.
  • The pain is due to acute inflammation, and the pus may discharge spontaneously, relieving symptoms.

Condition

Definition & Features

Treatment

External Hordeolum (Stye)
  • Acute suppurative inflammation of a lash follicle and associated glands of Zeis or Moll.
  • Most common causative organism - Staphylococcus aureus.
  • Symptoms: Acute pain with swelling on the anterior lid margin, watering and photophobia.

[[figure-1]]
  • Hot compresses 2-3 times daily.
  • Evacuate pus by epilating involved cilia when pus point forms.
  • Rarely, surgical incision for large abscess.
  • Antibiotic eye drops and ointment.
  • Systemic anti-inflammatory and analgesics.
  • Systemic antibiotics for early infection control.
  • Identify and treat predisposing conditions in recurrent cases.

Incorrect Options:

Meibomian gland (Option B): Sebaceous glands in the tarsal plate; acute infection → internal hordeolum (pus points to conjunctival side), chronic blockage → chalazion; not at eyelash base.

Lacrimal gland (Option C): Located in the superolateral orbit; inflammation (dacryoadenitis) causes painful swelling in outer upper eyelid — not localized to eyelash follicle.

Moll gland (Option D): Modified sweat glands at eyelash follicles; infection causes less common external hordeolum (Moll type), but opus point at eyelash base is more classically due to Zeis gland infection.

Explanation:

A 3-month-old infant presenting with:

  • Photophobia
  • Watering (epiphora)

Should immediately raise suspicion for conditions causing corneal irritation or corneal pathology.

The classic differential diagnosis of photophobia + watering in an infant includes:

  • Congenital glaucoma
  • Congenital entropion
  • Congenital distichiasis
  • Corneal disorders

Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction (CNLDO) causes watering, but does not typically cause photophobia.

Congenital Nasolacrimal Duct Obstruction (CNLDO)

Failure of canalization of the nasolacrimal duct, most commonly at the valve of Hasner.

Clinical Features

  • Watering since birth
  • Mucous or mucopurulent discharge
  • Crusting of lashes
  • Regurgitation on pressure over lacrimal sac
  • Photophobia is not a typical feature because the cornea is usually normal.

Congenital Entropion (Option B): Congenital entropion causes inward turning of the eyelid. The eyelashes rub against the cornea causing corneal irritation, watering, photophobia, and blepharospasm

Congenital Glaucoma (Option C): This is one of the most important causes of photophobia and watering in infants. Classical Triad include - Epiphora (watering), photophobia, blepharospasm. Other Features are corneal edema, corneal enlargement (buphthalmos), haab striae, and increased intraocular pressure

Congenital Distichiasis (Option D): Distichiasis refers to an additional row of eyelashes arising from the meibomian gland orifices. Aberrant lashes rub against the cornea leading to watering, photophobia, foreign body sensation, and corneal irritation

Ptosis in Horner syndrome is due to the paralysis of the Müller's muscle, a smooth muscle responsible for a minor portion of upper eyelid retraction.

Müller's (Superior Tarsal) Muscle

  • Smooth muscle located beneath the levator palpebrae superioris.
  • Provides about 1-2 mm of additional upper eyelid elevation.
  • Innervated by the sympathetic nervous system.

Horner's Syndrome

Clinical Features:

  • Miosis (due to uninhibited actions of iris sphincters
  • Ptosis: The ptosis is mild because it is the Müller’s muscle that is hampered in function.
  • Enophthalmos
  • Anhidrosis
  • Loss of Cilio-spinal reflex

Levator aponeurosis (Option B): The levator aponeurosis is the tendon of the levator palpebrae superioris. Defects cause aponeurotic ptosis, not Horner syndrome.

Horner muscle (Option C): No recognised eyelid muscle by this name.

Orbicularis oculi (Option D): Innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII). Responsible for eyelid closure, not eyelid elevation.

Correct Option C - Limited abduction:

  • Limited abduction (inability to move the eye outward) is not a feature of oculomotor nerve palsy.
  • This movement is controlled by the lateral rectus muscle, which is innervated by the abducens nerve (cranial nerve VI).

Incorrect Options:

Option A, B, and D: .

    • Ptosis: Drooping of the upper eyelid due to paralysis of the levator palpebrae superioris muscle.
    • Exotropia: Outward deviation of the eye because the medial rectus muscle (which normally pulls the eye inward) is paralyzed.
    • Dilated pupil: Also known as mydriasis, this occurs because the oculomotor nerve controls the constrictor pupillae muscle, and its dysfunction leads to unopposed action of the dilator pupillae muscle.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

A recurrent chalazion, especially in an elderly patient, should always raise suspicion for sebaceous gland carcinoma (SGC), one of the most important eyelid malignancies because it frequently masquerades as benign inflammatory conditions.

  • It often mimics a recurrent chalazion, especially in older adults.
  • Any chalazion that recurs or fails to resolve after standard treatment should raise suspicion for sebaceous carcinoma.
  • Early diagnosis is important because it is locally aggressive and can metastasize.

Sebaceous Gland Carcinoma (SGC)

  • Arises from:
    • Meibomian glands (most common)
    • Glands of Zeis
    • Sebaceous glands of the caruncle
  • Usually occurs in elderly patients.
  • More common in the upper eyelid due to the higher number of meibomian glands.
  • Yellowish material within the tumour is highly suggestive of SGC.

Presentation:

  1. Nodular SGC presents as a discrete, hard nodule, most commonly within the upper tarsal plate and may exhibit yellow discoloration due to the presence of lipid; it can be mistaken for a chalazion.
  2. Spreading SGC infiltrates into the dermis and causes a diffuse thickening of the lid margin, often with eyelash distortion and loss and can be mistaken for blepharitis.



Squamous cell carcinoma (Option B): Usually presents as a painless, slowly enlarging ulcerated or keratinized lesion or indurated plaque, Not as a recurrent chalazion.

Basal cell carcinoma (Option C): Common eyelid malignancy; presents as pearly nodules with telangiectasia, rarely mimicking chalazion.

Kaposi’s sarcoma (Option D) : Typically occurs in immunocompromised patients (HIV/AIDS) as violaceous plaques or nodules, not chalazion-like lesions.



Reference:

Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Pages 53, 54.

Explanation:

  • The presence of a painless, firm nodule in the upper eyelid that grows away from the lid margin is characteristic of a chalazion.
  • It is typically painless but can cause discomfort or cosmetic concerns if it becomes large.

Chalazion

  • A chalazion is a painless bump on the eyelid caused by blocked oil glands.
  • It is a lipogranulomatous inflammation of the meibomian gland
  • It can present as painless swelling on the lid.

Clinical Features

  • Painless swelling of the eyelid
  • Firm, localized nodule
  • More common in the upper eyelid (greater number of Meibomian glands)
  • Lesion points towards the conjunctival side (away from the lid margin)
  • Slowly enlarging
  • Overlying skin is freely mobile
  • Large lesions may induce astigmatism by pressing on the cornea

Treatment:

  • Antibiotics in case of infection
  • Warm compresses and lid hygiene in early cases
  • Intralesional steroid injection (selected cases)
  • Incision and curettage
  • It should always be a vertical incision.
  • If the horizontal incision is given, it can damage the ducts
  • Intralesional injection of TA (Triamcinolone acetonide)

Stye (Hordeolum Externum) (Option A)

  • Acute staphylococcal infection of the glands of Zeis or Moll
  • Painful, tender swelling
  • Points towards the lid margin
  • Associated with redness and inflammation

Entropion (Option B)

  • Inward turning of the eyelid margin
  • Causes irritation, watering, and trichiasis
  • Not a nodular lesion

Blepharitis (Option D)

  • Chronic inflammation of the eyelid margins
  • Presents with itching, crusting, burning, and redness
  • Does not produce a solitary firm nodule
Feature Chalazion Stye (Hordeolum)
Cause Meibomian gland blockage Acute bacterial infection
Pain Painless Painful
Consistency Firm Tender
Course Chronic Acute
Direction Away from lid margin Towards lid margin

Type

explanationHtml:
Explanation

  • Pleomorphic adenoma (benign mixed tumor) is the most frequently occurring tumor of the lacrimal gland.
  • It is typically benign, slow-growing, and presents as a painless, firm mass in the superotemporal orbit.

Pleomorphic Adenoma (Benign Mixed Tumor)

Pleomorphic adenoma is the most common epithelial tumor and the most common primary tumor of the lacrimal gland overall.

Pathology

  • Benign mixed tumor composed of:
    • Epithelial elements
    • Myoepithelial elements
    • Mesenchymal (stromal) components

Clinical Features

  • Age: Usually 30-50 years
  • Slow-growing painless mass
  • Progressive unilateral proptosis
  • Inferonasal displacement of the globe
  • Fullness in the superotemporal orbit
  • Diplopia may occur in large tumors

Imaging

  • Well-circumscribed lacrimal gland mass
  • Smooth expansion of the lacrimal fossa
  • No bony destruction

Treatment

  • Complete surgical excision with intact capsule is essential to prevent recurrence or malignant transformation.
  • Biopsy is generally avoided because rupture of the capsule increases the risk of recurrence and malignant transformation

Adenoid Cystic Carcinoma (Option A)

  • Most common malignant epithelial tumor of the lacrimal gland
  • Presents with:
    • Pain (due to perineural invasion)
    • Rapid progression
    • Proptosis
    • Diplopia
  • May cause bony destruction on imaging

Lymphoma (Option B)

  • Common orbital tumor in older adults
  • Presents as a painless "salmon-patch" conjunctival lesion or orbital mass
  • Not the most common lacrimal gland tumor overall

Mucoepidermoid Carcinoma (Option D)

  • Rare malignant epithelial tumor
  • Much less common than pleomorphic adenoma and adenoid cystic carcinoma

Lacrimal Gland Tumors

Tumors of the lacrimal gland are classified into:

  • Epithelial tumors
    • Benign: Pleomorphic adenoma (most common)
    • Malignant: Adenoid cystic carcinoma (most common malignant) > Mucoepidermoid carcinoma
  • Lymphoid tumors
  • Inflammatory lesions



Reference:
  1. Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Pages 140, 144.
  2. Parsons Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Pages 424-427.

question: A 50-year-old male presented to the ophthalmology clinic with complaints of difficulty in reading newspapers and books. Which among the following statements is inappropriate regarding the management of this patient?

correctAnswer: A. The patient has a reduced amplitude of accommodation B) The patient's far point is at infinity C) The patient has a myopic refractive error D) The patient’s near point has moved closer
explanationHtml:
• The amplitude of accommodation refers to the ability of the eye to focus on objects at different distances, specifically the difference between the near point and far point.
  • As individuals age, the amplitude of accommodation naturally decreases, resulting in difficulty focusing on nearby objects (presbyopia). This is likely the cause of the patient's difficulty reading up close.

Changes related to accommodation:

Far Point (Punctum Remotum)
  • Emmetropic eye - the far point is at infinity (Option B)
  • Hypermetropic eye - behind the eye
  • Myopic eye - in front of the eye

Near Point (Punctum Proximum)
  • Increases with age (Option D)

Range of Accommodation
  • The distance between the far point and the near point

Amplitude of Accommodation
  • The difference in dioptric power needed to focus between the near point (P) and the far point (R).
  • Expressed as A = P - R
  • The amplitude of accommodation decreases with age (Option A)

Explanation:

This is a case of with-the-rule astigmatism, in which a concave cylindrical lens at 180° or a convex cylindrical lens at 90° is used for correction

With-the-Rule Astigmatism (WTR)

Against-the-Rule Astigmatism (ATR)
  • The vertical meridian is more curved than the horizontal.
  • Correction requires a concave cylindrical lens at 180° or a convex cylindrical lens at 90°.
  • It is called "with-the-rule" because the vertical meridian is normally more convex than the horizontal due to eyelid pressure.
  • The horizontal meridian is more curved than the vertical meridian.
  • Correction requires a convex cylindrical lens at 180° or a concave cylindrical lens at 90°.

Astigmatism is classified based on where the two principal meridians focus:

question: Snellen chart is used to assess which of the following?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In a mature cataract, the posterior lens surface is obscured; therefore, the 4th image is absent.

  • Mature Cataract Effect: Total opacification of the lens cortex blocks light from passing backward.
  • Posterior Obscuration: Light cannot reach or bounce off the rear lens surface.
  • Resulting Absence: The fourth Purkinje image is completely eliminated.

Purkinje images: Reflections of light from ocular surfaces:

  • First image (Option A ruled out):
    • From the anterior corneal surface
    • Brightest reflection due to the air-cornea interface
  • Second image (Option B ruled out):
    • From the posterior corneal surface
    • Very faint and closely overlapped with the first image
  • Third image (Option C ruled out):
    • From the anterior lens surface
    • Largest image is due to the greater radius of curvature
    • Absent in aphakia
  • Fourth image (Option D):
    • From the posterior lens surface
    • Only real and inverted Purkinje image
    • Absent in aphakia and in mature cataract (clinically significant loss).

question: Which of the following is the most sensitive test for both congenital and acquired colour vision defects?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Optic neuritis, often associated with multiple sclerosis, commonly affects the optic nerve, leading to disturbances in vision, including red-green color vision defect.

Kollner’s Rule (for acquired color defects)

  • Optic nerve lesions → Red-Green defect (except Glaucoma → Blue-Yellow)

  • Retinal lesions → Blue-Yellow defect (except Stargardt’s disease → Red-Green)

Retinal vein occlusion (Option A) typically causes sudden vision loss, often associated with retinal hemorrhages, but does not cause a specific color vision defect in isolation.

Diabetic retinopathy (Option C) causes gradual vision loss due to retinal changes (like microaneurysms, hemorrhages, and edema) but does not typically present with acute color vision defects like those seen in optic neuritis.

Macular degeneration (Option D) primarily affects central vision and may cause difficulty with reading or recognizing faces but does not typically cause red-green color vision defects.

question: A 40-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of painful vision loss in her right eye. She has a history of multiple sclerosis. On examination, her visual acuity is 20/30 in the right eye, and a RAPD is noted. She reports difficulty distinguishing red and green colors in the right eye, but her left eye is normal on color vision testing. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her acquired color blindness?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Optic neuritis is an inflammatory demyelinating disorder of the optic nerve and is strongly associated with multiple sclerosis.

  • It classically presents with acute painful unilateral vision loss, RAPD, and acquired red-green dyschromatopsia (red desaturation).

Köllner's rule states that:

  • Optic nerve diseases typically produce red-green color vision defects (an important exception is glaucoma, which more commonly causes blue-yellow defects).
  • Retinal diseases usually produce blue-yellow color vision defects, although exceptions such as Stargardt disease may cause red-green defects.

Retinal vein occlusion (Option A) causes sudden painless visual loss with characteristic retinal haemorrhages and venous dilatation. It is not typically associated with isolated red-green dyschromatopsia as seen in optic neuritis.

Diabetic retinopathy (Option C) causes progressive visual impairment due to retinal microvascular disease. Although advanced macular involvement may affect colour vision, it does not typically present with acute painful vision loss, RAPD, and red-green dyschromatopsia.

Macular degeneration (Option D) primarily causes central visual loss and impaired colour discrimination due to macular dysfunction but is not associated with painful vision loss or RAPD, which are characteristic of optic neuritis.



Reference:
  1. Myron Yanoff and Duker’s textbook of ophthalmology, 6th Edition, Pages 625, 811, 834, 842, 934, 942

question: A 55-year-old male presents with complaints of difficulty driving at night and reading in dim light, despite having normal visual acuity during his eye exam. He underwent cataract surgery six months ago but still experiences these visual issues. Which of the following tests is most appropriate to assess his current visual problem?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The pinhole test reduces the amount of light scattering in the eye and sharpens vision by narrowing the beam of light entering the pupil.
  • An improvement in vision suggests a refractive error, such as myopia or astigmatism, that can be corrected with lenses.
    • Standard pinhole size: 1mm to 1.25mm

Cataracts (Option A): They cloud the lens, but using a pinhole does not typically improve vision, as the issue is related to lens opacification.

Optic nerve damage (Option C): This condition, such as optic neuropathy, does not improve with the pinhole, as the issue is with the nerve, not light entering the eye.

Macular degeneration (Option D): The visual acuity is unlikely to improve with a pinhole and may even decrease since the underlying problem is retinal damage, not a refractive error.

Explanation:

Seeing two red lights and three green lights on Worth's Four Dot Test indicates the presence of diplopia (double vision), where the patient perceives two distinct images due to misalignment.

Worth’s Four Dot test

Procedure:

  • The patient wears a red lens on the right eye and a green lens on the left eye.
  • They are shown a box with four lights: one red, two green, and one white.
  • The patient is asked how many lights they see.

Results:

  • All four lights: BSV (binocular single vision). (Option A ruled out)
  • All four lights with manifest squint: Harmonious ARC (anomalous retinal correspondence).
  • Two red lights: Right eye suppression. (Option C ruled out)
  • Three green lights: Left eye suppression. (Option B ruled out)
  • Alternating red and green lights: Alternating suppression.
  • Two red and three green lights: Diplopia (double vision).

[[figure-1]]

To calculate the refractive power along the 90° meridian:

  • Sphere (+2.00 D): This is the baseline power applied equally in all meridians.

  • Cylinder (–1.50 D, Axis 90°): The axis tells us the meridian with no cylinder effect.

    • At 90° (axis meridian) → only the sphere acts.

    • At 180° (perpendicular meridian) → sphere + cylinder = +2.00 + (–1.50) = +0.50 D.

  • So:

    • Power along 90° meridian = +2.00 D (Option A)

    • Power along 180° meridian = +0.50 D

Regular Astigmatism:

Type

Description

With-the-Rule (WTR)

The vertical meridian has greater curvature than the horizontal meridian. (Option A ruled out)

Against-the-Rule (ATR)

The horizontal meridian is more curved than the vertical meridian.

Principal meridians are at oblique angles (e.g., 45° and 135°), still perpendicular to each other.

Principal meridians are not perpendicular to each other (e.g., 30° and 100°). (Option D ruled out)

I. Surgical and Lens-Based Treatments for Presbyopia:

Treatment

Description

Can offer benefits for presbyopia.

Primarily used for hyperopia; results may not be permanent. (Option C ruled out)

II. Emerging and Experimental Treatments for Presbyopia:

Treatment

Description

Advantages

Limitations

Laser-Induced monovision

Uses LASIK or PRK to reshape one eye for near vision while keeping the other for distance, reducing the need for glasses or contacts.
  • Less need for glasses or contacts for both near and distant vision.
  • Vision correction tailored to individual needs.
  • Rapid visual recovery post-procedure.
  • Touch-ups can maintain optimal vision if needed.
  • Difficulty adjusting, leading to imbalance or discomfort.
  • Impaired spatial judgment, affecting activities like driving.
  • Less clarity in distance or near vision.
  • Further near vision deterioration with presbyopia, requires additional correction.

Corneal Multifocality

Laser procedures to reshape the cornea to create a multifocal effect.

Potential to address presbyopia without lens replacement.

(Option D ruled out)

Experimental; still in development.

Alters the sclera to restore accommodation.

Aims to restore accommodation.

Inconsistent results; less popular.

Intracorneal Inlays

Small devices are inserted into the cornea to correct presbyopia.

Can significantly benefit presbyopia.

Issues with biocompatibility; potential complications.

Laser Modification of the Natural Lens

Femtosecond lasers modify the natural lens's elasticity to restore accommodation.

An experimental approach aiming to restore natural focus.

Remains experimental; not widely available.

Type

Description

Functional Benefits

Explanation:

  • For effective occlusion therapy in treating amblyopia, it is typically recommended to patch the stronger eye for 4-6 hours per day as per ‘Amblyopia Treatment Study’.
  • This duration helps stimulate the weaker eye (amblyopic eye) and encourages improvement in its visual acuity.

Occlusion therapy:

  • Occlusion of the sound (normal) eye to force use of amblyopic eye is the main stay in the treatment of amblyopia
  • Full-time occlusion: Up to 2 years, the occlusion should be done in 2:1, i.e. 2 days in sound eye and one day in amblyopic eye; at the age of 3 years, 3:1; at the age of 4 years, 4:1; At the age of 5 years, 5:1; and after the age of 6 years 6:1.
  • Part-time occlusion: 4-6 hours/day, as shown by Amblyopia Treatment Study (ATS), and is as effective as full-time occlusion.
  • Maintenance occlusion: After vision equalization, part-time occlusion continues until at least 8 years of age.
  • Ensure no media opacity or refractive errors before starting occlusion therapy.

Type

Cause

Key Features

Strabismic Amblyopia (Option A ruled out)

The brain suppresses input from one eye due to constant squint (strabismus).

Common cause; underdevelopment of vision in the deviated eye.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Duochrome Test

  • Refines the spherical component of the prescription
  • The patient views red and green letters to check for chromatic aberration.
    • Individuals with myopia (nearsightedness) tend to see the red letters (longer wavelength) more clearly.
    • Conversely, individuals with hyperopia (farsightedness) would generally see the green letters (shorter wavelength) more clearly.
    • Both clear: Emmetropia.
  • The longer wavelength (red) is refracted less than the shorter (green).

[[figure-1]]

Hyperopia (Option A): These patients would see the Green letters more clearly because their eye is "too weak," pushing the green focus point closer to the retina.


Astigmatism (Option C): While astigmatism affects clarity, the duochrome test is specifically used to fine-tune the spherical component of a prescription, not the cylinder (astigmatism).


Presbyopia (Option D): This is an age-related loss of accommodation (near-focusing power). While it affects vision, the duochrome test is used to measure the refractive state of the eye at a distance.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, John F. Salmon, 10th Edition, Page 2
question: A 38-year-old patient presents for an eye examination. During the duochrome test, the patient reports that they can see the red letters more clearly than the green letters. What is the most likely refractive error for this patient?

correctAnswer: A. -3.00 D sphere -1.00 D cylinder at 180°
explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: A) -3.00 D sphere -1.00 D cylinder at 180°

Explanation:

  • -3.00 D sphere -1.00 D cylinder at 180° is the transposed spectacle prescription.

Transposition Process:

  1. Calculate the New Spherical Value:
    • Formula: New Spherical = Original Spherical + Cylinder
    • Calculation: -4.00 D sphere + 1.00 D cylinder
    • Result: -4.00 + 1.00 = -3.00 D sphere
  2. Change the Sign of the Cylinder:
    • Original Cylinder Value: +1.00 D
    • Transposed Cylinder Value: -1.00 D
  3. Adjust the Axis of the Cylinder:
    • Original Axis: 90°
    • Adjustment: Add 90° to the original axis
    • Calculation: 90° + 90° = 180°

Transposed Prescription:

  • New Spherical Value: -3.00 D
  • New Cylinder Value: -1.00 D
  • New Axis: 180°

Correct Transposed Prescription: -3.00 D sphere -1.00 D cylinder at 180°

explanationHtml:
• The prescription given is -1D spherical and -2D cylindrical at 180 degrees.
    • The spherical component (-1D) indicates a myopic refractive error.
    • The cylindrical component (-2D) at 180 degrees indicates astigmatism with the steepest curvature along the 180-degree axis.

In with-the-rule astigmatism, the steepest curvature (and therefore the highest cylinder value) is along the vertical axis (90 degrees), and the flatter axis is horizontal (0 or 180 degrees). Since the cylinder is placed at 180 degrees and the patient has a more negative cylindrical value at this axis, it indicates with-the-rule astigmatism.

With-the-Rule Astigmatism (WTR)

Against-the-Rule Astigmatism (ATR)
  • The vertical meridian is more curved than the horizontal.

  • Correction requires a concave cylindrical lens at 180° ± 20° or a convex cylindrical lens at 90° ± 20°.

  • It is called "with-the-rule" because the vertical meridian is normally more convex than the horizontal due to eyelid pressure.
  • The horizontal meridian is more curved than the vertical meridian.

  • Correction requires a convex cylindrical lens at 180° ± 20° or a concave cylindrical lens at 90° ± 20°.

Against the rule astigmatism (Option B): This occurs when the steepest curvature is along the horizontal axis (0 or 180 degrees) and the flatter axis is vertical (90 degrees), which is not the case here.

Simple astigmatism (Option C): This refers to astigmatism where one of the meridians has no refractive error (i.e., it's either emmetropic or has no cylinder correction), but this patient has both spherical and cylindrical components.

Mixed astigmatism (Option D): This occurs when one axis has a myopic refractive error and the other has a hypermetropic refractive error. In this case, the prescription is purely myopic in both axes.

Improvement in visual acuity with a pinhole is suggestive of a refractive error. Among the given options, Irregular astigmatism is the only refractive error. The pinhole test reduces the amount of light scattering in the eye and sharpens vision by narrowing the beam of light entering the pupil.

Pinhole and Stenopeic slit tests:

Pinhole Test

Stenopeic Slit Test

Mechanism

Uses a small opaque disc with holes to reduce retinal blur and improve visual acuity in refractive errors up to 4D.

Clinical Applications

question: The probable cause for a patient with a corneal scar having a visual acuity of 6/36, which improves to 6/18 with a pinhole, is most likely due to...

explanationHtml:
• Visual acuity of 6/6 means the patient has normal visual acuity, which is the ability to see clearly at a distance of 6 meters what should normally be seen at that distance.
  • The smallest angle at which the eye can differentiate two points is referred to as the angular resolution of the eye. For a person with normal vision (6/6), this is approximately 1 minute of arc per line on the Snellen chart.
  • However, the smallest angular separation that the human eye can typically distinguish under optimal conditions is 5 minutes of arc. This corresponds to the smallest angle at which a person with normal vision can resolve two separate points as distinct.
  • Normal visual acuity (6/6) corresponds to a subtended angle of 5 minutes of arc.

Snellen’s chart
  • Measures visual acuity by assessing the eye's ability to distinguish details or separate points.

[[figure-1]]

  • Rows of decreasing-sized letters fit within squares. Each letter subtends an angle of 5 minutes, and the lines forming letters subtend 1 minute of arc.

[[figure-2]]

Visual Acuity Notation
  • Snellen Fraction: Denoted as a fraction, with the numerator being 6 meters and the denominator indicating the distance at which normal vision reads the same letter (e.g., 6/18 means the patient reads at 6 meters what normal vision reads at 18 meters).
  • Metric/Imperial: 6/6 = 20/20 vision.
  • Decimal Acuity: 6/6 equals 1.0 decimal acuity.

Testing Procedure

The patient is positioned 6 meters from the chart, and each eye is tested individually, starting with the right eye. The patient reads the smallest visible letter.

Limitations
  • Refractive Errors: Primarily measures uncorrected vision. Pinhole tests help detect refractive errors that can be corrected with lenses.
  • Subjectivity: Dependent on patient literacy, language, and cognitive ability.
  • Scope: Assesses only visual acuity, not contrast sensitivity, color vision, or peripheral vision.

15 minutes of arc (Option A): This is too large an angle for normal visual acuity. It corresponds to a less sharp visual resolution.

10 minutes of arc (Option C): This is also larger than the typical 5 minutes of arc resolution of normal vision.

20 minutes of arc (Option D): This is even larger and would correspond to a more impaired level of visual acuity.



Reference:
  1. Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, John F. Salmon, 10th Edition, Page 2-3
  2. Myron Yanoff and Duker’s Textbook of Ophthalmology, 6th Edition, Page 35

explanationHtml:
• Myopia=shortsightedness- refractive error where parallel rays of light from distant objects focus in front of the retina when the eye's accommodation is relaxed.
  • Index myopia is a condition that often occurs in older individuals, typically associated with age-related changes in the lens. As we age, the lens of the eye becomes denser and less flexible, which can lead to myopia (nearsightedness) in some cases.
  • In index myopia, the refractive index of the lens increases, causing a shift in the focal point of the eye, making it easier for a person to focus on nearby objects, like reading a newspaper, without the aid of reading glasses. This would explain why the 70-year-old patient, who had been using presbyopia glasses (for near vision), is now able to read comfortably without them.

Type of Myopia

Cause

Axial Myopia

Increase in the anteroposterior length of the eyeball (most common form).

Curvatural Myopia

Increased curvature of the cornea, lens, or both.

Positional Myopia

Anterior placement of the crystalline lens in the eye.

Index Myopia

Increase in the refractive index of the crystalline lens, often due to nuclear sclerosis.

Myopia due to Excessive Accommodation

Caused by spasm of accommodation, leading to excessive focusing power.

Clinical features

  • Asthenopic symptoms
  • Half-shutting of eyes for better clarity
  • Prominent eyeball.
  • Prominent, large, and somewhat sluggishly reacting pupils.
  • Slightly deeper anterior chamber.
  • Normal fundus; rarely a temporal myopic crescent may be seen.

Treatment
  • Prescription of appropriate concave lenses
  • Surgical Treatment

Index hypermetropia (Option B): This would cause the opposite effect of index myopia. In this condition, the lens of the eye becomes more hypermetropic (farsighted), making near objects harder to focus on, which would make reading more difficult, not easier. Therefore, this is not consistent with the patient's improvement in near vision.

Presbyopia (Option C): This condition is a normal aging process that causes the loss of accommodation (the ability to focus on near objects). Presbyopia usually results in difficulty reading without corrective lenses (reading glasses). If the patient no longer needs glasses for reading, it is unlikely that they simply have presbyopia. The improvement in near vision suggests a different mechanism, such as index myopia.

None of the above (Option D): This option is incorrect because index myopia is a plausible explanation for the patient's improvement in near vision.



Reference:
  • Myron Yanoff and Duker’s textbook of ophthalmology, 6th edition, Page no: 28-30
  • Defining and Classifying Myopia
question: What is the probable medical condition for a 70-year-old individual who has relied on presbyopia glasses but can now comfortably read the newspaper without them?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Myopia = shortsightedness- refractive error where parallel rays of light from distant objects focus in front of the retina when the eye's accommodation is relaxed.
  • Index myopia is a condition that often occurs in older individuals, typically associated with age-related changes in the lens. As we age, the lens of the eye becomes denser and less flexible, which can lead to myopia (nearsightedness) in some cases.
  • The patient has reduced distant vision (a hallmark of myopia) but no longer needs glasses for near vision, which suggests that the lens has become more myopic (thicker or more curved) and is compensating for the near vision loss that typically occurs with presbyopia.
  • Index myopia is usually caused by the increase in refractive index of the lens with age, making it more myopic, particularly for distance vision.

Type of Myopia

Cause

Axial Myopia

Increase in the anteroposterior length of the eyeball (most common form).

Curvatural Myopia

Increased curvature of the cornea, lens, or both.

Positional Myopia

Anterior placement of the crystalline lens in the eye.

Index Myopia

Increase in the refractive index of the crystalline lens, often due to nuclear sclerosis.

Myopia due to Excessive Accommodation

Caused by spasm of accommodation, leading to excessive focusing power.

Clinical features

  • Asthenopic symptoms
  • Half-shutting of eyes for better clarity
  • Prominent eyeball.
  • Prominent, large, and somewhat sluggishly reacting pupils.
  • Slightly deeper anterior chamber.
  • Normal fundus; rarely a temporal myopic crescent may be seen.

Treatment
  • Prescription of appropriate concave lenses
  • Surgical Treatment

Incorrect Options:

Axial myopia (Option B): Caused by an elongated eyeball. This typically leads to myopia from birth or early in life and doesn’t relate to the lens changes seen with aging.

Curvatural myopia (Option C): Caused by a change in the curvature of the cornea, which affects the focusing power of the eye. It’s not related to the age-related changes in the lens.

Positional myopia (Option D): Refers to a refractive error caused by the position of the eye or the viewing distance (e.g., looking through different parts of the lens or an unusual gaze position). It's not linked to aging lens changes like index myopia.



Reference:
  1. Myron Yanoff and Duker’s textbook of ophthalmology, 6th edition, Page no: 28-30
  2. Defining and Classifying Myopia
question: What is the term used to describe the refractive error seen in the ocular examination image of a 60-year-old patient who has complained of reduced distant vision, but no longer requires spectacles for near vision?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Astigmatism is a refractive error caused by an irregular shape of the cornea or lens, leading to blurred or distorted vision. This results in multiple focal points instead of a single point of focus on the retina.
  • The image shows irregular, blurry distorted vision or varying focal points and is typically associated with astigmatism, where light entering the eye is refracted unevenly.

Astigmatism

  • A refractive error where the eye's refraction varies across different meridians.
  • As a result, light rays entering the eye do not converge to a single point, instead form focal lines.

[[figure-1]]

Regular Astigmatism
  • Refractive power changes uniformly from one meridian to another. There are 2 principal meridians.
    • Oblique Astigmatism- two principal meridians are not horizontal and vertical but are at right angles to each other (e.g., 45° and 135°).
    • Bioblique Astigmatism- two principal meridians are not at right angles to each other (e.g., one at 30° and the other at 100°).

Irregular Astigmatism
  • Irregular change in refractive power in different meridians, with multiple meridians that do not admit geometrical analysis

Incorrect Options:

Presbyopia (Option A): This is an age-related condition where the eye's ability to focus on near objects decreases, typically around age 40. It causes difficulty in reading or seeing close objects, but it's not associated with distorted vision like astigmatism.

Hypermetropia (Option C) (Farsightedness): In hypermetropia, distant objects are seen clearly, but near objects appear blurry. This is due to a shorter eyeball or less curved cornea, not irregular refraction.

Myopia (Option D) (Nearsightedness): In myopia, nearby objects are seen clearly, but distant objects appear blurry, typically due to a longer eyeball or steeper cornea. It does not cause distorted vision as seen in astigmatism.



Reference:
  1. Myron Yanoff and Duker’s textbook of ophthalmology, 6th edition, Page no: 31
  2. Astigmatism

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Radial Keratotomy (RK) involves making radial incisions in the cornea to flatten it and correct myopia. It is no longer recommended due to its unstable results and the risk of complications, especially in young, active individuals.

For a 21-year-old boxer, RK is contraindicated because it compromises the structural integrity of the cornea, increasing the risk of corneal weakening and potential rupture due to trauma, which is a significant concern in contact sports.

Refractive surgeries for myopia

Incisional Method

Radial Keratotomy (RK)
  • Involves radial cuts in the cornea to flatten it, correcting myopia.
  • Used for low to moderate myopia (2-6 D).
  • No longer recommended due to the advent of safer procedures like LASIK.

Newer Methods

Photorefractive Keratectomy (PRK)

(Option B ruled out)
  • It uses an excimer laser to reshape the cornea by removing a thin corneal layer.
  • Suitable for correcting myopia up to -6 D.

Refractive Lenticule Extraction (SMILE):

(Option D ruled out)
  • A minimally invasive laser procedure where a small lenticule is removed to reshape the cornea.
  • Effective for myopia up to -10 D, with or without astigmatism.

Intercorneal Rings (ICR):
  • Rings are inserted into the cornea to flatten it and reduce refractive power.
  • Results can be unpredictable, with risks such as corneal inflammation, so is not recommended

Orthokeratology
  • A non-surgical and reversible method involving rigid contact lenses worn overnight to reshape the cornea.
  • Corrects myopia up to -5 D temporarily.

High Myopia Solutions

Clear Lens Extraction
  • Removal of the natural lens (without cloudiness) to correct very high myopia (-16 D to -18 D).
  • Less common now due to risks like retinal detachment.

Phakic Intraocular Lens (IOL) Implantation
  • Implantable lens placed without removing the natural lens.
  • Best for myopia exceeding -8 D, especially in patients unsuitable for laser surgery.

PRK, LASIK, and SMILE are safer alternatives for myopia correction and are well-suited for active individuals like athletes. These methods involve laser reshaping of the cornea with less risk of trauma-related complications than RK.



Reference:

Myron Yanoff and Duker’s textbook of ophthalmology, 6th edition, Page no: 284-286
question: A 21 year old boxer wanted to improve the vision . Which of the following surgery is contraindicated?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option C - Astigmatism:

Explanation:

  • The image of Sturm’s conoid demonstrates that parallel light rays do not converge to a single focal point, but rather form two focal lines at different distances due to unequal refractive power in different meridians of the cornea or lens.
  • This optical phenomenon is characteristic of astigmatism, where light rays along one meridian focus in front of the retina while rays along the perpendicular meridian focus either behind or at a different point.
  • Astigmatism causes blurred or distorted vision and eye strain (asthenopia), especially with prolonged near tasks.

Sturm’s conoid in Astigmatism:

  1. Light rays from an object pass through two principal meridians with different curvatures.
  2. Each meridian has its own focal length → creates two focal lines (not a single point).
  3. The area between these two focal lines is called the Sturm’s conoid.
  4. The best vision is achieved at the circle of least confusion, located between the two focal lines.

[[figure-1]]

Incorrect Options:

  • Amblyopia (Option A): Reduced vision in one or both eyes due to abnormal visual development in childhood; unrelated to optical focusing errors like those shown in Sturm’s conoid.
  • Hypermetropia (Option B): Farsightedness due to the eye being too short or the cornea too flat, causing light to focus behind the retina; it produces a single focal point (not two) and does not show Sturm’s conoid.
  • Presbyopia (Option D): Age-related loss of accommodation due to decreased lens elasticity; affects near vision but does not produce two focal lines in different meridians.

Amblyopia: Definition, Types, and Clinical Characteristics

Definition:

  • Partial, reversible vision loss in one or both eyes.
  • Absence of organic diseases of ocular media, retina, visual pathway
  • The eye appears normal, but vision is impaired.

Types of Amblyopia:

Type

Cause

Key Features

Strabismic Amblyopia

The brain suppresses input from one eye due to constant squint (strabismus).

Common cause; underdevelopment of vision in the deviated eye.

Stimulus Deprivation Amblyopia

Hindered vision due to obstruction from early life (e.g., congenital cataracts, ptosis, dense central corneal opacity).

Lack of visual stimulation affects normal development.

Anisometropic Amblyopia (Option C ruled out)

A significant difference in refractive error between eyes.

The brain favours the clearer eye, leading to amblyopia in the other.

Ametropic Amblyopia

High uncorrected refractive errors in both eyes.

Bilateral; is less severe compared to other types.

Meridional Amblyopia

Uncorrected astigmatism affecting specific visual meridians.

Affects one or both eyes depending on the astigmatism degree.

Refractive errors (Option A) While the condition involves refractive errors, the key point is the significant difference in refractive powers between the two eyes. This disparity leads to anisometropia, which can cause amblyopia. General refractive errors alone do not necessarily lead to amblyopia.

Malingering (Option D) refers to the deliberate faking of symptoms.



Reference:
  1. Kanski’s clinical ophthalmology, John F. Salmon, 10th edition, Page no: 718-719

question: What is Anisometropia ?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option A - Right eye suppression:

  • The Right Eye (Red Filter): Can only see the Red dot and the White dot (which appears red). It is "blind" to the green light.

  • The Left Eye (Green Filter): Can only see the two Green dots and the White dot (which appears green). It is "blind" to the red light.

If the patient reports seeing only three green dots, they are using only their Left eye. The Left eye sees the two green dots plus the white dot (as a 3rd green dot). Because the patient sees no red dots, the brain is actively ignoring (suppressing) the signal from the Right eye.

Incorrect Options:

  • Option B (Left Eye Suppression): If the Left eye were suppressed, the patient would see only with their Right eye. They would report seeing two red dots (the one red dot plus the white dot appearing red).

  • Option C & D (Diplopia): In diplopia, neither eye is suppressed, but the brain fails to fuse the images. The patient will see the dots from both eyes simultaneously, totaling five dots (2 red and 3 green).

    • Esodeviation (Uncrossed) results in the red dots appearing to the right of the green dots.

    • Exodeviation (Crossed) results in the red dots appearing to the left of the green dots.

explanationHtml:
• Diabetic retinopathy often develops in stages, with initial mild symptoms that may progress to sudden vision loss due to complications.
  • Bilateral sudden painless loss of vision can be caused by diabetic retinopathy, particularly in its proliferative form, where there is a sudden onset of vision loss due macular edema, or retinal detachment.
  • Diabetic retinopathy affects both eyes and can lead to significant vision impairment if left untreated.

Clinical Features of Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR):

  • Includes all features of preproliferative diabetic retinopathy or severe NPDR: Multiple retinal hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, venous beading, vascular loops, intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMAs), and large areas of capillary nonperfusion along with neovascularization.

[[figure-1]]

  • Neovascularization (2 types):
    • Neovascularization of the Disc (NVD): Arises within 1 disc diameter of the optic nerve from the optic nerve head.
    • Neovascularization Elsewhere (NVE): Arises more than 1 disc diameter from the optic nerve, along the large vessels.
    • Appears adjacent to areas of capillary closure and the accompanying fibrous tissue varies in extent.
    • Fluorescein angiography (FA): Irregular expanding hyperfluorescence.
  • Severe Vision Loss: Result in vision as poor as hand movements or worse due to severe vitreous hemorrhage or retinal detachment.
  • Fibrovascular Tissue Formation:
    • Formed due to condensation of connective tissue around the new vessels.
    • Lie flat on the retina or attach to the posterior vitreous face.
    • Can lead to vitreous traction, retinal separation, and blood vessel tearing.
    • The most common cause of vitreous hemorrhage in adults.
  • Rubeosis Iridis: Neovascularization of iris.
  • Neovascular glaucoma: Occurs due neovascularization of anterior segment angle.

Acute congestive glaucoma (Option A): Acute congestive glaucoma is typically associated with painful loss of vision and is more often unilateral. The condition involves a sudden increase in intraocular pressure, causing symptoms such as severe eye pain, nausea, and vomiting.

Keratoconus (Option C): Keratoconus can lead to progressive vision loss due to the distortion of the cornea, but it usually presents gradually, not suddenly, and typically affects one eye more than the other initially.

Iridocyclitis (Option D): Iridocyclitis (anterior uveitis) is usually associated with pain, photophobia, and redness in the affected eye. It does not cause sudden, painless loss of vision in both eyes.

The likely cause of floaters in a 22-year-old patient with high myopia and thick glasses is Posterior Vitreous Detachment (PVD).

  • In high myopia, the elongated eyeball causes early liquefaction and shrinkage of the vitreous, leading to its detachment from the retina. This results in floaters (moving black spots) while vision remains normal.
  • A fundus exam is needed to rule out associated retinal tear or detachment.

Subarachnoid hemorrhage (Option A): This is a life-threatening brain bleed. The main symptom would be a severe, sudden headache ("worst headache of life"), not isolated floaters.

Vitreous hemorrhage (Option C): Causes sudden, dense floaters with decreased vision and a hazy fundus, not just mild floaters with normal vision.

Branched retinal artery occlusion (Option D): This is a vascular blockage causing sudden, localized vision loss and visual field defects. It does not typically present with floaters.

• The first image shows two dissimilar pictures meant to be seen simultaneously (e.g., dog and its kennel parts) — this is a test of Simultaneous Macular Perception (SMP).
  • The second image shows two complementary/similar pictures intended to be merged into one percept (one image completes the other) — that is a test for Fusion.

Binocular single vision:

  • SMP (Simultaneous Macular Perception): the baseline ability to perceive two images (one from each fovea) at the same time; absence suggests suppression.
  • Fusion: the cortex’s process of aligning and merging the two similar images into one percept — requires both motor alignment and sensory correspondence.
  • Functional relationship: SMP permits inputs; fusion integrates them; without SMP fusion is hard to establish.
  • Clinical tests: SMP and fusion are tested with synoptophore slides and Worth’s four-dot before testing stereopsis (Titmus/Randot).

Grade

Name

Description

Grade 1

Grade 2

Fusion

Merging of two similar images into one

Grade 3

Stereopsis

question: Binocular single vision consists of the following components:

explanationHtml:
Correction of refractive errors (Option A ruled out): This is a fundamental and often the first step in amblyopia treatment. Uncorrected significant refractive errors (like high farsightedness, nearsightedness, or astigmatism) can prevent clear image formation and lead to amblyopia. Correcting these errors with glasses or contact lenses allows the brain to receive a clear image, which is essential for visual development. This is an effective treatment.

Occlusion therapy (patching) (Option B rule out): This is a cornerstone of amblyopia treatment. It involves covering the stronger, non-amblyopic eye for specific periods each day, forcing the brain to use and develop the weaker, amblyopic eye. This is a highly effective and widely used treatment.

Strabismus surgery (Option C): Strabismus (misalignment of the eyes) is a common cause of amblyopia. While strabismus surgery can align the eyes, it primarily addresses the cosmetic and functional alignment issue. It does not directly treat the amblyopia itself, which is a brain-based vision deficit. However, aligning the eyes before or during amblyopia treatment can sometimes improve the chances of success, especially in preventing suppression. It is not a direct or primary treatment for the amblyopia deficit itself, but for its cause.

Use of video games for visual stimulation (Option D rule out): There has been research into using specially designed video games (often dichoptic, where each eye sees different parts of the game) to stimulate both eyes simultaneously and improve visual acuity in amblyopia. While this is a newer and emerging area of research, it has shown promise as an adjunctive or alternative therapy, particularly in older children or those who don't tolerate patching well. This is considered an emerging and potentially effective treatment.



Reference:
  1. Kanski’s clinical ophthalmology, John F. Salmon, 10th edition, Page no: 718-719
  2. pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2907781/

  • A posterior staphyloma is an outpouching of the weakened posterior sclera, visible as an ectatic area on fundus examination.
  • It occurs most commonly in pathological (high) myopia due to progressive elongation of the eyeball, leading to stretching and thinning of the sclera, choroid, and retina at the posterior pole.
  • This structural change can cause progressive visual decline and predispose to retinal degenerations/detachments.
  • Axial length usually >26 mm.
  • Fundus signs: temporal crescent, chorioretinal atrophy, lattice degeneration, and posterior staphyloma.
  • Etiology: mechanical stretching from axial elongation.
  • Clinical impact: distorted vision, higher retinal detachment risk.

Staphyloma:

  • It is ectasia of the outer coats of the eye (cornea, sclera, or both) with an incarceration of the uveal tissue.

Based on the site affected, staphyloma can be classified as

[[figure-1]]

Types of staphyloma

Causes

Anterior

Pseudocornea

Intercalary

Perforating injuries of the peripheral cornea, marginal corneal ulcer, anterior scleritis, and scleromalacia perforans

Ciliary

Glaucoma, scleritis, and trauma to the ciliary region

Equatorial (approx 14 mm behind the limbus)

Scleritis, degenerative myopia, and chronic uncontrolled glaucoma

Posterior

Degenerative high axial myopia

Treatment:

  • Treat underlying condition
  • Local excision and repair with a corneal and scleral patch graft
  • Large staphyloma: Staphylectomy and keratoplasty, or enucleated and replaced with an implant

Hypermetropia (Option B): Shorter axial length; no scleral ectasia; may cause narrow anterior chamber and angle-closure glaucoma but not posterior staphyloma.

Primary open-angle glaucoma (Option C): Optic nerve cupping and visual field loss without scleral ectasia; unrelated to posterior staphyloma formation.

Retinitis pigmentosa (Option D): Inherited retinal dystrophy; shows bone-spicule pigmentation, attenuated vessels, and waxy disc pallor — not posterior scleral outpouching.

explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - Aphakia:

Explanation:

  • Clinical reasoning:
    • Deep anterior chamber → suggests absence of crystalline lens.
    • Jet-black pupil → no lens reflections seen.
    • +12D prescription → large convex lens to replace lost refractive power of natural lens.
  • Aphakia = complete absence of the natural lens (usually post-cataract surgery without IOL implantation).
  • Without the lens, refractive power decreases drastically (~+15D needed), so strong convex lenses are prescribed.
  • Causes: Post-cataract extraction without IOL, trauma, congenital.
  • Features: Deep anterior chamber, iridodonesis, jet-black pupil, high hypermetropia (+10 to +15D).

Aphakia:

Definition
  • Absence of crystalline lens from the eye.

Aetiology
  • Congenital absence (rare)
  • Surgical removal (common)
  • Traumatic extrusion of lens (rare)
  • Posterior lens dislocation (optical aphakia)

Optical Effects
  • High hypermetropia
  • Reduced eye power to +44 D (from +60 D)

Symptoms
  • Defective vision (far and near)
  • Erythropsia and cyanopsia (abnormal red and blue color defect)

Signs
  • Limbal/corneal scar (in surgical cases)
  • Deep anterior chamber
  • Iridodonesis & Jet-black pupil
  • Only 2 Purkinje images (normal: 4)
  • Hypermetropic small optic disc

Treatment

Correct refractive error with:

  • Spectacles: the problem of spherical aberration and roving ring scotoma (jack-in-the-box phenomenon)
  • Contact lenses
  • Intraocular lenses (IOL) - best method
  • Refractive LASIK surgery

Incorrect Options:

  • Pseudophakia (Option A): Eye has an artificial intraocular lens post-cataract surgery; patient usually needs minimal refractive correction (not +12D).
  • Myopia (Option C): Nearsightedness; requires concave (minus) lenses; opposite of the strong convex lenses seen here.
  • Hypermetropia (Option D): Farsightedness; needs convex lenses, but typically much lower power (+1D to +4D), not as high as +12D.
question: A 45-year-old patient with eye examination findings of a deep anterior chamber and jet-black pupil is prescribed +12D glasses. Likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
Pupil dilatation and an increase in light sensitivity are the hallmark functional changes that occur when moving from a bright environment to a dark one.

Keeping a person in a dark room leads to dark adaptation, a process in which the eyes become more sensitive to low levels of light.

  • Changes include:
    • Pupil dilatation (mydriasis) → allows more light to enter the eye
    • Increased retinal sensitivity to light → enables vision in dim illumination
  • Dark adaptation involves:
    • Rapid neural adaptation
    • Slower chemical regeneration of photopigments
  • In darkness, Vitamin A is converted to retinal (11-cis retinal).
  • Retinal combines with opsin to regenerate rhodopsin, the visual pigment used in dim light vision.

Retinal pigment changes to Vitamin A (Statement 1): Occurs during light adaptation, not dark adaptation. In bright light, rhodopsin breaks down into opsin and retinal, and retinal may be converted to Vitamin A for storage.

Retinal opsin changes to photopigment (Statement 4): It is biochemically true because opsin combines with retinal to form rhodopsin in darkness. However, in standard exam interpretation, it is usually not considered among the directly “observed changes,” making option C the accepted answer.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 6.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The above case is suggestive of orbital cellulitis.
  • The superior ophthalmic vein directly drains blood from the orbit into the cavernous sinus, providing a pathway for infections to enter the cranial cavity.
  • This route is significant in cases of orbital infections, as it can lead to serious complications such as brain abscesses and cavernous sinus thrombosis.

The venous drainage of the eye primarily occurs through:

  • Superior ophthalmic vein:
    • It receives drainage from the angular, supratrochlear, and supraorbital veins, superior vortex veins, anterior ethmoidal vein, and receives collateral drainage from the inferior ophthalmic vein.
    • It continues posteriorly to drain into the cavernous sinus.
