question: A 32-year-old patient presents with an orbital infection characterized by severe pain, swelling, and redness around the eye. Despite treatment, the patient develops a headache, fever, and neurological deficits, leading to a diagnosis of a brain abscess. What is the most likely route of spread of the infection?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The left eye appears downward and abducted, commonly known as down and out pupil due to paralysis of the inferior oblique, and medial rectus muscles.
  • There is ptosis of left eye (upper eyelid droop), and the pupil is dilated in the left eye (as the constrictor pupillae is denervated).
  • These signs are suggestive of oculomotor nerve palsy (Left side).

Oculomotor nerve palsy:

  • Causes ptosis due to paralysis of levator palpebrae superioris.
  • Eye deviates “down and out” because only lateral rectus (VI) and superior oblique (IV) are functioning.
  • Diplopia (double vision) is common due to misalignment.
  • Pupil may be dilated (mydriasis) if parasympathetic fibers are involved.
  • Loss of accommodation and light reflex can occur.

Abducens nerve palsy (VI) (Option A): Causes inability to abduct the eye (lateral movement). Eye is pulled medially → medial deviation, not “down and out”.

Optic neuritis (II) (Option B): Affects vision (visual acuity, color vision), not eye movements. No ptosis or ocular deviation.

Trochlear nerve palsy (IV) (Option D): Affects superior oblique muscle → difficulty in looking down and in. Causes vertical diplopia, often with head tilt, not full 3rd nerve features.

Nerves of the eye:

Optic nerve (CN II)
  • Purely sensory
  • Senses the incoming light and image displayed on retina

Oculomotor nerve (CN III)
  • Innervates majority of the extraocular muscles
  • Motor innervation to the superior rectus muscle, medial rectus muscle, inferior rectus muscle, inferior oblique muscle, levator palpebrae superioris muscle, ciliary muscle, and the sphincter muscle.

Trochlear nerve (CN IV)
  • Motor innervation to the superior oblique muscle

Trigeminal Nerve (CN V)
  • Ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve provides sensory innervation to the eye
  • Afferent part of corneal and lacrimation reflex

Abducens Nerve (CN VI)
  • Motor innervation to the lateral rectus muscle

Facial Nerve (CN VII)
  • Motor innervation of the orbicularis oculi muscle
  • Efferent part of corneal and lacrimation reflex

Sympathetic Nervous System
  • Long ciliary nerves: Innervates the pupillary dilator muscles causing mydriasis

Parasympathetic nervous system
  • Short ciliary nerves: Innervates the sphincter pupillae muscles causing miosis



Reference:

Anatomy, Head and Neck: Eye Nerves - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf (nih.gov)

Explanation:
At birth, the eye has a relatively short axial length, causing parallel light rays to focus behind the retina. As a result, the normal physiological refractive state in newborns is hypermetropia.

With growth during early childhood, progressive axial elongation leads to a gradual reduction in hypermetropia through the process of emmetropization.


Physiological myopia (Option B) is not characteristic at birth. It may develop later in childhood, but it is not the usual neonatal refractive state.


Physiological emmetropia (Option C): Emmetropia is achieved gradually as eye growth progresses.

correctAnswer: C. Failure of embryonic fissure closure
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The keyhole-shaped defect in the inferior iris indicates an iris coloboma.

  • Coloboma is a congenital malformation of ocular structures (iris, retina, choroid, or optic disc) caused by failure of embryonic fissure closure.
  • The embryonic fissure is located inferonasally, making the inferonasal quadrant the most common site of coloboma.
  • Colobomas can be typical (inferonasal quadrant) or atypical (any other location).
  • Complete coloboma → extends from the pupil to the optic nerve (corresponding lens indentation).
  • Incomplete coloboma can involve:
    • Iris alone
    • Iris + ciliary body (most common)
    • Iris + ciliary body + part of choroid


Failure of lens vesicle separation (Option A) leads to lenticular anomalies, not coloboma.


Persistence of hyaloid artery (Option B) causes PHPV or Mittendorf dot, not iris coloboma.


Defective neural crest migration (Option D) produces anterior segment dysgenesis, not the typical inferonasal coloboma.



Reference:

Parsons Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page 604.

  3. Phototransduction leads to hyperpolarization of photoreceptors
  4. Rods and cones release acetylcholine at their synapses

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
Phototransduction begins when light converts 11-cis-retinal to all-trans-retinal, producing a series of unstable intermediates.

Metarhodopsin II → active form that interacts with transducin, triggering the cascade that leads to closure of sodium channels and hyperpolarization of the photoreceptor.


Lumirhodopsin (Option A): An early intermediate in rhodopsin bleaching but not the active form that initiates the cascade.


Bathorhodopsin (Option C): The first photoproduct after photon absorption, highly unstable and not directly involved in signal transduction.


Metarhodopsin I (Option D): Precedes Metarhodopsin II but does not effectively activate transducin.



Reference:

Parsons Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Pages 66-67.
question: During activation of rod photoreceptors, which intermediate form of rhodopsin directly initiates the phototransduction cascade?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Ametropia refers to any refractive state in which parallel rays of light do not focus on the retina when accommodation is at rest.
It includes:

  • Astigmatism: Unequal refractive power in different meridians. (Option 1)
  • Myopia: Rays focus in front of the retina. (Option 3)
  • Hypermetropia: Rays focus behind the retina. (Option 4)


Emmetropia (Option 2) is the normal refractive state in which light focuses precisely on the retina without accommodation.

Parsons Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page 133.
question:

  3. Myopia

correctAnswer: A. Increased axial length of the eyeball
explanationHtml:
Explanation:
Poor distance vision corrected by concave lenses indicates myopia, most commonly caused by axial elongation of the eyeball that makes parallel rays focus in front of the retina when accommodation is relaxed.

Type of Myopia

By Degree

< 3 D

Medium

3 - 6 D

High

Increased refractive index of the lens (Option B) may contribute to index myopia, but is less common than axial myopia.


Forward displacement of the crystalline lens (Option C) can produce myopia, but is not the usual mechanism.


Increased corneal curvature (Option D) may cause curvature myopia, but it is less frequent than axial elongation.

question: A 17-year-old student complains of difficulty seeing distant objects in class but can read books comfortably. Visual acuity improves with −4.50 D spherical lenses in both eyes. Fundus examination is normal. How is this refractive error best classified?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
Very high, progressive myopia with fundus changes like peripapillary crescent, tessellation, and chorioretinal atrophy indicates degenerative (pathological) myopia, which is caused by excessive axial elongation and posterior segment degeneration.

Pathological (degenerative) Myopia

Type

Progressive axial myopia

Onset

Childhood

Progression

Continues into adulthood; very high myopia (>15 D)

Cause

Strong genetic predisposition with excessive axial elongation

Anatomical change

Posterior pole elongation ± posterior staphyloma

Fundus changes

Myopic crescent, chorioretinal degeneration

Symptoms

Poor distance vision, eye strain on near work, photophobia, floaters, flashes

Other Forms of Pathologic Myopia

Curvature myopia in keratoconus; Index myopia in nuclear sclerosis, cataract or diabetes

Complications

Maculopathy, retinal detachment, vitreous degeneration

Macular Changes

Chorioretinal myopic degeneration; central visual impairment

Visual outcome

Poor vision even with correction

Prognosis

Poor in early-onset progressive myopia


School myopia (Option A): Usually a low to moderate degree and lacks degenerative fundus changes.


Night myopia (Option B): A functional phenomenon under low illumination, not associated with high refractive error or fundus pathology.


Curvature myopia (Option D) is caused by increased curvature of refractive surfaces and is usually not associated with degenerative retinal changes.



Reference:

Parsons Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Pages 179-183.
question: A 22-year-old woman presents with gradually worsening distance vision since childhood. She uses −9.00 D glasses. Fundus examination shows a temporal peripapillary crescent, a tessellated fundus, and areas of chorioretinal atrophy. Which type of myopia does this presentation most likely represent?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
High myopia with sudden central distortion and a pigmented macular scar indicates myopic choroidal neovascularization due to posterior pole stretching and Bruch’s membrane breaks, resulting in a Fuchs spot.

  • Pathophysiology:
    • Excessive axial elongation in pathological myopia causes breaks in Bruch’s membrane
    • Leads to myopic choroidal neovascularization (CNV)
    • Healed CNV forms a pigmented macular scar (Fuchs spot).
  • Features:
    • Tilted optic disc with peripapillary atrophy
    • Deep anterior chamber
    • Early posterior vitreous detachment
  • Posterior Segment Signs
    • Posterior staphyloma
    • Tessellated (tigroid) fundus
    • Peripapillary myopic crescent
    • Chorioretinal atrophy
    • Lacquer cracks
    • Fuchs spot
    • Peripheral retinal degeneration → risk of retinal detachment.

[[figure-1]]


Central serous chorioretinopathy (Option A) presents with serous detachment without a pigmented scar.


Diabetic maculopathy (Option C) requires background diabetic retinopathy changes.


Macular hole (Option D) produces a full-thickness defect, not a pigmented scar.



Reference:
  1. Parsons Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Pages 179-183.
  2. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5381305/
question: A 30-year-old woman with −11.00 D myopia presents with a sudden onset of central distortion and decreased vision in one eye. Fundus examination shows a small, dark pigmented lesion at the macula with surrounding subretinal changes. What is the most likely underlying pathology?

correctAnswer: B. Axial elongation causing peripheral retinal thinning
explanationHtml:
Explanation:
The given clinical scenario of high myopia with flashes, floaters, and a retinal tear indicates complications of degenerative myopia.

Excessive axial elongation stretches the retina and choroid, leading to peripheral retinal thinning, lattice degeneration and increased susceptibility to retinal breaks and rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.


Increased corneal curvature (Option A) may contribute to refractive error but does not explain peripheral retinal degeneration.


Decreased lens power (Option C) affects refraction only and has no role in vitreoretinal degeneration or tears.


Shallow anterior chamber crowding (Option D) is seen in hypermetropia and angle closure, not in high myopia, where the chamber is usually deep.



Reference:

Parsons Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, page 181.

options.text: Axial elongation causing peripheral retinal thinning

question: A 26-year-old woman with a history of −10.00 D myopia presents with a sudden onset of flashes of light and floaters in one eye. Fundus examination shows lattice degeneration with a peripheral retinal tear. Which underlying mechanism best explains her predisposition to this complication?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The given clinical scenario of high myopia with progressive central vision loss, tessellated fundus, peripapillary atrophy, and foveal lacquer cracks indicates myopic macular degeneration, the key complication of pathological myopia, causing irreversible central vision loss.

Major Complications of Pathological Myopia:

  • Retinal: Lattice degeneration, retinal holes/tears, rhegmatogenous retinal detachment
  • Macular: Myopic CNV, Fuchs spot, lacquer cracks, myopic macular degeneration, macular hole, foveoschisis
  • Choroid/sclera: Posterior staphyloma
  • Optic nerve: Tilted disc, peripapillary atrophy
  • Vitreous: Early posterior vitreous detachment
  • Anterior segment: Early cataract, increased risk of open-angle glaucoma.


Complicated cataract (Option B): Lens opacities from trauma or inflammation; may occur earlier in myopes but do not directly affect the macula.


Vitreous haemorrhage (Option C): Sudden vision loss with floaters from intraocular bleeding; unlike the gradual central vision loss seen here.


Retinal detachment (Option D) causes sudden peripheral vision loss or curtain defect; less common than macular degeneration for central vision loss in high myopia.

question: A patient undergoing refraction is found to have different refractive powers in two principal meridians, both of which are myopic. When accommodation is relaxed and parallel light rays enter the eye, where will the images be formed?

correctAnswer: B. Contraction of the ciliary muscle reducing zonular tension
explanationHtml:
Explanation:
During near vision, contraction of the ciliary muscle reduces tension on the zonular fibers, allowing the elastic lens capsule to make the lens more convex and thereby increasing its refractive power.

Accommodation is the eye’s ability to increase its refractive power so that near objects are sharply focused on the retina, achieved by increasing the curvature of the crystalline lens.

  • Near Triad:
    • Accommodation: Lens curvature increases
    • Convergence: Eyes turn medially
    • Miosis: Pupils constrict for better depth of focus
  • Factors affecting accommodation:
    • Age: Lens elasticity declines → presbyopia
    • Refractive status: Hypermetropes use more accommodation
    • Fatigue/health: Systemic weakness reduces accommodative ability
    • Drugs: Anticholinergics ↓, parasympathomimetics ↑ accommodation
    • Illumination: Dim light increases accommodative demand
    • Neurological status: Parasympathetic and oculomotor integrity essential.

[[figure-1]]

Increased zonular tension (Option A) occurs during distance vision and flattens the lens.

Activation of dilator pupillae (Option C) produces mydriasis, not accommodation.


Posterior displacement of the lens (Option D) does not account for the change in curvature required for accommodation.



Reference:

Parsons Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page 144.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

A patient has a near point at 25 cm and a far point at infinity. The amplitude of accommodation can be calculated as follows:

Amplitude of accommodation (A) is the difference between the refractive power of the eye when fully accommodated (at the near point) and the refractive power of the eye at rest (at the far point).

[[figure-1]]

where,

  • Pnear: Refractive power for the near point
    • 1/near point (m) = 1/0.25 (m) = 4D
  • Pfar: Refractive power for the far point
    • 1/far point (m) = 1/infinity = 0D

Amplitude of accommodation (A) = 4−0 = 4D (diopters).

question: Identify the instrument used for handling delicate tissues during eye surgery.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The Femtosecond laser is the most suitable laser for cataract surgery presently. It is used in a procedure called Femtosecond Laser-Assisted Cataract Surgery (FLACS).

Femtosecond lasers:

  • Mechanism: They use ultra-short pulses of laser light to ionize tissue, creating a plasma bubble that expands and allows for precise, controlled cutting of the tissue.
  • Advantages: It provides high precision, reduces thermal damage, and improves safety compared to traditional surgical methods.
  • Limitations: Femtosecond lasers are costly and require specialised surgeon training, which can limit their accessibility and increase the overall cost of surgery.
  • Applications:
    • Femtosecond lasers are commonly used in Femtosecond Laser-Assisted Cataract Surgery (FLACS) and Laser-Assisted In Situ Keratomileusis (LASIK) for precise lens fragmentation, corneal flap creation, and refractive correction.
    • PRK (photorefractive keratectomy)
    • SMILE (small incision lenticule extraction) for correction of myopia
    • Creation of tunnel for intracorneal rings
    • Arcuate incisions to correct corneal astigmatism
    • Keratoplasty incisions
    • Lamellar and full-thickness corneal transplants

Incorrect Options:

Nd-YAG laser (Option A) is primarily used for posterior capsulotomy for the management of posterior capsular opacification.. Nd-YAG laser is not the primary laser used for cataract removal.

Diode laser (Option B) are used in iridotomy for the management of glaucoma.

Excimer laser (Option C) are primarily used in refractive surgeries such as LASIK (laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis) to reshape the cornea and correct refractive errors

question: Which laser is considered the most appropriate for cataract surgery?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI), used for treating angle-closure glaucoma, uses an argon or Nd: YAG laser.
  • It operates via a photodisruptive mechanism, which vaporizes the iris tissue to create a precise and clean opening without causing significant thermal damage to surrounding structures.
  • This procedure involves creating a small hole in the peripheral iris to re-establish communication between the anterior and posterior chambers, bypassing the pupillary block and relieving angle crowding in glaucoma.

[[figure-1]]

Argon laser (Option A): The Argon laser is used for laser iridotomy but is typically employed to pre-treat the iris by thinning the tissue before creating an opening. It uses a photocoagulative mechanism, which involves thermal energy. However, it is less effective than the Nd:YAG laser for standalone iridotomy due to higher chances of tissue damage and incomplete penetration.

Excimer laser (Option C): Excimer lasers are not used for iridotomy. These lasers emit ultraviolet light and are designed for corneal refractive procedures like LASIK and PRK. They ablate corneal tissue rather than creating openings in the iris.

CO₂ laser (Option D): CO₂ lasers are suitable in ophthalmology to vaporize lymphangiomas and capillary hemangiomas and to provide hemostasis in patients with bleeding disorders.



Reference:
  • Parsons Diseases of the eye, 23rd Edition, Pg 357,673,675, 676.
  • Myron Yanoff & Duker Ophthalmology, 6th Edition, Page 98, 429
  • Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology, 10th Edition, Page 332, 381

explanationHtml:
• Posterior capsular opacification (PCO) is a common complication following cataract surgery, often referred to as a "secondary cataract." It occurs when the posterior capsule of the eye becomes cloudy after cataract extraction, leading to decreased visual acuity.
  • The treatment for PCO is laser capsulotomy, which involves using a laser to create an opening in the cloudy posterior capsule to restore vision. The Neodymium YAG (Nd YAG) laser is the standard laser used to treat posterior capsular opacification.

After cataract = Secondary cataract:

Definition
  • M/C postoperative complication following extracapsular lens extraction.

Clinical Types
  • Posterior Capsule Opacification (PCO): Common form of after cataract.
  • Dense Membranous After Cataract: Thick membrane formation.

[[figure-1]]

  • Soemmering's Ring: Thick ring behind the iris, enclosed between capsule layers.

[[figure-2]]

  • Elschnig's Pearls: Clustered, vacuolated subcapsular epithelial cells along the posterior capsule.

[[figure-3]]

Treatment
  • ND YAG laser posterior capsulotomy

Femto laser (Option A): The femtosecond laser is used in cataract surgery for making precise incisions and can be used for corneal surgery, but it is not used for treating posterior capsular opacification.

Argon fluoride (Option C): This laser is primarily used for retinal treatments, such as for retinal photocoagulation, and is not suitable for posterior capsular opacification.

Argon laser (Option D): The argon laser is used for retinal procedures (like retinal photocoagulation) and does not have the specific characteristics needed to treat PCO effectively.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Types of Tonometry:

1. Indentation Tonometry:

  • Concept: Measures IOP by how much a plunger indents the eye; softer eyes indent more than harder eyes.
  • Schiotz Tonometer (Option A):
    • Most widely used tonometer in the world.
    • Advantages: Inexpensive, simple, and reliable.
    • Disadvantages: Gives false readings in eyes with abnormal scleral rigidity (e.g., high myopes, post-surgery).

[[figure-1]]

2. Applanation Tonometry:

  • Concept: Measures IOP based on the force needed to flatten the cornea's surface (Imbert-Fick Law: P = W/A).
  • Goldmann Tonometer (Option B):
    • Most popular and accurate; uses a double prism on a slit lamp.
    • Technique:
      • Cornea is anesthetized and stained with fluorescein.
      • Cornea and biprisms are illuminated with cobalt blue light.
      • The prism touches the cornea, and the inner edges of two semicircles are adjusted to just touch.
      • IOP is read by multiplying the dial reading by ten.

[[figure-2]]

Variable force tonometers:

  • Goldmann applanation tonometer → Gold standard
  • Perkins tonometer (hand held version of goldmann)
  • Draeger tonometer (measures wide range of IOP)
  • Draeger tonometer is similar to Perkins
    • It has a different set of prisms
    • It operates with a motor
  • Pulsair (non-contact tonometer)
  • Airpuff (non-contact tonometer)
  • Grolman (non-contact tonometer)
  • Tonopen (based on both indentation and applanation)
  • MacKay Marg (based on both indentation and applanation)
  • Rebound tonometer
  • Transpalpebral Tonometer

Fixed force tonometer:

  1. Maklakov tonometer
  2. Barraquer tonometer

Tonopen (Option C) is a handheld electronic tonometer that measures IOP by using both applanation and indentation method..

Pascal dynamic contour (Option D) tonometer is a newer technology that measures IOP by analyzing the contour of the cornea during gentle deformation.

Anisometropia is a condition where there is a significant difference in the refractive power between the two eyes. In this case:

  • Right Eye (RE): -2D (Total refractive power: 62D → 60 + 2D)
  • Left Eye (LE): +1D (Total refractive power: 59D → 60 - 1D)
  • Difference in refractive power = 62D - 59D = 3D, which is greater than 2.5D, making it clinically significant anisometropia.

Anisometropia:

is a term used when the dioptric power of both eyes is not the same, and is significant if > 2.5D difference.

Myopia (Option A): Myopia (nearsightedness) is present in the right eye (-2D), but the left eye has hyperopia (+1D). The diagnosis should reflect the difference in refractive power rather than just the presence of myopia.

Hyperopia (Option B): Hyperopia (farsightedness) is present in the left eye (+1D), but since the right eye has myopia, this case is best classified as anisometropia rather than simple hyperopia.

Amblyopia (Option D): Amblyopia (lazy eye) can develop due to anisometropia if left untreated, but the question does not indicate decreased visual acuity. Therefore, anisometropia is the more accurate primary diagnosis at this stage.

explanationHtml:
• Image in the question shows Eyelid coloboma - incomplete closure of the embryonic cleft of eyelid, the patient is at the risk of developing Exposure Keratopathy due to increased exposure of corneal area.

Coloboma:

  • Congenital eye malformations caused by incomplete closure of the embryonic cleft, leading to underdeveloped or missing tissues in the uvea, retina, or extending onto the back of the iris.
  • Types of Coloboma:
    • Typical: Found along the inferior aspect of the eye structures, including the iris, lens, choroid, retina, and optic nerve.
    • Atypical: Occurs in the non-inferior location of the eye, like the upper iris or peripheral retina, which are not along the path of the embryonic fissure.

Types of Coloboma and their characteristics:

Iris Coloboma
  • Pear-shaped defect extending from the pupil but not always reaching the ciliary body. It may occur alone or be associated with colobomata of the lens, choroid, or retina.

[[figure-1]]

Coloboma of lens
  • Notch-shaped defect typically found along the inferior lens margin due to incomplete development of the suspensory ligament.

[[figure-2]]

Fundus Coloboma
  • Oval or comet-shaped defect with a rounded apex toward the optic disc, often with an irregularly depressed surface.

[[figure-3]]

Coloboma of Optic Disc
  • It appears as an inferior crescent at the lower edge of the disc due to incomplete closure of the embryonic fissure.
  • Found in Hypermetropic and Astigmatic eyes.

[[figure-4]]

Coloboma of Lid
  • Notch or gap in the eyelid edge, most commonly on the upper lid, often associated with iris coloboma or accessory auricles.
  • The corneal surface cannot stay lubricated and hence can lead to exposure keratopathy.

[[figure-5]]

Neurotrophic and Neuroparalytic Keratopathy:

Neurotrophic Keratopathy:

  • Caused by trigeminal nerve paralysis.
  • Decreased corneal sensation and epithelial desquamation.
  • May follow procedures like Gasserian ganglion removal or blockage, often used in treating trigeminal neuralgia.

Neuroparalytic Keratopathy:

  • This condition occurs due to facial nerve paralysis, leading to lagophthalmos (inability to close the eye) and subsequent corneal exposure.
  • The patient's history does not suggest facial nerve paralysis, making this less likely.


Reference:

Parsons Diseases of the eye 23rd Edition, Pages 604,605,643,1094

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In with-the-rule astigmatism, the cornea or lens has more curvature in the vertical meridian (90°) than the horizontal meridian (180°). Because the vertical meridian is too steep, it has excessive refractive power.

To correct this, a lens must do one (or both) of the following:

  • Add minus cylinder power at axis 180° (which corrects the steep vertical 90° meridian).
  • Add plus cylinder power at axis 90° (which adds power to the flatter horizontal 180° meridian).

Lens 1 (-3.00 DC x 180): A cylinder lens has its power acting 90° away from its axis. Therefore, a cylinder at axis 180° exerts its power in the vertical meridian (90°). A minus power here flattens the overly steep vertical meridian. This is a classic WTR correction.

Lens 2 (+1.00 DC x 90): A cylinder at axis 90° exerts its power in the horizontal meridian (180°). A plus power here steepens the flatter horizontal meridian. This also corrects WTR astigmatism.

Since both lenses in this combination actively work to correct WTR astigmatism, Option 4 is the correct choice.

+5.00 DC x 180, -3.00 DC x 90 (Option A): This combination of lenses corrects against-the-rule astigmatism. It cannot be used to correct with-the-rule astigmatism.

+7.00 DC x 180, +5.00 DC x 90 (Option B): This combination of lenses corrects against-the-rule astigmatism. It cannot be used to correct with-the-rule astigmatism.

-4.00 DC x 180, -5.00 DC x 90 (Option C): This combination of lenses corrects with-the-rule astigmatism. However, the powers are too high for a typical correction.

[[figure-1]]

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Viscoelastic substances are ophthalmic agents used in anterior segment surgeries like cataract surgery (phacoemulsification) to maintain anterior chamber stability, protect intraocular tissues, and facilitate intraocular lens (IOL) implantation.

Main functions:

  • Maintain anterior chamber depth
  • Protect corneal endothelium (Option A ruled out)
  • Facilitate IOL implantation
  • Stabilize intraocular tissues

Common examples:

  • Sodium hyaluronate (Healon, ProVisc)
  • Hydroxypropyl methylcellulose (HPMC)
  • Chondroitin sulfate-based OVDs (Viscoat)

Viscoelastic substances are not inert and must be removed at the end of surgery to prevent postoperative intraocular pressure (IOP) elevation. Residual viscoelastic substances can obstruct aqueous outflow, leading to IOP spikes. (Option C ruled out)

Silicone oil, perfluoropropane (C3F8), and sulfur hexafluoride (SF6) are not viscoelastic substances; they are tamponade agents used in retinal surgeries (e.g., retinal detachment repair). (Option D ruled out)

1. Uses of viscoelastics in Ophthalmic Surgery

  • Cataract Surgery – Capsulotomy, nucleus manipulation, endothelial protection.
  • Corneal Surgery – Keratoplasty, deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty (DALK), DSEK, DMEK.
  • Glaucoma Surgery – Trabeculectomy, viscocanalostomy.
  • Retinal Surgery – Membrane separation, traction release.
  • Other Uses – Strabismus surgery, pediatric cataract surgery, open globe repair, oculoplasty.

2. Ideal Properties of viscoelastics

  • Clear, sterile, non-toxic, non-inflammatory, and non-immunogenic.
  • Good viscosity – Prevents anterior chamber (AC) collapse.
  • Elastic and shock-absorbing – Protects intraocular structures.
  • Retention under pressure – High cohesion with minimal surface activity.
  • Easily removable – Should not obstruct aqueous outflow.
  • Coatability – Should protect endothelium and prevent cell loss.

3. Complications of viscoelastics

Complication

Cause & Features

Secondary Glaucoma

Retained OVD blocks trabecular meshwork → IOP spike (6–24 hrs post-op).

Capsular Block Syndrome (CBS)

Trapped OVD in capsular bag → anterior displacement of IOL/nucleus.

Pseudo-Anterior Uveitis

Clumping of RBCs/inflammatory cells due to negative charge.

Post-op Uveitis & Hypopyon

Inflammatory response post-OVD instillation.

Corneal Edema/Decompensation

Endothelial trauma from OVD residue.

IOL Crystallization

OVD residues on IOL surface → Fern-like deposits.

Calcific Band Keratopathy

Reported with chondroitin sulfate OVDs.

Hypersensitivity

Risk with sodium hyaluronate from rooster combs/streptococcal culture.



Reference:

  2. Agents for Vitreous Tamponade - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
The visual system is unique in that its primary receptors-photoreceptors (rods and cones)-are hyperpolarized by the stimulus (light).

In the dark, photoreceptors are actually in a depolarized state due to the "dark current" (influx of sodium ions). When light hits the photopigment, it initiates a biochemical cascade that closes sodium channels, making the cell membrane more negative.

  • In most sensory systems, a stimulus causes the receptor cell to depolarize (become more positive) to trigger an action potential.
  • However, in the eye, the absorption of light by rhodopsin activates the G-protein transducin, which then activates phosphodiesterase (PDE).
  • PDE breaks down cGMP, and the decrease in cGMP leads to the closure of cGMP-gated sodium channels, causing hyperpolarization and a decrease in the release of the neurotransmitter glutamate.

Olfactory (Option A): Binding of odorant molecules to receptors on olfactory cilia triggers a G-protein cascade that opens cation channels (Na+ and Ca2+), leading to depolarization of the olfactory receptor neuron.

Gustatory (Option B): Taste transduction (for salty, sour, sweet, bitter, and umami) ultimately leads to the depolarization of the taste bud cells, either through the direct entry of ions or through G-protein-coupled signaling that increases intracellular calcium.

Auditory (Option D): Sound waves cause the displacement of hair cell stereocilia. This physical movement opens mechanically gated potassium channels at the tips of the cilia, allowing potassium from the endolymph to enter and depolarize the hair cell.

  • X-rays of the chest and sacroiliac joints can help rule out conditions like ankylosing spondylitis, which can also present with episcleritis.
  • Therefore, a comprehensive approach including all listed investigations is appropriate.

Conditions associated with Episcleritis:

  • Idiopathic: The exact etiology is unknown in many cases.
  • Systemic Diseases:
    • Gout
    • Rosacea
    • Psoriasis
    • Connective tissue diseases (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, lupus)
  • Hypersensitivity Reactions:
    • Endogenous tubercular toxins
    • Streptococcal toxins
  • Infectious Episcleritis:
    • Herpes zoster virus
    • Syphilis
    • Lyme disease
    • Tuberculosis


Reference:
  1. Parson’s Diseases of the eye, 23rd Edition, Page 200.
  2. Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 292

question: A 40-year-old patient presents with recurrent episodes of episcleritis. After taking a detailed history and performing a thorough systemic examination, which of the following investigations would you consider ordering?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Severe pain, scleral thinning with adjacent congestion are hallmark signs of necrotizing scleritis, the most severe form of RA-associated scleritis.
  • RA leads to immune-mediated vasculitis, causing ischemic necrosis of the sclera.


Classification of Scleritis:

[[figure-1]]

Anterior Staphyloma (Option A):

  • Anterior staphyloma is a late-stage complication, where uveal tissue bulges through a thinned, scarred sclera.
  • This patient has active inflammation, whereas staphyloma occurs after chronic necrosis and healing.

Nodular Scleritis (Option C):

  • Nodular scleritis presents with discrete, firm nodules on the sclera, without necrosis.
  • This patient has scleral thinning and avascular necrosis, which rules out nodular scleritis.

Scleromalacia Perforans (Option D):

  • Scleromalacia perforans is a form of necrotizing scleritis WITHOUT inflammation (painless, non-red eye).
  • This patient has severe pain and congestion, so active necrotizing scleritis is the correct choice.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 294
question: A 45-year-old woman with a 15-year history of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) presents with severe ocular pain, redness, and progressively worsening vision in her left eye for the past 2 weeks. Examination reveals a localized area of scleral thinning with adjacent congestion. There is no posterior involvement on B-scan ultrasound. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:

Clinical classification:

  • Non-necrotizing anterior scleritis: Pain, redness, watering, discharge, and bluish or brownish discoloration.
    • Diffuse

  • Necrotizing anterior scleritis

[[figure-2]]

Necrotizing anterior scleritis with inflammation: (Option A)

  • Red, painful eye, and progressive worsening of symptoms

question: A 38-year-old male presents with persistent eye discomfort, redness, and watering. On examination, the left eye is diffusely tender, sclera appears uniformly reddened and swollen without localized thinning areas. There are no systemic signs of vasculitis or autoimmune disease on further investigation. Which type of anterior scleritis is most consistent with this presentation?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Given the clinical presentation of severe pain in the eye, proptosis, restricted ocular movements, reduced vision, disc, and macular edema, and the potential findings of choroidal folds, the diagnosis most consistent with these symptoms is posterior scleritis.
  • Thickening of the posterior sclera, retrobulbar thickening, and fluid surrounding the optic nerve creates a characteristic “T” sign in B-scan ultrasound.
    • In posterior scleritis, fluid accumulates in the sub-Tenon’s space due to inflammation.
    • On B-scan, this fluid tracks along the optic nerve sheath.
    • The horizontal line = scleral thickening + fluid
    • The vertical line = optic nerve
    • Together → form a “T-shaped” sign

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Moth-Eaten Appearance (Option B): Seen in Retinoblastoma, characterized by intraocular calcifications, typically in children, not adults.


Sunray Sign (Option C): Seen in Choroidal Melanoma, due to radial vascularity, but this patient lacks an intraocular mass.


Kiss Sign (Option D): Seen in Total Retinal Detachment, where the detached retina folds inward, but this case has no retinal involvement.

question: A 45-year-old woman presents with severe pain in her right eye, worsened by eye movements, and reduced vision. On examination, proptosis and restricted ocular movements were observed. Ophthalmoscopy shows disc, macular edema, and choroidal folds. Which of the following B-scan ultrasonography findings is most indicative of this disease?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The diagnosis in this scenario is Scleromalacia Perforans.

  • It is usually associated with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis and presents with scleral thinning, appearing bluish and without signs of inflammation.
  • The underlying cause of scleral thinning is due to Type III hypersensitivity caused by immune-mediated chronic granulomatous inflammation and chronic vaso-occlusion of episcleral vessels, leading to collagen necrosis.

[[figure-1]]

  • Type II hypersensitivity (Option B) involves antibody-mediated cellular dysfunction or destruction.
  • Type IV hypersensitivity (Option C): Scleromalacia perforans is caused by immune complex–mediated vasculitis, not delayed-type hypersensitivity.
  • Infective etiology (Option D): Scleromalacia perforans is a sterile, autoimmune complication of systemic diseases.



Reference:
  1. Parson’s Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page 527

question: Blue sclera is commonly associated with all of the following conditions except:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Aspergillus fumigatus is a common causative organism of keratomycosis in tropical and subtropical regions and is often associated with exposure to decaying organic matter.

Keratomycosis Etiology Summary

  • Most Common Causative Organisms:
    • Aspergillus fumigatus: Most common in India and tropical regions.
    • Fusarium(Option B ruled out): Common in warm climates like Brazil.
    • Candida albicans(Option A ruled out): More frequent in temperate climates.
  • Mode of Infection:
    • Injury with Vegetative Material: Typically occurs after trauma with objects like thorns, wooden sticks, crop leaves, or decaying vegetable matter.
    • Common in Field Workers: Especially during harvesting season in rural and tropical areas.
    • Immunocompromised Individuals: Higher risk for developing fungal keratitis.
  • Special Considerations:
    • Candida albicans: Leading cause of endogenous endophthalmitis.
    • Mucormycosis(Option C ruled out) & Invasive Aspergillosis: Considered as the cause of orbital cellulitis in immunocompromised patients.
