question:
Clinical question:
A 60 y/o man from a tropical region presents with a painful, red eye and a corneal ulcer following recent exposure to decaying vegetable matter. Which is the most common fungal infection affecting the cornea?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
Extensive corneal vascularization is generally absent in pure fungal keratitis, which distinguishes it from bacterial infections where vascularization is more common.

Keratomycosis

[[figure-1]]

Clinical Features

  • Pain & Foreign Body Sensation
  • Watering of the eye
  • Photophobia
  • Blurred Vision
  • Redness.

Examination Findings

  • Corneal Ulcer: Greyish-white, dry-looking with elevated, rolled-out margins.
  • Pigmented Ulcer: Brownish appearance, possible with dematiaceous fungi.
  • Feathery Extensions (Option A ruled out): Delicate, finger-like projections into the surrounding stroma.
  • Sterile Immune Ring (Option C ruled out): Yellow line of demarcation where fungal antigen and host antibodies meet.
  • Satellite Lesions: Multiple small lesions around the main ulcer.
  • Hypopyon: Large, non-sterile, even with a small ulcer.
  • Endothelial Plaque (Option D ruled out): Located under the stromal lesion, made of fibrin and leucocytes.
  • Corneal Vascularization: Typically absent in pure fungal ulcers.
  • Perforation: Rare but possible.

Investigations

  • Corneal Scraping: Performed under topical anaesthesia for microbiological examination.
  • Wet KOH Mount: Reveals filamentous fungi (branched, septate hyphae) or non-filamentous yeast-like fungi (Candida).
  • Gram's & Giemsa Stains: To detect fungal hyphae and inflammatory cells.
  • Culture: Sabouraud's agar medium is used for fungal culture.
  • PCR: Recommended for rapid identification of fungal pathogens.
  • Anterior Chamber Paracentesis: Considered if there is an intraocular extension.
  • Corneal Biopsy: Indicated for deep stromal abscess or when cultures are negative.
  • Confocal Microscopy: Used for identifying actual fungi within the cornea.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 216, 217.

options.text: Feathery extensions at the margins of the corneal ulcer

question: A 45 y/o man from a tropical region presents with a painful red eye, significant watering, and sensitivity to light after working in a garden with decaying plant material. The patient is diagnosed with keratomycosis. Which of the following is not an examination finding in keratomycosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The history of trauma with plant material, along with the presence of a corneal ulcer with feathery edges and satellite lesions, is highly suggestive of fungal keratitis.
  • Natamycin is the first-line treatment for fungal keratitis, especially caused by filamentous fungi like Fusarium and Aspergillus.
  • It is effective in treating the type of fungal infection that is suggested by the clinical presentation in this patient.

Treatment of Keratomycosis (Fungal Corneal Ulcer):

Primary Treatment: Antifungal Medications:

  • Topical Antifungal Agents:
    • Natamycin
    • Voriconazole
    • Amphotericin B (effective against Aspergillus and Fusarium)
    • Nystatin (effective against Candida)
  • Oral Antifungal Agents (for severe ulcers with specific features):
    • Ketoconazole
    • Voriconazole
    • Indications for Oral Therapy:
      • Hypopyon
      • Perforation
      • Suspicion of endophthalmitis

Surgical Management (if unresponsive to medical therapy):

  • Repeated Scraping: Removal of necrotic material
  • Cauterization Options:
    • Pure carbolic acid (100%)
    • Trichloroacetic acid (10%–20%)
    • Povidone-iodine 5%
  • Therapeutic Keratoplasty: Corneal transplantation

Management of Suspected Endophthalmitis:

  • Ultrasound: To check for exudates in the vitreous
  • Vitreous Tap & intravitreal injections of antibiotics and antifungals (amphotericin B) if confirmed
  • Surgical Options (if medical therapy fails):
    • Corneal graft
    • Conjunctival flap

Topical Moxifloxacin (Option A):

  • Moxifloxacin is an antibiotic effective against bacterial infections, not fungal infections.
  • Given the history of trauma with plant material and the appearance of a corneal ulcer with feathery edges and satellite lesions, the most likely diagnosis is fungal keratitis.
  • Therefore, moxifloxacin would not be appropriate.

Oral Acyclovir (Option C):

  • Acyclovir is an antiviral medication used primarily for herpes simplex virus infections.
  • It would not be effective for a fungal corneal ulcer, making it an inappropriate choice in this scenario.

Intravitreal Amphotericin B (Option D):

  • Intravitreal Amphotericin B is used in cases of fungal endophthalmitis, not as an initial treatment for keratitis.
  • Although hypopyon suggests severe infection, the primary treatment should still be topical antifungal agents unless there is confirmed or high suspicion of endophthalmitis requiring intravitreal therapy.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Pages 217, 218.
question: A 45 y/o male presents with redness, pain, and decreased vision in his right eye. He reports a history of trauma to the eye with a plant material three days ago. O/E, there is a corneal ulcer with feathery edges and satellite lesions. Hypopyon is also noted. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanations:

  • HSV keratitis is characterized by dendritic ulcers on the cornea, which are branching, tree-like lesions.
  • HSV also commonly causes decreased corneal sensation.

Examination Findings in Viral Keratitis:

Signs:

  • Swollen Epithelial Cells: Early signs presenting as swollen, opaque cells in a coarse punctate or stellate pattern.
  • Dendritic Ulcer: Characteristic linear, branching ulcer with terminal bulbs; stains with fluorescein.
  • Geographic Ulcer: Enlarged amoeboid-shaped ulcer, often due to inappropriate steroid use.
  • Rose Bengal Staining: Stains virus-laden cells at the ulcer edges, aiding in differentiation from other conditions.
  • Reduced Corneal Sensation: Result of corneal nerve damage.
  • Subepithelial Haze: Mild haziness was observed in the subepithelial layer.
  • Anterior Chamber Activity: Mild inflammatory reaction in the anterior chamber.
  • Elevated IOP: Increased intraocular pressure, requiring monitoring.
  • Persistent Punctate Erosions (PEE): Residual erosions and epithelial irregularities after healing, resolving spontaneously without indicating recurrence.

Specific Findings Based on Virus Type:

Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) Keratitis:

  • Dendritic Ulcers: Branching, tree-like ulcers.
  • Geographic Ulcers: Larger, amoeboid-shaped ulcers.
  • Stromal Keratitis: Inflammation of the corneal stroma, leading to oedema, infiltrates, and scarring.
  • Disciform Keratitis: Central, disc-shaped inflammation in the stroma.

Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus (HZO): (Option B)

  • Vesicles and Scars: Painful rash and blisters following the involvement of ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve.
  • Nummular Keratitis: Large, coin-shaped, subepithelial corneal infiltrates.

  • Scleritis: Inflammation of the sclera, causing pain and redness.
  • Iritis: Inflammation of the iris leading to pain, photophobia, and blurred vision.

Adenovirus (Option A):

  • Adenoviruses are known for causing epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC) and may present with conjunctivitis and keratitis.
  • They are less likely to cause dendritic ulcers, which are specific to HSV.

Chlamydia trachomatis (Option D):

  • Chlamydia typically causes trachoma or inclusion conjunctivitis, which may involve conjunctival scarring and corneal pannus, but not dendritic ulcers.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition 9, Pages 219, 220.
question: A 45 y/o patient presents with eye redness, excessive tearing, and sensitivity to light. O/E you observe dendritic ulcers, and decreased corneal sensation. Based on these findings, which virus is most likely responsible for the patient's condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient presents with pain, redness, photophobia, and decreased vision in the right eye, along with a dendritic ulcer on the cornea.
  • This clinical picture is classic for Herpes Simplex Keratitis (HSK), an infection of the cornea caused by the herpes simplex virus (HSV).

Treatment:

  • Topical Acyclovir:
    • This antiviral medication is the first-line treatment for HSV keratitis.
    • It directly targets the herpes simplex virus, reducing viral replication and promoting healing of the corneal ulcer.
  • Cycloplegics:
    • These medications help to relieve pain caused by ciliary muscle spasms and prevent the formation of synechiae (adhesions) in the iris.


Treatment of Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) Keratitis:

Topical Therapy:

  • Antivirals:
    • Common Agents:
      • Aciclovir 3% ointment: 5 times daily.
      • Ganciclovir 0.15% gel: 5 times daily.
      • Trifluridine: Up to 9 times daily.
    • Older Agents: Idoxuridine and vidarabine (less common due to lower efficacy/higher toxicity).
  • Other Topical Medications:
    • Antibiotics: Prevent secondary bacterial infections, especially with epithelial defects.
    • Cycloplegics: (e.g., Homatropine 1%) Relieve pain and photophobia by paralyzing ciliary muscles and dilating the pupil.
    • Steroids:
      • Epithelial Keratitis: Contraindicated due to the risk of worsening infection and corneal perforation.
      • Stromal Keratitis: Used cautiously with antivirals to control inflammation and reduce scarring.

Oral Therapy:

  • Antivirals:
    • Indications: immunocompromised patients, children, severe ocular surface disease, intolerance/resistance to topical treatment.
    • Prophylaxis:
      • Low-dose oral acyclovir (400 mg twice daily) reduces recurrence.
      • Alternatives include valaciclovir (500 mg once daily) and famciclovir.
  • Steroids: Generally avoided but may be used with caution in severe stromal inflammation as an adjunct to topical therapy.

Surgical Management:

  • Debridement: Removal of infected epithelial cells, helpful in resistant epithelial keratitis.
  • Keratoplasty:
    • Indication: Severe corneal scarring after at least a year of infection-free status.
    • Risk of Recurrence:
      • HSV keratitis may recur post-keratoplasty.
      • Eyes with extensive corneal vascularization are at higher risk of graft rejection and recurrence.
      • Prophylactic oral acyclovir is recommended.

Topical steroids and antibiotics (Option A):

  • Topical steroids are contraindicated in the treatment of active epithelial HSV keratitis, as they can suppress the immune response and worsen the viral infection, potentially leading to complications like corneal perforation.
  • Antibiotics are not needed unless there is a secondary bacterial infection, which is not indicated here.

Oral acyclovir and lubricants (Option B):

  • While oral acyclovir is used in more severe or recurrent cases of HSV keratitis, topical acyclovir is preferred as the initial treatment.
  • Lubricants can be supportive but are not the primary treatment.

Oral steroids and topical antibiotics (Option D):

  • Oral steroids are contraindicated in HSV keratitis, similar to topical steroids, as they can exacerbate the infection.
  • Topical antibiotics are unnecessary unless there's evidence of bacterial superinfection.


Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition 9, Page 221.
question: A 35 y/o patient presents with pain, redness, photophobia, and decreased vision in the right eye. Slit-lamp examination reveals a dendritic ulcer on the cornea. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The most likely diagnosis for a patient with long-standing, poorly controlled rheumatoid arthritis presenting with sudden, painless blurring of vision in the superior visual field of one eye, and a fundoscopic examination showing retinal hemorrhages and dilated, tortuous veins in the inferior retina, is Branch Retinal Vein Occlusion (BRVO).
  • It occurs when a single branch of the central retinal vein is occluded, causing retinal edema and hemorrhages localized to the area supplied by the blocked vein.
  • Visual Defects:
    • Visual loss is partial, superior or inferior field loss, depending on the location of the occlusion.
    • Prognosis for central vision is better unless the macula is involved, often seen in superior temporal vein occlusion.
  • Complications:
    • Neovascularization and secondary glaucoma are rare but can occur in cases of widespread capillary occlusion.
  • Diagnostic Features:
    • Fluorescein Angiography: Shows areas of hypofluorescence, incomplete perifoveal arcades, and capillary closure in poorly perfused areas.
    • Widespread capillary occlusion is associated with cotton-wool spots, delayed arteriovenous transit time, vessel leakage, and retinal edema.
  • Treatment:
    • No definitive treatment is effective once complete venous blockage occurs.
    • Panphotocoagulation or Cryotherapy: Used to prevent complications like neovascular glaucoma and rubeosis iridis in cases of widespread capillary occlusion.
    • Photocoagulation: Should only be performed after intraretinal blood absorption to address areas of poor perfusion, reducing edema and neovascularization risk.
    • Anti-VEGF Therapy: Intravitreal injections are now standard for improving visual recovery and preventing late complications.

Branched Retinal Artery Occlusion (Option A) a cherry red spot in the retina is noticed due to the surrounding edema.


Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (Option B) obstruction occurs at the level of the lamina cribrosa, causing sudden painless loss of vision within seconds.


Central Retinal Vein Occlusion (Option D) there is a mild blurring of vision, which improves over the day.



Reference:

Parsons Diseases of the Eye 23rd edition Pg.no:773,776
question: A patient with long-standing, poorly controlled rheumatoid arthritis presents with a sudden, painless blurring of vision in the superior visual field of one eye. Fundoscopic examination shows retinal hemorrhages and dilated, tortuous veins in the inferior retina. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Nodular swelling near the limbus, which blanches after administering phenylephrine and then recurs, is characteristic of episcleritis, particularly nodular episcleritis.

Episcleritis

  • Episcleritis is an inflammation of the episclera, the superficial vascular layer between the conjunctiva and sclera.
  • Benign and recurrent disease
  • It mainly affects middle-aged people (female > male)
  • It is a self-limiting disease.
  • It presents with:
    • Sectoral redness
    • Mild discomfort or irritation
    • Localized nodular swelling (in nodular episcleritis)
  • On examination
    • Nodular type: Nodule near limbus
    • Diffuse type
  • Confirmatory test: Phenylephrine test
    • Phenylephrine 2.5% or 10% blanches the superficial episcleral vessels, helping distinguish episcleritis from scleritis.
    • The redness may recur after the vasoconstrictive effect wears off.

Scleritis (Option B):

  • Deeper inflammation of the sclera
  • Severe, boring ocular pain (often radiating to the face/jaw)
  • Deep violaceous redness
  • Does not blanch with phenylephrine because the deeper scleral vessels are involved

Bitot spots (Option C): Bitot's spot consists of keratinized epithelium and is seen in vitamin A deficiency.

[[figure-1]]

Pterygium (Option D):

  • Fibrovascular triangular growth extending onto the cornea
  • Chronic lesion, not a nodular inflammatory swelling
  • Phenylephrine blanching is not a diagnostic feature

[[figure-2]]

Feature Episcleritis Scleritis
Pain Mild discomfort Severe boring pain
Redness Bright red Deep violaceous red
Vessel involvement Superficial episcleral vessels Deep scleral vessels
Phenylephrine test Blanches (+) No blanching (−)
Vision Usually normal May be affected
Association with systemic disease Less common Common (e.g., RA, vasculitis)


Reference:

Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Pages 292, 293.
question: A patient presents with a nodular swelling near the limbus, which blanches after administering phenylephrine and then recurs. What is the most probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient has painless redness of the eye which blanches (as shown in the image) following the application of 10% phenylephrine, suggesting episcleritis- Nodular episcleritis

Episcleritis

Definition

Episcleritis refers to inflammation of the loose connective tissue between the sclera and the conjunctiva

Etiology

Idiopathic

Systemic diseases - gout, rosacea, psoriasis, and connective tissue diseases.

Hypersensitivity reaction to endogenous tubercular or streptococcal toxins.

Infectious episcleritis - herpes zoster virus, syphilis, Lyme disease, and tuberculosis.

Clinical features
  • Common in young females
  • Acute onset redness
  • Discomfort - gritty/foreign body sensation
  • Mild to no pain
  • Resolves spontaneously
  • Recurrence is common

Clinical types
  1. Simple episcleritis: Sectorial (occasionally diffuse) inflammation of episclera. The engorged episcleral vessels are large and run in a radial direction beneath the conjunctiva
  2. Nodular episcleritis: Pink or purple flat nodule surrounded by injection, usually situated 2-3 mm away from the limbus. The nodule is firm, tender can be moved separately from the sclera and the overlying conjunctiva also moves freely.

Diagnosis

10% Topical phenylephrine blanches overlying conjunctival vessels and inflamed episcleral vessels.

Differential diagnosis
  • Conjunctivitis, which is more superficial; blanching occurs with 2.5% phenylephrine
  • Phlyctenulosis (Option C ruled out)
  • Inflamed pinguecula
  • Scleritis, which is deeper and more painful; does not blanch with 10% phenylephrine (Option B ruled out)

Treatment

  • Topical NSAIDs
  • Topical mild corticosteroid eye drops
  • Topical artificial tears,
  • Cold compresses applied to the closed lids may offer symptomatic relief from ocular discomfort.
  • Systemic NSAIDs

Scleral ectasia (Option D) refers to a thinning and bulging of the sclera, often associated with conditions like keratoconus. It is not an inflammatory condition, and it would not cause the blanching of vascularity seen with phenylephrine. The clinical presentation of scleral ectasia typically involves corneal changes rather than inflammation of the episclera.



Reference:
  • Parson’s Diseases of the eye, 23rd ed., page 198.
  • Yanoff and Duker Ophthalmology, 5e., page 212
  • Kanski’s Clinical ophthalmology, 9e., page 292
question: What is the probable diagnosis based on the observed blanching of vascularity following the administration of 10 % phenylephrine, as depicted in the provided image?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Dermoid cyst appears as a lenticular yellow tumor near the corneal margin and consists of epidermoid epithelium with sebaceous glands and hair.
  • Dermoid cyst is a congenital, often benign growth that contains skin-like structures, such as hair follicles, sweat glands, and sebaceous glands. It can present as a small, firm, yellowish nodule on the sclera or conjunctiva. These cysts are often located near the limbus (the junction between the cornea and sclera) and may be noticed in childhood, especially if they grow or become more noticeable over time.
  • A dermoid cyst may be diagnosed based on its characteristic appearance and location, and sometimes imaging or excision is needed for confirmation.

[[figure-1]]

Pterygium (Option A): A pterygium is a fibrovascular growth that extends from the conjunctiva onto the cornea, typically seen on the nasal side of the eye. It is usually triangular in shape and may cause visual disturbance. It is not typically a nodule confined to the sclera.

[[figure-2]]

Pinguecula (Option B): A yellowish, triangular patch on the conjunctiva near the limbus, typically in the elderly, associated with sun exposure and not extending onto the cornea.

[[figure-3]]

Dermolipoma (Option C): A dermolipoma is a benign tumor consisting of fat and skin-like tissue. While they may be located in the eye area, they typically present as larger, softer masses, and this does not match the presentation of a small nodule on the sclera.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th edition, Page- 197, 198.
question: A 5-year-old boy presents with a small nodule on the sclera as shown in the image below. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The history of a prolonged corneal ulcer is suggestive of low body immune response or infection by a virulent strain of bacteria leading to sloughing of the whole cornea, leaving a narrow rim behind along with iris prolapse resulting in the false cornea that cannot withstand raised intraocular pressure and results in forward bulging of the cornea with iris tissue. As a result an ectatic cicatrix forms called Anterior Staphyloma as seen in the image.

Staphyloma:

It is ectasia of the outer coats of the eye (cornea, sclera, or both) with an incarceration of the uveal tissue.

Based on the site affected, staphyloma can be classified as

[[figure-1]]

Types of staphyloma

Causes

Anterior

Pseudocornea (following corneal ulcer) (Option D)

Intercalary

Perforating injuries of the peripheral cornea, marginal corneal ulcer, anterior scleritis, and scleromalacia perforans

Ciliary

Glaucoma, scleritis, and trauma to the ciliary region

Equatorial (approx 14 mm behind the limbus)

Scleritis, degenerative myopia, and chronic uncontrolled glaucoma

Posterior

Degenerative high axial myopia

Treatment:

  • Treat underlying condition
  • Local excision and repair with a corneal and scleral patch graft
  • Large staphyloma: Staphylectomy and keratoplasty, or enucleated and replaced with an implant

Megalocornea (Option A): Rare bilateral nonprogressive congenital defect that is characterized by an increased corneal diameter greater than 12.5 to 13 mm at birth and a deep anterior chamber with normal intraocular pressures and clear cornea.

Conjunctivitis (Option B): Is the inflammation or infection of the transparent membrane that lines your eyelid and eyeball. Typical symptoms include redness and a gritty sensation in your eye, along with itching.

Buphthalmos (Option C): Meaning "bull-like eyes," is a condition characterized by the enlargement of the eyeball secondary to congenital Glaucoma. It typically manifests before the age of 3 years and results from the accumulation and retention of aqueous humor.

OP185



Reference:

Parsons Diseases of the Eye 23rd Edition, pages 531-533
question: What is the probable diagnosis of a 35-year-old male with a history of prolonged corneal ulcer who now presents with a deformed eye as shown in the image?

explanationHtml:
• The diagnosis in this scenario is scleromalacia perforans.
  • It is usually associated with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis and presents with scleral thinning appearing bluish and without signs of inflammation.
  • The underlying cause of scleral thinning is probably ischemia because of vessel damage (type III hypersensitivity).

Scleromalacia Perforans:

  • Most common in elderly females

Pathophysiology:

  • Associated with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis
  • Melting of the sclera is due to obliteration of arterial supply causing ischemia
  • Vessel damage is mediated by type III hypersensitivity (Option A)

Clinical manifestations:

  • Painless scleral thinning
  • Underlying dark uveal tissue is visible
  • Rarely perforation of the globe

[[figure-1]]

Scleromalacia perforans

Treatment:

  • No specific therapy
  • Protection of the eye from trauma is very crucial
  • Plenty of topical lubrication
  • Oral NSAIDs
  • Oral steroids
  • Immunomodulatory agents
  • Surgery-scleral patch grafting

Ciliary staphyloma (Option B): This condition involves outpouching of the eye wall near the ciliary body, typically associated with trauma or inflammatory conditions other than rheumatoid arthritis, but it is not a direct complication of RA.

Coloboma (Option C): A coloboma is a congenital defect in the eye, where part of the eye structure (such as the iris or retina) is missing. It is not associated with rheumatoid arthritis.

Malignant melanoma (Option D): This is a type of eye cancer that arises from pigment-producing cells. It is unrelated to rheumatoid arthritis and is not an autoimmune complication.



Reference:
  1. Parsons diseases of the eye 23e pg 527
  2. Scleromalacia Perforans - EyeWiki
  3. Image : https://eyewiki.org/Scleromalacia_Perforans
question: In the image, what are the associated complications observed in a 35-year-old woman who has been diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The valve of Hasner is a crucial structure located at the lower end of the nasolacrimal duct, where it opens into the inferior meatus of the nose.
  • Its primary function is to prevent the retrograde flow of fluid from the nasal cavity into the nasolacrimal duct, which is particularly important during actions like nose blowing.
  • This valve ensures that tears drain properly from the eye into the nasal cavity without backflow.

[[figure-1]]

The valve of Rosenmüller (Option B) is a mucosal fold located at the junction where the common canaliculus (formed by the superior and inferior canaliculi) opens into the lacrimal sac.

Orbital Lobe (Option C) is one of the two lobes of the main lacrimal gland, which is involved in the production of reflex tears.

[[figure-2]]

Glands of Krause (Option D) are accessory lacrimal glands found in the conjunctival fornices.



Reference:

Parsons’ Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Pg.1102,1103

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology 9th edition page 100-101
question: Which structure within the lacrimal passages prevents the backflow of tears from the nasal cavity into the nasolacrimal duct?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The lacrimal pump mechanism relies on the proper function of the orbicularis oculi muscle and the correct positioning of the punctum.
  • In Bell’s palsy, weakness of the orbicularis oculi muscle prevents proper eyelid closure and tear drainage, as the orbicularis oculi muscle is involved in both the tear suction and drainage phase of the lacrimal pump mechanism.
  • This leads to epiphora (excessive tearing).

Trauma to the canaliculus (Option A):

  • While an injury to the canaliculus can block the tear drainage system, it does not directly disrupt the lacrimal pump mechanism.

Obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct (Option C):

  • This condition involves a blockage in the nasolacrimal duct, preventing proper tear drainage.

Narrowing of the punctum (Option D):

  • Punctal stenosis refers to a narrowing or closure of the punctum (the opening at the corner of the eyelid that drains tears).



Reference:

Parsons Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page 1114
question: Which of the following is a cause of lacrimal pump failure, leading to excessive tearing (epiphora)?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Dacryocystography (DCG) provides highly detailed anatomical information about the entire lacrimal drainage system.
  • By injecting contrast dye into the lacrimal sac and taking X-rays, DCG can precisely identify the site, extent, and nature of the blockage, making it the investigation of choice when anatomical clarity is required.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Fluorescein Dye Disappearance Test (FDDT) (Option B):

  • It is mainly used to assess the overall efficiency of tear drainage and does not provide information on the exact location or nature of any obstruction within the lacrimal system.

Dacryoscintigraphy (Option C) or lacrimal scintillography is a functional test that evaluates the rate at which tears flow through the lacrimal drainage system by tracking a radioactive tracer.

  • While it is useful for identifying functional delays or blockages, it lacks the anatomical precision needed to determine the exact location or cause of the obstruction.

[[figure-3]]

Lacrimal Syringing (Option D):

  • Normal saline is injected into the lacrimal sac using a syringe.
  • Although it can identify the degree of blockage & approximate blockage site, it does not offer detailed anatomical information.



Reference:
  1. Parsons’ Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Pages 1114, 1115, 1116
  2. Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 104
  3. Yanoff & Duker Ophthalmology, 5th Edition, Pages 1339, 1340
question: A 65 y/o male presents with persistent tearing in his right eye that has worsened over the past year. The physician orders an imaging study to pinpoint the exact location of the blockage and assess the condition of the lacrimal sac. Which investigation is most appropriate for this purpose?

correctAnswer: A. Partial obstruction within the lacrimal passages
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • A positive Jones Test 2 indicates that the fluorescein dye was able to enter the lacrimal sac but could not reach the nasal cavity without syringing.
  • This finding is typical of a partial blockage somewhere along the lacrimal drainage system, allowing some tear flow but not enough for normal drainage.

[[figure-1]]

Jones Test 1:

  • Purpose: To distinguish between partial obstruction and excessive tear production.
  • Procedure: Fluorescein dye is placed in the conjunctival sac, and after 5 minutes, a cotton bud soaked in anaesthetic is placed in the inferior meatus inside the nose. The cotton bud is checked for dye.
  • Interpretation:
    • Positive: Dye on the cotton bud indicates patent tear drainage and suggests hypersecretion.
    • Negative: No dye indicates potential drainage issues, requiring further testing with Jones Test.

Jones Test 2:

  • Purpose: Performed if Jones Test 1 is negative to differentiate between partial obstruction and pump failure.
  • Procedure: Lacrimal syringing is done while the cotton bud remains in the nose.
  • Interpretation:
    • Positive: Dye flushed onto the cotton bud indicates partial obstruction.
    • Negative: No dye suggests lacrimal pump failure.

[[figure-2]]



Reference:
  1. Parsons’ Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page 1115
  2. Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Pages 103, 104

options.text: Partial obstruction within the lacrimal passages
Complete obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct

question: A 50 y/o man undergoes Jones Test 1 for chronic tearing, which shows no dye on the cotton bud placed in the inferior meatus. Following this, Jones Test 2 is performed, and fluorescein dye is detected after lacrimal syringing. What does this result suggest?

correctAnswer: B. Probing of the nasolacrimal duct
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction (CNLDO), persistent symptoms beyond 6–8 months of age, despite conservative management (e.g., Crigler massage and antibiotics), warrant nasolacrimal duct probing.
  • Since this child is 9 months old with no response to massage and antibiotics, the next step is probing, which is often successful when done before 12 months.

Congenital Nasolacrimal Duct Obstruction (CNLDO):

Aspect

Details

Definition

Blockage of the nasolacrimal duct, usually at the valve of Hasner

First-Line Management

• Crigler massage to open the duct

• Topical antibiotics for infection

Indications for Probing

• Persistence beyond 6–10 months

• Repeated infections or failure of conservative therapy

Continue massage and antibiotics (Option A): Incorrect because symptoms have already persisted beyond the expected resolution time despite these measures.

Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) (Option C): Incorrect as DCR is reserved for older children or adults when probing and intubation fail.

Balloon catheter dilation (Option D): Incorrect because balloon dacryoplasty is typically considered for recurrent or failed probing, not first-line.



Reference:
  1. Parson's Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page 1111
  2. Yanoff & Duker Ophthalmology, 5th Edition, Page 1341

options.text: Continue lacrimal sac massage and antibiotics

question: A 9-month-old infant is brought to the clinic with ongoing tearing and discharge from the right eye. Despite regular lacrimal sac massage and topical antibiotics, the symptoms persist. What is the next best step in management?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • External Dacryocystorhinostomy (External DCR) procedure is performed through an incision near the inner corner of the eye, providing direct access to the lacrimal sac and nasal mucosa.
  • It is widely done due to its high success rate, which exceeds 90%.
  • However, it leaves a visible scar and may result in greater blood loss compared to other methods.

Endonasal Dacryocystorhinostomy (Endonasal DCR) (Option B) involves using an endoscope inserted through the nasal cavity to create a drainage opening, thus avoiding any external incision.

  • While it has the advantage of being scarless and typically involves less bleeding, its success rate is slightly lower, ranging between 70-90%.

Endocanalicular Laser Dacryocystorhinostomy (Laser DCR) (Option C):

  • This method utilizes a laser passed through the canaliculli to create a drainage opening.
  • It is minimally invasive and can be performed quickly under local anaesthesia.
  • However, its success rate is lower than external or endonasal DCR

Conjunctivodacryocystorhinostomy (CDCR) (Option D):

  • CDCR is specifically used when both the canaliculi and the nasolacrimal duct are blocked.
  • It is a more specialized procedure compared to standard DCR and is not typically the first choice for isolated nasolacrimal duct obstruction.
  • CDCR involves creating a passage directly from the conjunctival sac to the nasal cavity, often using a Jones tube and is reserved for more complex cases where the canaliculi are also involved.


Reference:
  1. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5678323/
  2. Parsons’ Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Pg.1123,1124
  3. Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology 9th edition page 107, 108
question: Which of the following types of Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) is considered for treating nasolacrimal duct obstruction, offering the highest success rate?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The bluish swelling in the inner corner of the eye, along with excessive tearing and mucous discharge, is characteristic of congenital dacryocele.

Congenital Dacryocele:

  • A condition where obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct causes amniotic fluid accumulation in the lacrimal sac, leading to a cystic swelling below the inner corner of the eye.

[[figure-1]]

Dacryoadenitis (Option B):

  • Presents with a painful, red swelling of the outer third of the upper eyelid, often associated with systemic infections.

Dacryops (Option C):

  • Presents as a cystic swelling in the upper fornix due to blocked lacrimal ducts and would typically not be described as bluish or associated with mucous discharge in the medial canthal area.

Chronic Dacryocystitis (Option D):

  • Occurs when a blockage leads to recurrent infections of the lacrimal sac over time.
  • It is less likely in a 2-week-old infant presenting for the first time with these symptoms.
  • Additionally, chronic dacryocystitis would typically involve more prolonged symptoms and recurrent infections, which are not indicated in this scenario.


Reference:
  1. Parsons’ Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page 1104, 1105
  2. Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 109
  3. Congenital dacryocystocele: diagnosis and treatment - PMC (nih.gov)
  4. Prevalence and clinical characteristics of congenital dacryocystocele - PMC (nih.gov)
question: A 2-week-old infant presents with a bluish swelling in the inner corner of the right eye. The parents report excessive tearing and some slimy discharge from the eye. There is no history of trauma or illness. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The presence of a mucocele suggests chronic dacryocystitis where the lacrimal sac has been obstructed for a prolonged period, leading to the accumulation of mucoid fluid.
  • Milky or gelatinous mucoid fluid expressed from the lower punctum on pressing the swelling (positive Regurgitation test) indicates lacrimal mucocele.
  • Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) is the definitive surgical procedure designed to create a new drainage pathway between the lacrimal sac and the nasal cavity, thus resolving the obstruction and restoring proper tear drainage.
  • This approach addresses the underlying blockage and prevents recurrence.

Chronic Dacryocystitis

Chronic dacryocystitis is a chronic infection of the lacrimal sac caused by obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct, leading to stagnation of tears and secondary infection.

Etiology

The most common cause is: Nasolacrimal duct obstruction (NLDO)

This leads to:

Tear stasis → Lacrimal sac dilatation → Infection → Chronic inflammation

Clinical Features

Symptoms

  • Watering (epiphora)
  • Recurrent conjunctivitis
  • Mucoid or mucopurulent discharge
  • Swelling near the medial canthus

Signs

  • Soft/fluctuant swelling over lacrimal sac
  • Regurgitation of mucoid fluid on pressure over sac (ROPLAS positive)
  • Chronic discharge from puncta

Management

Definitive Treatment: Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR)

A surgical fistula is created between:

  • Lacrimal sac
  • Nasal cavity

This bypasses the obstructed nasolacrimal duct.

Acute vs Chronic Dacryocystitis

Feature Acute Dacryocystitis Chronic Dacryocystitis
Onset Sudden Gradual, long-standing
Pain Marked pain Usually painless or mild discomfort
Swelling Red, tender, inflamed swelling over lacrimal sac Soft, fluctuant swelling over lacrimal sac
Skin Changes Redness and warmth present Usually absent
Fever May be present Absent
Epiphora Present Present (prominent feature)
Discharge Acute purulent discharge Mucoid or mucopurulent regurgitation
Regurgitation on pressure over sac (ROPLAS) Often difficult due to pain Typically positive
Conjunctivitis Less prominent Recurrent conjunctivitis common
Complications Abscess, fistula, cellulitis Mucocele, pyocele, recurrent infection
Treatment Systemic antibiotics ± incision and drainage (Option C ruled out) Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR)
DCR Performed after acute infection subsides Treatment of choice

Dacryocystectomy (DCT) (Option D): DCT involves complete removal of the lacrimal sac. It is indicated in elderly patients unfit for DCR, lacrimal sac tumours, and failed DCR cases. It is not the routine treatment for uncomplicated chronic dacryocystitis.

Probing and Syringing (Option A): Lacrimal probing is primarily used in congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction. It is generally not the definitive treatment for chronic dacryocystitis in adults.



Reference:
  1. Parsons’ Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Pages 1110-1119
  2. Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th edition, Page 110

options.text: Acute Dacryocystitis; Systemic antibiotics and abscess drainage.

question: A 55 y/o woman presents with a persistent swelling below the inner corner of her left eye. She also reports a history of watery eyes and recurrent conjunctivitis. On examination, there is fluctuant swelling at the lacrimal sac, and mucoid fluid can be expressed. What is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate management?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Canaliculitis is diagnosed based on symptoms and clinical findings.
  • Actinomyces israelii is the most common cause of canaliculitis with yellow granules.
  • Canaliculotomy is the definitive treatment to remove concretions and resolve the infection.
  • It involves accessing and cleaning out the canaliculus to remove concretions and ensure thorough treatment of the infection.

Canaliculitis:

  • Canaliculitis is an inflammation or infection of the lacrimal canaliculus.

Causes:

  • Bacterial infection- most commonly Actinomyces israelii
  • Other bacteria: Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, Eikenella, Lactococcus, Nocardia
  • Fungal infections.
  • Viral infections.

[[figure-1]]

Treatment:

  • Initial: Topical and systemic antibiotics, warm compresses, local massage, irrigation and syringing of the tear duct
  • Definitive: Surgery often required for effective treatment
    • Canaliculotomy for direct access and curettage. Safe and effective procedure.
    • Punctal dilation or punctoplasty with curettage
    • Canaliculoplasty with intubation to avoid scarring
  • Follow-up with antibiotic treatment and addressing underlying causes, such as a loose punctal plug


Reference:
  1. Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 109
  2. Canaliculitis - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf (nih.gov)
  3. Canaliculitis: What It Is, Causes & Treatment (clevelandclinic.org)
  4. Lacrimal canaliculitis - PMC (nih.gov)

options.text: Eikenella corrodens; Oral antibiotics and steroid drops.
Staphylococcus aureus; Topical antibiotics and warm compresses
Chlamydia trachomatis; Irrigation and syringing of the tear duct.

question: A 60 y/o man presents with watery eyes, redness, swelling at the inner corner of his right eye, and persistent thick yellow discharge. O/E there is pouting of lacrimal puncta and yellow granules from the punctum upon massage. Which organism is most likely responsible, and what is the definitive treatment?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Pleomorphic Adenoma:

  • Pleomorphic adenoma is the most common tumor of the lacrimal gland.
  • It typically present’s as a benign, painless, firm, nontender and slow-growing mass.
  • Location: Upper eyelid or superotemporal orbit.
  • Occurs predominantly in young adult males.

Lacrimal gland carcinoma (Option C):

  • Lacrimal gland carcinoma is a rare but aggressive malignancy with high morbidity and mortality.
  • The most common type is adenoid cystic carcinoma (50%), followed by pleomorphic adenocarcinoma, mucoepidermoid carcinoma, and squamous cell carcinoma.

Lymphoma (Option B):

  • Lymphoma can present as a mass in the lacrimal gland but often has associated systemic symptoms and can cause more diffuse swelling rather than a distinct mass.

Dacryocystitis (Option D) :

  • It refers to inflammation of the nasolacrimal sac and would typically present with pain, redness, and possibly discharge, along with swelling in the lower eyelid.



Reference:

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology 9th edition page 141, 142
question: A 27 yeal old man presents with a painless, slow-growing, firm mass on the upper eyelid that has been gradually increasing in size over the past year. On examination, the lesion is well-circumscribed, mobile, and non-tender, with no signs of ulceration or inflammation. Imaging reveals a well-defined, lobulated mass without bony invasion. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
The gland described is the Glands of Moll, which are modified apocrine sweat glands located at the eyelid margin. They open either into the eyelash follicles or directly onto the lid margin, distinguishing them from sebaceous glands like Zeis and Meibomian glands.

Gland

Opening Location

Sebaceous gland (Option B ruled out)

Into eyelash follicles

Posterior lid margin, open onto the lid margin behind the lashes

Eccrine sweat glands

Open directly onto the skin surface (not specific to the eyelid margin)

Apoeccrine gland (Option D): Found in the axillary region; no role in eyelid anatomy.

question: A first-year ophthalmology resident examines a patient with chronic blepharitis and reviews the anatomy of eyelid glands. He is told that one of the eyelid glands opens either into the lash follicle or directly onto the lid margin and is a modified sweat gland. Which type of gland is being described?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
The clinical findings are suggestive of a chalazion (meibomian cyst), which presents as a painless, slowly progressive swelling of the eyelid.

  • It is a chronic lipogranulomatous inflammation caused by retained sebaceous secretions. (Option 1)
  • It involves the meibomian glands located within the tarsal plate. (Option 2)
  • It presents as a painless, slowly progressive eyelid swelling with conjunctival congestion on lid eversion.
  • Although benign, recurrent or atypical cases may mimic sebaceous gland carcinoma, it is not completely devoid of malignant potential. (Option 3 ruled out)
  • Persistent lesions may require surgical management such as incision and curettage or intralesional steroid injection. (Option 4)


Reference:

Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Pages 39-41.
question:
A 46-year-old man presents with a painless, slowly progressive swelling of the lower eyelid associated with watering. On lid eversion, a localized tarsal swelling with conjunctival congestion is seen, as shown in the image. Which of the following statements regarding this condition is/are true?

  1. It is a chronic lipogranulomatous inflammation
  2. It involves the meibomian glands
  3. It has no malignant potential
  4. It may require surgical management

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
A recurrent or atypical chalazion, especially in middle-aged or elderly patients, should raise suspicion of sebaceous gland carcinoma, an aggressive malignancy arising from the meibomian glands. Histopathological examination is mandatory in such cases to exclude malignant transformation.

Basal cell carcinoma (Option A): Common eyelid malignancy but typically presents as a nodular ulcerative lesion, not a recurrent chalazion.

Squamous cell carcinoma (Option C): Presents as an ulceroproliferative lesion, not as a chalazion-like swelling.

Adenosquamous carcinoma (Option D): Rare eyelid tumor, not classically associated with recurrent chalazion.



Reference:

Parsons Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page 1050.
question: A 52-year-old woman presents with a recurrent, painless eyelid swelling that was previously treated as a chalazion on two occasions. The lesion has recurred at the same site. To rule out malignant transformation, histopathological examination is advised to exclude which of the following conditions?

correctAnswer: C. Acute infection of the meibomian gland
explanationHtml:
Explanation:
The findings are characteristic of an internal hordeolum, which presents as an acute, painful, tender swelling on the palpebral conjunctival side of the eyelid. It is caused by an acute suppurative infection of the meibomian gland, usually due to Staphylococcus aureus.

Chronic infection of the meibomian gland (Option A): Describes chalazion, which is painless and chronic, not acute and tender.

Acute infection of the Zeis gland (Option B) causes external hordeolum (stye) at the lid margin, not on the palpebral conjunctival side.

Acute infection of the Moll gland (Option D) causes external hordeolum at the lid margin, not internal.



Reference:

Parsons Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Page 1047.

options.text: Chronic infection of the meibomian gland
Acute infection of the Zeis gland
Acute infection of the meibomian gland
Acute infection of the Moll gland

question: A 36-year-old man comes with a 2-day history of sudden-onset severe pain, watering, and a tender swelling of the lower eyelid. He is unable to keep the eye open comfortably because of pain. On everting the eyelid, a localized, red, tender swelling on the palpebral conjunctival surface is noted. What is the most likely underlying cause of this condition?

explanationHtml:

question: During evaluation of a patient planned for dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR), the resident revises the anatomy of the lacrimal drainage system. What is the approximate length of the nasolacrimal duct in an adult?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
Keratoconjunctivitis sicca is primarily due to aqueous layer deficiency from reduced lacrimal gland secretion, causing decreased tear volume, ocular surface dryness, irritation, and positive Rose Bengal staining of devitalized epithelial cells.

question: A 58-year-old woman complains of foreign body sensation, burning, and ocular discomfort for several months. Examination shows a dry, lustreless conjunctiva with positive Rose Bengal staining. She is diagnosed with keratoconjunctivitis sicca. Deficiency of which layer of the tear film is primarily responsible for this condition?

explanationHtml:
• Epiphora (excessive tearing) and a soft block at 7 mm on probing indicate that the level of obstruction is canalicular (in the canaliculus, not the nasolacrimal duct).
  • For canalicular obstruction, the preferred treatment is Conjunctival DCR (also known as Lester Jones tube placement). This procedure involves creating a bypass from the conjunctival sac to the nasal cavity using a glass tube (Lester Jones tube) to restore tear drainage.
  • Conjunctival DCR is specifically designed for proximal obstructions (e.g., canalicular blocks), whereas Endonasal DCR or External DCR is used for distal obstructions (e.g., nasolacrimal duct blocks).

[[figure-1]]

Endonasal Dacryocystorhinostomy (Option A): This is used for nasolacrimal duct obstructions, not for canalicular blockages.

External Dacryocystorhinostomy (Option C): This is more suitable for distal nasolacrimal duct obstructions and is not the first choice for canalicular obstructions.

Dacryocystectomy (Option D): This is a last-resort procedure used for chronic infections or tumors and is not indicated for a functional lacrimal system with a canalicular block.



Reference:

Parsons’ Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Pg.1123,1124

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology 9th edition page 107, 108
question: A 3-year-old child presents with epiphora, and probing reveals a soft block at 7 mm. What is the best treatment option for this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) is a surgical procedure performed to treat nasolacrimal duct obstruction, which causes epiphora due to impaired tear drainage. The surgery involves creating a new drainage pathway for tears from the lacrimal sac into the nasal cavity.

Indications for DCR:

  • Chronic dacryocystitis (infection of the lacrimal sac)
  • Obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct (either congenital or acquired, e.g., from trauma or aging)
  • Recurrent epiphora (despite conservative treatments)

Types of DCR:

  1. External DCR (Traditional):
    • Involves making an incision on the skin near the medial canthus of the eye .
    • The lacrimal bone (Mostly) and a portion of the maxillary bone are removed to create an opening between the lacrimal sac and the nasal cavity.
    • A stent is often placed to keep the passage open until healing is complete.
  2. Endoscopic DCR (Minimally invasive):
    • No external incision is made.
    • An endoscope is inserted through the nasal cavity to create a passage between the lacrimal sac and nasal cavity.
    • This approach is preferred for cosmetic reasons and for patients who may have anatomical difficulties with external incisions.

Postoperative Care:

  • Antibiotics are prescribed to prevent infection.
  • Stent removal (if placed) occurs after 6–8 weeks.
  • Nasal saline irrigation may be recommended to keep the new drainage pathway clear.

Complications:

  • Infection
  • Stenosis (narrowing) of the new drainage passage
  • Persistent epiphora or failure of the procedure

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK557851/

question: A 3-month-old child is brought to the outpatient department with watering of eyes and photophobia. On examination, both corneas appear hazy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
• The Canal of Petit (also known as Spatia Zonularia) is a sacculated canal that encircles the equator of the lens, formed by the zonular fibers (the zonule of Zinn) that anchor the lens to the ciliary body. This canal is located behind the suspensory ligament of the lens and contains aqueous humor in the interstices between the zonules. It is an important anatomical feature in the structure of the eye.

Zonular Spaces (Spatia Zonularia):

  • Zonular fibers, also known as the zonule of Zinn, anchor the lens to the ciliary body and the ciliary part of the retina. These fibers are separated by spaces filled with aqueous humor, referred to as zonular spaces.
  • Anatomy: The zonules form a fibrous ring around the equator of the lens, connecting it to the ciliary body. The spaces between the zonules form a sacculated canal known as Hannover’s Canal or Petit’s Canal or Petit’s spaces (spatia zonularia), which encircles the lens' equator.
  • Function: These spaces are involved in the structure and function of the ciliary zonule, providing mechanical support for the lens and contributing to accommodation. The canal can be inflated using a fine blowpipe inserted under the suspensory ligament.

[[figure-1]]

Canal of Hannover (Option B): Another term related to zonular anatomy, but it refers to a slightly different structure and is often used interchangeably with the Canal of Petit in some contexts. However, in this case, the correct answer is Canal of Petit.

Hyaloid Canal (Option C): This is a different structure in the eye, located within the vitreous body, and is the remnant of the fetal hyaloid artery. It is not related to the zonules or lens attachment.

Pars Plana (Option D): A region of the retina, part of the ciliary body, involved in ocular surgeries (like vitrectomy) but not related to the canal structures surrounding the lens.



Reference:

Zonular spaces - e-Anatomy - IMAIOS
question: Identify the marked structure:

explanationHtml:
In the management of dry eye syndrome, different stains are used to assess the health of the ocular surface. The typical order of staining is as follows:

  1. Fluorescein Stain:
    • First step: Fluorescein is typically used first to highlight epithelial defects and tear film stability. It is a bright yellow-green dye that fluoresces under cobalt blue light, marking areas of corneal epithelial damage. It can also help assess the tear break-up time (TBUT).
  2. Lissamine Green:
    • Second step: Lissamine green is a vital dye that stains dead or degenerated cells in the conjunctiva and cornea, often used to evaluate the conjunctival surface in dry eyes. It is less irritating than Rose Bengal, making it ideal for dry eye patients, and it stains areas with poor tear film or disrupted epithelial integrity.
  3. Rose Bengal Stain:
    • Third step: Rose Bengal stains damaged epithelial cells in the conjunctiva and cornea, particularly in cases of severe dryness. It can be more irritating to the eye than the other two stains, so it is typically used last in the staining sequence. It is helpful in identifying severe damage, such as conjunctival filaments or corneal ulcers.

Investigations of dry eye

1, Slit-lamp examination
  • Superficial corneal erosions
  • Inadequate tear lake volume
  • Early tear film break-up time
  • Conjunctival hyperemia
  • Conjunctival surface irregularities
  • Meibomian gland dysfunction

2. Schirmer’s Test:
  • Schirmer’s test is used to diagnose aqueous deficiency dry eye disease.

Schirmer's Test 1

  • Measures both basal and reflex tear secretions
  • Uses Whatman-4 filter paper, kept in the lower fornix at the junction of lateral one-third and medial two-thirds.
  • After 5 minutes, wetting of the filter strip from the bent end is measured.
  • Normal value: >15 mm
  • 5-10 mm: Mild to moderate keratoconjunctivitis sicca (KCS).
  • < 5 mm: Severe KCS

[[figure-1]]

[1]

Schirmer's Test 2

  • Measures only basal secretion under anesthesia

3. Phenol Red Test
  • A modified Schirmer’s test using a cotton thread impregnated with phenol red dye.
  • The thread is placed in the lower fornix for 15 seconds.
  • Phenol dye changes from yellow to red depending on the pH of the tears.
  • Wet length: >20 mm: Normal.
  • <10 mm: Severe dry eye.
  • ≤19 mm as borderline dry eye.

[[figure-2]]

4. Tear Film Break-Up Time (TBUT)
  • Tear film stained with sodium fluorescein 1% is observed under a slit lamp, and time is noted after the patient blinks.
  • The interval between the complete blink and the first appearance of a ‘dark’ dry spot on the cornea is recorded as TBUT.
  • It is an indicator of the adequacy of the mucin component of tears.
  • Normal: 15-35 seconds
  • < 10 seconds indicates unstable tear film.

[[figure-3]]

5. Rose Bengal or Lissamine Green

Stain devitalized, desiccated corneal and conjunctival epithelium red or green.

[[figure-4]]

[[figure-5]]

6. Alcian Blue

Stains particulate matter in the tear film due to mucus

7. Tear Osmolarity

Increased in dry eye

8. Tear to Lysozyme ratio

Between 0.9 and 0.6 indicates dry eye.

Options A, C, & D are incorrect.



Reference:
  • Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, Edition 9, Page- 160, 161, 162.
  • Diagnosis of dry eye disease and emerging technologies - PMC
  • Schirmer Test - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics
  • Evaluation of Phenol Red Thread test versus Schirmer test in dry eyes: A comparative study - PMC

question: A 60-year-old patient presents with chronic dacryocystitis. She complains of recurrent tearing, discharge, and mild swelling in the inner corner of the eye. The clinical findings and history are consistent with chronic dacryocystitis. What should be the treatment of choice for this patient?

explanationHtml:
• Chronic dacryocystitis is a condition characterized by inflammation and infection of the lacrimal sac, typically due to a blockage of the nasolacrimal duct. The patient’s symptoms of recurrent tearing, discharge, and mild swelling in the inner corner of the eye are classic signs of this condition.
  • Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) is the definitive surgical procedure designed to create a new drainage pathway between the lacrimal sac and the nasal cavity, thus resolving the obstruction and restoring proper tear drainage. This approach addresses the underlying blockage and prevents recurrence.

Aspect

Acute Dacryocystitis

Chronic Dacryocystitis

Aetiology
  • Acute exacerbation of chronic dacryocystitis
  • Spread from neighbouring infected structures (e.g., sinuses, bones, dental abscess)
  • Causative organisms: Streptococcus haemolyticus, Pneumococcus, Staphylococcus
  • Stasis and mild infection of long duration
  • Common in women aged 40-60
  • Causes: anatomical factors (narrow bony canal), nasal diseases, foreign bodies, infection.

Clinical Features/ Sequelae
  1. Stage of cellulitis: Painful swelling at the lacrimal sac, epiphora, fever, redness, and oedema.
  2. Lacrimal abscess: Pus-filled sac, fluctuant swelling, may rupture forming an abscess.
  3. Fistula formation: Untreated abscess leads to spontaneous discharge, forming a fistula.
  1. Stage of chronic catarrhal dacryocystitis: Watering eye, mild redness, NLD block
  2. Lacrimal mucocele: Swelling below inner canthus, mucoid fluid regurgitation.
  3. Chronic suppurative dacryocystitis: Purulent discharge (d/t infection), recurrent conjunctivitis.
  4. Chronic fibrotic sac: Thickened mucosa, persistent epiphora, irregular folds.

Image

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Complications

Conjunctivitis, corneal ulcer, lid abscess, orbital cellulitis, facial cellulitis, rarely cavernous sinus thrombosis.

Conjunctivitis, ectropion of lower lid, risk of corneal ulcers.

Treatment
  • Cellulitis: Systemic antibiotics, anti-inflammatory drugs, hot fomentation.
  • Lacrimal abscess: Drainage with incision, antibiotics, possible DCT or DCR later.
  • External fistula: Fistulectomy with DCT or DCR after controlling infection.
  • Conservative: Probing and syringing (early stages).
  • Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR): Preferred surgery to re-establish lacrimal drainage.
  • Dacryocystectomy (DCT): Indicated if DCR is contraindicated or in cases of fibrosis, infection, or old age.

Lacrimal sac massage (Option A): This is a conservative approach often recommended for mild or early cases of nasolacrimal duct obstruction, especially in infants. It helps express the accumulated tears and debris in the lacrimal sac. However, in chronic dacryocystitis in adults, this approach is typically insufficient and would not resolve the underlying obstruction.

Syringing (Option C) (irrigation of the lacrimal system) can help clear the obstruction in some cases and is often used diagnostically to confirm the presence of a blockage. However, it does not provide a long-term solution and is typically not effective for treating chronic dacryocystitis in adults, particularly when there is significant structural obstruction.

Probing (Option D) is a procedure used primarily in young children with congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction. It is typically not appropriate for adults with chronic dacryocystitis, especially in cases where there is long-standing obstruction or scarring of the nasolacrimal duct.



Reference:
  • Parsons’ Diseases of the Eye, 23rd Edition, Pg.1110-1119
  • Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology 9th edition page 110

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The instrument shown is Bone Punch, composed of a sturdy spring handle and two blades that are joined at a right angle. The upper blade features a sharp cutting edge and a small hole, while the lower blade has a cup-shaped indentation. This tool is utilized in DCR (dacryocystorhinostomy) surgery to expand the bony opening by punching the bone from the edges of the opening.

Types of DCR:

External Dacryocystorhinostomy (External DCR) procedure is performed through an incision near the inner corner of the eye, providing direct access to the lacrimal sac and nasal mucosa. The lacrimal sac is accessed via the Bone punch used to expand the opening (Option D). It is widely regarded as the gold standard due to its high success rate, which exceeds 90%. However, it leaves a visible scar and may result in greater blood loss compared to other methods.

[[figure-1]]

External DCR

[[figure-2]]

Endonasal Dacryocystorhinostomy (Endonasal DCR): involves using an endoscope inserted through the nasal cavity to create a drainage opening, thus avoiding any external incision. While it has the advantage of being scarless and typically involves less bleeding, its success rate is slightly lower, ranging between 70-90%.

Endocanalicular Laser Dacryocystorhinostomy (Laser DCR): This method utilizes a laser passed through the tear duct to create a drainage opening. It is minimally invasive and can be performed quickly under local anaesthesia. However, its success rate is lower than external or endonasal DCR, around 70%, and patients often require additional surgery if the initial procedure fails.

[[figure-3]]

Conjunctivodacryocystorhinostomy (CDCR): CDCR is specifically used when both the canaliculi and the nasolacrimal duct are blocked. It is a more specialized procedure compared to standard DCR and is not typically the first choice for isolated nasolacrimal duct obstruction. CDCR involves creating a passage directly from the conjunctival sac to the nasal cavity, often using a Jones tube and is reserved for more complex cases where the canaliculi are also involved.



Reference:
  1. Parsons’ Diseases of the Eye 23rd Edition, pages 1123,1124.
  2. Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology 9th edition, pages 107,108.

question: A 55-year-old woman is being counseled for surgery for her long-standing dacryocystitis. Which of the following is the surgery of choice?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • DCR creates a new drainage pathway between the lacrimal sac and the nasal cavity, bypassing an obstructed nasolacrimal duct.

  • Surgically, an osteotomy is made through the lacrimal bone and frontal process of maxilla, opening the sac into the middle meatus.

  • This allows direct tear drainage and prevents recurrence of epiphora.

Inferior meatus (Option A): This is where the nasolacrimal duct normally opens, but DCR bypasses the duct.


Superior/Supreme meatus (Option C & D): Not involved in lacrimal drainage.

Types of Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR)

1. External Dacryocystorhinostomy (External DCR)

  • Performed via a skin incision near the medial canthus

  • Provides direct access to the lacrimal sac and nasal mucosa

  • Gold standard procedure

  • Success rate: >90%

  • Disadvantages: Visible scar, relatively more blood loss

2. Endonasal (Endoscopic) Dacryocystorhinostomy

  • Performed through the nasal cavity using an endoscope

  • No external incision (scarless)

  • Less bleeding and faster recovery

  • Success rate: ~70–90%

  • Slightly lower success compared to external DCR

3. Endocanalicular Laser Dacryocystorhinostomy (Laser DCR)

  • Laser passed through the lacrimal canaliculus

  • Minimally invasive, quick, can be done under local anesthesia

  • Success rate: ~70%

  • Higher chance of failure → may need repeat surgery

4. Conjunctivodacryocystorhinostomy (CDCR)

  • Indicated when both canaliculi and nasolacrimal duct are obstructed

  • Creates a passage from conjunctival sac to nasal cavity

  • Uses a Jones tube

  • Reserved for complex cases, not first-line for simple NLD obstruction

[[figure-1]]

question: A young boy presents with severe itching of the eyes, worsening during the summer months. Ocular examination reveals raised, gelatinous nodules at the limbus as shown in the image. What is the best treatment for this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Diagnosis and Management of Trachoma:

Investigations

  • Micro-immunofluorescence (micro-IF): Using pooled antigens; For routine diagnostic purposes
  • Culture of C. trachomatis: In irradiated McCoy cells; Expensive
  • Monoclonal antibody direct tests: IgA-IPA light microscopy tests are the best combination for diagnosis

Management (SAFE strategy)

SAFE is a WHO-recommended combination of interventions to treat trachoma and prevent it from leading to blindness

  • Surgery for cicatricial entropion and trichiasis (Tertiary prevention)
  • Antibiotics to eliminate the organism (Secondary prevention)
  • Facial cleanliness to avoid infection (Primary prevention)
  • Environmental improvement with better hygiene and sanitation (Primordial prevention)

Surgery (Tertiary prevention) (Option B)

Epilation/ Bilamellar tarsal rotation

Antibiotics (Secondary prevention) (Option A)
  • For areas with 10% or more prevalence of active trachoma (TF in children 1-9 yrs): Azithromycin single oral dose 20 mg/kg to all community members
  • 5% to 10% prevalence: Antibiotic therapy targeted in the family and close contact only
  • Less than 5% prevalence: Only patients are treated

Facial cleanliness (Primary prevention) (Option D)

Frequent face wash with clean water, Avoid common towels, handkerchiefs, Surma rods, etc

Environmental improvement (Primordial prevention) (Option C)

Water latrines and good water supply to reduce flies, Sprays to control flies, Health education

question: Which of the following is not included in the SAFE strategy for trachoma?

explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: C) Chlamydia trachomatis

Explanation:

A 14-day-old neonate with Bilateral conjunctivitis and pneumonia-like presentation is suggestive of Chlamydia trachomatis infection. Neonatal conjunctivitis is also known as Ophthalmia neonatorum.

Ophthalmia neonatorum:



Definition

  • Ophthalmia neonatorum or neonatal conjunctivitis is a mucoid, mucopurulent, or purulent discharge from one or both eyes in the first month of life.
  • Any discharge, even watery, from a baby’s eyes in the first week of life must be viewed under suspicion as tears are not secreted so early in life.






Aetiology of ophthalmia neonatorum

Mode of infection:

  • Before birth:
    • Very rare through infected liquor amnii
  • During birth:
    • From an infected birth canal
  • After birth:
    • During the first bath of a newborn
    • Soiled clothes
    • Fingers with infected lochia

Source of infection:

  • Neisseria gonorrhoeae:
    • Transmitted at the time of delivery
    • Presents between 2-5 days of birth (Option B)
    • The discharge becomes mucopurulent and purulent quickly
    • Thick yellow pus and marked chemosis
    • Cornea seen at the bottom of a crater-like pit in severe cases
  • Chlamydia trachomatis:
    • Transmitted at the time of delivery
    • Onset at 5-14 days after birth (Option C)
    • Serotypes D to K are the most common cause of ophthalmia neonatorum in developed countries
    • Characteristic intracellular inclusion bodies are seen
    • Less severe inflammation
    • Purulent discharge +
  • Other causes:
    • Staphylococci/ Streptococcus pneumoniae (Option A)
    • Gram-negative coliforms
    • Herpes simplex virus
    • Chemical: silver nitrate solution previously used for prophylaxis immediately after birth: erythema, chemosis, lid edema, and discharge within the first 24 hours after birth.

Prophylaxis

  • Antenatal measures:
    • Treatment of genital infections and care of mother
    • Surveillance of pregnant women for STDs
  • Natal measures:
    • Aseptic, sterile precautions to be followed during deliveries
    • Clean the infant’s closed lids with sterile cotton soaked in normal saline and dried
  • Post-natal measures:
    • Povidone-iodine 2.5% solution
    • If the mother is under suspicion, 1% tetracycline or 0.5% erythromycin eye ointment is used in the baby immediately after birth and watched for a week.
    • Ceftriaxone 50mg/kg IM or IV single dose for infants born to mothers with untreated gonococcal infection.
  • Crede’s method:
    • Old method using 1% silver nitrate applied to infants' eyes right after birth
    • It is NOT used now as it can cause chemical neonatal conjunctivitis.

Diagnosis

Treatment

Neisseria gonorrhoea

Ceftriaxone IM, gentamicin drops, bacitracin eye ointment

Chemical

Wash eyes, erythromycin ointment, observe

Intraocular Foreign Bodies (IOFBs):

An IOFB can lodge in any part of the anterior or posterior segments, causing mechanical damage, infection, or toxic effects on intraocular structures.

Types:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The above case is suggestive of siderosis bulbi.

It is a degenerative eye condition caused by an iron-containing foreign body that is not promptly removed from the eye.

  • Mechanism: Oxidation and other chemical reactions with surrounding tissues, leading to toxic effects on cellular enzyme systems and subsequent cell death.
  • Clinical Manifestations:
    • Lens deposits
    • Heterochromia iridis (iris pigmentation)
    • Retinal changes (pigmentary retinopathy)
    • Glaucoma (trabecular damage)
    • Electroretinography (ERG): Progressive attenuation of the b-wave over time.

Chalcosis (Option A) is caused by copper, not iron, and shows distinct features like Kayser-Fleischer rings.

Retinitis pigmentosa (Option B) is genetic, not due to trauma.

Glaucoma (Option D) can be a complication but is not the primary diagnosis here.

question: A 28-year-old metalworker presents with gradual vision loss and a history of a metallic foreign body injury 4 months ago. Examination reveals iron deposits on Iris, rusty deposits on the lens and pigmentary changes in the retina. What is the most likely cause of his condition?

correctAnswer: C. Immediate irrigation with water or saline for 20-30 minutes
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The above clinical case is suggestive of chemical injury. Irrigation with water or saline is the priority to dilute and remove the chemical, minimizing damage.

Management of Chemical Injury

  • Immediate irrigation: Copious water/saline for 20–30 min or until pH normal; double eversion of lids.
  • Debridement: Removal of dead conjunctiva/corneal epithelium with cotton swab (Option A).
  • Antibiotics: To prevent secondary infection (Option A).
  • Cycloplegics: For ciliary muscle relaxation and pain relief.Steroids: Only for initial 7 days (reduce inflammation but impair healing) (Option B).
  • Vitamin C (Ascorbic acid): 10% eye drops 2-hourly to promote collagen synthesis.
  • Collagenase inhibitors: Citrate 10% drops, tetracycline, acetylcysteine 10%.
  • Early surgical options: Tenon advancement, limbal cell transplant, amniotic membrane graft.
  • Late surgical options: Symblepharon release with conjunctival/mucous graft, keratoplasty (Option D). if corneal opacity.

Complications: Secondary glaucoma, limbal stem cell deficiency, pseudopterygium, corneal opacity

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 10th Edition, Pages 929-931.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The "teardrop sign" or “hanging drop sign” on the X-ray suggests an orbital floor fracture, often associated with muscle entrapment, which leads to restricted eye movement and diplopia.
  • The appropriate next step in management would be to evaluate for surgical intervention to relieve the entrapment and repair the fracture.

Orbital imaging:

  • X-rays: A nose-chin (Water's) view showing 'hanging drop' opacity of the superior maxillary antrum from orbital contents herniating through the floor.

[[figure-1]]

  • Computerised tomography (CT) scanning and magnetic resonance imaging(MRI): Evaluate the extent of the fracture and herniation of contents into maxillary antrum (hanging drop or tear drop sign).

[[figure-2]]

CT scan of coronal section of orbit showing fracture floor with herniation of orbital contents

Management:

  • Antibiotics and anti-inflammatory drugs
  • Ice packs and nasal decongestants
  • Surgery (dislodge the muscle and do microplating)
    • Indications for surgery:

      • Enopthalmos is > 2mm
      • Half of the floor is fractured

He complains of diplopia and difficulty moving his left eye upwards. On examination, there is significant periorbital swelling. The X-ray is shown below. What does this X-ray indicate in this patient, and what is the most appropriate next step in management?

correctAnswer: C. Irrigation of the eye with normal saline
explanationHtml:
• Chemical injury to the conjunctiva and cornea is a severe ocular emergency that must be treated immediately.
  • The first and the most crucial step in treating chemical injuries is copious eye irrigation by double eversion of the lid with normal saline.
  • Deliver a minimum of 2 liters of water in 20-30 minutes or until pH is restored.

Management of Alkali Burns in the Eye:

Initial Evaluation and Emergency Response

  • Immediate Irrigation:
    • Continue irrigation during transport to the hospital until ocular surface pH normalizes to 7.0–7.2.
    • Borate buffer (e.g., Cederroth Eye Wash) may be more effective than saline or water.
  • Monitor pH:
    • Check ocular pH with narrow-range strips (6–8) every 15–30 minutes to confirm stabilization.

Ophthalmic Examination: Perform a full exam after pH normalization:

Treatment Based on Severity (Grade I–IV):

Grade I (Mild Injuries):

  • Treatment:
    • Topical antibiotic ointments (e.g., bacitracin, erythromycin).(Option A ruled out)
    • Preservative-free artificial tears for lubrication.
    • Topical steroids (e.g., prednisolone acetate) for 1 week to reduce inflammation. (Option D ruled out)
    • Cycloplegic agents (e.g., cyclopentolate) for comfort.

Grades II–IV (Moderate to Severe Injuries):

  • Anti-inflammatory Measures:
    • Hourly topical prednisolone acetate in the first week, tapered after day 10.
    • Long-acting cycloplegics (e.g., atropine) for pain relief.
    • Oral tetracyclines (e.g., doxycycline) to inhibit matrix metalloproteinases and reduce corneal melting risk.
    • High-dose vitamin C (topical/oral) to prevent corneal ulceration.
  • Antibiotics:
    • Topical broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g., fluoroquinolones) to prevent superinfection.
  • IOP Management:
    • Use aqueous suppressants to control elevated IOP.
  • Amniotic Membrane:
    • Early placement of amniotic membrane (e.g., Prokera) for grades II–IV injuries to support epithelial healing.

Surgical Management

  • Debridement: Remove necrotic corneal and conjunctival epithelium with sponges or surgical instruments.
  • Persistent Epithelial Defects: Use amniotic membranes for healing (sutured or Prokera).

Ascorbic eye drops (Option B) promote collagen synthesis and improve wound healing but it is not the initial step.



Reference:

https://www.aao.org/eyenet/article/treating-acute-chemical-injuries-of-cornea
