question: A patient presents with a foreign body (chuna) in the eye and complaints of irritability and lacrimation. What is the first step in management for this patient?

explanationHtml:
• Chemical eye injuries, particularly alkali burns (such as chuna, calcium hydroxide, or lime), are ophthalmic emergencies.
  • Immediate and aggressive irrigation is the first and most critical step to minimize ocular damage.

Chemical Injuries
  • Eye injuries caused by chemicals range from mild irritation to vision loss.
  • Sources of Injury
    • Domestic: Ammonia, detergents, cosmetics
    • Agriculture: Fertilizers, insecticides
    • Laboratory: Acids, alkalis
    • Assaults & Warfare: Acid attacks, chemical weapons
    • Self-inflicted: Malingering or mental health conditions
  • Alkali vs. Acid Burns
    • Alkali: More severe, deeper penetration due to saponification, hygroscopic nature, and soluble compounds formation.
    • Acid: Less severe, protein coagulation forms a protective barrier.

Clinical Stages
  • Acute: Conjunctival swelling, corneal epithelial loss, iris inflammation, possible corneal sloughing and staphyloma.
  • Reparation: Epithelial regeneration, corneal vascularization, iris inflammation subsides.
  • Complications: Symblepharon, recurrent ulcers, cataracts, secondary glaucoma.

Emergency Management
  • Immediate irrigation: Use water or saline for at least 20-30 minutes or until the eye’s pH is restored. A minimum of 2 liters should be used. (Option B)
  • Mechanical removal: Gently remove any chemical particles with a cotton swab, particularly in lime burns.
  • Necrotic tissue removal: Carefully excise dead conjunctiva and corneal epithelium using a cotton swab.

Healing & Complication Prevention
  • Topical antibiotics: Use broad-spectrum antibiotics like moxifloxacin to prevent infection.
  • Topical steroids: Control inflammation and anterior uveitis. Use cautiously after two weeks to avoid hindering collagen production.
  • Cycloplegics: Alleviate pain and dilate the pupil with agents like atropine.
  • Ascorbic acid: Promote wound healing and collagen synthesis using topical and systemic Vitamin C.
  • Lubricants: Use preservative-free artificial tears to keep the eye moist and support healing.
  • Autologous serum: Use serum eye drops to provide essential growth factors for healing.
  • Sodium citrate: Stabilise neutrophils and reduce collagenase activity with topical sodium citrate.
  • Doxycycline: Inhibit collagenase activity with oral doxycycline.
  • Symblepharon Prevention:Use a glass shell or sweep a glass rod in the fornices (spaces between the eyelid and eyeball) twice daily to prevent adhesions.

Complication Management
  • Secondary glaucoma: Control intraocular pressure with beta-blockers like timolol or carbonic anhydrase inhibitors such as acetazolamide.
  • Limbal stem cell deficiency: Consider amniotic membrane or limbal stem cell transplantation.
  • Pseudopterygium: Surgically remove abnormal conjunctival growth and consider autografting or amniotic membrane transplantation.
  • Corneal opacity: Consider keratoplasty or keratoprosthesis for severe corneal damage.

Implications

Chemical injuries can cause permanent vision loss, physical disfigurement and psychological impact despite treatment.

Take history (Option A): Taking history is important but not the priority in an emergency. Every second matters in chemical burns, and delaying irrigation can worsen corneal damage.

Check vision in both eyes (Option C): Checking vision can be done after irrigation, but delaying decontamination increases ocular morbidity.

Check IOP and plan for surgery (Option D): Checking intraocular pressure (IOP) and planning for surgery is important after initial management. Alkali burns can cause secondary glaucoma, but irrigation takes precedence over any diagnostic steps.



Reference:

AK Khurana Comprehensive Ophthalmology 7th edition, page 456-459

options.text: Check IOP and plan for surgery

question: A factory worker presented with a history of chuna (lime) exposure in both eyes a few hours ago. What is the first immediate management?

explanationHtml:
Hemochromatosis is a condition characterized by excessive iron accumulation in the body. In the context of a flying foreign body injury, if the foreign body were made of iron, it could lead to iron deposition in the affected tissues, contributing to the development of hemochromatosis.

Intraocular Foreign Bodies (IOFBs)

Description

An IOFB can lodge in any part of the anterior or posterior segments, causing mechanical damage, infection, or toxic effects on intraocular structures.

Types

Inert: Glass, wood, plastic, rubber, gold, silver, platinum

Reactive: Organic and Inorganic (iron causing siderosis, copper causing chalcosis).

Diagnosis

  • History.
  • Examination (wound examination, foreign body location, associated signs such as lid laceration and anterior segment damage should be noted).
  • CT (investigation of choice) with axial and coronal cuts detects and localizes a metallic IOFB.
  • MRI is contraindicated (metallic IOFB).

Treatment

  • Magnetic removal (metallic IOFB)
  • Forceps removal through pars plana vitrectomy
  • Prophylaxis against infection (topical/systemic antibiotics)
  • Conservative and supportive management (topical corticosteroids, analgesics, etc).

Modes of Damage:

  1. Mechanical Effects
    • Depend on the size and velocity of the foreign body (FB).
  2. Introduction of Infection
    • Metallic FB are usually sterile due to the heat generated on their emission.
    • Pieces of wood or stone carry a greater chance of infection, often leading to endophthalmitis.
  3. Reactions to a Foreign Body (FB)
    • Inert FB: No reaction. (Options C and D)
    • Lead & Aluminium: Cause fibrosis (Option B).
    • Toxic Non-Metallic FB (Zinc, Copper, Mercury, Aluminium): Incite suppuration.
    • Siderosis (Iron FB - Degenerative Changes Due to Electrolytic Dissociation and Dissemination):
      • Earliest sign: Deposition in the anterior capsule of the lens, appearing as a rusty ring (pathognomonic).
      • Heterochromia iridis: Hyperchromic.
      • Visual loss: Due to pigmentary retinal dystrophy.
      • Secondary chronic glaucoma.
      • Diagnosis: Prussian blue reaction.
    • Chalcosis (Copper from Alloy Deposited on Membranous Structures):
      • Kayser-Fleischer Ring: Deposition in Descemet’s membrane (seen in Wilson’s disease).
      • Sunflower cataract.
      • No degenerative changes: Visual prognosis is good.
    • Caterpillar Hair: Produces granulomatous iridocyclitis, known as Ophthalmia Nodosa.


Reference:

Yanoff and Duker Ophthalmology, 5th Edition, Pages 675-676.

Kanski’s Clinical Ophthalmology, 10th Edition, Pages 927-928.
question: A patient has a history of a flying foreign body injury to the eye. Hemochromatosis is subsequently diagnosed. Which of the following substances is most likely involved in the deposition?

correctAnswer: C. Irrigation of eye with normal saline
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Chemical injury to the conjunctiva and cornea is a severe ocular emergency that must be treated immediately.
  • The first and most crucial step in treating chemical injuries is copious eye irrigation by double eversion of the lid with normal saline.
  • Deliver a minimum of 2 litres of water in 20-30 minutes or until pH is restored.

Management of chemical injury to eye

  • Irrigation with normal saline
  • Antibiotic drops in the eye (Option A): Antibiotics are used to prevent infection, but it is not the initial step.
  • Cycloplegics to relax ciliary muscles
  • Steroids (Option D): Steroids reduce inflammation, neutrophil infiltration, and address anterior uveitis. Cautious use is recommended after 7-10 days, as steroids may interfere with collagen synthesis.
  • Ascorbic acid eye drops (Option B): Ascorbic acid eye drops promote collagen synthesis and improve wound healing, but it is not the initial step.
  • Sodium citrate- reduce collagenase release
  • Tetracycline- reduce collagenase release
  • Acetylcysteine- reduce collagenase release

Grading of Chemical injury (Roper-Hall system):

  • Grade 1: Clear cornea (epithelial damage only) and no limbal ischaemia (excellent prognosis).
  • Grade 2: Shows a hazy cornea but with visible iris detail and less than one-third of the limbus being ischaemic (good prognosis).
  • Grade 3: Total loss of corneal epithelium, stromal haze obscuring iris detail and between one-third and one-half limbal ischaemia (guarded prognosis).
  • Grade 4: Manifests with an opaque cornea and more than 50% of the limbus showing ischaemia (poor prognosis).



Reference:

Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Pages 913, 914.

options.text: Irrigation of eye with normal saline

question: The patient presents with foreign body (chuna) in his eyes and complaints of irritability and lacrimation. What is the first step management in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

CT scan is the investigation of choice in case of an intraocular foreign body and MRI is contraindicated in cases where there is a risk of metallic foreign bodies.

Intraocular Foreign Bodies (IOFBs):

Definition
  • An IOFB is a foreign object that penetrates the eye and remains lodged inside. It is a serious injury that can result in permanent vision loss.

Common Types of IOFBs
  • Metallic (90% of cases): Iron, steel.
  • Others: Glass, stone, lead pellets, copper, aluminium, plastic, wood.

Foreign Body Reactions
  • Inorganic Materials: Glass, plastic are inert; lead, aluminium, copper cause inflammatory responses.
  • Organic Materials: Wood causes giant cell reactions and granulomatous inflammation.

Diagnosis
  • Detailed History: Understand injury mechanism for IOFB type.
  • Ocular Examination:
    • Slit-lamp examination
    • Gonioscopy
    • Ophthalmoscopy (back of the eye)
  • Signs:
    • Subconjunctival hemorrhage
    • Corneal scars/ Iris holes
    • Opaque tracks in the lens/ IOFB in vitreous or retina
  • Investigations:
    • X-rays: Less common; CT is preferred. (Option C)
    • Ultrasonography: B-mode USG locates both radiopaque and non-radiopaque IOFBs. (Option A)
    • CT Scan: Investigation of choice/ Gold standard for detailed cross-sectional images.(Option B)
    • MRI: Contra-indicated in case of metal foreign bodies (Option D)

Treatment
  • IOFB Removal: Essential except for inert, sterile IOFBs not affecting vision or if removal is too risky.
    • Magnetic IOFBs: Removed using a handheld electromagnet.
    • Non-magnetic IOFBs: Requires specialized procedures.
  • Removal Methods:
    • Anterior Chamber:
      • Corneal incision, avoiding central cornea.
      • Magnetic IOFBs: Handheld magnet.
      • Non-magnetic IOFBs: Specialized forceps.
    • Iris: Sector iridectomy for IOFBs in the iris.
    • Lens: Extracapsular cataract extraction (ECCE) with or without lens removal.
    • Vitreous and Retina: Pars plana vitrectomy

Post-Removal Management
  • Topical/systemic antibiotics for infection prevention.
  • Topical corticosteroids to reduce inflammation.
  • Cycloplegic agents (e.g., atropine) for pupil dilation and pain relief.



Reference:

: AK Khurana Comprehensive Ophthalmology 7th edition, page 450-454
question: Which investigation is most suitable for localizing a foreign body in the eye of an industrial worker admitted to the hospital due to an eye injury caused by cutting stone with a hammer and iron chisel?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Symptoms like fever, pain and swelling limited to the region anterior to the orbital septum with no abnormal ocular findings is suggestive of Preseptal cellulitis.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Orbital cellulitis:

Definition

Orbital cellulitis is an acute infection of the soft tissues of the orbit located behind the orbital septum.

Etiology
  • Sinusitis: Ethmoid sinusitis (most common) carries a high risk of causing orbital cellulitis. (Option A)
  • Underlying dental problem.
  • Dacryocystitis (inflammation of the lacrimal sac).
  • Endogenous cause: Septicemia
  • Exogenous cause: Fracture or surgery of the orbit.

Causative Organisms
  • Staphylococcus aureus (most common)
  • Haemophilus influenzae (most common in children)
  • Streptococcus pneumoniae
  • Streptococcus pyogenes

Clinical Features
  • Preseptal cellulitis: Fever, pain, swelling, tenderness on the outer eyelid region. (Option D)
  • Orbital cellulitis: (Option A)
    • Painful, unilateral Proptosis (swelling and severe pain worsened by eye movement or pressure)
    • Restriction of eye movements (due to proptosis)
    • Decreased visual acuity

Staging

Modified Chandler staging system:

  • Stage I: Preseptal cellulitis/ periorbital cellulitis (limited anterior to the orbital septum) (Option D)
  • Stage II: Inflammatory orbital oedema/ Orbital cellulitis (Posterior to orbital septum)
  • Stage III: Subperiosteal abscess
  • Stage IV: Orbital abscess
  • Stage V: Cavernous sinus thrombosis

[[figure-3]]

Treatment

  • Antibiotics (IV): Empirical therapy treats orbital cellulitis by giving Ceftazidime, Vancomycin, and Metronidazole.
  • Monitoring of optic nerve function
  • Surgery: Drainage of an orbital abscess or infected sinuses should be considered if there is a lack of response to antibiotics.


Reference:
  • Parson’s Diseases of the eye 23rd edition, Page 137.
  • Kanski’s Clinical ophthalmology 9th edition, Page 125
question: A patient was brought to the outpatient department with a history of trauma near the eye and now presents with symptoms of fever, severe pain, and swelling in the left eye. On examination, no abnormal findings were observed. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Floor is the weakest wall of orbit due to the presence of Inferior orbital fissure (although medial wall of the orbit is the thinnest wall). Trauma to the orbit can result in fracture of the floor of the orbit - known as ‘Blowout fracture’

Blow-out fracture:

Description
  • Blow-out orbital fractures result from trauma causing backward displacement of the eyeball and an increase in intraorbital pressure, leading to a resultant fracture.

Classification
  • Pure blow-out fractures: Not associated with involvement of the orbital rim.
  • Impure blow-out fractures: Associated with other fractures in the middle third of the facial skeleton.

Clinical Features
  • Periorbital oedema and blood extravasation (e.g., subconjunctival ecchymosis)
  • Emphysema of the eyelids, more common with medial wall fractures
  • Paraesthesia and anaesthesia in the distribution of the infraorbital nerve (lower lid, cheek, side of nose, upper lip, and upper teeth)
  • Ipsilateral epistaxis (bleeding from maxillary sinus)
  • Proptosis, often due to orbital oedema and haemorrhage
  • Enophthalmos (due to orbital fat escape, muscle entrapment, and cavity enlargement)
  • Diplopia

Radiography
  • X-ray: Water’s view shows ‘hanging drop’ opacity of the superior maxillary antrum due to herniated orbital contents.

[[figure-1]]

  • CT/MRI: Coronal sections show extent of the fracture and herniation- hanging drop or tear drop sign

[[figure-2]]

Management

General Measures and Medical Treatment:

  • Avoid nose blowing
  • Systemic antibiotics to prevent sinus infection
  • Analgesics and anti-inflammatory drugs
  • Cold compresses to decrease swelling

Surgical Management:

  • Optimal surgery time: 10-14 days after injury
  • Surgical indications: Persistent diplopia, large herniation, tissue incarceration, enophthalmos >3mm

Orbital Surgeries:

  • Orbitotomy: 4 approaches: anterior, lateral, transfrontal, and temporofrontal
  • Exenteration: Removal of all orbital contents and periorbita through an incision along orbital margins.


Reference:

AK Khurana Comprehensive Ophthalmology 7th edition, pages 440-442.
question: A man suffered trauma to the eye from a punch while fighting with another person. What is the most common site of fracture in orbit?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The given image is suggestive of Vossius ring, a condition that is typically detected during an ophthalmological examination following a blunt trauma to the eye. The Vossius ring itself is identified by the presence of pigment dispersion in a circular shape on the anterior surface of the lens following blunt trauma to the eye.

[[figure-1]]

Blunt trauma to the eye:

Damage Mechanisms
  • Direct Impact: Greatest damage at impact site.
  • Compression Wave Force: Distant damage ("contrecoup").
  • Indirect Force: Damage from impact against orbital walls.

Specific Injuries
  • Cornea: Descemet's membrane tears
  • Conjunctiva: Subconjunctival haemorrhage
  • Anterior Chamber: Hyphema (most common sign), exudates.
  • Iris, Pupil, Ciliary Body: Iridodialysis,Iridodonesis.
  • Lens: Rosette shaped cataract, ectopia lentis, Vossius ring
  • Vitreous: Liquefaction, opacities, detachment.
  • Choroid: choroidal rupture(bucket handle type)
  • Retina: Commotio retinae, Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, Gray white retina due to Berlin's edema.
  • Intraocular Pressure: Traumatic glaucoma, hypotony, ghost cell glaucoma, angle recession glaucoma
  • Traumatic optic neuropathy-RAPD (relative afferent pupillary defect)

Incorrect Options:

Weiss Ring (Option B): This is an opacified ring-shaped structure that can be seen floating within the vitreous humor of the eye, often signifying a posterior vitreous detachment, a condition in which the vitreous gel separates from the retina.

[[figure-2]]

Fleischer's Ring (Option C): This refers to a pigmented, circular line found at the edge of the cornea in keratoconus patients due to iron deposition in the corneal epithelial layer. It's composed of iron deposits and signifies corneal thinning and protrusion.

[[figure-3]]

Kayser-Fleischer Ring (Option D): This is a brown-colored ring found at the periphery of the cornea, most commonly seen in patients with Wilson's disease, a rare genetic disorder leading to excessive copper deposition in the body.

[[figure-4]]



Reference:

AK Khurana Comprehensive Ophthalmology 7th edition, pages 445-449

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • MRI is contraindicated in cases where there is a risk of metallic foreign bodies, such as in this industrial worker with a suspected foreign body in the eye.
  • The strong magnetic field of an MRI can cause movement or displacement of the metallic object, potentially leading to further injury or damage to the eye.

Intraocular Foreign Bodies (IOFBs):

Definition
  • An IOFB is a foreign object that penetrates the eye and remains lodged inside. It is a serious injury that can result in permanent vision loss.

Common Types of IOFBs
  • Metallic (90% of cases): Iron, steel.
  • Others: Glass, stone, lead pellets, copper, aluminium, plastic, wood.

Foreign Body Reactions
  • Inorganic Materials: Glass, plastic are inert; lead, aluminium, copper cause inflammatory responses.
  • Organic Materials: Wood causes giant cell reactions and granulomatous inflammation.

Diagnosis
  • Detailed History: Understand injury mechanism for IOFB type.
  • Ocular Examination:
    • Slit-lamp examination
    • Gonioscopy
    • Ophthalmoscopy (back of the eye)
  • Signs:
    • Subconjunctival hemorrhage
    • Corneal scars/ Iris holes
    • Opaque tracks in the lens/ IOFB in vitreous or retina
  • Investigations:
    • X-rays: Less common; CT is preferred.
    • Ultrasonography: B-mode USG locates both radiopaque and non-radiopaque IOFBs.
    • CT Scan: Investigation of choice/ Gold standard for detailed cross-sectional images.
    • MRI: Contra-indicated in case of metal foreign bodies (Option D)

Treatment
  • IOFB Removal: Essential except for inert, sterile IOFBs not affecting vision or if removal is too risky.
    • Magnetic IOFBs: Removed using a handheld electromagnet.
    • Non-magnetic IOFBs: Requires specialized procedures.
  • Removal Methods:
    • Anterior Chamber:
      • Corneal incision, avoiding central cornea.
      • Magnetic IOFBs: Handheld magnet.
      • Non-magnetic IOFBs: Specialized forceps.
    • Iris: Sector iridectomy for IOFBs in the iris.
    • Lens: Extracapsular cataract extraction (ECCE) with or without lens removal.
    • Vitreous and Retina: Pars plana vitrectomy

Post-Removal Management
  • Topical/systemic antibiotics for infection prevention.
  • Topical corticosteroids to reduce inflammation.
  • Cycloplegic agents (e.g., atropine) for pupil dilation and pain relief.


Reference:

AK Khurana Comprehensive Ophthalmology 7th edition, page 450-454
question: An industrial worker was admitted to the hospital after an eye injury sustained while cutting stone with a hammer and iron chisel. A foreign body was suspected to be impacted in his eye. Which investigation can be detrimental to this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Blunt trauma to the eye (hit by a tennis ball) and development of hyphema (blood in the anterior chamber) suggest rupture of blood vessels within the iris and ciliary body region, which most commonly occurs due to tearing of vessels of the major arterial circle of the iris (Circulus arteriosus major) following blunt ocular trauma.

Hyphema is the presence of blood within the anterior chamber, usually accumulating between the cornea and iris.

[[figure-1]]

Common Causes

  • Blunt ocular trauma (most common)
  • Penetrating eye injury
  • Iris neovascularization
  • Intraocular tumors
  • Blood dyscrasias
  • Postoperative complications

Source of Bleeding:

  • The bleeding most commonly originates from the: Major arterial circle of the iris (Circulus arteriosus major)
  • This arterial circle lies near the root of the iris within the ciliary body and is particularly vulnerable to rupture during blunt trauma.

Blood Supply of the Iris: The iris receives blood supply through two arterial circles:

Feature

Circulus Arteriosus Major

Circulus Arteriosus Minor

Location

Near iris root in ciliary body

Near pupillary margin

Formation

Anastomosis of long posterior ciliary arteries and anterior ciliary arteries

Branches from major circle

Clinical Importance

Most common source of traumatic hyphema

Less commonly involved

The major arterial circle is formed by:

  • Long posterior ciliary arteries
  • Anterior ciliary arteries

This circle gives rise to radial vessels that course through the iris toward the pupil.

Anterior Ciliary Artery (Option B):

  • Anterior ciliary arteries contribute to the formation of the major arterial circle but are not themselves the usual direct source identified in traumatic hyphema.
  • The bleeding classically originates from the major arterial circle, not from an isolated anterior ciliary artery.
  • These arteries primarily accompany the rectus muscles before entering the globe.
  • Anterior ciliary arteries + long posterior ciliary arteries → Circulus arteriosus major.

Posterior Ciliary Artery (Option C):

  • Posterior ciliary arteries mainly supply the choroid, optic nerve head, and ciliary body.
  • They are not the classic vessel implicated in traumatic hyphema.
  • The exam-favorite answer is the major arterial circle of the iris, which is formed partly by long posterior ciliary arteries.
  • Short posterior ciliary arteries are important in the blood supply of the optic nerve head and choroid.

Circulus Arteriosus Minor (Option D):

  • Located near the pupillary margin.
  • Supplies the inner portion of the iris.
  • Less susceptible to rupture during blunt trauma.
  • Not the usual source of blood in traumatic hyphema.
  • The minor arterial circle is derived from branches of the major arterial circle and lies closer to the pupil.


Reference:
  1. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8291460/
  2. Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th Edition, Page 900
